External Resources, Videos and Talks L73: # 1.4. Support Vector Machinescite66†# L74: 
L75: Support vector machines (SVMs) are a set of supervised learning methods used for cite67†classification , cite68†regression and cite69†outliers detection .
L76: 
L77: The advantages of support vector machines are:
L78: 
L79:   * Effective in high dimensional spaces.
L80: 
L81:   * Still effective in cases where number of dimensions is greater than the number of samples.
L82: 
L83:   * Uses a subset of training points in the decision function (called support vectors), so it is also memory efficient.
L84:   * Versatile: different cite70†Kernel functions can be specified for the decision function. Common kernels are provided, but it is also possible to specify custom kernels.
L85: 
L86: The disadvantages of support vector machines include:
L87: 
L88:   * If the number of features is much greater than the number of samples, avoid over-fitting in choosing cite70†Kernel functions and regularization term is crucial.
L89:   * SVMs do not directly provide probability estimates, these are calculated using an expensive five-fold cross-validation (see cite71†Scores and probabilities , below).
L90: The support vector machines in scikit-learn support both dense (`numpy.ndarray` and convertible to that by `numpy.asarray`) and sparse (any `scipy.sparse`) sample vectors as input. However, to use an SVM to make predictions for sparse data, it must have been fit on such data. For optimal performance, use C-ordered `numpy.ndarray` (dense) or `scipy.sparse.csr_matrix` (sparse) with `dtype=float64`.
L91: ## 1.4.1. Classificationcite72†# L92: 
L93: cite73†`SVC` , cite74†`NuSVC` and cite75†`LinearSVC` are classes capable of performing binary and multi-class classification on a dataset.
L94: cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` are similar methods, but accept slightly different sets of parameters and have different mathematical formulations (see section cite76†Mathematical formulation ). On the other hand, cite75†`LinearSVC` is another (faster) implementation of Support Vector Classification for the case of a linear kernel. It also lacks some of the attributes of cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` , like `support_`.
L95: cite75†`LinearSVC` uses `squared_hinge` loss and due to its implementation in `liblinear` it also regularizes the intercept, if considered. This effect can however be reduced by carefully fine tuning its `intercept_scaling` parameter, which allows the intercept term to have a different regularization behavior compared to the other features. The classification results and score can therefore differ from the other two classifiers.
L96: As other classifiers, cite73†`SVC` , cite74†`NuSVC` and cite75†`LinearSVC` take as input two arrays: an array `X` of shape `(n_samples, n_features)` holding the training samples, and an array `y` of class labels (strings or integers), of shape `(n_samples)`:
L97: 
L98:     >>> from sklearn import svm
L99:     >>> X = [[0, 0], [1, 1]]
L100:     >>> y = [0, 1]
L101:     >>> clf = svm.SVC()
L102:     >>> clf.fit(X, y)
L103:     SVC()
L104: After being fitted, the model can then be used to predict new values:
L105: 
L106:     >>> clf.predict([[2., 2.]])
L107:     array([1])
L108: SVMs decision function (detailed in the cite76†Mathematical formulation ) depends on some subset of the training data, called the support vectors. Some properties of these support vectors can be found in attributes `support_vectors_`, `support_` and `n_support_`:
L109: 
L110:     >>> # get support vectors
L111:     >>> clf.support_vectors_
L112:     array([[0., 0.],
L113:            [1., 1.]])
L114:     >>> # get indices of support vectors
L115:     >>> clf.support_
L116:     array([0, 1]...)
L117:     >>> # get number of support vectors for each class
L118:     >>> clf.n_support_
L119:     array([1, 1]...)
L120: Examples
L121: 
L122:   * cite77†SVM: Maximum margin separating hyperplane L123: 
L124:   * cite78†SVM-Anova: SVM with univariate feature selection L125: 
L126:   * cite79†Plot classification probability L127: ### 1.4.1.1. Multi-class classificationcite80†# L128: cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` implement the “one-versus-one” (“ovo”) approach for multi-class classification, which constructs `n_classes * (n_classes - 1) / 2` classifiers, each trained on data from two classes. Internally, the solver always uses this “ovo” strategy to train the models.
L129: However, by default, the `decision_function_shape` parameter is set to `"ovr"` (“one-vs-rest”), to have a consistent interface with other classifiers by monotonically transforming the “ovo” decision function into an “ovr” decision function of shape `(n_samples, n_classes)`.
L130: 
L131:     >>> X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]]
L132:     >>> Y = [0, 1, 2, 3]
L133:     >>> clf = svm.SVC(decision_function_shape='ovo')
L134:     >>> clf.fit(X, Y)
L135:     SVC(decision_function_shape='ovo')
L136:     >>> dec = clf.decision_function([[1]])
L137:     >>> dec.shape[1] # 6 classes: 4*3/2 = 6
L138:     6
L139:     >>> clf.decision_function_shape = "ovr"
L140:     >>> dec = clf.decision_function([[1]])
L141:     >>> dec.shape[1] # 4 classes
L142:     4
L143: On the other hand, cite75†`LinearSVC` implements a “one-vs-rest” (“ovr”) multi-class strategy, thus training `n_classes` models.
L144: 
L145:     >>> lin_clf = svm.LinearSVC()
L146:     >>> lin_clf.fit(X, Y)
L147:     LinearSVC()
L148:     >>> dec = lin_clf.decision_function([[1]])
L149:     >>> dec.shape[1]
L150:     4
L151: 
L152: 
L153: See cite76†Mathematical formulation for a complete description of the decision function.
L154: 
L155: Details on multi-class strategiescite81†# L156: Note that the cite75†`LinearSVC` also implements an alternative multi-class strategy, the so-called multi-class SVM formulated by Crammer and Singer cite82†[16] , by using the option `multi_class='crammer_singer'`. In practice, one-vs-rest classification is usually preferred, since the results are mostly similar, but the runtime is significantly less.
L157: For “one-vs-rest” cite75†`LinearSVC` the attributes `coef_` and `intercept_` have the shape `(n_classes, n_features)` and `(n_classes,)` respectively. Each row of the coefficients corresponds to one of the `n_classes` “one-vs-rest” classifiers and similar for the intercepts, in the order of the “one” class.
L158: In the case of “one-vs-one” cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` , the layout of the attributes is a little more involved. In the case of a linear kernel, the attributes `coef_` and `intercept_` have the shape `(n_classes * (n_classes - 1) / 2, n_features)` and `(n_classes * (n_classes - 1) / 2)` respectively. This is similar to the layout for cite75†`LinearSVC` described above, with each row now corresponding to a binary classifier.
L159: The order for classes 0 to n is “0 vs 1”, “0 vs 2” , … “0 vs n”, “1 vs 2”, “1 vs 3”, “1 vs n”, . . . “n-1 vs n”.
L160: The shape of `dual_coef_` is `(n_classes-1, n_SV)` with a somewhat hard to grasp layout. The columns correspond to the support vectors involved in any of the `n_classes * (n_classes - 1) / 2` “one-vs-one” classifiers. Each support vector `v` has a dual coefficient in each of the `n_classes - 1` classifiers comparing the class of `v` against another class. Note that some, but not all, of these dual coefficients, may be zero.
L161: The `n_classes - 1` entries in each column are these dual coefficients, ordered by the opposing class.
L162: This might be clearer with an example: consider a three class problem with class 0 having three support vectors \(v^{0}_0, v^{1}_0, v^{2}_0\) and class 1 and 2 having two support vectors \(v^{0}_1, v^{1}_1\) and \(v^{0}_2, v^{1}_2\) respectively. For each support vector \(v^{j}_i\), there are two dual coefficients. Let’s call the coefficient of support vector \(v^{j}_i\) in the classifier between classes \(i\) and \(k\) \(\alpha^{j}_{i,k}\). Then `dual_coef_` looks like this:
L163: \(\alpha^{0}_{0,1}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{0,1}\)  | \(\alpha^{2}_{0,1}\)  | \(\alpha^{0}_{1,0}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{1,0}\)  | \(\alpha^{0}_{2,0}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{2,0}\)
L164: \(\alpha^{0}_{0,2}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{0,2}\)  | \(\alpha^{2}_{0,2}\)  | \(\alpha^{0}_{1,2}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{1,2}\)  | \(\alpha^{0}_{2,1}\)  | \(\alpha^{1}_{2,1}\)
L165: Coefficients for SVs of class 0  | Coefficients for SVs of class 1  | Coefficients for SVs of class 2

L169:   * cite83†Plot different SVM classifiers in the iris dataset L170: ### 1.4.1.2. Scores and probabilitiescite84†# L171: The `decision_function` method of cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` gives per-class scores for each sample (or a single score per sample in the binary case). When the constructor option `probability` is set to `True`, class membership probability estimates (from the methods `predict_proba` and `predict_log_proba`) are enabled. In the binary case, the probabilities are calibrated using Platt scaling cite85†[9] : logistic regression on the SVM’s scores, fit by an additional cross-validation on the training data.
L172: In the multiclass case, this is extended as per cite86†[10] .
L173: Note
L174: 
L175: The same probability calibration procedure is available for all estimators via the cite87†`CalibratedClassifierCV` (see cite88†Probability calibration ). In the case of cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` , this procedure is builtin to cite89†libsvm†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw which is used under the hood, so it does not rely on scikit-learn’s cite87†`CalibratedClassifierCV` .
L176: The cross-validation involved in Platt scaling is an expensive operation for large datasets. In addition, the probability estimates may be inconsistent with the scores:
L177: 
L178:   * the “argmax” of the scores may not be the argmax of the probabilities
L179: 
L180:   * in binary classification, a sample may be labeled by `predict` as belonging to the positive class even if the output of `predict_proba` is less than 0.5; and similarly, it could be labeled as negative even if the output of `predict_proba` is more than 0.5.
L181: Platt’s method is also known to have theoretical issues. If confidence scores are required, but these do not have to be probabilities, then it is advisable to set `probability=False` and use `decision_function` instead of `predict_proba`.
L182: Please note that when `decision_function_shape='ovr'` and `n_classes > 2`, unlike `decision_function`, the `predict` method does not try to break ties by default. You can set `break_ties=True` for the output of `predict` to be the same as `np.argmax(clf.decision_function(...), axis=1)`, otherwise the first class among the tied classes will always be returned; but have in mind that it comes with a computational cost. See cite90†SVM Tie Breaking Example for an example on tie breaking.
L183: ### 1.4.1.3. Unbalanced problemscite91†# L184: 
L185: In problems where it is desired to give more importance to certain classes or certain individual samples, the parameters `class_weight` and `sample_weight` can be used.
L186: cite73†`SVC` (but not cite74†`NuSVC` ) implements the parameter `class_weight` in the `fit` method. It’s a dictionary of the form `{class_label : value}`, where value is a floating point number > 0 that sets the parameter `C` of class `class_label` to `C * value`. The figure below illustrates the decision boundary of an unbalanced problem, with and without weight correction.
L187: cite73†`SVC` , cite74†`NuSVC` , cite92†`SVR` , cite93†`NuSVR` , cite75†`LinearSVC` , cite94†`LinearSVR` and cite95†`OneClassSVM` implement also weights for individual samples in the `fit` method through the `sample_weight` parameter. Similar to `class_weight`, this sets the parameter `C` for the i-th example to `C * sample_weight[i]`, which will encourage the classifier to get these samples right. The figure below illustrates the effect of sample weighting on the decision boundary.

L193:   * cite97†SVM: Weighted samples L194: ## 1.4.2. Regressioncite98†# L195: 
L196: The method of Support Vector Classification can be extended to solve regression problems. This method is called Support Vector Regression.
L197: The model produced by support vector classification (as described above) depends only on a subset of the training data, because the cost function for building the model does not care about training points that lie beyond the margin. Analogously, the model produced by Support Vector Regression depends only on a subset of the training data, because the cost function ignores samples whose prediction is close to their target.
L198: There are three different implementations of Support Vector Regression: cite92†`SVR` , cite93†`NuSVR` and cite94†`LinearSVR` . cite94†`LinearSVR` provides a faster implementation than cite92†`SVR` but only considers the linear kernel, while cite93†`NuSVR` implements a slightly different formulation than cite92†`SVR` and cite94†`LinearSVR` . Due to its implementation in `liblinear` cite94†`LinearSVR` also regularizes the intercept, if considered.
L199: This effect can however be reduced by carefully fine tuning its `intercept_scaling` parameter, which allows the intercept term to have a different regularization behavior compared to the other features. The classification results and score can therefore differ from the other two classifiers. See cite99†Implementation details for further details.
L200: As with classification classes, the fit method will take as argument vectors X, y, only that in this case y is expected to have floating point values instead of integer values:
L201: 
L202:     >>> from sklearn import svm
L203:     >>> X = [[0, 0], [2, 2]]
L204:     >>> y = [0.5, 2.5]
L205:     >>> regr = svm.SVR()
L206:     >>> regr.fit(X, y)
L207:     SVR()
L208:     >>> regr.predict([[1, 1]])
L209:     array([1.5])
L210: 
L211:

L218:

L220: ## 1.4.4. Complexitycite103†# L221: Support Vector Machines are powerful tools, but their compute and storage requirements increase rapidly with the number of training vectors. The core of an SVM is a quadratic programming problem (QP), separating support vectors from the rest of the training data.
L222: The QP solver used by the cite89†libsvm†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw -based implementation scales between \(O(n_{features} \times n_{samples}^2)\) and \(O(n_{features} \times n_{samples}^3)\) depending on how efficiently the cite89†libsvm†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw cache is used in practice (dataset dependent). If the data is very sparse \(n_{features}\) should be replaced by the average number of non-zero features in a sample vector.
L223: For the linear case, the algorithm used in cite75†`LinearSVC` by the cite104†liblinear†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw implementation is much more efficient than its cite89†libsvm†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw -based cite73†`SVC` counterpart and can scale almost linearly to millions of samples and/or features.
L224: ## 1.4.5. Tips on Practical Usecite105†# L225: 
L226:   * Avoiding data copy: For cite73†`SVC` , cite92†`SVR` , cite74†`NuSVC` and cite93†`NuSVR` , if the data passed to certain methods is not C-ordered contiguous and double precision, it will be copied before calling the underlying C implementation. You can check whether a given numpy array is C-contiguous by inspecting its `flags` attribute.
L227: For cite75†`LinearSVC` (and cite106†`LogisticRegression` ) any input passed as a numpy array will be copied and converted to the cite104†liblinear†www.csie.ntu.edu.tw internal sparse data representation (double precision floats and int32 indices of non-zero components). If you want to fit a large-scale linear classifier without copying a dense numpy C-contiguous double precision array as input, we suggest to use the cite107†`SGDClassifier` class instead.
L228: The objective function can be configured to be almost the same as the cite75†`LinearSVC` model.
L229:   * Kernel cache size: For cite73†`SVC` , cite92†`SVR` , cite74†`NuSVC` and cite93†`NuSVR` , the size of the kernel cache has a strong impact on run times for larger problems. If you have enough RAM available, it is recommended to set `cache_size` to a higher value than the default of 200(MB), such as 500(MB) or 1000(MB).
L230: 
L231:   * Setting C: `C` is `1` by default and it’s a reasonable default choice. If you have a lot of noisy observations you should decrease it: decreasing C corresponds to more regularization.
L232: cite75†`LinearSVC` and cite94†`LinearSVR` are less sensitive to `C` when it becomes large, and prediction results stop improving after a certain threshold. Meanwhile, larger `C` values will take more time to train, sometimes up to 10 times longer, as shown in cite108†[11] .
L233:   * Support Vector Machine algorithms are not scale invariant, so it is highly recommended to scale your data. For example, scale each attribute on the input vector X to [0,1] or [-1,+1], or standardize it to have mean 0 and variance 1. Note that the same scaling must be applied to the test vector to obtain meaningful results. This can be done easily by using a cite109†`Pipeline` :
L234: 
L235:     >>> from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
L236:     >>> from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
L237:     >>> from sklearn.svm import SVC
L238: 
L239:     >>> clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC())
L240: See section cite110†Preprocessing data for more details on scaling and normalization.
L241: 
L242:   * Regarding the `shrinking` parameter, quoting cite111†[12] : We found that if the number of iterations is large, then shrinking can shorten the training time. However, if we loosely solve the optimization problem (e.g., by using a large stopping tolerance), the code without using shrinking may be much faster
L243:   * Parameter `nu` in cite74†`NuSVC` /cite95†`OneClassSVM` /cite93†`NuSVR` approximates the fraction of training errors and support vectors.
L244: 
L245:   * In cite73†`SVC` , if the data is unbalanced (e.g. many positive and few negative), set `class_weight='balanced'` and/or try different penalty parameters `C`.
L246:   * Randomness of the underlying implementations: The underlying implementations of cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` use a random number generator only to shuffle the data for probability estimation (when `probability` is set to `True`). This randomness can be controlled with the `random_state` parameter. If `probability` is set to `False` these estimators are not random and `random_state` has no effect on the results.
L247: The underlying cite95†`OneClassSVM` implementation is similar to the ones of cite73†`SVC` and cite74†`NuSVC` . As no probability estimation is provided for cite95†`OneClassSVM` , it is not random.
L248: The underlying cite75†`LinearSVC` implementation uses a random number generator to select features when fitting the model with a dual coordinate descent (i.e. when `dual` is set to `True`). It is thus not uncommon to have slightly different results for the same input data. If that happens, try with a smaller `tol` parameter. This randomness can also be controlled with the `random_state` parameter.
L249: When `dual` is set to `False` the underlying implementation of cite75†`LinearSVC` is not random and `random_state` has no effect on the results.
L250:   * Using L1 penalization as provided by `LinearSVC(penalty='l1', dual=False)` yields a sparse solution, i.e. only a subset of feature weights is different from zero and contribute to the decision function. Increasing `C` yields a more complex model (more features are selected). The `C` value that yields a “null” model (all weights equal to zero) can be calculated using cite112†`l1_min_c` .
L251: ## 1.4.6. Kernel functionscite113†# L252: 
L253: The kernel function can be any of the following:
L254: 
L255:   * linear: \(\langle x, x'\rangle\).
L256: 
L257:   * polynomial: \((\gamma \langle x, x'\rangle + r)^d\), where \(d\) is specified by parameter `degree`, \(r\) by `coef0`.
L258: 
L259:   * rbf: \(\exp(-\gamma \|x-x'\|^2)\), where \(\gamma\) is specified by parameter `gamma`, must be greater than 0.
L260: 
L261:   * sigmoid \(\tanh(\gamma \langle x,x'\rangle + r)\), where \(r\) is specified by `coef0`.
L262: Different kernels are specified by the `kernel` parameter:
L263: 
L264:     >>> linear_svc = svm.SVC(kernel='linear')
L265:     >>> linear_svc.kernel
L266:     'linear'
L267:     >>> rbf_svc = svm.SVC(kernel='rbf')
L268:     >>> rbf_svc.kernel
L269:     'rbf'
L270: 
L271: 
L272: See also cite114†Kernel Approximation for a solution to use RBF kernels that is much faster and more scalable.
L273: ### 1.4.6.1. Parameters of the RBF Kernelcite115†# L274: When training an SVM with the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, two parameters must be considered: `C` and `gamma`. The parameter `C`, common to all SVM kernels, trades off misclassification of training examples against simplicity of the decision surface. A low `C` makes the decision surface smooth, while a high `C` aims at classifying all training examples correctly. `gamma` defines how much influence a single training example has.
L275: The larger `gamma` is, the closer other examples must be to be affected.
L276: Proper choice of `C` and `gamma` is critical to the SVM’s performance. One is advised to use cite116†`GridSearchCV` with `C` and `gamma` spaced exponentially far apart to choose good values.
L277: 
L278: Examples
L279: 
L280:   * cite117†RBF SVM parameters L281: 
L282:   * cite118†Scaling the regularization parameter for SVCs L283: ### 1.4.6.2. Custom Kernelscite119†# L284: 
L285: You can define your own kernels by either giving the kernel as a python function or by precomputing the Gram matrix.
L286: 
L287: Classifiers with custom kernels behave the same way as any other classifiers, except that:
L288: 
L289:   * Field `support_vectors_` is now empty, only indices of support vectors are stored in `support_`
L290:   * A reference (and not a copy) of the first argument in the `fit()` method is stored for future reference. If that array changes between the use of `fit()` and `predict()` you will have unexpected results.
L291: 
L292: Using Python functions as kernelscite120†# L293: 
L294: You can use your own defined kernels by passing a function to the `kernel` parameter.
L295: Your kernel must take as arguments two matrices of shape `(n_samples_1, n_features)`, `(n_samples_2, n_features)` and return a kernel matrix of shape `(n_samples_1, n_samples_2)`.
L296: 
L297: The following code defines a linear kernel and creates a classifier instance that will use that kernel:
L298: 
L299:     >>> import numpy as np
L300:     >>> from sklearn import svm
L301:     >>> def my_kernel(X, Y):
L302:     ...     return np.dot(X, Y.T)
L303:     ...
L304:     >>> clf = svm.SVC(kernel=my_kernel)
L305: 
L306: 
L307: Using the Gram matrixcite121†# L308: You can pass pre-computed kernels by using the `kernel='precomputed'` option. You should then pass Gram matrix instead of X to the `fit` and `predict` methods. The kernel values between all training vectors and the test vectors must be provided:
L309: 
L310:     >>> import numpy as np
L311:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
L312:     >>> from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
L313:     >>> from sklearn import svm
L314:     >>> X, y = make_classification(n_samples=10, random_state=0)
L315:     >>> X_train , X_test , y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
L316:     >>> clf = svm.SVC(kernel='precomputed')
L317:     >>> # linear kernel computation
L318:     >>> gram_train = np.dot(X_train, X_train.T)
L319:     >>> clf.fit(gram_train, y_train)
L320:     SVC(kernel='precomputed')
L321:     >>> # predict on training examples
L322:     >>> gram_test = np.dot(X_test, X_train.T)
L323:     >>> clf.predict(gram_test)
L324:     array([0, 1, 0])

L453: torch.nn.functional.softmax(input, dim=None, _stacklevel=3, dtype=None)cite245†[source]†github.com cite246†# L454: 
L455: 
L456: Apply a softmax function.
L457: 
L458: Softmax is defined as:
L459: 
L460: $\text{Softmax}(x_{i}) = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j)}$Softmax(x i​)=∑j​e x p(x j​)e x p(x i​)​
L461: 
L462: It is applied to all slices along dim, and will re-scale them so that the elements lie in the range [0, 1] and sum to 1.
L463: 
L464: See cite247†`Softmax` for more details.
L465: 
L466: Parameters:
L467:   * input (cite248†Tensor ) – input
L468: 
L469:   * dim (cite249†int†docs.python.org ) – A dimension along which softmax will be computed.
L470: 
L471:   * dtype (cite250†`torch.dtype` , optional) – the desired data type of returned tensor. If specified, the input tensor is casted to `dtype` before the operation is performed. This is useful for preventing data type overflows. Default: None.
L472: 
L473: Return type:
L474: 
L475: 
L476: cite248†Tensor L477: 
L478: Note
L479: This function doesn’t work directly with NLLLoss, which expects the Log to be computed between the Softmax and itself. Use log_softmax instead (it’s faster and has better numerical properties).

L2: Linear learner hyperparameters - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: # Linear learner hyperparameters
L4: The following table contains the hyperparameters for the linear learner algorithm. These are parameters that are set by users to facilitate the estimation of model parameters from data. The required hyperparameters that must be set are listed first, in alphabetical order. The optional hyperparameters that can be set are listed next, also in alphabetical order. When a hyperparameter is set to `auto`, Amazon SageMaker AI will automatically calculate and set the value of that hyperparameter.
L5: Parameter Name  | Description
L6: --- | ---
L7: `num_classes`  | The number of classes for the response variable. The algorithm assumes that classes are labeled `0`, ..., `num_classes - 1`. Required when `predictor_type` is `multiclass_classifier`. Otherwise, the algorithm ignores it. Valid values: Integers from 3 to 1,000,000
L8: `predictor_type`  | Specifies the type of target variable as a binary classification, multiclass classification, or regression. Required Valid values: `binary_classifier`, `multiclass_classifier`, or `regressor`
L9: `accuracy_top_k`  | When computing the top-k accuracy metric for multiclass classification, the value of k. If the model assigns one of the top-k scores to the true label, an example is scored as correct. Optional Valid values: Positive integers Default value: 3
L10: `balance_multiclass_weights`  | Specifies whether to use class weights, which give each class equal importance in the loss function. Used only when the `predictor_type` is `multiclass_classifier`. Optional Valid values: `true`, `false` Default value: `false`
L11: `beta_1`  | The exponential decay rate for first-moment estimates. Applies only when the `optimizer` value is `adam`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or floating-point value between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L12: `beta_2`  | The exponential decay rate for second-moment estimates. Applies only when the `optimizer` value is `adam`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L13: `bias_lr_mult`  | Allows a different learning rate for the bias term. The actual learning rate for the bias is `learning_rate` * `bias_lr_mult`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default value: `auto`
L14: `bias_wd_mult`  | Allows different regularization for the bias term. The actual L2 regularization weight for the bias is `wd` * `bias_wd_mult`. By default, there is no regularization on the bias term. Optional Valid values: `auto` or non-negative floating-point integer Default value: `auto`
L15: `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria`  | When `predictor_type` is set to `binary_classifier`, the model evaluation criteria for the validation dataset (or for the training dataset if you don't provide a validation dataset). Criteria include:
L16:   * `accuracy`—The model with the highest accuracy.
L17:   * `f_beta`—The model with the highest F1 score. The default is F1.
L18:   * `precision_at_target_recall`—The model with the highest precision at a given recall target.
L19:   * `recall_at_target_precision`—The model with the highest recall at a given precision target.
L20:   * `loss_function`—The model with the lowest value of the loss function used in training.
L21: Optional Valid values: `accuracy`, `f_beta`, `precision_at_target_recall`, `recall_at_target_precision`, or `loss_function` Default value: `accuracy`
L22: `early_stopping_patience`  | If no improvement is made in the relevant metric, the number of epochs to wait before ending training. If you have provided a value for `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria`. the metric is that value. Otherwise, the metric is the same as the value specified for the `loss` hyperparameter. The metric is evaluated on the validation data.
L23: If you haven't provided validation data, the metric is always the same as the value specified for the `loss` hyperparameter and is evaluated on the training data. To disable early stopping, set `early_stopping_patience` to a value greater than the value specified for `epochs`.Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 3
L24: `early_stopping_tolerance`  | The relative tolerance to measure an improvement in loss. If the ratio of the improvement in loss divided by the previous best loss is smaller than this value, early stopping considers the improvement to be zero. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.001
L25: `epochs`  | The maximum number of passes over the training data. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 15
L26: `f_beta`  | The value of beta to use when calculating F score metrics for binary or multiclass classification. Also used if the value specified for `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria` is `f_beta`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integers Default value: 1.0
L27: `feature_dim`  | The number of features in the input data. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default values: `auto`
L28: `huber_delta`  | The parameter for Huber loss. During training and metric evaluation, compute L2 loss for errors smaller than delta and L1 loss for errors larger than delta. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 1.0
L29: `init_bias`  | Initial weight for the bias term. Optional Valid values: Floating-point integer Default value: 0
L30: `init_method`  | Sets the initial distribution function used for model weights. Functions include:
L31:   * `uniform`—Uniformly distributed between (-scale, +scale)
L32:   * `normal`—Normal distribution, with mean 0 and sigma
L33: Optional Valid values: `uniform` or `normal` Default value: `uniform`
L34: `init_scale`  | Scales an initial uniform distribution for model weights. Applies only when the `init_method` hyperparameter is set to `uniform`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.07
L35: `init_sigma`  | The initial standard deviation for the normal distribution. Applies only when the `init_method` hyperparameter is set to `normal`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.01
L36: `l1`  | The L1 regularization parameter. If you don't want to use L1 regularization, set the value to 0. Optional Valid values: `auto` or non-negative float Default value: `auto`
L37: `learning_rate`  | The step size used by the optimizer for parameter updates. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default value: `auto`, whose value depends on the optimizer chosen.
L38: `loss`  | Specifies the loss function. The available loss functions and their default values depend on the value of `predictor_type`:
L39:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `regressor`, the available options are `auto`, `squared_loss`, `absolute_loss`, `eps_insensitive_squared_loss`, `eps_insensitive_absolute_loss`, `quantile_loss`, and `huber_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `squared_loss`.
L40:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `binary_classifier`, the available options are `auto`,`logistic`, and `hinge_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `logistic`.
L41:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `multiclass_classifier`, the available options are `auto` and `softmax_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `softmax_loss`.
L42: Valid values: `auto`, `logistic`, `squared_loss`, `absolute_loss`, `hinge_loss`, `eps_insensitive_squared_loss`, `eps_insensitive_absolute_loss`, `quantile_loss`, or `huber_loss` Optional Default value: `auto`
L43: `loss_insensitivity`  | The parameter for the epsilon-insensitive loss type. During training and metric evaluation, any error smaller than this value is considered to be zero. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.01
L44: `lr_scheduler_factor`  | For every `lr_scheduler_step` hyperparameter, the learning rate decreases by this quantity. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer between 0 and 1 Default value: `auto`
L45: `lr_scheduler_minimum_lr`  | The learning rate never decreases to a value lower than the value set for `lr_scheduler_minimum_lr`. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default values: `auto`
L46: `lr_scheduler_step`  | The number of steps between decreases of the learning rate. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default value: `auto`
L47: `margin`  | The margin for the `hinge_loss` function. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 1.0
L48: `mini_batch_size`  | The number of observations per mini-batch for the data iterator. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 1000
L49: `momentum`  | The momentum of the `sgd` optimizer. Optional Valid values: `auto` or a floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L50: `normalize_data`  | Normalizes the feature data before training. Data normalization shifts the data for each feature to have a mean of zero and scales it to have unit standard deviation. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `true`
L51: `normalize_label`  | Normalizes the label. Label normalization shifts the label to have a mean of zero and scales it to have unit standard deviation. The `auto` default value normalizes the label for regression problems but does not for classification problems. If you set the `normalize_label` hyperparameter to `true` for classification problems, the algorithm ignores it. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `auto`
L52: `num_calibration_samples`  | The number of observations from the validation dataset to use for model calibration (when finding the best threshold). Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default value: `auto`
L53: `num_models`  | The number of models to train in parallel. For the default, `auto`, the algorithm decides the number of parallel models to train. One model is trained according to the given training parameter (regularization, optimizer, loss), and the rest by close parameters. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default values: `auto`
L54: `num_point_for_scaler`  | The number of data points to use for calculating normalization or unbiasing of terms. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 10,000
L55: `optimizer`  | The optimization algorithm to use. Optional Valid values:
L56:   * `auto`—The default value.
L57:   * `sgd`—Stochastic gradient descent.
L58:   * `adam`—cite1†Adaptive momentum estimation†arxiv.org .
L59:   * `rmsprop`—A gradient-based optimization technique that uses a moving average of squared gradients to normalize the gradient.
L60: Default value: `auto`. The default setting for `auto` is `adam`.
L61: `positive_example_weight_mult`  | The weight assigned to positive examples when training a binary classifier. The weight of negative examples is fixed at 1. If you want the algorithm to choose a weight so that errors in classifying negative vs. positive examples have equal impact on training loss, specify `balanced`. If you want the algorithm to choose the weight that optimizes performance, specify `auto`. Optional Valid values: `balanced`, `auto`, or a positive floating-point integer Default value: 1.0
L62: `quantile`  | The quantile for quantile loss. For quantile q, the model attempts to produce predictions so that the value of `true_label` is greater than the prediction with probability q. Optional Valid values: Floating-point integer between 0 and 1 Default value: 0.5
L63: `target_precision`  | The target precision. If `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria` is `recall_at_target_precision`, then precision is held at this value while recall is maximized. Optional Valid values: Floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: 0.8
L64: `target_recall`  | The target recall. If `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria` is `precision_at_target_recall`, then recall is held at this value while precision is maximized. Optional Valid values: Floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: 0.8
L65: `unbias_data`  | Unbiases the features before training so that the mean is 0. By default data is unbiased as the `use_bias` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `auto`
L66: `unbias_label`  | Unbiases labels before training so that the mean is 0. Applies to regression only if the `use_bias` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `auto`
L67: `use_bias`  | Specifies whether the model should include a bias term, which is the intercept term in the linear equation. Optional Valid values: `true` or `false` Default value: `true`
L68: `use_lr_scheduler`  | Whether to use a scheduler for the learning rate. If you want to use a scheduler, specify `true`. Optional Valid values: `true` or `false` Default value: `true`

Image Classification - MXNet - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/image-classification.html)
citeturn59view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/image-classification.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 114

L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the Image Classification Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Image Classification Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # Image Classification - MXNet
L6: 
L7: The Amazon SageMaker image classification algorithm is a supervised learning algorithm that supports multi-label classification. It takes an image as input and outputs one or more labels assigned to that image. It uses a convolutional neural network that can be trained from scratch or trained using transfer learning when a large number of training images are not available
L8: The recommended input format for the Amazon SageMaker AI image classification algorithms is Apache MXNet cite4†RecordIO†mxnet.apache.org . However, you can also use raw images in .jpg or .png format. Refer to cite5†this discussion†mxnet.apache.org for a broad overview of efficient data preparation and loading for machine learning systems.
L9: ###### Note
L10: 
L11: To maintain better interoperability with existing deep learning frameworks, this differs from the protobuf data formats commonly used by other Amazon SageMaker AI algorithms.
L12: 
L13: For more information on convolutional networks, see:
L14: 
L15:   * cite6†Deep residual learning for image recognition†arxiv.org Kaiming He, et al., 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
L16: 
L17:   * cite7†ImageNet image database†www.image-net.org L18:   * cite8†Image classification with Gluon-CV and MXNet†gluon-cv.mxnet.io L19: ###### Topics
L20: 
L21:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the Image Classification Algorithm L22: 
L23:   * cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Image Classification Algorithm L24: 
L25:   * cite3†Image Classification Sample Notebooks L26: 
L27:   * cite9†How Image Classification Works L28: 
L29:   * cite10†Image Classification Hyperparameters L30: 
L31:   * cite11†Tune an Image Classification Model L32: ## Input/Output Interface for the Image Classification Algorithm
L33: The SageMaker AI Image Classification algorithm supports both RecordIO (`application/x-recordio`) and image (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image`) content types for training in file mode, and supports the RecordIO (`application/x-recordio`) content type for training in pipe mode. However, you can also train in pipe mode using the image files (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image`), without creating RecordIO files, by using the augmented manifest format.
L34: Distributed training is supported for file mode and pipe mode. When using the RecordIO content type in pipe mode, you must set the `S3DataDistributionType` of the `S3DataSource` to `FullyReplicated`. The algorithm supports a fully replicated model where your data is copied onto each machine.
L35: 
L36: The algorithm supports `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image` for inference.
L37: ### Train with RecordIO Format
L38: 
L39: If you use the RecordIO format for training, specify both `train` and `validation` channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of the cite12†`CreateTrainingJob` request. Specify one RecordIO (`.rec`) file in the `train` channel and one RecordIO file in the `validation` channel. Set the content type for both channels to `application/x-recordio`.
L40: ### Train with Image Format
L41: 
L42: If you use the Image format for training, specify `train`, `validation`, `train_lst`, and `validation_lst` channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of the cite12†`CreateTrainingJob` request. Specify the individual image data (`.jpg` or `.png` files) for the `train` and `validation` channels. Specify one `.lst` file in each of the `train_lst` and `validation_lst` channels. Set the content type for all four channels to `application/x-image`.
L43: ###### Note
L44: 
L45: SageMaker AI reads the training and validation data separately from different channels, so you must store the training and validation data in different folders.
L46: A `.lst` file is a tab-separated file with three columns that contains a list of image files. The first column specifies the image index, the second column specifies the class label index for the image, and the third column specifies the relative path of the image file. The image index in the first column must be unique across all of the images. The set of class label indices are numbered successively and the numbering should start with 0.
L47: For example, 0 for the cat class, 1 for the dog class, and so on for additional classes.
L48: The following is an example of a `.lst` file:
L49: 
L50:     `5      1   your_image_directory/train_img_dog1.jpg
L51:     1000   0   your_image_directory/train_img_cat1.jpg
L52:     22     1   your_image_directory/train_img_dog2.jpg`
L53: For example, if your training images are stored in `s3://<your_bucket>/train/class_dog`, `s3://<your_bucket>/train/class_cat`, and so on, specify the path for your `train` channel as `s3://<your_bucket>/train`, which is the top-level directory for your data. In the `.lst` file, specify the relative path for an individual file named `train_image_dog1.jpg` in the `class_dog` class directory as `class_dog/train_image_dog1.jpg`.
L54: You can also store all your image files under one subdirectory inside the `train` directory. In that case, use that subdirectory for the relative path. For example, `s3://<your_bucket>/train/your_image_directory`.
L55: ### Train with Augmented Manifest Image Format
L56: The augmented manifest format enables you to do training in Pipe mode using image files without needing to create RecordIO files. You need to specify both train and validation channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of the cite12†`CreateTrainingJob` request. While using the format, an S3 manifest file needs to be generated that contains the list of images and their corresponding annotations.
L57: The manifest file format should be in cite13†JSON Lines†jsonlines.org format in which each line represents one sample. The images are specified using the `'source-ref'` tag that points to the S3 location of the image. The annotations are provided under the `"AttributeNames"` parameter value as specified in the cite12†`CreateTrainingJob` request. It can also contain additional metadata under the `metadata` tag, but these are ignored by the algorithm.
L58: In the following example, the `"AttributeNames"` are contained in the list of image and annotation references `["source-ref", "class"]`. The corresponding label value is `"0"` for the first image and `“1”` for the second image:
L59: 
L60:     `{"source-ref":"s3://image/filename1.jpg", "class":"0"}
L61:     {"source-ref":"s3://image/filename2.jpg", "class":"1", "class-metadata": {"class-name": "cat", "type" : "groundtruth/image-classification"}}`
L62: The order of `"AttributeNames"` in the input files matters when training the ImageClassification algorithm. It accepts piped data in a specific order, with `image` first, followed by `label`. So the "AttributeNames" in this example are provided with `"source-ref"` first, followed by `"class"`. When using the ImageClassification algorithm with Augmented Manifest, the value of the `RecordWrapperType` parameter must be `"RecordIO"`.
L63: Multi-label training is also supported by specifying a JSON array of values. The `num_classes` hyperparameter must be set to match the total number of classes. There are two valid label formats: multi-hot and class-id.
L64: In the multi-hot format, each label is a multi-hot encoded vector of all classes, where each class takes the value of 0 or 1. In the following example, there are three classes. The first image is labeled with classes 0 and 2, while the second image is labeled with class 2 only:
L65: 
L66:     `{"image-ref": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/sample01/image1.jpg", "class": "[1, 0, 1]"}
L67:     {"image-ref": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/sample02/image2.jpg", "class": "[0, 0, 1]"}`
L68: In the class-id format, each label is a list of the class ids, from [0, `num_classes`), which apply to the data point. The previous example would instead look like this:
L69: 
L70:     `{"image-ref": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/sample01/image1.jpg", "class": "[0, 2]"}
L71:     {"image-ref": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/sample02/image2.jpg", "class": "[2]"}`
L72: The multi-hot format is the default, but can be explicitly set in the content type with the `label-format` parameter: `"application/x-recordio; label-format=multi-hot".` The class-id format, which is the format outputted by GroundTruth, must be set explicitly: `"application/x-recordio; label-format=class-id".`
L73: 
L74: For more information on augmented manifest files, see cite14†Augmented Manifest Files for Training Jobs .
L75: ### Incremental Training
L76: 
L77: You can also seed the training of a new model with the artifacts from a model that you trained previously with SageMaker AI. Incremental training saves training time when you want to train a new model with the same or similar data. SageMaker AI image classification models can be seeded only with another built-in image classification model trained in SageMaker AI.
L78: To use a pretrained model, in the cite12†`CreateTrainingJob` request, specify the `ChannelName` as "model" in the `InputDataConfig` parameter. Set the `ContentType` for the model channel to `application/x-sagemaker-model`. The input hyperparameters of both the new model and the pretrained model that you upload to the model channel must have the same settings for the `num_layers`, `image_shape` and `num_classes` input parameters. These parameters define the network architecture.
L79: For the pretrained model file, use the compressed model artifacts (in .tar.gz format) output by SageMaker AI. You can use either RecordIO or image formats for input data.
L80: ### Inference with the Image Classification Algorithm
L81: The generated models can be hosted for inference and support encoded `.jpg` and `.png` image formats as `image/png, image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image` content-type. The input image is resized automatically. The output is the probability values for all classes encoded in JSON format, or in cite13†JSON Lines text format†jsonlines.org for batch transform. The image classification model processes a single image per request and so outputs only one line in the JSON or JSON Lines format.
L82: The following is an example of a response in JSON Lines format:
L83: 
L84:     `accept: application/jsonlines
L85: 
L86:      {"prediction": [prob_0, prob_1, prob_2, prob_3, ...]}`
L87: For more details on training and inference, see the image classification sample notebook instances referenced in the introduction.
L88: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Image Classification Algorithm
L89: 
L90: For image classification, we support P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 instances. We recommend using GPU instances with more memory for training with large batch sizes. You can also run the algorithm on multi-GPU and multi-machine settings for distributed training. Both CPU (such as C4) and GPU (P2, P3, G4dn, or G5) instances can be used for inference.
L91: ## Image Classification Sample Notebooks
L92: For a sample notebook that uses the SageMaker AI image classification algorithm, see cite15†Build and Register an MXNet Image Classification Model via SageMaker Pipelines†github.com . For instructions how to create and access Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite16†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances . Once you have created a notebook instance and opened it, select the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI samples.
L93: The example image classification notebooks are located in the Introduction to Amazon algorithms section. To open a notebook, click on its Use tab and select Create copy.

External Resources, Videos and Talks L73: # 1.1. Linear Modelscite66†# L74: 
L75: The following are a set of methods intended for regression in which the target value is expected to be a linear combination of the features. In mathematical notation, the predicted value \(\hat{y}\) can be written as:
L76: 
L77: \[\hat{y}(w, x) = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + ... + w_p x_p\]
L78: 
L79: Across the module, we designate the vector \(w = (w_1, ..., w_p)\) as `coef_` and \(w_0\) as `intercept_`.
L80: 
L81: To perform classification with generalized linear models, see cite67†Logistic regression .
L82: ## 1.1.1. Ordinary Least Squarescite68†# L83: 
L84: cite69†`LinearRegression` fits a linear model with coefficients \(w = (w_1, ..., w_p)\) to minimize the residual sum of squares between the observed targets in the dataset, and the targets predicted by the linear approximation. Mathematically it solves a problem of the form:
L85: 
L86: \[\min_{w} || X w - y||_2^2\]
L87: cite69†`LinearRegression` takes in its `fit` method arguments `X`, `y`, `sample_weight` and stores the coefficients \(w\) of the linear model in its `coef_` and `intercept_` attributes:
L88: 
L89:     >>> from sklearn import linear_model
L90:     >>> reg = linear_model.LinearRegression()
L91:     >>> reg.fit([[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2]], [0, 1, 2])
L92:     LinearRegression()
L93:     >>> reg.coef_
L94:     array([0.5, 0.5])
L95:     >>> reg.intercept_
L96:     0.0
L97: The coefficient estimates for Ordinary Least Squares rely on the independence of the features. When features are correlated and some columns of the design matrix \(X\) have an approximately linear dependence, the design matrix becomes close to singular and as a result, the least-squares estimate becomes highly sensitive to random errors in the observed target, producing a large variance. This situation of multicollinearity can arise, for example, when data are collected without an experimental design.
L98: Examples
L99: 
L100:   * cite70†Ordinary Least Squares and Ridge Regression L101: ### 1.1.1.1. Non-Negative Least Squarescite71†# L102: 
L103: It is possible to constrain all the coefficients to be non-negative, which may be useful when they represent some physical or naturally non-negative quantities (e.g., frequency counts or prices of goods). cite69†`LinearRegression` accepts a boolean `positive` parameter: when set to `True` cite72†Non-Negative Least Squares†en.wikipedia.org are then applied.

L107:   * cite73†Non-negative least squares L108: ### 1.1.1.2. Ordinary Least Squares Complexitycite74†# L109: 
L110: The least squares solution is computed using the singular value decomposition of \(X\). If \(X\) is a matrix of shape `(n_samples, n_features)` this method has a cost of \(O(n_{\text{samples}} n_{\text{features}}^2)\), assuming that \(n_{\text{samples}} \geq n_{\text{features}}\).

L112: ## 1.1.2. Ridge regression and classificationcite75†# L113: ### 1.1.2.1. Regressioncite76†# L114: 
L115: cite77†`Ridge` regression addresses some of the problems of cite68†Ordinary Least Squares by imposing a penalty on the size of the coefficients. The ridge coefficients minimize a penalized residual sum of squares:
L116: 
L117: \[\min_{w} || X w - y||_2^2 + \alpha ||w||_2^2\]
L118: 
L119: The complexity parameter \(\alpha \geq 0\) controls the amount of shrinkage: the larger the value of \(\alpha\), the greater the amount of shrinkage and thus the coefficients become more robust to collinearity.
L120: As with other linear models, cite77†`Ridge` will take in its `fit` method arrays `X`, `y` and will store the coefficients \(w\) of the linear model in its `coef_` member:
L121: 
L122:     >>> from sklearn import linear_model
L123:     >>> reg = linear_model.Ridge(alpha=.5)
L124:     >>> reg.fit([[0, 0], [0, 0], [1, 1]], [0, .1, 1])
L125:     Ridge(alpha=0.5)
L126:     >>> reg.coef_
L127:     array([0.34545455, 0.34545455])
L128:     >>> reg.intercept_
L129:     np.float64(0.13636)
L130: Note that the class cite77†`Ridge` allows for the user to specify that the solver be automatically chosen by setting `solver="auto"`. When this option is specified, cite77†`Ridge` will choose between the `"lbfgs"`, `"cholesky"`, and `"sparse_cg"` solvers. cite77†`Ridge` will begin checking the conditions shown in the following table from top to bottom. If the condition is true, the corresponding solver is chosen.
L131: Solver  | Condition
L132: ‘lbfgs’  | The `positive=True` option is specified.
L133: ‘cholesky’  | The input array X is not sparse.
L134: ‘sparse_cg’  | None of the above conditions are fulfilled.
L135:

L144:   * cite80†Ridge coefficients as a function of the L2 Regularization L145: ### 1.1.2.2. Classificationcite81†# L146: 
L147: The cite77†`Ridge` regressor has a classifier variant: cite82†`RidgeClassifier` . This classifier first converts binary targets to `{-1, 1}` and then treats the problem as a regression task, optimizing the same objective as above. The predicted class corresponds to the sign of the regressor’s prediction. For multiclass classification, the problem is treated as multi-output regression, and the predicted class corresponds to the output with the highest value.
L148: It might seem questionable to use a (penalized) Least Squares loss to fit a classification model instead of the more traditional logistic or hinge losses. However, in practice, all those models can lead to similar cross-validation scores in terms of accuracy or precision/recall, while the penalized least squares loss used by the cite82†`RidgeClassifier` allows for a very different choice of the numerical solvers with distinct computational performance profiles.
L149: The cite82†`RidgeClassifier` can be significantly faster than e.g. cite83†`LogisticRegression` with a high number of classes because it can compute the projection matrix \((X^T X)^{-1} X^T\) only once.
L150: 
L151: This classifier is sometimes referred to as a cite84†Least Squares Support Vector Machine†en.wikipedia.org with a linear kernel.

L159: ### 1.1.2.4. Setting the regularization parameter: leave-one-out Cross-Validationcite87†# L160: 
L161: cite88†`RidgeCV` and cite89†`RidgeClassifierCV` implement ridge regression/classification with built-in cross-validation of the alpha parameter. They work in the same way as cite90†`GridSearchCV` except that it defaults to efficient Leave-One-Out cite91†cross-validation . When using the default cite91†cross-validation , alpha cannot be 0 due to the formulation used to calculate Leave-One-Out error. See cite92†[RL2007] for details.

L163: 
L164:     >>> import numpy as np
L165:     >>> from sklearn import linear_model
L166:     >>> reg = linear_model.RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-6, 6, 13))
L167:     >>> reg.fit([[0, 0], [0, 0.1], [1, 1]], [0, -0.1, 1])
L168:     RidgeCV(alphas=array([1.e-06, 1.e-05, 1.e-04, 1.e-03, 1.e-02, 1.e-01, 1.e+00, 1.e+01,
L169:           1.e+02, 1.e+03, 1.e+04, 1.e+05, 1.e+06]))
L170:     >>> reg.alpha_
L171:     np.float64(0.1)

L179: ## 1.1.3. Lassocite98†# L180: The cite99†`Lasso` is a linear model that estimates sparse coefficients, i.e., it is able to set coefficients exactly to zero. It is useful in some contexts due to its tendency to prefer solutions with fewer non-zero coefficients, effectively reducing the number of features upon which the given solution is dependent. For this reason, Lasso and its variants are fundamental to the field of compressed sensing.
L181: Under certain conditions, it can recover the exact set of non-zero coefficients (see cite100†Compressive sensing: tomography reconstruction with L1 prior (Lasso) ).
L182: Mathematically, it consists of a linear model with an added regularization term. The objective function to minimize is:
L183: 
L184: \[\min_{w} P(w) = {\frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}} ||X w - y||_2 ^ 2 + \alpha ||w||_1}\]
L185: 
L186: The lasso estimate thus solves the least-squares with added penalty \(\alpha ||w||_1\), where \(\alpha\) is a constant and \(||w||_1\) is the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the coefficient vector.
L187: The implementation in the class cite99†`Lasso` uses coordinate descent as the algorithm to fit the coefficients. See cite101†Least Angle Regression for another implementation:
L188: 
L189:     >>> from sklearn import linear_model
L190:     >>> reg = linear_model.Lasso(alpha=0.1)
L191:     >>> reg.fit([[0, 0], [1, 1]], [0, 1])
L192:     Lasso(alpha=0.1)
L193:     >>> reg.predict([[1, 1]])
L194:     array([0.8])
L195: The function cite102†`lasso_path` is useful for lower-level tasks, as it computes the coefficients along the full path of possible values.

L218: ### 1.1.3.1. Coordinate Descent with Gap Safe Screening Rulescite109†# L219: 
L220: Coordinate descent (CD) is a strategy to solve a minimization problem that considers a single feature \(j\) at a time. This way, the optimization problem is reduced to a 1-dimensional problem which is easier to solve:
L221: 
L222: \[\min_{w_j} {\frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}} ||x_j w_j + X_{-j}w_{-j} - y||_2 ^ 2 + \alpha |w_j|}\]
L223: 
L224: with index \(-j\) meaning all features but \(j\). The solution is
L225: \[w_j = \frac{S(x_j^T (y - X_{-j}w_{-j}), \alpha)}{||x_j||_2^2}\]
L226: with the soft-thresholding function \(S(z, \alpha) = \operatorname{sign}(z) \max(0, |z|-\alpha)\). Note that the soft-thresholding function is exactly zero whenever \(\alpha \geq |z|\). The CD solver then loops over the features either in a cycle, picking one feature after the other in the order given by `X` (`selection="cyclic"`), or by randomly picking features (`selection="random"`). It stops if the duality gap is smaller than the provided tolerance `tol`.
L227: 
L228: Mathematical detailscite110†# L229: The duality gap \(G(w, v)\) is an upper bound of the difference between the current primal objective function of the Lasso, \(P(w)\), and its minimum \(P(w^\star)\), i.e. \(G(w, v) \geq P(w) - P(w^\star)\). It is given by \(G(w, v) = P(w) - D(v)\) with dual objective function
L230: 
L231: \[D(v) = \frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}}(y^Tv - ||v||_2^2)\]
L232: subject to \(v \in ||X^Tv||_{\infty} \leq n_{\text{samples}}\alpha\). At optimum, the duality gap is zero, \(G(w^\star, v^\star) = 0\) (a property called strong duality). With (scaled) dual variable \(v = c r\), current residual \(r = y - Xw\) and dual scaling
L233: 
L234: \[\begin{split}c = \begin{cases} 1, & ||X^Tr||_{\infty} \leq n_{\text{samples}}\alpha, \\ \frac{n_{\text{samples}}\alpha}{||X^Tr||_{\infty}}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\end{split}\]
L235: 
L236: the stopping criterion is
L237: \[\text{tol} \frac{||y||_2^2}{n_{\text{samples}}} < G(w, cr)\,.\]
L238: 
L239: A clever method to speedup the coordinate descent algorithm is to screen features such that at optimum \(w_j = 0\). Gap safe screening rules are such a tool. Anywhere during the optimization algorithm, they can tell which feature we can safely exclude, i.e., set to zero with certainty.
L240:

Gap Safe Screening Rules for Sparsity Enforcing Penalties. Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(128):1-33, 2017.†arxiv.org L248: ### 1.1.3.2. Setting regularization parametercite115†# L249: 
L250: The `alpha` parameter controls the degree of sparsity of the estimated coefficients.
L251: #### 1.1.3.2.1. Using cross-validationcite116†# L252: 
L253: scikit-learn exposes objects that set the Lasso `alpha` parameter by cross-validation: cite117†`LassoCV` and cite118†`LassoLarsCV` . cite118†`LassoLarsCV` is based on the cite101†Least Angle Regression algorithm explained below.
L254: For high-dimensional datasets with many collinear features, cite117†`LassoCV` is most often preferable. However, cite118†`LassoLarsCV` has the advantage of exploring more relevant values of `alpha` parameter, and if the number of samples is very small compared to the number of features, it is often faster than cite117†`LassoCV` .
L255: #### 1.1.3.2.2. Information-criteria based model selectioncite119†# L256: 
L257: Alternatively, the estimator cite120†`LassoLarsIC` proposes to use the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayes Information criterion (BIC). It is a computationally cheaper alternative to find the optimal value of alpha as the regularization path is computed only once instead of k+1 times when using k-fold cross-validation.
L258: Indeed, these criteria are computed on the in-sample training set. In short, they penalize the over-optimistic scores of the different Lasso models by their flexibility (cf. to “Mathematical details” section below).
L259: However, such criteria need a proper estimation of the degrees of freedom of the solution, are derived for large samples (asymptotic results) and assume the correct model is candidates under investigation. They also tend to break when the problem is badly conditioned (e.g. more features than samples).
L260:

L262:

L265:   * cite121†Lasso model selection via information criteria L266: #### 1.1.3.2.3. AIC and BIC criteriacite122†# L267: 
L268: The definition of AIC (and thus BIC) might differ in the literature. In this section, we give more information regarding the criterion computed in scikit-learn.
L269: 
L270: Mathematical detailscite123†# L271: 
L272: The AIC criterion is defined as:
L273: 
L274: \[AIC = -2 \log(\hat{L}) + 2 d\]
L275: 
L276: where \(\hat{L}\) is the maximum likelihood of the model and \(d\) is the number of parameters (as well referred to as degrees of freedom in the previous section).
L277: The definition of BIC replaces the constant \(2\) by \(\log(N)\):
L278: 
L279: \[BIC = -2 \log(\hat{L}) + \log(N) d\]
L280: 
L281: where \(N\) is the number of samples.
L282: 
L283: For a linear Gaussian model, the maximum log-likelihood is defined as:
L284: 
L285: \[\log(\hat{L}) = - \frac{n}{2} \log(2 \pi) - \frac{n}{2} \log(\sigma^2) - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\]
L286: where \(\sigma^2\) is an estimate of the noise variance, \(y_i\) and \(\hat{y}_i\) are respectively the true and predicted targets, and \(n\) is the number of samples.
L287: 
L288: Plugging the maximum log-likelihood in the AIC formula yields:
L289: 
L290: \[AIC = n \log(2 \pi \sigma^2) + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sigma^2} + 2 d\]
L291: The first term of the above expression is sometimes discarded since it is a constant when \(\sigma^2\) is provided. In addition, it is sometimes stated that the AIC is equivalent to the \(C_p\) statistic cite124†[12] . In a strict sense, however, it is equivalent only up to some constant and a multiplicative factor.
L292: At last, we mentioned above that \(\sigma^2\) is an estimate of the noise variance. In cite120†`LassoLarsIC` when the parameter `noise_variance` is not provided (default), the noise variance is estimated via the unbiased estimator cite125†[13] defined as:
L293: 
L294: \[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n - p}\]
L295: 
L296: where \(p\) is the number of features and \(\hat{y}_i\) is the predicted target using an ordinary least squares regression. Note, that this formula is valid only when `n_samples > n_features`.

L309: ## 1.1.4. Multi-task Lassocite131†# L310: 
L311: The cite132†`MultiTaskLasso` is a linear model that estimates sparse coefficients for multiple regression problems jointly: `y` is a 2D array, of shape `(n_samples, n_tasks)`. The constraint is that the selected features are the same for all the regression problems, also called tasks.

L320: Mathematical detailscite134†# L321: Mathematically, it consists of a linear model trained with a mixed \(\ell_1\) \(\ell_2\)-norm for regularization. The objective function to minimize is:
L322: 
L323: \[\min_{W} { \frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}} ||X W - Y||_{\text{Fro}} ^ 2 + \alpha ||W||_{21}}\]
L324: 
L325: where \(\text{Fro}\) indicates the Frobenius norm
L326: 
L327: \[||A||_{\text{Fro}} = \sqrt{\sum_{ij} a_{ij}^2}\]
L328: 
L329: and \(\ell_1\) \(\ell_2\) reads
L330: 
L331: \[||A||_{2 1} = \sum_i \sqrt{\sum_j a_{ij}^2}.\]
L332: The implementation in the class cite132†`MultiTaskLasso` uses coordinate descent as the algorithm to fit the coefficients.
L333: ## 1.1.5. Elastic-Netcite135†# L334: 
L335: cite136†`ElasticNet` is a linear regression model trained with both \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\)-norm regularization of the coefficients. This combination allows for learning a sparse model where few of the weights are non-zero like cite99†`Lasso` , while still maintaining the regularization properties of cite77†`Ridge` . We control the convex combination of \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) using the `l1_ratio` parameter.
L336: Elastic-net is useful when there are multiple features that are correlated with one another. Lasso is likely to pick one of these at random, while elastic-net is likely to pick both.
L337: 
L338: A practical advantage of trading-off between Lasso and Ridge is that it allows Elastic-Net to inherit some of Ridge’s stability under rotation.
L339: 
L340: The objective function to minimize is in this case
L341: 
L342: \[\min_{w} { \frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}} ||X w - y||_2 ^ 2 + \alpha \rho ||w||_1 + \frac{\alpha(1-\rho)}{2} ||w||_2 ^ 2}\]
L343: The class cite137†`ElasticNetCV` can be used to set the parameters `alpha` (\(\alpha\)) and `l1_ratio` (\(\rho\)) by cross-validation.

L357:   * “An Interior-Point Method for Large-Scale L1-Regularized Least Squares,” S. J. Kim, K. Koh, M. Lustig, S. Boyd and D. Gorinevsky, in IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing, 2007 (cite108†Paper†web.stanford.edu )
L358: ## 1.1.6. Multi-task Elastic-Netcite142†# L359: 
L360: The cite143†`MultiTaskElasticNet` is an elastic-net model that estimates sparse coefficients for multiple regression problems jointly: `Y` is a 2D array of shape `(n_samples, n_tasks)`. The constraint is that the selected features are the same for all the regression problems, also called tasks.
L361: 
L362: Mathematically, it consists of a linear model trained with a mixed \(\ell_1\) \(\ell_2\)-norm and \(\ell_2\)-norm for regularization. The objective function to minimize is:
L363: \[\min_{W} { \frac{1}{2n_{\text{samples}}} ||X W - Y||_{\text{Fro}}^2 + \alpha \rho ||W||_{2 1} + \frac{\alpha(1-\rho)}{2} ||W||_{\text{Fro}}^2}\]

L6: # Data and model quality monitoring with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
L7: ###### Note
L8: 
L9: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is no longer open to new customers. Existing customers can continue to use the service as normal. AWS continues to invest in security and availability improvements for Model Monitor, but we do not plan to introduce new features. For more information, see cite2†Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor availability change .
L10: 
L11: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor monitors the quality of Amazon SageMaker AI machine learning models in production. With Model Monitor, you can set up:
L12:   * Continuous monitoring with a real-time endpoint.
L13: 
L14:   * Continuous monitoring with a batch transform job that runs regularly.
L15: 
L16:   * On-schedule monitoring for asynchronous batch transform jobs.
L17: With Model Monitor, you can set alerts that notify you when there are deviations in the model quality. Early and proactive detection of these deviations lets you to take corrective actions. You can take actions like retraining models, auditing upstream systems, or fixing quality issues without having to monitor models manually or build additional tooling. You can use Model Monitor prebuilt monitoring capabilities that do not require coding.
L18: You also have the flexibility to monitor models by coding to provide custom analysis.
L19: Model Monitor provides the following types of monitoring:
L20: 
L21:   * cite3†Data quality - Monitor drift in data quality.
L22: 
L23:   * cite4†Model quality - Monitor drift in model quality metrics, such as accuracy.
L24: 
L25:   * cite5†Bias drift for models in production - Monitor bias in your model's predictions.
L26: 
L27:   * cite6†Feature attribution drift for models in production - Monitor drift in feature attribution.

L60: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor automatically monitors machine learning (ML) models in production and notifies you when quality issues happen. Model Monitor uses rules to detect drift in your models and alerts you when it happens. The following figure shows how this process works in the case that your model is deployed to a real-time endpoint.
L61: 
L62: cite15†Image: The model monitoring process with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor. L63: You can also use Model Monitor to monitor a batch transform job instead of a real-time endpoint. In this case, instead of receiving requests to an endpoint and tracking the predictions, Model Monitor monitors inference inputs and outputs. The following figure diagrams the process of monitoring a batch transform job.
L64: 
L65: cite16†Image: The model monitoring process with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor. L66: To enable model monitoring, take the following steps. These steps follow the path of the data through the various data collection, monitoring, and analysis processes.
L67: 
L68:   * For a real-time endpoint, enable the endpoint to capture data from incoming requests to a trained ML model and the resulting model predictions.
L69: 
L70:   * For a batch transform job, enable data capture of the batch transform inputs and outputs.
L71:   * Create a baseline from the dataset that was used to train the model. The baseline computes metrics and suggests constraints for the metrics. Real-time or batch predictions from your model are compared to the constraints. They are reported as violations if they are outside the constrained values.
L72: 
L73:   * Create a monitoring schedule specifying what data to collect, how often to collect it, how to analyze it, and which reports to produce.
L74:   * Inspect the reports, which compare the latest data with the baseline. Watch for any violations reported, metrics, and notifications from Amazon CloudWatch.
L75: ###### Notes
L76: 
L77:   * Model Monitor computes model metrics and statistics on tabular data only. For example, an image classification model that takes images as input and outputs a label based on that image can still be monitored. Model Monitor would be able to calculate metrics and statistics for the output, not the input.
L78:   * Model Monitor currently supports only endpoints that host a single model and does not support monitoring multi-model endpoints. For information on using multi-model endpoints, see cite17†Multi-model endpoints .
L79: 
L80:   * Model Monitor supports monitoring inference pipelines. However, capturing and analyzing data is done for the entire pipeline, not for individual containers in the pipeline.
L81:   * To prevent impact to inference requests, Data Capture stops capturing requests at high levels of disk usage. We recommended that you keep your disk utilization below 75% to ensure data capture continues capturing requests.
L82:   * If you launch SageMaker Studio in a custom Amazon VPC, you must create VPC endpoints to let Model Monitor communicate with Amazon S3 and CloudWatch. For information about VPC endpoints, see cite18†VPC endpoints in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide. For information about launching SageMaker Studio in a custom VPC, see cite19†Connect Studio notebooks in a VPC to external resources .
