# Amazon SageMaker Feature Store now supports feature metadata and search

Posted on: Jul 6, 2022

Amazon SageMaker Feature Store is a fully managed, purpose-built repository to store, update, search, and share machine learning (ML) features. The service provides feature management capabilities such as enabling easy feature reuse, low latency serving, time travel, and ensuring consistency between features used in training and inference workflows. A feature group is a logical grouping of ML features whose organization and structure is defined by a feature group schema. Until today, customers could add metadata tags only to feature groups which in turn enabled easy search and discovery of a feature group. To search for a specific feature however was more complicated. Customers needed to know which feature group the feature belongs and then scan for the relevant feature in the feature group, leading to additional overhead while searching for features..

Today, Amazon SageMaker Feature Store is announcing the ability to add custom metadata at a feature level and the ability to directly search for features in addition to feature groups. The custom metadata fields include description and parameters to help make features discoverable. You can use the UpdateFeatureMetadata API to add or update metadata for a feature, and use the DescribeFeatureMetadata API to view all metadata for a feature. You can also update and view feature metadata in SageMaker Studio, an integrated development environment for ML.

Using either the Feature Store user interface in SageMaker Studio or the Search API, you can search for features across feature groups within the same AWS account, and discover features relevant for your use case by performing a text based search of the feature metadata attributes.

To learn more, please view the documentation here. To get started, log into the Amazon SageMaker console.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The third challenge is ambiguity, and it runs deeper than view selection. Consider a search for “swimming pools” that returns a tile where the pool is visible only in the ortho photo but not in any oblique view. It is unclear whether that result is correct. The reverse case is equally ambiguous: a tile where the pool is visible from the south oblique but not from above.

Zoom level compounds this. Depending on tile resolution, a single tile might cover a city block or an entire neighborhood. In a dense suburban area, one tile could contain a dozen swimming pools. Should the ground truth require the system to return a tile if it contains a matching feature, or should it account for every instance within that tile? A tile-level match (at least one pool present) and a feature-level match (every pool accounted for) are fundamentally different evaluation criteria, and they reward different system behaviors. We had to define what “correct” means before we could measure it.

L28: cite11†Image: Example histogram chart in the Data Wrangler console. L29: You can use the Facet by feature to create histograms of one column, for each value in another column. For example, the following diagram shows histograms of user reviews of best-selling books on Amazon if faceted by year.
L30: 
L31: cite12†Image: Example histograms in the Data Wrangler console. L32: ## Scatter Plot
L33: 
L34: Use the Scatter Plot feature to inspect the relationship between features. To create a scatter plot, select a feature to plot on the X axis and the Y axis. Both of these columns must be numeric typed columns.
L35: 
L36: You can color scatter plots by an additional column. For example, the following example shows a scatter plot comparing the number of reviews against user ratings of top-selling books on Amazon between 2009 and 2019. The scatter plot is colored by book genre.
L37: cite13†Image: Example scatter plot in the Data Wrangler console. L38: 
L39: Additionally, you can facet scatter plots by features. For example, the following image shows an example of the same review versus user rating scatter plot, faceted by year.
L40: 
L41: cite14†Image: Example faceted scatter plot in the Data Wrangler console. L42: ## Table Summary
L43: 
L44: Use the Table Summary analysis to quickly summarize your data.
L45: 
L46: For columns with numerical data, including log and float data, a table summary reports the number of entries (count), minimum (min), maximum (max), mean, and standard deviation (stddev) for each column.
L47: 
L48: For columns with non-numerical data, including columns with string, Boolean, or date/time data, a table summary reports the number of entries (count), least frequent value (min), and most frequent value (max).
L49: ## Quick Model
L50: Use the Quick Model visualization to quickly evaluate your data and produce importance scores for each feature. A cite15†feature importance score†spark.apache.org score indicates how useful a feature is at predicting a target label. The feature importance score is between [0, 1] and a higher number indicates that the feature is more important to the whole dataset. On the top of the quick model chart, there is a model score. A classification problem shows an F1 score.
L51: A regression problem has a mean squared error (MSE) score.
L52: When you create a quick model chart, you select a dataset you want evaluated, and a target label against which you want feature importance to be compared. Data Wrangler does the following:
L53: 
L54:   * Infers the data types for the target label and each feature in the dataset selected.
L55:   * Determines the problem type. Based on the number of distinct values in the label column, Data Wrangler determines if this is a regression or classification problem type. Data Wrangler sets a categorical threshold to 100. If there are more than 100 distinct values in the label column, Data Wrangler classifies it as a regression problem; otherwise, it is classified as a classification problem.
L56:   * Pre-processes features and label data for training. The algorithm used requires encoding features to vector type and encoding labels to double type.
L57: 
L58:   * Trains a random forest algorithm with 70% of data. Spark’s cite16†RandomForestRegressor†spark.apache.org is used to train a model for regression problems. The cite17†RandomForestClassifier†spark.apache.org is used to train a model for classification problems.
L59:   * Evaluates a random forest model with the remaining 30% of data. Data Wrangler evaluates classification models using an F1 score and evaluates regression models using an MSE score.
L60: 
L61:   * Calculates feature importance for each feature using the Gini importance method.
L62: 
L63: The following image shows the user interface for the quick model feature.
L64: 
L65: cite18†Image: Example UI of the quick model feature in the Data Wrangler console. L66: ## Target Leakage
L67: 
L68: Target leakage occurs when there is data in a machine learning training dataset that is strongly correlated with the target label, but is not available in real-world data. For example, you may have a column in your dataset that serves as a proxy for the column you want to predict with your model.
L69: 
L70: When you use the Target Leakage analysis, you specify the following:
L71: 
L72:   * Target: This is the feature about which you want your ML model to be able to make predictions.
L73:   * Problem type: This is the ML problem type on which you are working. Problem type can either be classification or regression.
L74: 
L75:   * (Optional) Max features: This is the maximum number of features to present in the visualization, which shows features ranked by their risk of being target leakage.
L76: For classification, the target leakage analysis uses the area under the receiver operating characteristic, or AUC - ROC curve for each column, up to Max features. For regression, it uses a coefficient of determination, or R2 metric.
L77: The AUC - ROC curve provides a predictive metric, computed individually for each column using cross-validation, on a sample of up to around 1000 rows. A score of 1 indicates perfect predictive abilities, which often indicates target leakage. A score of 0.5 or lower indicates that the information on the column could not provide, on its own, any useful information towards predicting the target.
L78: Although it can happen that a column is uninformative on its own but is useful in predicting the target when used in tandem with other features, a low score could indicate the feature is redundant.
L79: For example, the following image shows a target leakage report for a diabetes classification problem, that is, predicting if a person has diabetes or not. An AUC - ROC curve is used to calculate the predictive ability of five features, and all are determined to be safe from target leakage.
L80: 
L81: cite19†Image: Example target leakage report in the Data Wrangler console. L82: ## Multicollinearity
L83: 
L84: Multicollinearity is a circumstance where two or more predictor variables are related to each other. The predictor variables are the features in your dataset that you're using to predict a target variable. When you have multicollinearity, the predictor variables are not only predictive of the target variable, but also predictive of each other.
L85: You can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), or Lasso feature selection as measures for the multicollinearity in your data. For more information, see the following.
L86: 
L87: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
L88: 
L89: 
L90: The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) is a measure of collinearity among variable pairs. Data Wrangler returns a VIF score as a measure of how closely the variables are related to each other. A VIF score is a positive number that is greater than or equal to 1.
L91: A score of 1 means that the variable is uncorrelated with the other variables. Scores greater than 1 indicate higher correlation.
L92: 
L93: Theoretically, you can have a VIF score with a value of infinity. Data Wrangler clips high scores to 50. If you have a VIF score greater than 50, Data Wrangler sets the score to 50.
L94: 
L95: You can use the following guidelines to interpret your VIF scores:
L96: 
L97:   * A VIF score less than or equal to 5 indicates that the variables are moderately correlated with the other variables.
L98:   * A VIF score greater than or equal to 5 indicates that the variables are highly correlated with the other variables.
L99: 
L100: Principle Component Analysis (PCA)
L101: 
L102: 
L103: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) measures the variance of the data along different directions in the feature space. The feature space consists of all the predictor variables that you use to predict the target variable in your dataset.
L104: For example, if you're trying to predict who survived on the RMS Titanic after it hit an iceberg, your feature space can include the passengers' age, gender, and the fare that they paid.
L105: 
L106: From the feature space, PCA generates an ordered list of variances. These variances are also known as singular values. The values in the list of variances are greater than or equal to 0. We can use them to determine how much multicollinearity there is in our data.
L107: When the numbers are roughly uniform, the data has very few instances of multicollinearity. When there is a lot of variability among the values, we have many instances of multicollinearity. Before it performs PCA, Data Wrangler normalizes each feature to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
L108: ###### Note
L109: 
L110: PCA in this circumstance can also be referred to as Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).
L111: 
L112: Lasso feature selection
L113: 
L114: 
L115: Lasso feature selection uses the L1 regularization technique to only include the most predictive features in your dataset.
L116: For both classification and regression, the regularization technique generates a coefficient for each feature. The absolute value of the coefficient provides an importance score for the feature. A higher importance score indicates that it is more predictive of the target variable. A common feature selection method is to use all the features that have a non-zero lasso coefficient.
L117: ## Detect Anomalies In Time Series Data
L118: 
L119: You can use the anomaly detection visualization to see outliers in your time series data. To understand what determines an anomaly, you need to understand that we decompose the time series into a predicted term and an error term. We treat the seasonality and trend of the time series as the predicted term. We treat the residuals as the error term.
L120: For the error term, you specify a threshold as the number of standard of deviations the residual can be away from the mean for it to be considered an anomaly. For example, you can specify a threshold as being 3 standard deviations. Any residual greater than 3 standard deviations away from the mean is an anomaly.
L121: 
L122: You can use the following procedure to perform an Anomaly detection analysis.
L123: 
L124:   1. Open your Data Wrangler data flow.
L125:   2. In your data flow, under Data types, choose the +, and select Add analysis.
L126: 
L127:   3. For Analysis type, choose Time Series.
L128: 
L129:   4. For Visualization, choose Anomaly detection.
L130: 
L131:   5. For Anomaly threshold, choose the threshold that a value is considered an anomaly.
L132: 
L133:   6. Choose Preview to generate a preview of the analysis.
L134: 
L135:   7. Choose Add to add the transform to the Data Wrangler data flow.
L136: ## Seasonal Trend Decomposition In Time Series Data
L137: You can determine whether there's seasonality in your time series data by using the Seasonal Trend Decomposition visualization. We use the STL (Seasonal Trend decomposition using LOESS) method to perform the decomposition. We decompose the time series into its seasonal, trend, and residual components. The trend reflects the long term progression of the series. The seasonal component is a signal that recurs in a time period.
L138: After removing the trend and the seasonal components from the time series, you have the residual.
L139: You can use the following procedure to perform a Seasonal-Trend decomposition analysis.
L140: 
L141:   1. Open your Data Wrangler data flow.
L142: 
L143:   2. In your data flow, under Data types, choose the +, and select Add analysis.
L144: 
L145:   3. For Analysis type, choose Time Series.
L146: 
L147:   4. For Visualization, choose Seasonal-Trend decomposition.
L148: 
L149:   5. For Anomaly threshold, choose the threshold that a value is considered an anomaly.
L150: 
L151:   6. Choose Preview to generate a preview of the analysis.
L152:   7. Choose Add to add the transform to the Data Wrangler data flow.
L153: ## Bias Report
L154: 
L155: You can use the bias report in Data Wrangler to uncover potential biases in your data. To generate a bias report, you must specify the target column, or Label, that you want to predict and a Facet, or the column that you want to inspect for biases.
L156: Label: The feature about which you want a model to make predictions. For example, if you are predicting customer conversion, you may select a column containing data on whether or not a customer has placed an order. You must also specify whether this feature is a label or a threshold. If you specify a label, you must specify what a positive outcome looks like in your data.
L157: In the customer conversion example, a positive outcome may be a 1 in the orders column, representing the positive outcome of a customer placing an order within the last three months. If you specify a threshold, you must specify a lower bound defining a positive outcome. For example, if your customer orders columns contains the number of orders placed in the last year, you may want to specify 1.
L158: Facet: The column that you want to inspect for biases. For example, if you are trying to predict customer conversion, your facet may be the age of the customer. You may choose this facet because you believe that your data is biased toward a certain age group. You must identify whether the facet is measured as a value or threshold. For example, if you wanted to inspect one or more specific ages, you select Value and specify those ages.
L159: If you want to look at an age group, you select Threshold and specify the threshold of ages you want to inspect.
L160: After you select your feature and label, you select the types of bias metrics you want to calculate.
L161: 
L162: To learn more, see cite20†Generate reports for bias in pre-training data .
L163: ## Create Custom Visualizations
L164: 
L165: You can add an analysis to your Data Wrangler flow to create a custom visualization. Your dataset, with all the transformations you've applied, is available as a cite21†Pandas DataFrame†pandas.pydata.org . Data Wrangler uses the `df` variable to store the dataframe. You access the dataframe by calling the variable.
L166: You must provide the output variable, `chart`, to store an cite22†Altair†altair-viz.github.io output chart. For example, you can use the following code block to create a custom histogram using the Titanic dataset.
L167: 
L168:     `import altair as alt
L169:     df = df.iloc[:30]
L170:     df = df.rename(columns={"Age": "value"})
L171:     df = df.assign(count=df.groupby('value').value.transform('count'))
L172:     df = df[["value", "count"]]
L173:     base = alt.Chart(df)
L174:     bar = base.mark_bar().encode(x=alt.X('value', bin=True, axis=None), y=alt.Y('count'))
L175:     rule = base.mark_rule(color='red').encode(
L176:         x='mean(value):Q',
L177:         size=alt.value(5))
L178:     chart = bar + rule`
L179: ###### To create a custom visualization:
L180: 
L181:   1. Next to the node containing the transformation that you'd like to visualize, choose the +.
L182: 
L183:   2. Choose Add analysis.
L184: 
L185:   3. For Analysis type, choose Custom Visualization.
L186: 
L187:   4. For Analysis name, specify a name.
L188: 
L189:   5. Enter your code in the code box.
L190: 
L191:   6. Choose Preview to preview your visualization.
L192: 
L193:   7. Choose Save to add your visualization.
L194: 
L195: cite23†Image: Example on how to add your visualization in the Data Wrangler console. L196: If you don’t know how to use the Altair visualization package in Python, you can use custom code snippets to help you get started.
L197: 
L198: Data Wrangler has a searchable collection of visualization snippets. To use a visualization snippet, choose Search example snippets and specify a query in the search bar.
L199: 
L200: The following example uses the Binned scatterplot code snippet. It plots a histogram for 2 dimensions.
L201: The snippets have comments to help you understand the changes that you need to make to the code. You usually need to specify the column names of your dataset in the code.
L202: 
L203:     `
L204:     import altair as alt
L205: 
L206:     # Specify the number of top rows for plotting
L207:     rows_number = 1000
L208:     df = df.head(rows_number)
L209:     # You can also choose bottom rows or randomly sampled rows
L210:     # df = df.tail(rows_number)
L211:     # df = df.sample(rows_number)
L212: 
L213: 
L214:     chart = (
L215:         alt.Chart(df)
L216:         .mark_circle()
L217:         .encode(
L218:             # Specify the column names for binning and number of bins for X and Y axis
L219:             x=alt.X("col1:Q", bin=alt.Bin(maxbins=20)),
L220:             y=alt.Y("col2:Q", bin=alt.Bin(maxbins=20)),
L221:             size="count()",
L222:         )
L223:     )
L224: 
L225:     # :Q specifies that label column has quantitative type.
L226:     # For more details on Altair typing refer to
L227:     # https://altair-viz.github.io/user_guide/encoding.html#encoding-data-types
L228:             `

L5: 
L6: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler provides numerous ML data transforms to streamline cleaning, transforming, and featurizing your data. When you add a transform, it adds a step to the data flow. Each transform you add modifies your dataset and produces a new dataframe. All subsequent transforms apply to the resulting dataframe.
L7: Data Wrangler includes built-in transforms, which you can use to transform columns without any code. You can also add custom transformations using PySpark, Python (User-Defined Function), pandas, and PySpark SQL. Some transforms operate in place, while others create a new output column in your dataset.
L8: 
L9: You can apply transforms to multiple columns at once. For example, you can delete multiple columns in a single step.
L10: You can apply the Process numeric and Handle missing transforms only to a single column.
L11: 
L12: Use this page to learn more about these built-in and custom transforms.
L13: ## Transform UI
L14: 
L15: Most of the built-in transforms are located in the Prepare tab of the Data Wrangler UI. You can access the join and concatenate transforms through the data flow view. Use the following table to preview these two views.
L16: 
L17: Transform
L18: 
L19: 
L20: You can add a transform to any step in your data flow. Use the following procedure to add a transform to your data flow.
L21: 
L22: To add a step to your data flow, do the following.
L23: 
L24:   1. Choose the + next to the step in the data flow.
L25: 
L26:   2. Choose Add transform.
L27:   3. Choose Add step.
L28: 
L29: cite29†Image: Add step located toward the top of the Transforms section. L30: 
L31:   4. Choose a transform.
L32: 
L33:   5. (Optional) You can search for the transform that you want to use. Data Wrangler highlights the query in the results.
L34: 
L35: cite30†Image: Search box located toward the top of the ADD TRANSFORM section. L36: 
L37: Join View
L38: To join two datasets, select the first dataset in your data flow and choose Join. When you choose Join, you see results similar to those shown in the following image. Your left and right datasets are displayed in the left panel. The main panel displays your data flow, with the newly joined dataset added.
L39: 
L40: cite31†Image: The joined dataset flow in the data flow section of the Data Wrangler console. L41: When you choose Configure to configure your join, you see results similar to those shown in the following image. Your join configuration is displayed in the left panel. You can use this panel to choose the joined dataset name, join type, and columns to join. The main panel displays three tables. The top two tables display the left and right datasets on the left and right respectively. Under this table, you can preview the joined dataset.
L42: cite32†Image: The joined dataset tables in the data flow section of the Data Wrangler console. L43: 
L44: See cite2†Join Datasets to learn more.
L45: 
L46: Concatenate View
L47: 
L48: 
L49: To concatenate two datasets, you select the first dataset in your data flow and choose Concatenate. When you select Concatenate, you see results similar to those shown in the following image. Your left and right datasets are displayed in the left panel. The main panel displays your data flow, with the newly concatenated dataset added.
L50: cite33†Image: Example concatenated dataset flow in the data flow section in the Data Wrangler console. L51: When you choose Configure to configure your concatenation, you see results similar to those shown in the following image. Your concatenate configuration displays in the left panel. You can use this panel to choose the concatenated dataset's name, and choose to remove duplicates after concatenation and add columns to indicate the source dataframe. The main panel displays three tables. The top two tables display the left and right datasets on the left and right respectively.
L52: Under this table, you can preview the concatenated dataset.
L53: cite34†Image: Example concatenated dataset tables in the data flow section in the Data Wrangler console. L54: 
L55: See cite3†Concatenate Datasets to learn more.
L56: ## Join Datasets
L57: 
L58: You join dataframes directly in your data flow. When you join two datasets, the resulting joined dataset appears in your flow. The following join types are supported by Data Wrangler.
L59: 
L60:   * Left Outer – Include all rows from the left table. If the value for the column joined on a left table row does not match any right table row values, that row contains null values for all right table columns in the joined table.
L61:   * Left Anti – Include rows from the left table that do not contain values in the right table for the joined column.
L62: 
L63:   * Left semi – Include a single row from the left table for all identical rows that satisfy the criteria in the join statement. This excludes duplicate rows from the left table that match the criteria of the join.
L64:   * Right Outer – Include all rows from the right table. If the value for the joined column in a right table row does not match any left table row values, that row contains null values for all left table columns in the joined table.
L65: 
L66:   * Inner – Include rows from left and right tables that contain matching values in the joined column.
L67:   * Full Outer – Include all rows from the left and right tables. If the row value for the joined column in either table does not match, separate rows are created in the joined table. If a row doesn’t contain a value for a column in the joined table, null is inserted for that column.
L68:   * Cartesian Cross – Include rows which combine each row from the first table with each row from the second table. This is a cite35†Cartesian product†en.wikipedia.org of rows from tables in the join. The result of this product is the size of the left table times the size of the right table. Therefore, we recommend caution in using this join between very large datasets.
L69: 
L70: Use the following procedure to join two dataframes.
L71:   1. Select + next to the left dataframe that you want to join. The first dataframe you select is always the left table in your join.
L72: 
L73:   2. Choose Join.
L74: 
L75:   3. Select the right dataframe. The second dataframe you select is always the right table in your join.
L76: 
L77:   4. Choose Configure to configure your join.
L78: 
L79:   5. Give your joined dataset a name using the Name field.
L80: 
L81:   6. Select a Join type.
L82: 
L83:   7. Select a column from the left and right tables to join.
L84:   8. Choose Apply to preview the joined dataset on the right.
L85: 
L86:   9. To add the joined table to your data flow, choose Add.
L87: ## Concatenate Datasets
L88: ###### Concatenate two datasets:
L89: 
L90:   1. Choose + next to the left dataframe that you want to concatenate. The first dataframe you select is always the left table in your concatenate.
L91: 
L92:   2. Choose Concatenate.
L93: 
L94:   3. Select the right dataframe. The second dataframe you select is always the right table in your concatenate.
L95: 
L96:   4. Choose Configure to configure your concatenate.
L97: 
L98:   5. Give your concatenated dataset a name using the Name field.
L99:   6. (Optional) Select the checkbox next to Remove duplicates after concatenation to remove duplicate columns.
L100: 
L101:   7. (Optional) Select the checkbox next to Add column to indicate source dataframe if, for each column in the new dataset, you want to add an indicator of the column's source.
L102: 
L103:   8. Choose Apply to preview the new dataset.
L104: 
L105:   9. Choose Add to add the new dataset to your data flow.
L106: ## Balance Data
L107: 
L108: You can balance the data for datasets with an underrepresented category. Balancing a dataset can help you create better models for binary classification.
L109: ###### Note
L110: 
L111: You can't balance datasets containing column vectors.
L112: 
L113: You can use the Balance data operation to balance your data using one of the following operators:
L114: 
L115:   * Random oversampling – Randomly duplicates samples in the minority category. For example, if you're trying to detect fraud, you might only have cases of fraud in 10% of your data. For an equal proportion of fraudulent and non-fraudulent cases, this operator randomly duplicates fraud cases within the dataset 8 times.
L116:   * Random undersampling – Roughly equivalent to random oversampling. Randomly removes samples from the overrepresented category to get the proportion of samples that you desire.
L117: 
L118:   * Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) – Uses samples from the underrepresented category to interpolate new synthetic minority samples. For more information about SMOTE, see the following description.
L119: You can use all transforms for datasets containing both numeric and non-numeric features. SMOTE interpolates values by using neighboring samples. Data Wrangler uses the R-squared distance to determine the neighborhood to interpolate the additional samples. Data Wrangler only uses numeric features to calculate the distances between samples in the underrepresented group.
L120: For two real samples in the underrepresented group, Data Wrangler interpolates the numeric features by using a weighted average. It randomly assigns weights to those samples in the range of [0, 1]. For numeric features, Data Wrangler interpolates samples using a weighted average of the samples. For samples A and B, Data Wrangler could randomly assign a weight of 0.7 to A and 0.3 to B. The interpolated sample has a value of 0.7A + 0.3B.
L121: Data Wrangler interpolates non-numeric features by copying from either of the interpolated real samples. It copies the samples with a probability that it randomly assigns to each sample. For samples A and B, it can assign probabilities 0.8 to A and 0.2 to B. For the probabilities it assigned, it copies A 80% of the time.
L122: ## Custom Transforms
L123: The Custom Transforms group allows you to use Python (User-Defined Function), PySpark, pandas, or PySpark (SQL) to define custom transformations. For all three options, you use the variable `df` to access the dataframe to which you want to apply the transform. To apply your custom code to your dataframe, assign the dataframe with the transformations that you've made to the `df` variable. If you're not using Python (User-Defined Function), you don't need to include a return statement.
L124: Choose Preview to preview the result of the custom transform. Choose Add to add the custom transform to your list of Previous steps.
L125: You can import the popular libraries with an `import` statement in the custom transform code block, such as the following:
L126: 
L127:   * NumPy version 1.19.0
L128: 
L129:   * scikit-learn version 0.23.2
L130: 
L131:   * SciPy version 1.5.4
L132: 
L133:   * pandas version 1.0.3
L134: 
L135:   * PySpark version 3.0.0
L136: ###### Important
L137: Custom transform doesn't support columns with spaces or special characters in the name. We recommend that you specify column names that only have alphanumeric characters and underscores. You can use the Rename column transform in the Manage columns transform group to remove spaces from a column's name. You can also add a Python (Pandas) Custom transform similar to the following to remove spaces from multiple columns in a single step.
L138: This example changes columns named `A column` and `B column` to `A_column` and `B_column` respectively.

L140:     `df.rename(columns={"A column": "A_column", "B column": "B_column"})`

L147: Python (User-Defined Function)

L208: ## Custom Formula
L209:

You can use the Rename column transform in the Manage columns transform group to remove spaces from a column's name. You can also add a Python (Pandas) Custom transform similar to the following to remove spaces from multiple columns in a single step.

L216: You can use this transform to perform operations on columns, referencing the columns by name. L232: ## Reduce Dimensionality within a Dataset
L233: 
L234: Reduce the dimensionality in your data by using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The dimensionality of your dataset corresponds to the number of features. When you use dimensionality reduction in Data Wrangler, you get a new set of features called components. Each component accounts for some variability in the data.
L235: The first component accounts for the largest amount of variation in the data. The second component accounts for the second largest amount of variation in the data, and so on.
L236: 
L237: You can use dimensionality reduction to reduce the size of the data sets that you use to train models. Instead of using the features in your dataset, you can use the principal components instead.
L238: To perform PCA, Data Wrangler creates axes for your data. An axis is an affine combination of columns in your dataset. The first principal component is the value on the axis that has the largest amount of variance. The second principal component is the value on the axis that has the second largest amount of variance. The nth principal component is the value on the axis that has the nth largest amount of variance.
L239: You can configure the number of principal components that Data Wrangler returns. You can either specify the number of principal components directly or you can specify the variance threshold percentage. Each principal component explains an amount of variance in the data. For example, you might have a principal component with a value of 0.5. The component would explain 50% of the variation in the data.
L240: When you specify a variance threshold percentage, Data Wrangler returns the smallest number of components that meet the percentage that you specify.
L241: The following are example principal components with the amount of variance that they explain in the data.
L242: 
L243:   * Component 1 – 0.5
L244: 
L245:   * Component 2 – 0.45
L246: 
L247:   * Component 3 – 0.05
L248: 
L249: If you specify a variance threshold percentage of `94` or `95`, Data Wrangler returns Component 1 and Component 2. If you specify a variance threshold percentage of `96`, Data Wrangler returns all three principal components.
L250: 
L251: You can use the following procedure to run PCA on your dataset.
L252: To run PCA on your dataset, do the following.
L253: 
L254:   1. Open your Data Wrangler data flow.
L255: 
L256:   2. Choose the +, and select Add transform.
L257: 
L258:   3. Choose Add step.
L259: 
L260:   4. Choose Dimensionality Reduction.
L261: 
L262:   5. For Input Columns, choose the features that you're reducing into the principal components.
L263:   6. (Optional) For Number of principal components, choose the number of principal components that Data Wrangler returns in your dataset. If specify a value for the field, you can't specify a value for Variance threshold percentage.
L264:   7. (Optional) For Variance threshold percentage, specify the percentage of variation in the data that you want explained by the principal components. Data Wrangler uses the default value of `95` if you don't specify a value for the variance threshold. You can't specify a variance threshold percentage if you've specified a value for Number of principal components.
L265:   8. (Optional) Deselect Center to not use the mean of the columns as the center of the data. By default, Data Wrangler centers the data with the mean before scaling.
L266: 
L267:   9. (Optional) Deselect Scale to not scale the data with the unit standard deviation.
L268: 
L269:   10. (Optional) Choose Columns to output the components to separate columns. Choose Vector to output the components as a single vector.
L270:   11. (Optional) For Output column, specify a name for an output column. If you're outputting the components to separate columns, the name that you specify is a prefix. If you're outputting the components to a vector, the name that you specify is the name of the vector column.
L271: 
L272:   12. (Optional) Select Keep input columns. We don't recommend selecting this option if you plan on only using the principal components to train your model.
L273: 
L274:   13. Choose Preview.
L275: 
L276:   14. Choose Add.
L277: ## Encode Categorical
L278: Categorical data is usually composed of a finite number of categories, where each category is represented with a string. For example, if you have a table of customer data, a column that indicates the country a person lives in is categorical. The categories would be Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, and so on. Categorical data can be nominal or ordinal. Ordinal categories have an inherent order, and nominal categories do not.
L279: The highest degree obtained (High school, Bachelors, Masters, and so on) is an example of ordinal categories.
L280: Encoding categorical data is the process of creating a numerical representation for categories. For example, if your categories are Dog and Cat, you may encode this information into two vectors, `[1,0]` to represent Dog, and `[0,1]` to represent Cat.
L281: 
L282: When you encode ordinal categories, you may need to translate the natural order of categories into your encoding. For example, you can represent the highest degree obtained with the following map: `{"High school": 1, "Bachelors": 2, "Masters":3}`.
L283: Use categorical encoding to encode categorical data that is in string format into arrays of integers.
L284: The Data Wrangler categorical encoders create encodings for all categories that exist in a column at the time the step is defined. If new categories have been added to a column when you start a Data Wrangler job to process your dataset at time t, and this column was the input for a Data Wrangler categorical encoding transform at time t-1, these new categories are considered missing in the Data Wrangler job. The option you select for Invalid handling strategy is applied to these missing values.
L285: Examples of when this can occur are:
L286:   * When you use a .flow file to create a Data Wrangler job to process a dataset that was updated after the creation of the data flow. For example, you may use a data flow to regularly process sales data each month. If that sales data is updated weekly, new categories may be introduced into columns for which an encode categorical step is defined.
L287: 
L288:   * When you select Sampling when you import your dataset, some categories may be left out of the sample.
L289: In these situations, these new categories are considered missing values in the Data Wrangler job.
L290: 
L291: You can choose from and configure an ordinal and a one-hot encode. Use the following sections to learn more about these options.
L292: 
L293: Both transforms create a new column named Output column name. You specify the output format of this column with Output style:
L294: 
L295:   * Select Vector to produce a single column with a sparse vector.
L296:   * Select Columns to create a column for every category with an indicator variable for whether the text in the original column contains a value that is equal to that category.
L297: ### Ordinal Encode
L298: 
L299: Select Ordinal encode to encode categories into an integer between 0 and the total number of categories in the Input column you select.
L300: 
L301: Invalid handing strategy: Select a method to handle invalid or missing values.
L302: 
L303:   * Choose Skip if you want to omit the rows with missing values.
L304: 
L305:   * Choose Keep to retain missing values as the last category.
L306: 
L307:   * Choose Error if you want Data Wrangler to throw an error if missing values are encountered in the Input column.
L308:   * Choose Replace with NaN to replace missing with NaN. This option is recommended if your ML algorithm can handle missing values. Otherwise, the first three options in this list may produce better results.
L309: ### One-Hot Encode
L310: 
L311: Select One-hot encode for Transform to use one-hot encoding. Configure this transform using the following:
L312: 
L313:   * Drop last category: If `True`, the last category does not have a corresponding index in the one-hot encoding. When missing values are possible, a missing category is always the last one and setting this to `True` means that a missing value results in an all zero vector.
L314: 
L315:   * Invalid handing strategy: Select a method to handle invalid or missing values.
L316:     * Choose Skip if you want to omit the rows with missing values.
L317: 
L318:     * Choose Keep to retain missing values as the last category.
L319: 
L320:     * Choose Error if you want Data Wrangler to throw an error if missing values are encountered in the Input column.
L321: 
L322:   * Is input ordinal encoded: Select this option if the input vector contains ordinal encoded data. This option requires that input data contain non-negative integers. If True, input i is encoded as a vector with a non-zero in the ith location.
L323: ### Similarity encode
L324: 
L325: Use similarity encoding when you have the following:
L326: 
L327:   * A large number of categorical variables
L328: 
L329:   * Noisy data
L330: 
L331: The similarity encoder creates embeddings for columns with categorical data. An embedding is a mapping of discrete objects, such as words, to vectors of real numbers. It encodes similar strings to vectors containing similar values. For example, it creates very similar encodings for "California" and "Calfornia".
L332: Data Wrangler converts each category in your dataset into a set of tokens using a 3-gram tokenizer. It converts the tokens into an embedding using min-hash encoding.
L333: 
L334: The following example shows how the similarity encoder creates vectors from strings.
L335: 
L336: cite40†Image: Example on using ENCODE CATEGORICAL for a table in the Data Wrangler console. L337: 
L338: cite41†Image: Example vector representation of a variable found in a table in the Data Wrangler console. L339: 
L340: The similarity encodings that Data Wrangler creates:
L341:   * Have low dimensionality
L342: 
L343:   * Are scalable to a large number of categories
L344: 
L345:   * Are robust and resistant to noise
L346: 
L347: For the preceding reasons, similarity encoding is more versatile than one-hot encoding.
L348: 
L349: To add the similarity encoding transform to your dataset, use the following procedure.
L350: 
L351: To use similarity encoding, do the following.
L352: 
L353:   1. Sign in to the cite42†Amazon SageMaker AI Console†console.aws.amazon.com .
L354: 
L355:   2. Choose Open Studio Classic.
L356: 
L357:   3. Choose Launch app.
L358: 
L359:   4. Choose Studio.
L360:   5. Specify your data flow.
L361: 
L362:   6. Choose a step with a transformation.
L363: 
L364:   7. Choose Add step.
L365: 
L366:   8. Choose Encode categorical.
L367: 
L368:   9. Specify the following:
L369: 
L370:      * Transform – Similarity encode
L371: 
L372:      * Input column – The column containing the categorical data that you're encoding.
L373: 
L374:      * Target dimension – (Optional) The dimension of the categorical embedding vector. The default value is 30. We recommend using a larger target dimension if you have a large dataset with many categories.
L375:      * Output style – Choose Vector for a single vector with all of the encoded values. Choose Column to have the encoded values in separate columns.
L376: 
L377:      * Output column – (Optional) The name of the output column for a vector encoded output. For a column-encoded output, this is the prefix of the column names followed by listed number.
L378: ## Featurize Text
L379: 
L380: Use the Featurize Text transform group to inspect string-typed columns and use text embedding to featurize these columns.
L381: 
L382: This feature group contains two features, Character statistics and Vectorize. Use the following sections to learn more about these transforms. For both options, the Input column must contain text data (string type).
L383: ### Character Statistics
L384: 
L385: Use Character statistics to generate statistics for each row in a column containing text data.
L386: 
L387: This transform computes the following ratios and counts for each row, and creates a new column to report the result. The new column is named using the input column name as a prefix and a suffix that is specific to the ratio or count.
L388: 
L389:   * Number of words: The total number of words in that row. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_word_count`.
L390:   * Number of characters: The total number of characters in that row. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_char_count`.
L391: 
L392:   * Ratio of upper: The number of uppercase characters, from A to Z, divided by all characters in the column. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_capital_ratio`.
L393: 
L394:   * Ratio of lower: The number of lowercase characters, from a to z, divided by all characters in the column. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_lower_ratio`.
L395:   * Ratio of digits: The ratio of digits in a single row over the sum of digits in the input column. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_digit_ratio`.
L396: 
L397:   * Special characters ratio: The ratio of non-alphanumeric (characters like #$&%:@) characters to over the sum of all characters in the input column. The suffix for this output column is `-stats_special_ratio`.
L398: ### Vectorize
L399: 
L400: Text embedding involves mapping words or phrases from a vocabulary to vectors of real numbers. Use the Data Wrangler text embedding transform to tokenize and vectorize text data into term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) vectors.
L401: 
L402: When TF-IDF is calculated for a column of text data, each word in each sentence is converted to a real number that represents its semantic importance. Higher numbers are associated with less frequent words, which tend to be more meaningful.
L403: When you define a Vectorize transform step, Data Wrangler uses the data in your dataset to define the count vectorizer and TF-IDF methods . Running a Data Wrangler job uses these same methods.
L404: 
L405: You configure this transform using the following:
L406: 
L407:   * Output column name: This transform creates a new column with the text embedding. Use this field to specify a name for this output column.
L408: 
L409:   * Tokenizer: A tokenizer converts the sentence into a list of words, or tokens.
L410: Choose Standard to use a tokenizer that splits by white space and converts each word to lowercase. For example, `"Good dog"` is tokenized to `["good","dog"]`.
L411: 
L412: Choose Custom to use a customized tokenizer. If you choose Custom, you can use the following fields to configure the tokenizer:
L413:     * Minimum token length: The minimum length, in characters, for a token to be valid. Defaults to `1`. For example, if you specify `3` for minimum token length, words like `a, at, in` are dropped from the tokenized sentence.
L414: 
L415:     * Should regex split on gaps: If selected, regex splits on gaps. Otherwise, it matches tokens. Defaults to `True`.
L416: 
L417:     * Regex pattern: Regex pattern that defines the tokenization process. Defaults to `' \\ s+'`.
L418:     * To lowercase: If chosen, Data Wrangler converts all characters to lowercase before tokenization. Defaults to `True`.
L419: 
L420: To learn more, see the Spark documentation on cite43†Tokenizer†spark.apache.org .
L421: 
L422:   * Vectorizer: The vectorizer converts the list of tokens into a sparse numeric vector. Each token corresponds to an index in the vector and a non-zero indicates the existence of the token in the input sentence. You can choose from two vectorizer options, Count and Hashing.
L423:     * Count vectorize allows customizations that filter infrequent or too common tokens. Count vectorize parameters include the following:

L6: 
L7: You can use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to import data from the following data sources: Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Snowflake. The dataset that you import can include up to 1000 columns.
L8: ###### Topics
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†Import data from Amazon S3 L11: 
L12:   * cite2†Import data from Athena L13: 
L14:   * cite3†Import data from Amazon Redshift L15: 
L16:   * cite4†Import data from Amazon EMR L17: 
L18:   * cite5†Import data from Databricks (JDBC) L19: 
L20:   * cite6†Import data from Salesforce Data Cloud L21: 
L22:   * cite7†Import data from Snowflake L23: 
L24:   * cite8†Import Data From Software as a Service (SaaS) Platforms L25: 
L26:   * cite9†Imported Data Storage L27: 
L28: Some data sources allow you to add multiple data connections:
L29:   * You can connect to multiple Amazon Redshift clusters. Each cluster becomes a data source.
L30: 
L31:   * You can query any Athena database in your account to import data from that database.
L32: 
L33: When you import a dataset from a data source, it appears in your data flow. Data Wrangler automatically infers the data type of each column in your dataset. To modify these types, select the Data types step and select Edit data types.
L34: When you import data from Athena or Amazon Redshift, the imported data is automatically stored in the default SageMaker AI S3 bucket for the AWS Region in which you are using Studio Classic. Additionally, Athena stores data you preview in Data Wrangler in this bucket. To learn more, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L35: ###### Important
L36: 
L37: The default Amazon S3 bucket may not have the least permissive security settings, such as bucket policy and server-side encryption (SSE). We strongly recommend that you cite10†Add a Bucket Policy To Restrict Access to Datasets Imported to Data Wrangler .
L38: ###### Important
L39: 
L40: In addition, if you use the managed policy for SageMaker AI, we strongly recommend that you scope it down to the most restrictive policy that allows you to perform your use case. For more information, see cite11†Grant an IAM Role Permission to Use Data Wrangler .
L41: 
L42: All data sources except for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) require you to specify a SQL query to import your data. For each query, you must specify the following:
L43: 
L44:   * Data catalog
L45: 
L46:   * Database
L47: 
L48:   * Table
L49: You can specify the name of the database or the data catalog in either the drop down menus or within the query. The following are example queries:
L50: 
L51:   * `select * from `example-data-catalog-name`.`example-database-name`.`example-table-name`` – The query doesn't use anything specified in the dropdown menus of the user-interface (UI) to run. It queries `example-table-name` within `example-database-name` within `example-data-catalog-name`.
L52:   * `select * from `example-database-name`.`example-table-name`` – The query uses the data catalog that you've specified in the Data catalog dropdown menu to run. It queries `example-table-name` within `example-database-name` within the data catalog that you've specified.
L53:   * `select * from `example-table-name`` – The query requires you to select fields for both the Data catalog and Database name dropdown menus. It queries `example-table-name` within the data catalog within the database and data catalog that you've specified.
L54: 
L55: The link between Data Wrangler and the data source is a connection. You use the connection to import data from your data source.
L56: 
L57: There are the following types of connections:
L58: 
L59:   * Direct
L60: 
L61:   * Cataloged
L62: Data Wrangler always has access to the most recent data in a direct connection. If the data in the data source has been updated, you can use the connection to import the data. For example, if someone adds a file to one of your Amazon S3 buckets, you can import the file.
L63: A cataloged connection is the result of a data transfer. The data in the cataloged connection doesn't necessarily have the most recent data. For example, you might set up a data transfer between Salesforce and Amazon S3. If there's an update to the Salesforce data, you must transfer the data again. You can automate the process of transferring data. For more information about data transfers, see cite8†Import Data From Software as a Service (SaaS) Platforms .
L64: ## Import data from Amazon S3
L65: You can use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) to store and retrieve any amount of data, at any time, from anywhere on the web. You can accomplish these tasks using the AWS Management Console, which is a simple and intuitive web interface, and the Amazon S3 API. If you've stored your dataset locally, we recommend that you add it to an S3 bucket for import into Data Wrangler. To learn how, see cite12†Uploading an object to a bucket in the Amazon Simple Storage Service User Guide.
L66: Data Wrangler uses cite13†S3 Select†aws.amazon.com to allow you to preview your Amazon S3 files in Data Wrangler. You incur standard charges for each file preview. To learn more about pricing, see the Requests & data retrievals tab on cite14†Amazon S3 pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L67: ###### Important
L68: 
L69: If you plan to export a data flow and launch a Data Wrangler job, ingest data into a SageMaker AI feature store, or create a SageMaker AI pipeline, be aware that these integrations require Amazon S3 input data to be located in the same AWS region.
L70: ###### Important
L71: 
L72: If you're importing a CSV file, make sure it meets the following requirements:
L73: 
L74:   * A record in your dataset can't be longer than one line.
L75: 
L76:   * A backslash, `\`, is the only valid escape character.
L77: 
L78:   * Your dataset must use one of the following delimiters:
L79: 
L80:     * Comma – `,`
L81: 
L82:     * Colon – `:`
L83: 
L84:     * Semicolon – `;`
L85: 
L86:     * Pipe – `|`
L87: 
L88:     * Tab – `[TAB]`
L89: 
L90: To save space, you can import compressed CSV files.
L91: Data Wrangler gives you the ability to either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Amazon S3, it provides the following sampling options:
L92: 
L93:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L94: 
L95:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L96: 
L97:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L98: 
L99:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L100: After you've imported your data, you can also use the sampling transformer to take one or more samples from your entire dataset. For more information about the sampling transformer, see cite15†Sampling .
L101: 
L102: You can use one of the following resource identifiers to import your data:
L103: 
L104:   * An Amazon S3 URI that uses an Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon S3 access point
L105: 
L106:   * An Amazon S3 access point alias
L107: 
L108:   * An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) that uses an Amazon S3 access point or Amazon S3 bucket
L109: Amazon S3 access points are named network endpoints that are attached to the buckets. Each access point has distinct permissions and network controls that you can configure. For more information about access points, see cite16†Managing data access with Amazon S3 access points .
L110: ###### Important
L111: 
L112: If you're using an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) to import your data, it must be for a resource located in the same AWS Region that you're using to access Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic.
L113: You can import either a single file or multiple files as a dataset. You can use the multifile import operation when you have a dataset that is partitioned into separate files. It takes all of the files from an Amazon S3 directory and imports them as a single dataset. For information on the types of files that you can import and how to import them, see the following sections.
L114: 
L115: Single File Import
L116: 
L117: 
L118: You can import single files in the following formats:
L119: 
L120:   * Comma Separated Values (CSV)
L121: 
L122:   * Parquet
L123:   * Javascript Object Notation (JSON)
L124: 
L125:   * Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)
L126: 
L127:   * Image – Data Wrangler uses OpenCV to import images. For more information about supported image formats, see cite17†Image file reading and writing†docs.opencv.org .
L128: For files formatted in JSON, Data Wrangler supports both JSON lines (.jsonl) and JSON documents (.json). When you preview your data, it automatically shows the JSON in tabular format. For nested JSON documents that are larger than 5 MB, Data Wrangler shows the schema for the structure and the arrays as values in the dataset. Use the Flatten structured and Explode array operators to display the nested values in tabular format. For more information, see cite18†Unnest JSON Data and cite19†Explode Array .
L129: When you choose a dataset, you can rename it, specify the file type, and identify the first row as a header.
L130: 
L131: You can import a dataset that you've partitioned into multiple files in an Amazon S3 bucket in a single import step.
L132: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from a single file that you've stored in Amazon S3:
L133: 
L134:   1. If you are not currently on the Import tab, choose Import.
L135: 
L136:   2. Under Available, choose Amazon S3.
L137: 
L138:   3. From the Import tabular, image, or time-series data from S3, do one of the following:
L139: 
L140:      * Choose an Amazon S3 bucket from the tabular view and navigate to the file that you're importing.
L141:      * For S3 source, specify an Amazon S3 bucket or an Amazon S3 URI and select Go. The Amazon S3 URIs can be in one of the following formats:
L142: 
L143:        * `s3://`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`/`example-prefix`/`example-file``
L144: 
L145:        * `example-access-point`-`aqfqprnstn7aefdfbarligizwgyfouse1a`-s3alias/datasets/`example-file`
L146: 
L147:        * `s3://arn:aws:s3:`AWS-Region`:`111122223333`:accesspoint/`example-prefix`/`example-file``
L148: 
L149:   4. Choose the dataset to open the Import settings pane.
L150:   5. If your CSV file has a header, select the checkbox next to Add header to table.
L151: 
L152:   6. Use the Preview table to preview your dataset. This table shows up to 100 rows.
L153: 
L154:   7. In the Details pane, verify or change the Name and File Type for your dataset. If you add a Name that contains spaces, these spaces are replaced with underscores when your dataset is imported.
L155: 
L156:   8. Specify the sampling configuration that you'd like to use.
L157: 
L158:   9. Choose Import.
L159: 
L160: Multifile Import
L161: The following are the requirements for importing multiple files:
L162: 
L163:   * The files must be in the same folder of your Amazon S3 bucket.
L164: 
L165:   * The files must either share the same header or have no header.
L166: 
L167: Each file must be in one of the following formats:
L168: 
L169:   * CSV
L170: 
L171:   * Parquet
L172: 
L173:   * Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)
L174: 
L175:   * Image – Data Wrangler uses OpenCV to import images. For more information about supported image formats, see cite17†Image file reading and writing†docs.opencv.org .
L176: Use the following procedure to import multiple files.
L177: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from multiple files that you've stored in an Amazon S3 directory
L178: 
L179:   1. If you are not currently on the Import tab, choose Import.
L180: 
L181:   2. Under Available, choose Amazon S3.
L182: 
L183:   3. From the Import tabular, image, or time-series data from S3, do one of the following:
L184: 
L185:      * Choose an Amazon S3 bucket from the tabular view and navigate to the folder containing the files that you're importing.
L186:      * For S3 source, specify the Amazon S3 bucket or an Amazon S3 URI with your files and select Go. The following are valid URIs:
L187: 
L188:        * `s3://`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`/`example-prefix`/`example-prefix``
L189: 
L190:        * ``example-access-point`-`aqfqprnstn7aefdfbarligizwgyfouse1a`-s3alias/`example-prefix`/`
L191: 
L192:        * `s3://arn:aws:s3:AWS-Region:`111122223333`:accesspoint/`example-prefix``
L193:   4. Select the folder containing the files that you want to import. Each file must be in one of the supported formats. Your files must be the same data type.
L194: 
L195:   5. If your folder contains CSV files with headers, select the checkbox next to First row is header.
L196: 
L197:   6. If your files are nested within other folders, select the checkbox next to Include nested directories.
L198: 
L199:   7. (Optional) Choose Add filename column add a column to the dataset that shows the filename for each observation.
L200:   8. (Optional) By default, Data Wrangler doesn't show you a preview of a folder. You can activate previewing by choosing the blue Preview off button. A preview shows the first 10 rows of the first 10 files in the folder.
L201: 
L202:   9. In the Details pane, verify or change the Name and File Type for your dataset. If you add a Name that contains spaces, these spaces are replaced with underscores when your dataset is imported.
L203: 
L204:   10. Specify the sampling configuration that you'd like to use.
L205:   11. Choose Import dataset.
L206: 
L207: You can also use parameters to import a subset of files that match a pattern. Parameters help you more selectively pick the files that you're importing. To start using parameters, edit the data source and apply them to the path that you're using to import the data. For more information, see cite20†Reusing Data Flows for Different Datasets .
L208: ## Import data from Athena
L209: 
L210: Use Amazon Athena to import your data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) into Data Wrangler. In Athena, you write standard SQL queries to select the data that you're importing from Amazon S3. For more information, see cite21†What is Amazon Athena? L211: You can use the AWS Management Console to set up Amazon Athena. You must create at least one database in Athena before you start running queries. For more information about getting started with Athena, see cite22†Getting started .
L212: 
L213: Athena is directly integrated with Data Wrangler. You can write Athena queries without having to leave the Data Wrangler UI.
L214: 
L215: In addition to writing simple Athena queries in Data Wrangler, you can also use:
L216:   * Athena workgroups for query result management. For more information about workgroups, see cite23†Managing query results .
L217: 
L218:   * Lifecycle configurations for setting data retention periods. For more information about data retention, see cite24†Setting data retention periods .
L219: ### Query Athena within Data Wrangler
L220: ###### Note
L221: 
L222: Data Wrangler does not support federated queries.
L223: 
L224: If you use AWS Lake Formation with Athena, make sure your Lake Formation IAM permissions do not override IAM permissions for the database `sagemaker_data_wrangler`.
L225: 
L226: Data Wrangler gives you the ability to either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Athena, it provides the following sampling options:
L227: 
L228:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L229:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L230: 
L231:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L232: 
L233:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L234: 
L235: The following procedure shows how to import a dataset from Athena into Data Wrangler.
L236: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from Athena
L237: 
L238:   1. Sign into cite25†Amazon SageMaker AI Console†console.aws.amazon.com .
L239: 
L240:   2. Choose Studio.
L241: 
L242:   3. Choose Launch app.
L243: 
L244:   4. From the dropdown list, select Studio.
L245: 
L246:   5. Choose the Home icon.
L247: 
L248:   6. Choose Data.
L249: 
L250:   7. Choose Data Wrangler.
L251: 
L252:   8. Choose Import data.
L253: 
L254:   9. Under Available, choose Amazon Athena.
L255: 
L256:   10. For Data Catalog, choose a data catalog.
L257:   11. Use the Database dropdown list to select the database that you want to query. When you select a database, you can preview all tables in your database using the Tables listed under Details.
L258: 
L259:   12. (Optional) Choose Advanced configuration.
L260: 
L261:     1. Choose a Workgroup.
L262: 
L263:     2. If your workgroup hasn't enforced the Amazon S3 output location or if you don't use a workgroup, specify a value for Amazon S3 location of query results.
L264:     3. (Optional) For Data retention period, select the checkbox to set a data retention period and specify the number of days to store the data before it's deleted.
L265: 
L266:     4. (Optional) By default, Data Wrangler saves the connection. You can choose to deselect the checkbox and not save the connection.
L267: 
L268:   13. For Sampling, choose a sampling method. Choose None to turn off sampling.
L269:   14. Enter your query in the query editor and use the Run button to run the query. After a successful query, you can preview your result under the editor.
L270: ###### Note
L271: 
L272: Salesforce data uses the `timestamptz` type. If you're querying the timestamp column that you've imported to Athena from Salesforce, cast the data in the column to the `timestamp` type. The following query casts the timestamp column to the correct type.
L273: 
L274:     `
L275:     # cast column timestamptz_col as timestamp type, and name it as timestamp_col
L276:     select cast(timestamptz_col as timestamp) as timestamp_col from table
L277:                             `
L278:   15. To import the results of your query, select Import.
L279: 
L280: After you complete the preceding procedure, the dataset that you've queried and imported appears in the Data Wrangler flow.
L281: By default, Data Wrangler saves the connection settings as a new connection. When you import your data, the query that you've already specified appears as a new connection. The saved connections store information about the Athena workgroups and Amazon S3 buckets that you're using. When you're connecting to the data source again, you can choose the saved connection.
L282: ### Managing query results
L283: 
L284: Data Wrangler supports using Athena workgroups to manage the query results within an AWS account. You can specify an Amazon S3 output location for each workgroup. You can also specify whether the output of the query can go to different Amazon S3 locations. For more information, see cite26†Using Workgroups to Control Query Access and Costs .
L285: Your workgroup might be configured to enforce the Amazon S3 query output location. You can't change the output location of the query results for those workgroups.
L286: If you don't use a workgroup or specify an output location for your queries, Data Wrangler uses the default Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region in which your Studio Classic instance is located to store Athena query results. It creates temporary tables in this database to move the query output to this Amazon S3 bucket. It deletes these tables after data has been imported; however the database, `sagemaker_data_wrangler`, persists. To learn more, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L287: To use Athena workgroups, set up the IAM policy that gives access to workgroups. If you're using a `SageMaker AI-Execution-Role`, we recommend adding the policy to the role. For more information about IAM policies for workgroups, see cite27†IAM policies for accessing workgroups . For example workgroup policies, see cite28†Workgroup example policies .
L288: ### Setting data retention periods
L289: Data Wrangler automatically sets a data retention period for the query results. The results are deleted after the length of the retention period. For example, the default retention period is five days. The results of the query are deleted after five days. This configuration is designed to help you clean up data that you're no longer using. Cleaning up your data prevents unauthorized users from gaining access. It also helps control the costs of storing your data on Amazon S3.
L290: If you don't set a retention period, the Amazon S3 lifecycle configuration determines the duration that the objects are stored. The data retention policy that you've specified for the lifecycle configuration removes any query results that are older than the lifecycle configuration that you've specified. For more information, see cite29†Setting lifecycle configuration on a bucket .
L291: Data Wrangler uses Amazon S3 lifecycle configurations to manage data retention and expiration. You must give your Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic IAM execution role permissions to manage bucket lifecycle configurations. Use the following procedure to give permissions.
L292: 
L293: To give permissions to manage the lifecycle configuration do the following.
L294: 
L295:   1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the IAM console at cite30†https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/†console.aws.amazon.com .
L296: 
L297:   2. Choose Roles.
L298:   3. In the search bar, specify the Amazon SageMaker AI execution role that Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic is using.
L299: 
L300:   4. Choose the role.
L301: 
L302:   5. Choose Add permissions.
L303: 
L304:   6. Choose Create inline policy.
L305: 
L306:   7. For Service, specify S3 and choose it.
L307: 
L308:   8. Under the Read section, choose GetLifecycleConfiguration.
L309: 
L310:   9. Under the Write section, choose PutLifecycleConfiguration.
L311: 
L312:   10. For Resources, choose Specific.
L313: 
L314:   11. For Actions, select the arrow icon next to Permissions management.
L315:   12. Choose PutResourcePolicy.
L316: 
L317:   13. For Resources, choose Specific.
L318: 
L319:   14. Choose the checkbox next to Any in this account.
L320: 
L321:   15. Choose Review policy.
L322: 
L323:   16. For Name, specify a name.
L324: 
L325:   17. Choose Create policy.
L326: ## Import data from Amazon Redshift
L327: 
L328: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service in the cloud. The first step to create a data warehouse is to launch a set of nodes, called an Amazon Redshift cluster. After you provision your cluster, you can upload your dataset and then perform data analysis queries.
L329: You can connect to and query one or more Amazon Redshift clusters in Data Wrangler. To use this import option, you must create at least one cluster in Amazon Redshift. To learn how, see cite31†Getting started with Amazon Redshift .
L330: 
L331: You can output the results of your Amazon Redshift query in one of the following locations:
L332: 
L333:   * The default Amazon S3 bucket
L334: 
L335:   * An Amazon S3 output location that you specify
L336: You can either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Amazon Redshift, it provides the following sampling options:
L337: 
L338:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L339: 
L340:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L341: 
L342:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L343: 
L344:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L345: The default Amazon S3 bucket is in the same AWS Region in which your Studio Classic instance is located to store Amazon Redshift query results. For more information, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L346: 
L347: For either the default Amazon S3 bucket or the bucket that you specify, you have the following encryption options:
L348: 
L349:   * The default AWS service-side encryption with an Amazon S3 managed key (SSE-S3)
L350: 
L351:   * An AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that you specify
L352: An AWS KMS key is an encryption key that you create and manage. For more information on KMS keys, see cite32†AWS Key Management Service .
L353: 
L354: You can specify an AWS KMS key using either the key ARN or the ARN of your AWS account.
L355: 
L356: If you use the IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, to grant a role permission to use Data Wrangler in Studio Classic, your Database User name must have the prefix `sagemaker_access`.
L357: 
L358: Use the following procedures to learn how to add a new cluster.
L359: ###### Note
L360: 
L361: Data Wrangler uses the Amazon Redshift Data API with temporary credentials. To learn more about this API, refer to cite33†Using the Amazon Redshift Data API in the Amazon Redshift Management Guide.

L429: ## Import data from Amazon EMR
L430: 
L431: You can use Amazon EMR as a data source for your Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler flow. Amazon EMR is a managed cluster platform that you can use process and analyze large amounts of data. For more information about Amazon EMR, see cite38†What is Amazon EMR? . To import a dataset from EMR, you connect to it and query it.
L432: 
L433: ###### Important
L434: 
L435: You must meet the following prerequisites to connect to an Amazon EMR cluster:
L436: ###### Prerequisites
L437: 
L438:   * ###### Network configurations
L439: 
L440:     * You have an Amazon VPC in the Region that you're using to launch Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic and Amazon EMR.
L441: 
L442:     * Both Amazon EMR and Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must be launched in private subnets. They can be in the same subnet or in different ones.
L443: 
L444:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must be in VPC-only mode.
L445: 
L446: For more information about creating a VPC, see cite39†Create a VPC .
L447: For more information about creating a VPC, see cite40†Connect SageMaker Studio Classic Notebooks in a VPC to External Resources .
L448: 
L449:     * The Amazon EMR clusters that you're running must be in the same Amazon VPC.
L450: 
L451:     * The Amazon EMR clusters and the Amazon VPC must be in the same AWS account.
L452: 
L453:     * Your Amazon EMR clusters are running Hive or Presto.
L454: 
L455:       * Hive clusters must allow inbound traffic from Studio Classic security groups on port 10000.
L456:       * Presto clusters must allow inbound traffic from Studio Classic security groups on port 8889.
L457: ###### Note
L458: 
L459: The port number is different for Amazon EMR clusters using IAM roles. Navigate to the end of the prerequisites section for more information.
L460: 
L461:   * ###### SageMaker Studio Classic
L462: 
L463:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must run Jupyter Lab Version 3. For information about updating the Jupyter Lab Version, see cite41†View and update the JupyterLab version of an application from the console .
L464:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic has an IAM role that controls user access. The default IAM role that you're using to run Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic doesn't have policies that can give you access to Amazon EMR clusters. You must attach the policy granting permissions to the IAM role. For more information, see cite42†Configure listing Amazon EMR clusters .
L465: 
L466:     * The IAM role must also have the following policy attached `secretsmanager:PutResourcePolicy`.
L467:     * If you're using a Studio Classic domain that you've already created, make sure that its `AppNetworkAccessType` is in VPC-only mode. For information about updating a domain to use VPC-only mode, see cite43†Shut Down and Update Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic .
L468: 
L469:   * ###### Amazon EMR clusters
L470: 
L471:     * You must have Hive or Presto installed on your cluster.
L472: 
L473:     * The Amazon EMR release must be version 5.5.0 or later.
L474: ###### Note
