L233: ## cite79†Artificial Intelligence L234: # Pruning machine learning models with Amazon SageMaker Debugger and Amazon SageMaker Experiments
L235: 
L236: by Nathalie Rauschmayr, cite80†Julien Simon , and Satadal Bhattacharjee on 31 MAR 2020 in cite81†Amazon SageMaker , cite82†Artificial Intelligence cite83†Permalink cite84†Comments cite85†Share L237: In the past decade, deep learning has advanced many different areas, such as computer vision and natural language processing. State-of-the-art models now achieve near-human performance in tasks such as image classification. Deep neural networks can achieve this because they consist of millions of parameters that you train on large training datasets. For instance, the cite86†BERT (Large)†arxiv.org model consists of 340 million parameters, and cite87†Resnet-152†arxiv.org consists of 60 million parameters.
L238: Training such models from scratch is computationally intensive and can take hours, days, or even weeks.
L239: Typically, data scientists perform transfer learning, which is the process of using knowledge gained by solving one problem to a related but different problem. With transfer learning, you fine-tune a pretrained model on a smaller dataset to improve accuracy. In such scenarios, you may not need a large number of parameters in the model—a smaller model may just perform as well.
L240: In the context of machine learning (ML) at the edge, having small models is essential. Due to hardware constraints, factors such as latency, memory footprint, and compute time are as important as model accuracy. For instance, autonomous driving requires models with high accuracy and low latency. In such a scenario, a model that achieves 1% better accuracy but takes twice the time for prediction is not favorable.
L241: Model pruning can significantly reduce model size without sacrificing accuracy. The idea is simple: identify the redundant parameters in the model that contribute little to the training process.
L242: 
L243: This post demonstrates iterative model pruning with cite88†Amazon SageMaker . The post walks through a sample application that uses a pretrained model and iteratively prunes it by more than a factor of three with no significant loss in accuracy.
L244: ## Model pruning
L245: Model pruning aims to remove weights that don’t contribute much to the training process. Weights are learnable parameters: they are randomly initialized and optimized during the training process. During the forward pass, data passes through the model. The loss function evaluates model output given the labels; during the backward pass, weights are updated to minimize the loss. To do so, the gradients of the loss with respect to the weights are computed, and each weight receives a different update.
L246: After a few iterations, certain weights are typically more impactful than others; the goal of pruning is to remove the useless ones without significantly reducing model accuracy. The following diagram illustrates this workflow.
L247: cite89†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L248: 
L249: You can use the following heuristics to measure the importance of weights:
L250: 
L251:   * Magnitudes of weights – Remove weights if their absolute value is smaller than a threshold: smaller weights have less effect on the output.
L252:   * Average activation – If a neuron is mostly not active throughout the training, you can infer that the weights going into the activation function are less relevant.
L253: 
L254: You can distinguish between non-structured and structured weight pruning:
L255:   * Non-structured pruning removes arbitrary weights (as in the preceding diagram)
L256:   * Structured pruning removes entire convolutional filters and associated channels
L257: Structured pruning is especially relevant for computer vision models that typically consist of many convolutional layers. A filter is a collection of kernels (one kernel for every single input channel). A filter produces one feature map, also referred to as an output channel. The following diagram shows three kernels that produce three output feature maps.
L258: The number of parameters that the model has to learn (its weights) is 3 x input_channels x kernel_width x kernel_height, where the number of input channels in this example is 1. For simplification, you can assume in this diagram that there is no bias tensor. You can rank the filters to identify those of least importance (for instance, the yellow filter). You reduce the number of parameters by 1 x input_channels x kernel_width x kernel_height by removing it.
L259: cite90†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L260: To rank the importance of each filter, you employ the ranking method as described in the paper cite91†“Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks for Resource Efficient Inference”†arxiv.org : they estimate the impact of a pruned filter on the loss. The goal is to remove the ones that do not impact the loss. A filter receives a low rank if its activation outputs and corresponding gradients are small.
L261: You can get an estimate of filter importance by accumulating the product of activation outputs and gradients throughout the training.
L262: You then remove the lowest-ranked filters and fine-tune the model to recover from the pruning and regain accuracy. You can repeat these steps several times.
L263: ## Iterative model pruning on Amazon SageMaker
L264: cite92†Amazon SageMaker Debugger†docs.aws.amazon.com allows you to emit tensors from your training jobs and run built-in rules that automatically detect training issues. You can retrieve gradients and activation outputs to compute filter ranks. For more information, see cite93†Amazon SageMaker Debugger – Debug Your Machine Learning Models . Amazon SageMaker Experiments lets you customize, visualize, and track ML experiments at scale.
L265: For more information, see cite94†Amazon SageMaker Experiments – Organize, Track and Compare Your Machine Learning Trainings . For this post, you use it to track the different pruning iterations. You can quickly identify and deploy the model that yields the best accuracy and size trade-off with the Experiments view in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
L266: To walk through iterative model pruning step-by-step, this post uses a cite87†Resnet18†arxiv.org model pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tunes it on the cite95†Caltech101†www.vision.caltech.edu dataset, which consists of only 101 classes. You resize images during retraining. ResNet is a convolutional neural network consisting of multiple residual blocks. A block is made up of convolutional layers followed by a batch normalization layer and ReLu function. Skip connections allow the input to bypass the block.
L267: For this post, you use ResNet18, the smallest version of ResNet models with about 11 million parameters. In each pruning iteration, you remove the 200 lowest-ranked filters.
L268: The following diagram illustrates the solution workflow:
L269: 
L270: cite96†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L271: 
L272: The steps are as follows:
L273: 
L274:   1. Start the training job
L275:   2. Acquire the weights, gradients, biases, and activation outputs
L276:   3. Compute filter ranks
L277:   4. Prune low-ranking filters
L278:   5. Set new weights
L279:   6. Start the training job with the pruned model
L280: ## Creating the experiment and debugger hook configuration
L281: Before you implement the solution, create a model pruning experiment. An experiment is a collection of trials, whereby a trial is a collection of training steps. See the following code:
L282: 
L283:     `from smexperiments.experiment import Experiment
L284: 
L285:     Experiment.create(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment",
L286:                         description="Iterative model pruning of ResNet18 trained on Caltech101",
L287:                         sagemaker_boto_client=sagemaker_boto_client)
L288:     `
L289: In each pruning iteration, you start a new Amazon SageMaker training job, which is a new trial within the experiment. See the following code:
L290: 
L291:     `from smexperiments.trial import Trial
L292: 
L293:     trial = Trial.create(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment",
L294:     sagemaker_boto_client=sagemaker_boto_client)`
L295: You next define the `experiment_config`, which is a dictionary that is passed to the Amazon SageMaker training job. This allows Amazon SageMaker to associate the training job with the experiment and trial. See the following code:
L296: 
L297:     `experiment_config = { "ExperimentName": "model_pruning_experiment",
L298:                             "TrialName":  trial.trial_name,
L299:                             "TrialComponentDisplayName": "Training"}`
L300: Before you can start the training job, you must define a debugger hook configuration. Amazon SageMaker Debugger provides default collections for weights, biases, gradients, and losses . For this post, you must also store  activation outputs. To retrieve those, create a custom collection in which a regular expression indicates the tensor names to include. Because ResNet consists of batch norm layers, you also store the batch norm statistics running mean and variance.
L301: Tensors are saved every 100 steps, wherein a step presents one forward and backward pass. See the following code:
L302: 
L303:     `from sagemaker.debugger import DebuggerHookConfig, CollectionConfig
L304: 
L305:     debugger_hook_config = DebuggerHookConfig(
L306:           collection_configs=[
L307:               CollectionConfig(
L308:                     name="custom_collection",
L309:                     parameters={ "include_regex": ".*relu|.*weight|.*bias|.*running_mean|.*running_var",
L310:                                  "save_interval": "100" })])`
L311: ## Starting your training job
L312: You are now ready to train the ResNet18 model with Amazon SageMaker. The training loop is defined in the `entry_point` file `train.py`. For more information, see the cite97†GitHub repo†github.com . To emit tensors, pass the debugger hook configuration into the PyTorch Estimator. See the following code:
L313: 
L314:     `import sagemaker
L315:     from sagemaker.pytorch import PyTorch
L316: 
L317:     estimator = PyTorch(role=sagemaker.get_execution_role(),
L318:                       train_instance_count=1,
L319:                       train_instance_type='ml.p3.2xlarge',
L320:                       train_volume_size=400,
L321:                       source_dir='src',
L322:                       entry_point='train.py',
L323:                       framework_version='1.3.1',
L324:                       py_version='py3',
L325:                       debugger_hook_config=debugger_hook_config
L326:             )
L327:     `
L328: After you define the estimator object, you can call `fit`. This launches a managed ml.p3.2xlarge instance to run your training script. As discussed previously, you pass the `experiment_config` to the training job. See the following code:
L329: 
L330:     `estimator.fit(experiment_config=experiment_config)`
L331: ## Getting gradients, weights, and biases
L332: After the training job is complete, you retrieve its tensors, such as gradients, weights, and biases. You can use the cite98†smdebug†pypi.org library, which provides functions to read and filter tensors. First, create a cite99†trial†github.com that allows access to the tensors that the debugger saved. For more information, see the cite99†GitHub repo†github.com . In the context of Amazon SageMaker Debugger, a trial is an object that lets you query tensors for a given training job.
L333: In the context of Amazon SageMaker Experiments, a trial is part of an experiment and presents a collection of training steps involved in a single training job. See the following code:
L334: 
L335:     `from smdebug.trials import create_trial
L336: 
L337:     path = estimator.latest_job_debugger_artifacts_path()
L338:     smdebug_trial = create_trial(path)`
L339: To access tensor values, call `smdebug_trial.tensor()`. For instance, to get the activation outputs of the first convolution layer, enter the following code:
L340: 
L341:     `smdebug_trial.tensor('layer1.0.relu_0_output_0').value(0, mode=modes.TRAIN)`
L342: ## Computing filter ranks
L343: Now that you have access to the tensors, you can compute their filter ranks. Iterate the available training steps and retrieve the activation outputs and their gradients. For instance, the following code segment computes the filter ranks of the first feature layer of the model, and you then compute a single value (rank) for each filter:
L344: 
L345:     `rank = 0
L346:     for step in smdebug_trial.steps(mode=modes.TRAIN):
L347:         activation_output = smdebug_trial.tensor( 'layer1.0.relu_0_output_0').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L348:         gradient = smdebug_trial.tensor( 'gradient/layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L349:         product = activation_output * gradient
L350:         rank += np.mean(product, axis=(0,2,3))`
L351: Afterwards, you normalize filter ranks and sort them by size.
L352: ## Pruning low-ranking filters
L353: 
L354: You can now retrieve the smallest filters. The following code shows that you can prune filter 1, 36, and 127 in `layer1.0` because they have a rank of 0.0:
L355: 
L356:     `[('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 1, 0.0),
L357:     ('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 127, 0.0),
L358:     ('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 36, 0.0)]`
L359: To prune those filters, use SageMaker Debugger to get the weight tensor of the first convolutional layer in `layer1.0` and delete the preceding entries in the second dimension (`axis=1`). See the following code:
L360: 
L361:     `weight = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.conv1.weight').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L362:     weight = np.delete(weight, [1,36,127], axis=1)`
L363: ## Setting new weights
L364: You also need to adjust the convolution parameters. The convolutional layer in `layer1.0` in the Resnet18 model has 64 output channels. After removing three filters, it only has 61 output channels. You also need to adjust the weights of the subsequent batch norm layer. Therefore, remove the entries in the first dimension (`axis=0`). See the following code:
L365: 
L366:     `weight = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.bn1.weight').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L367:     bias = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.bn1.bias').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L368:     weight = np.delete(weight, [1,36,127], axis=0)
L369:     bias =  np.delete(bias, [1,36,127], axis=0)`
L370: ## Starting the next pruning iteration
L371: 
L372: After you prune the 200 smallest filters, save the new model definition with the latest weights and start the next pruning iteration. You can complete these steps multiple times, which leads to a smaller model in each iteration.
L373: ## Results
L374: You can track and visualize the iterative model pruning experiment in Amazon SageMaker Studio. The training script uses SageMaker Debugger’s `save_scalar` method to store the number of model parameters and model accuracy. For more information, see the cite100†GitHub repo†github.com . The values that `save_scalar` writes go into a data store that Amazon SageMaker Studio uses to create visualizations.
L375: The following graph shows a scatterplot in which the x-axis shows the number of model parameters and the y-axis shows the validation accuracy.
L376: cite101†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L377: 
L378: Initially, the model consisted of 11 million parameters. After 11 iterations, the number of parameters reduced to 706,000, and accuracy increased to 90% and started dropping after eight pruning iterations. The following screenshot shows the experiment view where the different trials and details are listed.
L379: 
L380: cite102†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L381: ## Running iterative model pruning with a custom rule
L382: In the previous example, accuracy drops when the model has fewer than 4 million parameters. You want to stop the experiment when you reach this point. SageMaker Debugger provides built-in rules that trigger when the model training runs into issues, such as for instance vanishing gradients or the loss is not decreasing. If the model does not have enough capacity (too few parameters), it doesn’t learn well. One of the implications is that the loss may not decrease.
L383: For more information, see cite103†Built-in Rules Provided by Amazon SageMaker Debugger†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L384: For this post, you can define a custom rule that compares the accuracy of the current model with the accuracy of the previous training job. For example, if it drops by more than 10%, the rule triggers and returns `True`. You can then set up an cite104†Amazon CloudWatch alarm and cite105†AWS Lambda function that stops the training job and prevents your model pruning experiment from wasting resources on jobs that produce low-quality models. For more information, see the cite106†GitHub repo†github.com .
L385: The following code shows a high-level overview of the custom rule:
L386: 
L387:     `from smdebug.rules.rule import Rule
L388: 
L389:     class check_accuracy(Rule):
L390:         def __init__(self, base_trial,
L391:                      previous_accuracy=0.0):
L392:               self.previous_accuracy = float(previous_accuracy)
L393: 
L394:         def invoke_at_step(self, step):
L395:             predictions = np.argmax(self.base_trial.tensor('CrossEntropyLoss_0_input_0').value(step, mode=modes.EVAL), axis=1)
L396:             labels = self.base_trial.tensor('CrossEntropyLoss_0_input_1').value(step, mode=modes.EVAL)
L397:             current_accuracy = compute_accurcay(predictions, labels)
L398: 
L399:             if self.previous_accuracy - current_accuracy > 0.10:
L400:                 return True
L401: 
L402:              return False
L403:     `
L404: The rule implements a Python class that inherits from the `smdebug` rule class. It takes as argument the accuracy of the previous training job. The class implements the function `invoke_at_step` that is called every time tensors of a new step are available. With `smdebug`, you get the inputs into the loss function, which are the model predictions and labels. You can then compute the accuracy and compare it to the previous training job.
L405: For more information about the full implementation of the rule, see the cite107†GitHub repo†github.com .
L406: To run the rule with your training job, you need to pass it to the PyTorch estimator object. You first need to create a custom rule configuration. See the following code:
L407: 
L408:     `from sagemaker.debugger import Rule, CollectionConfig, rule_configs
L409: 
L410:     check_accuracy_rule = Rule.custom(
L411:         name='CheckAccuracy',
L412:         image_uri='840043622174.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sagemaker-debugger-rule-evaluator:latest',
L413:         instance_type='ml.c4.xlarge',
L414:         volume_size_in_gb=400,
L415:         source='custom_rule/check_accuracy.py',
L416:         rule_to_invoke='check_accuracy',
L417:         rule_parameters={"previous_accuracy": "0.0"},
L418:     )
L419:     `
L420: The rule configuration specifies the location of the rule definition, its input parameters, and the instance type where the rule container is going to run. You need to specify the image for the rule container. For more information, see cite108†Amazon SageMaker Custom Rule Evaluator Registry Ids†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L421: 
L422: After you define the rule, pass the argument `rules = [check_accuracy_rule]` to the Pytorch estimator.
L423: In each pruning iteration, you need to pass the accuracy of the previous training job to the rule, which is retrievable via SageMaker Experiments and the `ExperimentAnalytics` module. See the following code:
L424: 
L425:     `from sagemaker.analytics import ExperimentAnalytics
L426: 
L427:     trial_component_analytics = ExperimentAnalytics(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment")
L428:     accuracy = trial_component_analytics.dataframe()['scalar/accuracy_EVAL - Max'][0]
L429:     `
L430: Overwrite the value in the rule configuration with the following code:
L431: 
L432:     `check_accuracy_rule.rule_parameters["previous_accuracy"] = str(accuracy)`
L433: In each iteration, check the job status. If the previous job stops, exit the loop. See the following code:
L434: 
L435:     `job_name = estimator.latest_training_job.name
L436:     client = estimator.sagemaker_session.sagemaker_client
L437:     description = client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=job_name)
L438:     if description['TrainingJobStatus'] == 'Stopped':
L439:         break
L440:     `
L441: The following graph shows the number of parameters versus accuracy. In contrast to the previous experiment, the training job stops when it produces a low-quality model, and the experiment ends. As a consequence, it only runs eight iterations.
L442: 
L443: cite109†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L444: 
L445: The following screenshot shows the Debugger view in SageMaker Studio. It shows that the custom rule found an issue.
L446: 
L447: cite110†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L448: For more information about defining and running custom rules with SageMaker Debugger, see cite111†How to Use Custom Rules†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L449: ## Conclusion
L450: 
L451: This post discussed iterative model pruning with Amazon SageMaker and how you can significantly reduce the size of your models and retain accuracy by identifying redundant parameters that contribute little to the training process. You walked through a sample application that uses a pretrained model and saw that the model did not lose accuracy when iteratively pruned.

L2: Export - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Export to Amazon S3 cite2†Export to Pipelines cite3†Export to an Inference Endpoint cite4†Export to Python Code cite5†Export to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store cite6†Refit Transforms to The Entire Dataset and Export Them cite7†Create a Schedule to Automatically Process New Data L5: # Export
L6: 
L7: In your Data Wrangler flow, you can export some or all of the transformations that you've made to your data processing pipelines.
L8: A Data Wrangler flow is the series of data preparation steps that you've performed on your data. In your data preparation, you perform one or more transformations to your data. Each transformation is done using a transform step. The flow has a series of nodes that represent the import of your data and the transformations that you've performed. For an example of nodes, see the following image.
L9: 
L10: cite8†Image: Example data flow in the Data Wrangler console. L11: The preceding image shows a Data Wrangler flow with two nodes. The Source - sampled node shows the data source from which you've imported your data. The Data types node indicates that Data Wrangler has performed a transformation to convert the dataset into a usable format.
L12: Each transformation that you add to the Data Wrangler flow appears as an additional node. For information on the transforms that you can add, see cite9†Transform Data . The following image shows a Data Wrangler flow that has a Rename-column node to change the name of a column in a dataset.
L13: 
L14: You can export your data transformations to the following:
L15: 
L16:   * Amazon S3
L17: 
L18:   * Pipelines
L19: 
L20:   * Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
L21: 
L22:   * Python Code
L23: ###### Important
L24: 
L25: We recommend that you use the IAM `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess` managed policy to grant AWS permission to use Data Wrangler. If you don't use the managed policy, you can use an IAM policy that gives Data Wrangler access to an Amazon S3 bucket. For more information on the policy, see cite10†Security and Permissions .
L26: When you export your data flow, you're charged for the AWS resources that you use. You can use cost allocation tags to organize and manage the costs of those resources. You create these tags for your user-profile and Data Wrangler automatically applies them to the resources used to export the data flow. For more information, see cite11†Using Cost Allocation Tags .
L27: ## Export to Amazon S3
L28: 
L29: Data Wrangler gives you the ability to export your data to a location within an Amazon S3 bucket. You can specify the location using one of the following methods:
L30: 
L31:   * Destination node – Where Data Wrangler stores the data after it has processed it.
L32: 
L33:   * Export to – Exports the data resulting from a transformation to Amazon S3.
L34: 
L35:   * Export data – For small datasets, can quickly export the data that you've transformed.
L36: Use the following sections to learn more about each of these methods.
L37: 
L38: Destination Node
L39: If you want to output a series of data processing steps that you've performed to Amazon S3, you create a destination node. A destination node tells Data Wrangler where to store the data after you've processed it. After you create a destination node, you create a processing job to output the data. A processing job is an Amazon SageMaker processing job. When you're using a destination node, it runs the computational resources needed to output the data that you've transformed to Amazon S3.
L40: You can use a destination node to export some of the transformations or all of the transformations that you've made in your Data Wrangler flow.
L41: 
L42: You can use multiple destination nodes to export different transformations or sets of transformations. The following example shows two destination nodes in a single Data Wrangler flow.
L43: 
L44: cite12†Image: Example data flow showing two destination nodes in the Data Wrangler console. L45: You can use the following procedure to create destination nodes and export them to an Amazon S3 bucket.
L46: 
L47: To export your data flow, you create destination nodes and a Data Wrangler job to export the data. Creating a Data Wrangler job starts a SageMaker Processing job to export your flow. You can choose the destination nodes that you want to export after you've created them.
L48: ###### Note
L49: 
L50: You can choose Create job in the Data Wrangler flow to view the instructions to use a processing job.
L51: 
L52: Use the following procedure to create destination nodes.
L53: 
L54:   1. Choose the + next to the nodes that represent the transformations that you want to export.
L55: 
L56:   2. Choose Add destination.
L57: 
L58: cite13†Image: Example data flow showing how to add a destination in the Data Wrangler console. L59: 
L60:   3. Choose Amazon S3.
L61: 
L62: cite14†Image: Example dataflow showing how to add destination in the Data Wrangler console. L63:   4. Specify the following fields.
L64: 
L65:      * Dataset name – The name that you specify for the dataset that you're exporting.
L66: 
L67:      * File type – The format of the file that you're exporting.
L68: 
L69:      * Delimiter (CSV and Parquet files only) – The value used to separate other values.
L70: 
L71:      * Compression (CSV and Parquet files only) – The compression method used to reduce the file size. You can use the following compression methods:
L72: 
L73:        * bzip2
L74: 
L75:        * deflate
L76: 
L77:        * gzip
L78:      * (Optional) Amazon S3 location – The S3 location that you're using to output the files.
L79: 
L80:      * (Optional) Number of partitions – The number of datasets that you're writing as the output of the processing job.
L81: 
L82:      * (Optional) Partition by column – Writes all data with the same unique value from the column.
L83:      * (Optional) Inference Parameters – Selecting Generate inference artifact applies all of the transformations you've used in the Data Wrangler flow to data coming into your inference pipeline. The model in your pipeline makes predictions on the transformed data.
L84: 
L85:   5. Choose Add destination.
L86: 
L87: Use the following procedure to create a processing job.
L88: 
L89: Create a job from the Data flow page and choose the destination nodes that you want to export.
L90: ###### Note
L91: 
L92: You can choose Create job in the Data Wrangler flow to view the instructions for creating a processing job.
L93: 
L94:   1. Choose Create job. The following image shows the pane that appears after you select Create job.
L95: 
L96: cite15†Image: Example data flow create job pane in the Data Wrangler console. L97: 
L98:   2. For Job name, specify the name of the export job.
L99: 
L100:   3. Choose the destination nodes that you want to export.
L101:   4. (Optional) Specify a AWS KMS key ARN. A AWS KMS key is a cryptographic key that you can use to protect your data. For more information about AWS KMS keys, see cite16†AWS Key Management Service .
L102: 
L103:   5. (Optional) Under Trained parameters. choose Refit if you've done the following:
L104: 
L105:      * Sampled your dataset
L106: 
L107:      * Applied a transform that uses your data to create a new column in the dataset
L108: For more information about refitting the transformations you've made to an entire dataset, see cite6†Refit Transforms to The Entire Dataset and Export Them .
L109: ###### Note
L110: 
L111: For image data, Data Wrangler exports the transformations that you've made to all of the images. Refitting the transformations isn't applicable to your use case.
L112: 
L113:   6. Choose Configure job. The following image shows the Configure job page.
L114: 
L115: cite17†Image: Example data flow configure job page in the Data Wrangler console. L116: 
L117:   7. (Optional) Configure the Data Wrangler job. You can make the following configurations:
L118: 
L119:      * Job configuration
L120: 
L121:      * Spark memory configuration
L122:      * Network configuration
L123: 
L124:      * Tags
L125: 
L126:      * Parameters
L127: 
L128:      * Associate Schedules
L129: 
L130:   8. Choose Run.
L131: 
L132: Export to
L133: 
L134: 
L135: As an alternative to using a destination node, you can use the Export to option to export your Data Wrangler flow to Amazon S3 using a Jupyter notebook. You can choose any data node in your Data Wrangler flow and export it. Exporting the data node exports the transformation that the node represents and the transformations that precede it.
L136: Use the following procedure to generate a Jupyter notebook and run it to export your Data Wrangler flow to Amazon S3.
L137: 
L138:   1. Choose the + next to the node that you want to export.
L139: 
L140:   2. Choose Export to.
L141: 
L142:   3. Choose Amazon S3 (via Jupyter Notebook).
L143: 
L144:   4. Run the Jupyter notebook.
L145: 
L146: cite18†Image: Example data flow showing how to export your Data Wrangler flow in the Data Wrangler console. L147: 
L148: When you run the notebook, it exports your data flow (.flow file) in the same AWS Region as the Data Wrangler flow.
L149: The notebook provides options that you can use to configure the processing job and the data that it outputs.
L150: ###### Important
L151: 
L152: We provide you with job configurations to configure the output of your data. For the partitioning and driver memory options, we strongly recommend that you don't specify a configuration unless you already have knowledge about them.
L153: 
L154: Under Job Configurations, you can configure the following:
L155: 
L156:   * `output_content_type` – The content type of the output file. Uses `CSV` as the default format, but you can specify `Parquet`.
L157:   * `delimiter` – The character used to separate values in the dataset when writing to a CSV file.
L158: 
L159:   * `compression` – If set, compresses the output file. Uses gzip as the default compression format.
L160: 
L161:   * `num_partitions` – The number of partitions or files that Data Wrangler writes as the output.
L162: 
L163:   * `partition_by` – The names of the columns that you use to partition the output.
L164: To change the output file format from CSV to Parquet, change the value from `"CSV"` to `"Parquet"`. For the rest of the preceding fields, uncomment the lines containing the fields that you want to specify.
L165: 
L166: Under (Optional) Configure Spark Cluster Driver Memory you can configure Spark properties for the job, such as the Spark driver memory, in the `config` dictionary.
L167: The following shows the `config` dictionary.
L168: 
L169:     `
L170:     config = json.dumps({
L171:         "Classification": "spark-defaults",
L172:         "Properties": {
L173:             "spark.driver.memory": f"{driver_memory_in_mb}m",
L174:         }
L175:     })
L176:                         `
L177: To apply the configuration to the processing job, uncomment the following lines:
L178: 
L179:     `
L180:     # data_sources.append(ProcessingInput(
L181:     #     source=config_s3_uri,
L182:     #     destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/conf",
L183:     #     input_name="spark-config",
L184:     #     s3_data_type="S3Prefix",
L185:     #     s3_input_mode="File",
L186:     #     s3_data_distribution_type="FullyReplicated"
L187:     # ))
L188: 
L189:                         `
L190: 
L191: Export data
L192: If you have a transformation on a small dataset that you want to export quickly, you can use the Export data method. When you start choose Export data, Data Wrangler works synchronously to export the data that you've transformed to Amazon S3. You can't use Data Wrangler until either it finishes exporting your data or you cancel the operation.
L193: 
L194: For information on using the Export data method in your Data Wrangler flow, see the following procedure.
L195: 
L196: To use the Export data method:
L197:   1. Choose a node in your Data Wrangler flow by opening (double-clicking on) it.
L198: 
L199: cite19†Image: Example data flow showing how to export data in the Data Wrangler console. L200: 
L201:   2. Configure how you want to export the data.
L202: 
L203:   3. Choose Export data.
L204: When you export your data flow to an Amazon S3 bucket, Data Wrangler stores a copy of the flow file in the S3 bucket. It stores the flow file under the data_wrangler_flows prefix. If you use the default Amazon S3 bucket to store your flow files, it uses the following naming convention: `sagemaker-`region`-`account number``. For example, if your account number is 111122223333 and you are using Studio Classic in us-east-1, your imported datasets are stored in `sagemaker-us-east-1-111122223333`.
L205: In this example, your .flow files created in us-east-1 are stored in `s3://sagemaker-`region`-`account number`/data_wrangler_flows/`.
L206: ## Export to Pipelines
L207: 
L208: When you want to build and deploy large-scale machine learning (ML) workflows, you can use Pipelines to create workflows that manage and deploy SageMaker AI jobs. With Pipelines, you can build workflows that manage your SageMaker AI data preparation, model training, and model deployment jobs. You can use the first-party algorithms that SageMaker AI offers by using Pipelines. For more information on Pipelines, see cite20†SageMaker Pipelines .
L209: When you export one or more steps from your data flow to Pipelines, Data Wrangler creates a Jupyter notebook that you can use to define, instantiate, run, and manage a pipeline.
L210: ### Use a Jupyter Notebook to Create a Pipeline
L211: 
L212: Use the following procedure to create a Jupyter notebook to export your Data Wrangler flow to Pipelines.
L213: 
L214: Use the following procedure to generate a Jupyter notebook and run it to export your Data Wrangler flow to Pipelines.
L215: 
L216:   1. Choose the + next to the node that you want to export.
L217: 
L218:   2. Choose Export to.
L219: 
L220:   3. Choose Pipelines (via Jupyter Notebook).
L221: 
L222:   4. Run the Jupyter notebook.
L223: cite18†Image: Example data flow showing how to export your Data Wrangler flow in the Data Wrangler console. L224: 
L225: You can use the Jupyter notebook that Data Wrangler produces to define a pipeline. The pipeline includes the data processing steps that are defined by your Data Wrangler flow.
L226: You can add additional steps to your pipeline by adding steps to the `steps` list in the following code in the notebook:
L227: 
L228:     `pipeline = Pipeline(
L229:         name=pipeline_name,
L230:         parameters=[instance_type, instance_count],
L231:         steps=[step_process], #Add more steps to this list to run in your Pipeline
L232:     )`
L233: 
L234: For more information on defining pipelines, see cite21†Define SageMaker AI Pipeline .
L235: ## Export to an Inference Endpoint
L236: Use your Data Wrangler flow to process data at the time of inference by creating a SageMaker AI serial inference pipeline from your Data Wrangler flow. An inference pipeline is a series of steps that results in a trained model making predictions on new data. A serial inference pipeline within Data Wrangler transforms the raw data and provides it to the machine learning model for a prediction. You create, run, and manage the inference pipeline from a Jupyter notebook within Studio Classic.
L237: For more information about accessing the notebook, see cite22†Use a Jupyter Notebook to create an inference endpoint .
L238: Within the notebook, you can either train a machine learning model or specify one that you've already trained. You can either use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot or XGBoost to train the model using the data that you've transformed in your Data Wrangler flow.
L239: 
L240: The pipeline provides the ability to perform either batch or real-time inference. You can also add the Data Wrangler flow to SageMaker Model Registry. For more information about hosting models, see cite23†Multi-model endpoints .
L241: ###### Important
L242: 
L243: You can't export your Data Wrangler flow to an inference endpoint if it has the following transformations:
L244: 
L245:   * Join
L246: 
L247:   * Concatenate
L248: 
L249:   * Group by
L250: 
L251: If you must use the preceding transforms to prepare your data, use the following procedure.
L252: ###### To prepare your data for inference with unsupported transforms
L253: 
L254:   1. Create a Data Wrangler flow.
L255: 
L256:   2. Apply the preceding transforms that aren't supported.
L257: 
L258:   3. Export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
L259: 
L260:   4. Create a separate Data Wrangler flow.
L261: 
L262:   5. Import the data that you've exported from the preceding flow.
L263: 
L264:   6. Apply the remaining transforms.
L265: 
L266:   7. Create a serial inference pipeline using the Jupyter notebook that we provide.
L267: For information about exporting your data to an Amazon S3 bucket see cite1†Export to Amazon S3 . For information about opening the Jupyter notebook used to create the serial inference pipeline, see cite22†Use a Jupyter Notebook to create an inference endpoint .
L268: 
L269: Data Wrangler ignores transforms that remove data at the time of inference. For example, Data Wrangler ignores the cite24†Handle Missing Values transform if you use the Drop missing configuration.
L270: If you've refit transforms to your entire dataset, the transforms carry over to your inference pipeline. For example, if you used the median value to impute missing values, the median value from refitting the transform is applied to your inference requests. You can either refit the transforms from your Data Wrangler flow when you're using the Jupyter notebook or when you're exporting your data to an inference pipeline.
L271: For information about refitting transforms, see cite6†Refit Transforms to The Entire Dataset and Export Them .
L272: The serial inference pipeline supports the following data types for the input and output strings. Each data type has a set of requirements.
L273: ###### Supported datatypes
L274: 
L275:   * `text/csv` – the datatype for CSV strings
L276: 
L277:     * The string can't have a header.
L278: 
L279:     * Features used for the inference pipeline must be in the same order as features in the training dataset.
L280: 
L281:     * There must be a comma delimiter between features.
L282: 
L283:     * Records must be delimited by a newline character.
L284: The following is an example of a validly formatted CSV string that you can provide in an inference request.
L285: 
L286:     `
L287:     abc,0.0,"Doe, John",12345\ndef,1.1,"Doe, Jane",67890
L288:                     `
L289: 
L290:   * `application/json` – the datatype for JSON strings
L291: 
L292:     * The features used in the dataset for the inference pipeline must be in the same order as the features in the training dataset.
L293:     * The data must have a specific schema. You define schema as a single `instances` object that has a set of `features`. Each `features` object represents an observation.
L294: The following is an example of a validly formatted JSON string that you can provide in an inference request.
L295: 
L296:     `{
L297:         "instances": [
L298:             {
L299:                 "features": ["abc", 0.0, "Doe, John", 12345]
L300:             },
L301:             {
L302:                 "features": ["def", 1.1, "Doe, Jane", 67890]
L303:             }
L304:         ]
L305:     }
L306:                     `
L307: ### Use a Jupyter Notebook to create an inference endpoint
L308: 
L309: Use the following procedure to export your Data Wrangler flow to create an inference pipeline.
L310: 
L311: To create an inference pipeline using a Jupyter notebook, do the following.
L312: 
L313:   1. Choose the + next to the node that you want to export.
L314: 
L315:   2. Choose Export to.
L316: 
L317:   3. Choose SageMaker AI Inference Pipeline (via Jupyter Notebook).
L318: 
L319:   4. Run the Jupyter notebook.
L320: When you run the Jupyter notebook, it creates an inference flow artifact. An inference flow artifact is a Data Wrangler flow file with additional metadata used to create the serial inference pipeline. The node that you're exporting encompasses all of the transforms from the preceding nodes.
L321: ###### Important
L322: 
L323: Data Wrangler needs the inference flow artifact to run the inference pipeline. You can't use your own flow file as the artifact. You must create it by using the preceding procedure.
L324: ## Export to Python Code
L325: 
L326: To export all steps in your data flow to a Python file that you can manually integrate into any data processing workflow, use the following procedure.
L327: 
L328: Use the following procedure to generate a Jupyter notebook and run it to export your Data Wrangler flow to Python Code.
L329: 
L330:   1. Choose the + next to the node that you want to export.
L331: 
L332:   2. Choose Export to.
L333: 
L334:   3. Choose Python Code.
L335: 
L336:   4. Run the Jupyter notebook.
L337: cite18†Image: Example data flow showing how to export your Data Wrangler flow in the Data Wrangler console. L338: 
L339: You might need to configure the Python script to make it run in your pipeline. For example, if you're running a Spark environment, make sure that you are running the script from an environment that has permission to access AWS resources.
L340: ## Export to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
L341: You can use Data Wrangler to export features you've created to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store. A feature is a column in your dataset. Feature Store is a centralized store for features and their associated metadata. You can use Feature Store to create, share, and manage curated data for machine learning (ML) development. Centralized stores make your data more discoverable and reusable. For more information about Feature Store, see cite25†Amazon SageMaker Feature Store .
L342: A core concept in Feature Store is a feature group. A feature group is a collection of features, their records (observations), and associated metadata. It's similar to a table in a database.
L343: 
L344: You can use Data Wrangler to do one of the following:
L345: 
L346:   * Update an existing feature group with new records. A record is an observation in the dataset.
L347: 
L348:   * Create a new feature group from a node in your Data Wrangler flow. Data Wrangler adds the observations from your datasets as records in your feature group.
L349: If you're updating an existing feature group, your dataset's schema must match the schema of the feature group. All the records in the feature group are replaced with the observations in your dataset.
L350: 
L351: You can use either a Jupyter notebook or a destination node to update your feature group with the observations in the dataset.
L352: If your feature groups with the Iceberg table format have a custom offline store encryption key, make sure you grant the IAM that you're using for the Amazon SageMaker Processing job permissions to use it. At a minimum, you must grant it permissions to encrypt the data that you're writing to Amazon S3. To grant the permissions, give the IAM role the ability to use the cite26†GenerateDataKey .
L353: For more information about granting IAM roles permissions to use AWS KMS keys see cite27†https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html L354: Destination Node
L355: If you want to output a series of data processing steps that you've performed to a feature group, you can create a destination node. When you create and run a destination node, Data Wrangler updates a feature group with your data. You can also create a new feature group from the destination node UI. After you create a destination node, you create a processing job to output the data. A processing job is an Amazon SageMaker processing job.
L356: When you're using a destination node, it runs the computational resources needed to output the data that you've transformed to the feature group.
L357: You can use a destination node to export some of the transformations or all of the transformations that you've made in your Data Wrangler flow.
L358: 
L359: Use the following procedure to create a destination node to update a feature group with the observations from your dataset.
L360: 
L361: To update a feature group using a destination node, do the following.

L370: cite28†Image: Example data flow showing how to add destination in the Data Wrangler console. L371:   3. Choose (double-click) the feature group. Data Wrangler checks whether the schema of the feature group matches the schema of the data that you're using to update the feature group.
L372: 
L373:   4. (Optional) Select Export to offline store only for feature groups that have both an online store and an offline store. This option only updates the offline store with observations from your dataset.

L376: Use the following procedure to create a new feature group with data from your dataset.
L377: 
L378: You can store your feature group in one of the following ways:
L379: 
L380:   * Online – Low-latency, high-availability cache for a feature group that provides real-time lookup of records. The online store allows quick access to the latest value for a record in a feature group.
L381:   * Offline – Stores data for your feature group in an Amazon S3 bucket. You can store your data offline when you don't need low-latency (sub-second) reads. You can use an offline store for features used in data exploration, model training, and batch inference.
L382: 
L383:   * Both online and offline – Stores your data in both an online store and an offline store.
L384: 
L385: To create a feature group using a destination node, do the following.
L386:   1. Choose the + symbol next to the node containing the dataset that you'd like to export.
L387: 
L388:   2. Under Add destination, choose SageMaker AI Feature Store.
L389: 
L390:   3. Choose Create Feature Group.

L392:   4. In the following dialog box, if your dataset doesn't have an event time column, select Create "EventTime" column.
L393: 
L394:   5. Choose Next.
L395: 
L396:   6. Choose Copy JSON Schema. When you create a feature group, you paste the schema into the feature definitions.
L397: 
L398:   7. Choose Create.
L399:   8. For Feature group name, specify a name for your feature group.
L400: 
L401:   9. For Description (optional), specify a description to make your feature group more discoverable.
L402: 
L403:   10. To create a feature group for an online store, do the following.
L404: 
L405:     1. Select Enable storage online.
L406: 
L407:     2. For Online store encryption key, specify an AWS managed encryption key or an encryption key of your own.
L408: 
L409:   11. To create a feature group for an offline store, do the following.
L410:     1. Select Enable storage offline. Specify values for the following fields:
L411: 
L412:        * S3 bucket name – The name of the Amazon S3 bucket that stores the feature group.
L413: 
L414:        * (Optional) Dataset directory name – The Amazon S3 prefix that you're using to store the feature group.
L415: 
L416:        * IAM Role ARN – The IAM role that has access to Feature Store.
L417: 
L418:        * Table Format – Table format of your offline store. You can specify Glue or Iceberg. Glue is the default format.
L419:        * Offline store encryption key – By default, Feature Store uses an AWS Key Management Service managed key, but you can use the field to specify a key of your own.
L420: 
L421:     2. Specify values for the following fields:
L422: 
L423:        * S3 bucket name – The name of the bucket storing the feature group.
L424: 
L425:        * (Optional) Dataset directory name – The Amazon S3 prefix that you're using to store the feature group.
L426: 
L427:        * IAM Role ARN – The IAM role that has access to feature store.
L428:        * Offline store encryption key – By default, Feature Store uses an AWS managed key, but you can use the field to specify a key of your own.
L429: 
L430:   12. Choose Continue.
L431: 
L432:   13. Choose JSON.
L433: 
L434:   14. Remove the placeholder brackets in the window.
L435: 
L436:   15. Paste the JSON text from Step 6.
L437: 
L438:   16. Choose Continue.

L440:   17. For RECORD IDENTIFIER FEATURE NAME, choose the column in your dataset that has unique identifiers for each record in your dataset.
L441:   18. For EVENT TIME FEATURE NAME, choose the column with the timestamp values.

L443:   19. Choose Continue.

L446: 
L447:   21. Choose Continue.

L451:   23. Navigate back to your Data Wrangler flow and choose the refresh icon next to the Feature Group search bar.

L3: # Automatic model tuning with SageMaker AI
L4: 
L5: Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning (AMT) finds the best version of a model by running many training jobs on your dataset. Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning (AMT) is also known as hyperparameter tuning. To do this, AMT uses the algorithm and ranges of hyperparameters that you specify. It then chooses the hyperparameter values that creates a model that performs the best, as measured by a metric that you choose.
L6: For example, running a cite1†binary classification problem on a marketing dataset. Your goal is to maximize the cite2†area under the curve (AUC) metric of the algorithm by training an cite3†XGBoost algorithm with Amazon SageMaker AI model. You want to find which values for the `eta`, `alpha`, `min_child_weight`, and `max_depth` hyperparameters that will train the best model. Specify a range of values for these hyperparameters.
L7: Then, SageMaker AI hyperparameter tuning searches within the ranges to find a combination that creates a training job that creates a model with the highest AUC. To conserve resources or meet a specific model quality expectation, set up completion criteria to stop tuning after the criteria have been met.
L8: You can use SageMaker AI AMT with built-in algorithms, custom algorithms, or SageMaker AI pre-built containers for machine learning frameworks.
L9: 
L10: SageMaker AI AMT can use an Amazon EC2 Spot instance to optimize costs when running training jobs. For more information, see cite4†Managed Spot Training in Amazon SageMaker AI .
L11: 
L12: Before you start using hyperparameter tuning, you should have a well-defined machine learning problem, including the following:
L13: 
L14:   * A dataset
L15:   * An understanding of the type of algorithm that you need to train
L16: 
L17:   * A clear understanding of how you measure success
L18: 
L19: Prepare your dataset and algorithm so that they work in SageMaker AI and successfully run a training job at least once. For information about setting up and running a training job, see cite5†Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI .

L6: 
L7: To create a new hyperparameter optimization (HPO) job with Amazon SageMaker AI that tunes multiple algorithms, you must provide job settings that apply to all of the algorithms to be tested and a training definition for each of these algorithms. You must also specify the resources you want to use for the tuning job.
L8:   * The job settings to configure include warm starting, early stopping, and the tuning strategy. Warm starting and early stopping are available only when tuning a single algorithm.
L9:   * The training job definition to specify the name, algorithm source, objective metric, and the range of values, when required, to configure the set of hyperparameter values for each training job. It configures the channels for data inputs, data output locations, and any checkpoint storage locations for each training job. The definition also configures the resources to deploy for each training job, including instance types and counts, managed spot training, and stopping conditions.
L10:   * The tuning job resources: to deploy, including the maximum number of concurrent training jobs that a hyperparameter tuning job can run concurrently and the maximum number of training jobs that the hyperparameter tuning job can run.
L11: ## Get Started
L12: 
L13: You can create a new hyperparameter tuning job, clone a job, add, or edit tags to a job from the console. You can also use the search feature to find jobs by their name, creation time, or status. Alternatively, you can also hyperparameter tuning jobs with the SageMaker AI API.
L14:   * In the console: To create a new job, open the Amazon SageMaker AI console at cite2†https://console.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/†console.aws.amazon.com , choose Hyperparameter tuning jobs from the Training, menu, and then choose Create hyperparameter tuning job. Then following the configuration steps to create a training job for each algorithm that you want to use. These steps are documented in the cite3†Create a Hyperparameter Optimization Tuning Job for One or More Algorithms (Console) topic.

L17: When you start the configuration steps, note that the warm start and early stopping features are not available to use with multi-algorithm HPO. If you want to use these features, you can only tune a single algorithm at a time.
L18:   * With the API: For instructions on using the SageMaker API to create a hyperparameter tuning job, see cite4†Example: Hyperparameter Tuning Job . L6: # Give SageMaker AI Training Jobs Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC
L7: ###### Note
L8: 
L9: For training jobs, you can configure only subnets with a default tenancy VPC in which your instance runs on shared hardware. For more information on the tenancy attribute for VPCs, see cite3†Dedicated Instances .
L10: ## Configure a Training Job for Amazon VPC Access
L11: 
L12: To control access to your training jobs, run them in an Amazon VPC with private subnets that don’t have internet access.
L13: 
L14: You configure the training job to run in the VPC by specifying its subnets and security group IDs. You don’t need to specify the subnet for the container of the training job. Amazon SageMaker AI automatically pulls the training container image from Amazon ECR.
L15: When you create a training job, you can specify the subnets and security groups in your VPC using the Amazon SageMaker AI console or the API.
L16: To use the API, you specify the subnets and security group IDs in the `VpcConfig` parameter of the cite4†CreateTrainingJob operation. SageMaker AI uses the subnet and security group details to create the network interfaces and attaches them to the training containers. The network interfaces provide the training containers with a network connection within your VPC. This allows the training job to connect to resources that exist in your VPC.
L17: The following is an example of the `VpcConfig` parameter that you include in your call to the `CreateTrainingJob` operation:
L18: 
L19:     `VpcConfig: {
L20:           "Subnets": [
L21:               "subnet-0123456789abcdef0",
L22:               "subnet-0123456789abcdef1",
L23:               "subnet-0123456789abcdef2"
L24:               ],
L25:           "SecurityGroupIds": [
L26:               "sg-0123456789abcdef0"
L27:               ]
L28:             }`
L29: ## Configure Your Private VPC for SageMaker AI Training
L30: 
L31: When configuring the private VPC for your SageMaker AI training jobs, use the following guidelines. For information about setting up a VPC, see cite5†Working with VPCs and Subnets in the Amazon VPC User Guide.
L32: ###### Topics
L33: 
L34:   * cite6†Ensure That Subnets Have Enough IP Addresses L35: 
L36:   * cite7†Create an Amazon S3 VPC Endpoint L37: 
L38:   * cite8†Use a Custom Endpoint Policy to Restrict Access to S3 L39: 
L40:   * cite9†Configure Route Tables L41: 
L42:   * cite10†Configure the VPC Security Group L43: 
L44:   * cite11†Connect to Resources Outside Your VPC L45: 
L46:   * cite12†Monitor Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics L47: ### Ensure That Subnets Have Enough IP Addresses
L48: 
L49: Training instances that don't use an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) should have at least 2 private IP addresses. Training instances that use an EFA should have at least 5 private IP addresses. For more information, see cite13†Multiple IP addresses in the Amazon EC2 User Guide.
L50: Your VPC subnets should have at least two private IP addresses for each instance in a training job. For more information, see cite14†VPC and Subnet Sizing for IPv4 in the Amazon VPC User Guide.
L51: ### Create an Amazon S3 VPC Endpoint
L52: If you configure your VPC so that training containers don't have access to the internet, they can't connect to the Amazon S3 buckets that contain your training data unless you create a VPC endpoint that allows access. By creating a VPC endpoint, you allow your training containers to access the buckets where you store your data and model artifacts. We recommend that you also create a custom policy that allows only requests from your private VPC to access to your S3 buckets.
L53: For more information, see cite15†Endpoints for Amazon S3 .
L54: ###### To create an S3 VPC endpoint:
L55: 
L56:   1. Open the Amazon VPC console at cite16†https://console.aws.amazon.com/vpc/†console.aws.amazon.com .
L57: 
L58:   2. In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then choose Create Endpoint
L59: 
L60:   3. For Service Name, search for com.amazonaws.`region`.s3, where `region` is the name of the region where your VPC resides.
L61: 
L62:   4. Choose the Gateway type.
L63: 
L64:   5. For VPC, choose the VPC you want to use for this endpoint.
L65:   6. For Configure route tables, select the route tables to be used by the endpoint. The VPC service automatically adds a route to each route table you select that points any S3 traffic to the new endpoint.
L66: 
L67:   7. For Policy, choose Full Access to allow full access to the S3 service by any user or service within the VPC. Choose Custom to restrict access further. For information, see cite8†Use a Custom Endpoint Policy to Restrict Access to S3 .
L68: ### Use a Custom Endpoint Policy to Restrict Access to S3
L69: 
L70: The default endpoint policy allows full access to S3 for any user or service in your VPC. To further restrict access to S3, create a custom endpoint policy. For more information, see cite17†Using Endpoint Policies for Amazon S3 . You can also use a bucket policy to restrict access to your S3 buckets to only traffic that comes from your Amazon VPC. For information, see cite18†Using Amazon S3 Bucket Policies .
L71: #### Restrict Package Installation on the Training Container
L72: The default endpoint policy allows users to install packages from the Amazon Linux and Amazon Linux 2 repositories on the training container. If you don't want users to install packages from that repository, create a custom endpoint policy that explicitly denies access to the Amazon Linux and Amazon Linux 2 repositories. The following is an example of a policy that denies access to these repositories:
L73: 
L74:     `{
L75:         "Statement": [
L76:           {
L77:             "Sid": "AmazonLinuxAMIRepositoryAccess",
L78:             "Principal": "*",
L79:             "Action": [
L80:                 "s3:GetObject"
L81:             ],
L82:             "Effect": "Deny",
L83:             "Resource": [
L84:                 "arn:aws:s3:::packages.*.amazonaws.com/*",
L85:                 "arn:aws:s3:::repo.*.amazonaws.com/*"
L86:             ]
L87:           }
L88:         ]
L89:     }
L90: 
L91:     {
L92:         "Statement": [
L93:             { "Sid": "AmazonLinux2AMIRepositoryAccess",
L94:               "Principal": "*",
L95:               "Action": [
L96:                   "s3:GetObject"
L97:                   ],
L98:               "Effect": "Deny",
L99:               "Resource": [
L100:                   "arn:aws:s3:::amazonlinux.*.amazonaws.com/*"
L101:                   ]
L102:              }
L103:         ]
L104:     } `
L105: ### Configure Route Tables
L106: 
L107: Use default DNS settings for your endpoint route table, so that standard Amazon S3 URLs (for example, `http://s3-aws-region.amazonaws.com/amzn-s3-demo-bucket`) resolve. If you don't use default DNS settings, ensure that the URLs that you use to specify the locations of the data in your training jobs resolve by configuring the endpoint route tables. For information about VPC endpoint route tables, see cite19†Routing for Gateway Endpoints in the Amazon VPC User Guide.
L108: ### Configure the VPC Security Group
L109: 
L110: In distributed training, you must allow communication between the different containers in the same training job. To do that, configure a rule for your security group that allows inbound connections between members of the same security group. For EFA-enabled instances, ensure that both inbound and outbound connections allow all traffic from the same security group. For information, see cite20†Security Group Rules in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide.
L111: ### Connect to Resources Outside Your VPC
L112: 
L113: If you configure your VPC so that it doesn't have internet access, training jobs that use that VPC do not have access to resources outside your VPC. If your training job needs access to resources outside your VPC, provide access with one of the following options:
L114:   * If your training job needs access to an AWS service that supports interface VPC endpoints, create an endpoint to connect to that service. For a list of services that support interface endpoints, see cite21†VPC Endpoints in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide. For information about creating an interface VPC endpoint, see cite22†Interface VPC Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide.
L115:   * If your training job needs access to an AWS service that doesn't support interface VPC endpoints or to a resource outside of AWS, create a NAT gateway and configure your security groups to allow outbound connections. For information about setting up a NAT gateway for your VPC, see cite23†Scenario 2: VPC with Public and Private Subnets (NAT) in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide.
L116: ### Monitor Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics
L117: 
L118: Amazon SageMaker AI provides Amazon CloudWatch logs and metrics to monitor training jobs. CloudWatch provides CPU, GPU, memory, GPU memory, and disk metrics, and event logging. For more information about monitoring Amazon SageMaker training jobs, see cite24†Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and cite25†SageMaker AI job metrics .

L2: Managed Spot Training in Amazon SageMaker AI - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: # Managed Spot Training in Amazon SageMaker AI
L4: 
L5: Amazon SageMaker AI makes it easy to train machine learning models using managed Amazon EC2 Spot instances. Managed spot training can optimize the cost of training models up to 90% over on-demand instances. SageMaker AI manages the Spot interruptions on your behalf.
L6: Managed Spot Training uses Amazon EC2 Spot instance to run training jobs instead of on-demand instances. You can specify which training jobs use spot instances and a stopping condition that specifies how long SageMaker AI waits for a job to run using Amazon EC2 Spot instances. Metrics and logs generated during training runs are available in CloudWatch.
L7: Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning, also known as hyperparameter tuning, can use managed spot training. For more information on automatic model tuning, see cite1†Automatic model tuning with SageMaker AI .
L8: Spot instances can be interrupted, causing jobs to take longer to start or finish. You can configure your managed spot training job to use checkpoints. SageMaker AI copies checkpoint data from a local path to Amazon S3. When the job is restarted, SageMaker AI copies the data from Amazon S3 back into the local path. The training job can then resume from the last checkpoint instead of restarting. For more information about checkpointing, see cite2†Checkpoints in Amazon SageMaker AI .
L9: ###### Note
L10: 
L11: Unless your training job will complete quickly, we recommend you use checkpointing with managed spot training. SageMaker AI built-in algorithms and marketplace algorithms that do not checkpoint are currently limited to a `MaxWaitTimeInSeconds` of 3600 seconds (60 minutes).
L12: To use managed spot training, create a training job. Set `EnableManagedSpotTraining` to `True` and specify the `MaxWaitTimeInSeconds`. `MaxWaitTimeInSeconds` must be larger than `MaxRuntimeInSeconds`. For more information about creating a training job, see cite3†DescribeTrainingJob .
L13: You can calculate the savings from using managed spot training using the formula `(1 - (BillableTimeInSeconds / TrainingTimeInSeconds)) * 100`. For example, if `BillableTimeInSeconds` is 100 and `TrainingTimeInSeconds` is 500, this means that your training job ran for 500 seconds, but you were billed for only 100 seconds. Your savings is (1 - (100 / 500)) * 100 = 80%.
L14: To learn how to run training jobs on Amazon SageMaker AI spot instances and how managed spot training works and reduces the billable time, see the following example notebooks:
L15: 
L16:   * cite4†Managed Spot Training with TensorFlow†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io L17: 
L18:   * cite5†Managed Spot Training with PyTorch†github.com L19:

citeturn92view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/automatic-model-tuning-how-it-works.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 91

L2: Understand the hyperparameter tuning strategies available in Amazon SageMaker AI - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Grid search cite2†Random search cite3†Bayesian optimization cite4†Hyperband L5: # Understand the hyperparameter tuning strategies available in Amazon SageMaker AI
L6: When you build complex machine learning systems like deep learning neural networks, exploring all of the possible combinations is impractical. Hyperparameter tuning can accelerate your productivity by trying many variations of a model. It looks for the best model automatically by focusing on the most promising combinations of hyperparameter values within the ranges that you specify. To get good results, you must choose the right ranges to explore.
L7: This page provides a brief explanation of the different hyperparameter tuning strategies that you can use with Amazon SageMaker AI.
L8: Use the cite5†API reference guide to understand how to interact with hyperparameter tuning. You can use the tuning strategies described on this page with the cite6†HyperParameterTuningJobConfig and cite7†HyperbandStrategyConfig APIs.
L9: ###### Note
L10: 
L11: Because the algorithm itself is stochastic, the hyperparameter tuning model may fail to converge on the best answer. This can occur even if the best possible combination of values is within the ranges that you choose.
L12: ## Grid search
L13: When using grid search, hyperparameter tuning chooses combinations of values from the range of categorical values that you specify when you create the job. Only categorical parameters are supported when using the grid search strategy. You do not need to specify the `MaxNumberOfTrainingJobs`. The number of training jobs created by the tuning job is automatically calculated to be the total number of distinct categorical combinations possible.
L14: If specified, the value of `MaxNumberOfTrainingJobs` should equal the total number of distinct categorical combinations possible.
L15: ## Random search
L16: 
L17: When using random search, hyperparameter tuning chooses a random combination of hyperparameter values in the ranges that you specify for each training job it launches. The choice of hyperparameter values doesn't depend on the results of previous training jobs. As a result, you can run the maximum number of concurrent training jobs without changing the performance of the tuning.
L18: For an example notebook that uses random search, see the cite8†Random search and hyperparameter scaling with SageMaker XGBoost and Automatic Model Tuning†github.com notebook.
L19: ## Bayesian optimization
L20: Bayesian optimization treats hyperparameter tuning like a cite9†regression problem. Given a set of input features (the hyperparameters), hyperparameter tuning optimizes a model for the metric that you choose. To solve a regression problem, hyperparameter tuning makes guesses about which hyperparameter combinations are likely to get the best results. It then runs training jobs to test these values.
L21: After testing a set of hyperparameter values, hyperparameter tuning uses regression to choose the next set of hyperparameter values to test.
L22: Hyperparameter tuning uses an Amazon SageMaker AI implementation of Bayesian optimization.
L23: When choosing the best hyperparameters for the next training job, hyperparameter tuning considers everything that it knows about this problem so far. Sometimes it chooses a combination of hyperparameter values close to the combination that resulted in the best previous training job to incrementally improve performance. This allows hyperparameter tuning to use the best known results. Other times, it chooses a set of hyperparameter values far removed from those it has tried.
L24: This allows it to explore the range of hyperparameter values to try to find new areas that are not yet well understood. The explore/exploit trade-off is common in many machine learning problems.
L25: For more information about Bayesian optimization, see the following:
L26: ###### Basic Topics on Bayesian Optimization
L27: 
L28:   * cite10†A Tutorial on Bayesian Optimization of Expensive Cost Functions, with Application to Active User Modeling and Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning†arxiv.org L29: 
L30:   * cite11†Practical Bayesian Optimization of Machine Learning Algorithms†arxiv.org L31: 
L32:   * cite12†Taking the Human Out of the Loop: A Review of Bayesian Optimization†ieeexplore.ieee.org L33: ###### Speeding up Bayesian Optimization
L34: 
L35:   * cite13†Google Vizier: A Service for Black-Box Optimization†dl.acm.org L36: 
L37:   * cite14†Learning Curve Prediction with Bayesian Neural Networks†openreview.net L38: 
L39:   * cite15†Speeding up automatic hyperparameter optimization of deep neural networks by extrapolation of learning curves†dl.acm.org L40: ###### Advanced Modeling and Transfer Learning
L41: 
L42:   * cite16†Scalable Hyperparameter Transfer Learning†papers.nips.cc L43: 
L44:   * cite17†Bayesian Optimization with Tree-structured Dependencies†proceedings.mlr.press L45: 
L46:   * cite18†Bayesian Optimization with Robust Bayesian Neural Networks†papers.nips.cc L47: 
L48:   * cite19†Scalable Bayesian Optimization Using Deep Neural Networks†proceedings.mlr.press L49: 
L50:   * cite20†Input Warping for Bayesian Optimization of Non-stationary Functions†arxiv.org L51: ## Hyperband
L52: 
L53: Hyperband is a multi-fidelity based tuning strategy that dynamically reallocates resources. Hyperband uses both intermediate and final results of training jobs to re-allocate epochs to well-utilized hyperparameter configurations and automatically stops those that underperform. It also seamlessly scales to using many parallel training jobs. These features can significantly speed up hyperparameter tuning over random search and Bayesian optimization strategies.
L54: Hyperband should only be used to tune iterative algorithms that publish results at different resource levels. For example, Hyperband can be used to tune a neural network for image classification which publishes accuracy metrics after every epoch.
L55: 
L56: For more information about Hyperband, see the following links:
L57: 
L58:   * cite21†Hyperband: A Novel Bandit-Based Approach to Hyperparameter Optimization†arxiv.org L59: 
L60:   * cite22†Massively Parallel Hyperparameter Tuning†liamcli.com L61:   * cite23†BOHB: Robust and Efficient Hyperparameter Optimization at Scale†proceedings.mlr.press L62: 
L63:   * cite24†Model-based Asynchronous Hyperparameter and Neural Architecture Search†openreview.net L64: ### Hyperband with early stopping
L65: 
L66: Training jobs can be stopped early when they are unlikely to improve the objective metric of the hyperparameter tuning job. This can help reduce compute time and avoid overfitting your model. Hyperband uses an advanced internal mechanism to apply early stopping. The parameter `TrainingJobEarlyStoppingType` in the `HyperParameterTuningJobConfig` API must be set to `OFF` when using the Hyperband internal early stopping feature.
L67: ###### Note
L68: 
L69: Hyperparameter tuning might not improve your model. It is an advanced tool for building machine solutions. As such, it should be considered part of the scientific development process.
