citeturn93view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/notebook-interface-endpoint.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 169
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Connect to a Notebook Instance Through a VPC Interface Endpoint - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Connect Your Private Network to Your VPC cite2†Create a VPC Endpoint Policy for SageMaker AI Notebook Instances cite3†Restrict Access to Connections from Within Your VPC L5: # Connect to a Notebook Instance Through a VPC Interface Endpoint
L6: 
L7: You can connect to your notebook instance from your VPC through an cite4†interface endpoint in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) instead of connecting over the public internet. When you use a VPC interface endpoint, communication between your VPC and the notebook instance is conducted entirely and securely within the AWS network.
L8: SageMaker notebook instances support cite5†Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) interface endpoints that are powered by cite6†AWS PrivateLink . Each VPC endpoint is represented by one or more cite7†Elastic Network Interfaces with private IP addresses in your VPC subnets.
L9: ###### Note
L10: 
L11: Before you create an interface VPC endpoint to connect to a notebook instance, create an interface VPC endpoint to connect to the SageMaker API. That way, when users call cite8†
L12: CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl to get the URL to connect to the notebook instance, that call also goes through the interface VPC endpoint. For information, see cite9†Connect to SageMaker AI Within your VPC .
L13: You can create an interface endpoint to connect to your notebook instance with either the AWS Management Console or AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) commands. For instructions, see cite10†Creating an Interface Endpoint . Make sure that you create an interface endpoint for all of the subnets in your VPC from which you want to connect to the notebook instance.
L14: When you create the interface endpoint, specify aws.sagemaker.`Region`.notebook as the service name. After you create a VPC endpoint, enable private DNS for your VPC endpoint. Anyone using the SageMaker API, the AWS CLI, or the console to connect to the notebook instance from within the VPC connects to the notebook instance through the VPC endpoint instead of the public internet.
L15: SageMaker notebook instances support VPC endpoints in all AWS Regions where both cite11†Amazon VPC and cite12†SageMaker AI are available.
L16: ###### Topics
L17: 
L18:   * cite1†Connect Your Private Network to Your VPC L19: 
L20:   * cite2†Create a VPC Endpoint Policy for SageMaker AI Notebook Instances L21: 
L22:   * cite3†Restrict Access to Connections from Within Your VPC L23: ## Connect Your Private Network to Your VPC
L24: To connect to your notebook instance through your VPC, you either have to connect from an instance that is inside the VPC, or connect your private network to your VPC by using an AWS Virtual Private Network (Site-to-Site VPN) or Direct Connect. For information about Site-to-Site VPN, see cite13†VPN Connections in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide. For information about AWS Direct Connect, see cite14†Creating a Connection in the AWS Direct Connect User Guide.
L25: ## Create a VPC Endpoint Policy for SageMaker AI Notebook Instances
L26: 
L27: You can create a policy for Amazon VPC endpoints for SageMaker notebook instances to specify the following:
L28: 
L29:   * The principal that can perform actions.
L30: 
L31:   * The actions that can be performed.
L32: 
L33:   * The resources on which actions can be performed.
L34: 
L35: For more information, see cite15†Controlling Access to Services with VPC Endpoints in the Amazon VPC User Guide.
L36: The following example of a VPC endpoint policy specifies that all users that have access to the endpoint are allowed to access the notebook instance named `myNotebookInstance`.
L37: 
L38:     `{
L39:       "Statement": [
L40:           {
L41:               "Action": "sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl",
L42:               "Effect": "Allow",
L43:               "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:123456789012:notebook-instance/myNotebookInstance",
L44:               "Principal": "*"
L45:           }
L46:       ]
L47:     }`
L48: Access to other notebook instances is denied.
L49: ## Restrict Access to Connections from Within Your VPC
L50: 
L51: Even if you set up an interface endpoint in your VPC, individuals outside the VPC can connect to the notebook instance over the internet.
L52: ###### Important
L53: 
L54: If you apply an IAM policy similar to one of the following, users can't access the specified SageMaker APIs or the notebook instance through the console.
L55: 
L56: To restrict access to only connections made from within your VPC, create an AWS Identity and Access Management policy that restricts access to only calls that come from within your VPC. Then add that policy to every AWS Identity and Access Management user, group, or role used to access the notebook instance.
L57: ###### Note
L58: 
L59: This policy allows connections only to callers within a subnet where you created an interface endpoint.
L60: 
L61: JSON
L62: 
L63: 
L64:     ``{
L65:         "Id": "notebook-example-1",
L66:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L67:         "Statement": [
L68:             {
L69:                 "Sid": "EnableNotebookAccess",
L70:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L71:                 "Action": [
L72:                     "sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl",
L73:                     "sagemaker:DescribeNotebookInstance"
L74:                 ],
L75:                 "Resource": "*",
L76:                 "Condition": {
L77:                     "StringEquals": {
L78:                         "aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-111bbaaa"
L79:                     }
L80:                 }
L81:             }
L82:         ]
L83:     }`
L84:     `
L85: If you want to restrict access to the notebook instance to only connections made using the interface endpoint, use the `aws:SourceVpce` condition key instead of `aws:SourceVpc:`
L86: 
L87: JSON
L88: 
L89: 
L90:     ``{
L91:         "Id": "notebook-example-1",
L92:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L93:         "Statement": [
L94:             {
L95:                 "Sid": "EnableNotebookAccess",
L96:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L97:                 "Action": [
L98:                     "sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl",
L99:                     "sagemaker:DescribeNotebookInstance"
L100:                 ],
L101:                 "Resource": "*",
L102:                 "Condition": {
L103:                     "ForAnyValue:StringEquals": {
L104:                         "aws:sourceVpce": [
L105:                             "vpce-111bbccc",
L106:                             "vpce-111bbddd"
L107:                         ]
L108:                     }
L109:                 }
L110:             }
L111:         ]
L112:     }`
L113:     `
L114: Both of these policy examples assume that you have also created an interface endpoint for the SageMaker API. For more information, see cite9†Connect to SageMaker AI Within your VPC . Object Detection - MXNet - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/object-detection.html)
citeturn94view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/object-detection.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 138
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Object Detection - MXNet - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the Object Detection Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Object Detection Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # Object Detection - MXNet
L6: The Amazon SageMaker AI Object Detection - MXNet algorithm detects and classifies objects in images using a single deep neural network. It is a supervised learning algorithm that takes images as input and identifies all instances of objects within the image scene. The object is categorized into one of the classes in a specified collection with a confidence score that it belongs to the class. Its location and scale in the image are indicated by a rectangular bounding box.
L7: It uses the cite4†Single Shot multibox Detector (SSD)†arxiv.org framework and supports two base networks: cite5†VGG†arxiv.org and cite6†ResNet†arxiv.org . The network can be trained from scratch, or trained with models that have been pre-trained on the cite7†ImageNet†www.image-net.org dataset.
L8: ###### Topics
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the Object Detection Algorithm L11: 
L12:   * cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Object Detection Algorithm L13: 
L14:   * cite3†Object Detection Sample Notebooks L15: 
L16:   * cite8†How Object Detection Works L17: 
L18:   * cite9†Object Detection Hyperparameters L19: 
L20:   * cite10†Tune an Object Detection Model L21: 
L22:   * cite11†Object Detection Request and Response Formats L23: ## Input/Output Interface for the Object Detection Algorithm
L24: The SageMaker AI Object Detection algorithm supports both RecordIO (`application/x-recordio`) and image (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image`) content types for training in file mode and supports RecordIO (`application/x-recordio`) for training in pipe mode. However you can also train in pipe mode using the image files (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, and `application/x-image`), without creating RecordIO files, by using the augmented manifest format.
L25: The recommended input format for the Amazon SageMaker AI object detection algorithms is cite12†Apache MXNet RecordIO†mxnet.apache.org . However, you can also use raw images in .jpg or .png format. The algorithm supports only `application/x-image` for inference.
L26: ###### Note
L27: 
L28: To maintain better interoperability with existing deep learning frameworks, this differs from the protobuf data formats commonly used by other Amazon SageMaker AI algorithms.
L29: 
L30: See the cite3†Object Detection Sample Notebooks for more details on data formats.
L31: ### Train with the RecordIO Format
L32: If you use the RecordIO format for training, specify both train and validation channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of the cite13†`CreateTrainingJob` request. Specify one RecordIO (.rec) file in the train channel and one RecordIO file in the validation channel. Set the content type for both channels to `application/x-recordio`. An example of how to generate RecordIO file can be found in the object detection sample notebook.
L33: You can also use tools from the cite14†MXNet's GluonCV†gluon-cv.mxnet.io to generate RecordIO files for popular datasets like the cite15†PASCAL Visual Object Classes†host.robots.ox.ac.uk and cite16†Common Objects in Context (COCO)†cocodataset.org .
L34: ### Train with the Image Format
L35: If you use the image format for training, specify `train`, `validation`, `train_annotation`, and `validation_annotation` channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of cite13†`CreateTrainingJob` request. Specify the individual image data (.jpg or .png) files for the train and validation channels. For annotation data, you can use the JSON format. Specify the corresponding .json files in the `train_annotation` and `validation_annotation` channels.
L36: Set the content type for all four channels to `image/png` or `image/jpeg` based on the image type. You can also use the content type `application/x-image` when your dataset contains both .jpg and .png images. The following is an example of a .json file.
L37: 
L38:     `{
L39:        "file": "your_image_directory/sample_image1.jpg",
L40:        "image_size": [
L41:           {
L42:              "width": 500,
L43:              "height": 400,
L44:              "depth": 3
L45:           }
L46:        ],
L47:        "annotations": [
L48:           {
L49:              "class_id": 0,
L50:              "left": 111,
L51:              "top": 134,
L52:              "width": 61,
L53:              "height": 128
L54:           },
L55:           {
L56:              "class_id": 0,
L57:              "left": 161,
L58:              "top": 250,
L59:              "width": 79,
L60:              "height": 143
L61:           },
L62:           {
L63:              "class_id": 1,
L64:              "left": 101,
L65:              "top": 185,
L66:              "width": 42,
L67:              "height": 130
L68:           }
L69:        ],
L70:        "categories": [
L71:           {
L72:              "class_id": 0,
L73:              "name": "dog"
L74:           },
L75:           {
L76:              "class_id": 1,
L77:              "name": "cat"
L78:           }
L79:        ]
L80:     }`
L81: Each image needs a .json file for annotation, and the .json file should have the same name as the corresponding image. The name of above .json file should be "sample_image1.json". There are four properties in the annotation .json file. The property "file" specifies the relative path of the image file.
L82: For example, if your training images and corresponding .json files are stored in s3://`your_bucket`/train/sample_image and s3://`your_bucket`/train_annotation, specify the path for your train and train_annotation channels as s3://`your_bucket`/train and s3://`your_bucket`/train_annotation, respectively.
L83: In the .json file, the relative path for an image named sample_image1.jpg should be sample_image/sample_image1.jpg. The `"image_size"` property specifies the overall image dimensions. The SageMaker AI object detection algorithm currently only supports 3-channel images. The `"annotations"` property specifies the categories and bounding boxes for objects within the image. Each object is annotated by a `"class_id"` index and by four bounding box coordinates (`"left"`, `"top"`, `"width"`, `"height"`).
L84: The `"left"` (x-coordinate) and `"top"` (y-coordinate) values represent the upper-left corner of the bounding box. The `"width"` (x-coordinate) and `"height"` (y-coordinate) values represent the dimensions of the bounding box. The origin (0, 0) is the upper-left corner of the entire image. If you have multiple objects within one image, all the annotations should be included in a single .json file. The `"categories"` property stores the mapping between the class index and class name.
L85: The class indices should be numbered successively and the numbering should start with 0. The `"categories"` property is optional for the annotation .json file
L86: ### Train with Augmented Manifest Image Format
L87: The augmented manifest format enables you to do training in pipe mode using image files without needing to create RecordIO files. You need to specify both train and validation channels as values for the `InputDataConfig` parameter of the cite13†`CreateTrainingJob` request. While using the format, an S3 manifest file needs to be generated that contains the list of images and their corresponding annotations.
L88: The manifest file format should be in cite17†JSON Lines†jsonlines.org format in which each line represents one sample. The images are specified using the `'source-ref'` tag that points to the S3 location of the image. The annotations are provided under the `"AttributeNames"` parameter value as specified in the cite13†`CreateTrainingJob` request. It can also contain additional metadata under the `metadata` tag, but these are ignored by the algorithm.
L89: In the following example, the `"AttributeNames` are contained in the list `["source-ref", "bounding-box"]`:
L90: 
L91:     `{"source-ref": "s3://your_bucket/image1.jpg", "bounding-box":{"image_size":[{ "width": 500, "height": 400, "depth":3}], "annotations":[{"class_id": 0, "left": 111, "top": 134, "width": 61, "height": 128}, {"class_id": 5, "left": 161, "top": 250, "width": 80, "height": 50}]}, "bounding-box-metadata":{"class-map":{"0": "dog", "5": "horse"}, "type": "groundtruth/object-detection"}}
L92:     {"source-ref": "s3://your_bucket/image2.jpg", "bounding-box":{"image_size":[{ "width": 400, "height": 300, "depth":3}], "annotations":[{"class_id": 1, "left": 100, "top": 120, "width": 43, "height": 78}]}, "bounding-box-metadata":{"class-map":{"1": "cat"}, "type": "groundtruth/object-detection"}}`
L93: The order of `"AttributeNames"` in the input files matters when training the Object Detection algorithm. It accepts piped data in a specific order, with `image` first, followed by `annotations`. So the "AttributeNames" in this example are provided with `"source-ref"` first, followed by `"bounding-box"`. When using Object Detection with Augmented Manifest, the value of parameter `RecordWrapperType` must be set as `"RecordIO"`.
L94: For more information on augmented manifest files, see cite18†Augmented Manifest Files for Training Jobs .
L95: ### Incremental Training
L96: 
L97: You can also seed the training of a new model with the artifacts from a model that you trained previously with SageMaker AI. Incremental training saves training time when you want to train a new model with the same or similar data. SageMaker AI object detection models can be seeded only with another built-in object detection model trained in SageMaker AI.
L98: To use a pretrained model, in the cite13†`CreateTrainingJob` request, specify the `ChannelName` as "model" in the `InputDataConfig` parameter. Set the `ContentType` for the model channel to `application/x-sagemaker-model`. The input hyperparameters of both the new model and the pretrained model that you upload to the model channel must have the same settings for the `base_network` and `num_classes` input parameters. These parameters define the network architecture.
L99: For the pretrained model file, use the compressed model artifacts (in .tar.gz format) output by SageMaker AI. You can use either RecordIO or image formats for input data.
L100: For more information on incremental training and for instructions on how to use it, see cite19†Use Incremental Training in Amazon SageMaker AI .
L101: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Object Detection Algorithm
L102: 
L103: The object detection algorithm supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 GPU instance families. We recommend using GPU instances with more memory for training with large batch sizes. You can run the object detection algorithm on multi-GPU and mult-machine settings for distributed training.
L104: 
L105: You can use both CPU (such as C5 and M5) and GPU (such as P3 and G4dn) instances for inference.
L106: ## Object Detection Sample Notebooks
L107: 
L108: For a sample notebook that shows how to use the SageMaker AI Object Detection algorithm to train and host a model on the
L109: cite20†Caltech Birds (CUB 200 2011)†www.vision.caltech.edu dataset using the Single Shot multibox Detector algorithm, see cite21†Amazon SageMaker AI Object Detection for Bird Species†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io . For instructions how to create and access Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite22†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances .
L110: Once you have created a notebook instance and opened it, select the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI samples. The object detection example notebook using the Object Detection algorithm is located in the Introduction to Amazon Algorithms section. To open a notebook, click on its Use tab and select Create copy.
L111: For more information about the Amazon SageMaker AI Object Detection algorithm, see the following blog posts:
L112: 
L113:   * cite23†Training the Amazon SageMaker AI object detection model and running it on AWS IoT Greengrass – Part 1 of 3: Preparing training data†aws.amazon.com L114: 
L115:   * cite24†Training the Amazon SageMaker AI object detection model and running it on AWS IoT Greengrass – Part 2 of 3: Training a custom object detection model†aws.amazon.com L116:   * cite25†Training the Amazon SageMaker AI object detection model and running it on AWS IoT Greengrass – Part 3 of 3: Deploying to the edge†aws.amazon.com L117:

Linear learner hyperparameters - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/ll_hyperparameters.html)
citeturn95view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/ll_hyperparameters.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 90
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Linear learner hyperparameters - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: # Linear learner hyperparameters
L4: The following table contains the hyperparameters for the linear learner algorithm. These are parameters that are set by users to facilitate the estimation of model parameters from data. The required hyperparameters that must be set are listed first, in alphabetical order. The optional hyperparameters that can be set are listed next, also in alphabetical order. When a hyperparameter is set to `auto`, Amazon SageMaker AI will automatically calculate and set the value of that hyperparameter.
L5: Parameter Name  | Description
L6: --- | ---
L7: `num_classes`  | The number of classes for the response variable. The algorithm assumes that classes are labeled `0`, ..., `num_classes - 1`. Required when `predictor_type` is `multiclass_classifier`. Otherwise, the algorithm ignores it. Valid values: Integers from 3 to 1,000,000
L8: `predictor_type`  | Specifies the type of target variable as a binary classification, multiclass classification, or regression. Required Valid values: `binary_classifier`, `multiclass_classifier`, or `regressor`
L9: `accuracy_top_k`  | When computing the top-k accuracy metric for multiclass classification, the value of k. If the model assigns one of the top-k scores to the true label, an example is scored as correct. Optional Valid values: Positive integers Default value: 3
L10: `balance_multiclass_weights`  | Specifies whether to use class weights, which give each class equal importance in the loss function. Used only when the `predictor_type` is `multiclass_classifier`. Optional Valid values: `true`, `false` Default value: `false`
L11: `beta_1`  | The exponential decay rate for first-moment estimates. Applies only when the `optimizer` value is `adam`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or floating-point value between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L12: `beta_2`  | The exponential decay rate for second-moment estimates. Applies only when the `optimizer` value is `adam`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L13: `bias_lr_mult`  | Allows a different learning rate for the bias term. The actual learning rate for the bias is `learning_rate` * `bias_lr_mult`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default value: `auto`
L14: `bias_wd_mult`  | Allows different regularization for the bias term. The actual L2 regularization weight for the bias is `wd` * `bias_wd_mult`. By default, there is no regularization on the bias term. Optional Valid values: `auto` or non-negative floating-point integer Default value: `auto`
L15: `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria`  | When `predictor_type` is set to `binary_classifier`, the model evaluation criteria for the validation dataset (or for the training dataset if you don't provide a validation dataset). Criteria include:
L16:   * `accuracy`—The model with the highest accuracy.
L17:   * `f_beta`—The model with the highest F1 score. The default is F1.
L18:   * `precision_at_target_recall`—The model with the highest precision at a given recall target.
L19:   * `recall_at_target_precision`—The model with the highest recall at a given precision target.
L20:   * `loss_function`—The model with the lowest value of the loss function used in training.
L21: Optional Valid values: `accuracy`, `f_beta`, `precision_at_target_recall`, `recall_at_target_precision`, or `loss_function` Default value: `accuracy`
L22: `early_stopping_patience`  | If no improvement is made in the relevant metric, the number of epochs to wait before ending training. If you have provided a value for `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria`. the metric is that value. Otherwise, the metric is the same as the value specified for the `loss` hyperparameter. The metric is evaluated on the validation data.
L23: If you haven't provided validation data, the metric is always the same as the value specified for the `loss` hyperparameter and is evaluated on the training data. To disable early stopping, set `early_stopping_patience` to a value greater than the value specified for `epochs`.Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 3
L24: `early_stopping_tolerance`  | The relative tolerance to measure an improvement in loss. If the ratio of the improvement in loss divided by the previous best loss is smaller than this value, early stopping considers the improvement to be zero. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.001
L25: `epochs`  | The maximum number of passes over the training data. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 15
L26: `f_beta`  | The value of beta to use when calculating F score metrics for binary or multiclass classification. Also used if the value specified for `binary_classifier_model_selection_criteria` is `f_beta`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integers Default value: 1.0
L27: `feature_dim`  | The number of features in the input data. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default values: `auto`
L28: `huber_delta`  | The parameter for Huber loss. During training and metric evaluation, compute L2 loss for errors smaller than delta and L1 loss for errors larger than delta. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 1.0
L29: `init_bias`  | Initial weight for the bias term. Optional Valid values: Floating-point integer Default value: 0
L30: `init_method`  | Sets the initial distribution function used for model weights. Functions include:
L31:   * `uniform`—Uniformly distributed between (-scale, +scale)
L32:   * `normal`—Normal distribution, with mean 0 and sigma
L33: Optional Valid values: `uniform` or `normal` Default value: `uniform`
L34: `init_scale`  | Scales an initial uniform distribution for model weights. Applies only when the `init_method` hyperparameter is set to `uniform`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.07
L35: `init_sigma`  | The initial standard deviation for the normal distribution. Applies only when the `init_method` hyperparameter is set to `normal`. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.01
L36: `l1`  | The L1 regularization parameter. If you don't want to use L1 regularization, set the value to 0. Optional Valid values: `auto` or non-negative float Default value: `auto`
L37: `learning_rate`  | The step size used by the optimizer for parameter updates. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default value: `auto`, whose value depends on the optimizer chosen.
L38: `loss`  | Specifies the loss function. The available loss functions and their default values depend on the value of `predictor_type`:
L39:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `regressor`, the available options are `auto`, `squared_loss`, `absolute_loss`, `eps_insensitive_squared_loss`, `eps_insensitive_absolute_loss`, `quantile_loss`, and `huber_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `squared_loss`.
L40:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `binary_classifier`, the available options are `auto`,`logistic`, and `hinge_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `logistic`.
L41:   * If the `predictor_type` is set to `multiclass_classifier`, the available options are `auto` and `softmax_loss`. The default value for `auto` is `softmax_loss`.
L42: Valid values: `auto`, `logistic`, `squared_loss`, `absolute_loss`, `hinge_loss`, `eps_insensitive_squared_loss`, `eps_insensitive_absolute_loss`, `quantile_loss`, or `huber_loss` Optional Default value: `auto`
L43: `loss_insensitivity`  | The parameter for the epsilon-insensitive loss type. During training and metric evaluation, any error smaller than this value is considered to be zero. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 0.01
L44: `lr_scheduler_factor`  | For every `lr_scheduler_step` hyperparameter, the learning rate decreases by this quantity. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer between 0 and 1 Default value: `auto`
L45: `lr_scheduler_minimum_lr`  | The learning rate never decreases to a value lower than the value set for `lr_scheduler_minimum_lr`. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive floating-point integer Default values: `auto`
L46: `lr_scheduler_step`  | The number of steps between decreases of the learning rate. Applies only when the `use_lr_scheduler` hyperparameter is set to `true`. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default value: `auto`
L47: `margin`  | The margin for the `hinge_loss` function. Optional Valid values: Positive floating-point integer Default value: 1.0
L48: `mini_batch_size`  | The number of observations per mini-batch for the data iterator. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 1000
L49: `momentum`  | The momentum of the `sgd` optimizer. Optional Valid values: `auto` or a floating-point integer between 0 and 1.0 Default value: `auto`
L50: `normalize_data`  | Normalizes the feature data before training. Data normalization shifts the data for each feature to have a mean of zero and scales it to have unit standard deviation. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `true`
L51: `normalize_label`  | Normalizes the label. Label normalization shifts the label to have a mean of zero and scales it to have unit standard deviation. The `auto` default value normalizes the label for regression problems but does not for classification problems. If you set the `normalize_label` hyperparameter to `true` for classification problems, the algorithm ignores it. Optional Valid values: `auto`, `true`, or `false` Default value: `auto`
L52: `num_calibration_samples`  | The number of observations from the validation dataset to use for model calibration (when finding the best threshold). Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default value: `auto`
L53: `num_models`  | The number of models to train in parallel. For the default, `auto`, the algorithm decides the number of parallel models to train. One model is trained according to the given training parameter (regularization, optimizer, loss), and the rest by close parameters. Optional Valid values: `auto` or positive integer Default values: `auto`
L54: `num_point_for_scaler`  | The number of data points to use for calculating normalization or unbiasing of terms. Optional Valid values: Positive integer Default value: 10,000

L6: 
L7: You can connect directly to the SageMaker API or to Amazon SageMaker Runtime through an cite6†interface endpoint in your virtual private cloud (VPC) instead of connecting over the internet. When you use a VPC interface endpoint, communication between your VPC and the SageMaker AI API or Runtime is conducted entirely and securely within an AWS network.
L8: ## Connect to SageMaker AI through a VPC interface endpoint
L9: The SageMaker API and SageMaker AI Runtime support cite7†Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) interface endpoints that are powered by cite8†AWS PrivateLink†aws.amazon.com . Each VPC endpoint is represented by one or more cite9†Elastic Network Interfaces with private IP addresses in your VPC subnets. For example, an application inside your VPC uses AWS PrivateLink to communicate with SageMaker AI Runtime. SageMaker AI Runtime in turn communicates with the SageMaker AI endpoint.
L10: Using AWS PrivateLink allows you to invoke your SageMaker AI endpoint from within your VPC, as shown in the following diagram.
L11: cite10†Image: A VPC uses AWS PrivateLink to communicate with a SageMaker AI endpoint. L12: 
L13: The VPC interface endpoint connects your VPC directly to the SageMaker API or SageMaker AI Runtime using AWS PrivateLink without using an internet gateway, NAT device, VPN connection, or Direct Connect connection. The instances in your VPC do not need to connect to the public internet in order to communicate with the SageMaker API or SageMaker AI Runtime.
L14: You can create an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint to connect to SageMaker AI or to SageMaker AI Runtime using either the AWS Management Console or AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). For instructions, see cite11†Access an AWS service using an interface VPC endpoint .
L15: If you haven't enabled a private Domain Name System (DNS) hostname for your VPC endpoint, after you have created a VPC endpoint, specify the internet endpoint URL to the SageMaker API or SageMaker AI Runtime. Example code using AWS CLI commands to specify the `endpoint-url` parameter follows.
L16: 
L17:     `aws sagemaker list-notebook-instances --endpoint-url `VPC_Endpoint_ID`.api.sagemaker.`Region`.vpce.amazonaws.com
L18:     aws sagemaker list-training-jobs --endpoint-url `VPC_Endpoint_ID.api`.sagemaker.`Region`.vpce.amazonaws.com
L19: 
L20:     aws sagemaker-runtime invoke-endpoint --endpoint-url https://`VPC_Endpoint_ID`.runtime.sagemaker.`Region`.vpce.amazonaws.com  \
L21:         --endpoint-name `Endpoint_Name` \
L22:         --body "`Endpoint_Body`" \
L23:         --content-type "`Content_Type`" \
L24:                 `Output_File``
L25: If you enable private DNS hostnames for your VPC endpoint, you don't need to specify the endpoint URL because the default hostname (https://api.sagemaker.`Region`.amazon.com) resolves to your VPC endpoint. Similarly, the default SageMaker AI Runtime DNS hostname (https://runtime.sagemaker.`Region`.amazonaws.com) also resolves to your VPC endpoint.
L26: The SageMaker API and SageMaker AI Runtime support VPC endpoints in all AWS Regions where both cite12†Amazon VPC and cite13†SageMaker AI ares available. SageMaker AI supports making calls to all of its cite14†`Operations` inside your VPC. If you use the `AuthorizedUrl` from the cite15†
L27:  CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl command, your traffic will go over the public internet. You can't only use a VPC endpoint to access the presigned URL, the request must go through the internet gateway.
L28: By default, your users can share the presigned URL to people outside of your corporate network. For additional security, you must add IAM permissions to restrict the URL only be usable within your network. For information about IAM permissions, see cite16†How AWS PrivateLink works with IAM .
L29: ###### Note
L30: 
L31: When setting up a VPC interface endpoint for the SageMaker AI Runtime service (https://runtime.sagemaker.``Region``.amazonaws.com), you must ensure that the VPC interface endpoint is activated in the Availability Zone of your client in order for private DNS resolution to work. Otherwise, you may see DNS failures when attempting to resolve the URL.
L32: To learn more about AWS PrivateLink, see the cite17†AWS PrivateLink documentation . Refer to cite18†AWS PrivateLink Pricing†aws.amazon.com for the price of VPC endpoints. To learn more about VPC and endpoints, see cite19†Amazon VPC†aws.amazon.com . For information about how to use identity-based AWS Identity and Access Management policies to restrict access to the SageMaker API and SageMaker AI Runtime, see cite20†Control access to the SageMaker AI API by using identity-based policies .
L33: ## Using SageMaker training and hosting with resources inside your VPC
L34: SageMaker AI uses your execution role to download and upload information from an Amazon S3 bucket and Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), in isolation from your training or inference container. If you have resources that are located inside your VPC, you can still grant SageMaker AI access to those resources. The following sections explain how to make your resources available to SageMaker AI with or without network isolation.
L35: ### Without network isolation enabled
L36: 
L37: If you haven't set network isolation on your training job or model, SageMaker AI can access resources using either of the following methods.
L38:   * SageMaker training and deployed inference containers can access the internet by default. SageMaker AI containers are able to access external services and resources on the public internet as part of your training and inference workloads. SageMaker AI containers are not able to access resources inside your VPC without a VPC configuration, as shown in the following illustration.
L39: 
L40: cite21†Image: SageMaker AI cannot access resources inside your VPC without a VPC configuration. L41:   * Use a VPC configuration to communicate with resources inside your VPC through an elastic network interface (ENI). The communication between the container and the resources in your VPC takes place securely within your VPC network, as shown in the following illustration. In this case, you manage networking access to your VPC resources and internet.
L42: 
L43: cite22†Image: SageMaker AI can access and communicate with resources inside your VPC with a VPC configuration. L44: ### With network isolation
L45: 
L46: If you employ network isolation, the SageMaker AI container can't communicate with resources inside your VPC or make any network calls, as shown in the following illustration. If you provide a VPC configuration, the download and upload operations will be run through your VPC. For more information about hosting and training with network isolation while using a VPC, see cite23†Network Isolation .
L47: cite24†Image: SageMaker AI can access and communicate with resources inside your VPC with a VPC configuration. L48: ## Create a VPC Endpoint Policy for SageMaker AI

L62: The following example VPC endpoint policy specifies that all users who have access to the VPC interface endpoint are allowed to invoke the SageMaker AI hosted endpoint named `myEndpoint`.

citeturn96view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 3 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/automatic-model-tuning-warm-start.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 168

L2: Run a Warm Start Hyperparameter Tuning Job - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Types of Warm Start Tuning Jobs cite2†Warm Start Tuning Restrictions cite3†Sample Notebook cite4†Create a Warm Start Tuning Job L5: # Run a Warm Start Hyperparameter Tuning Job
L6: Use warm start to start a hyperparameter tuning job using one or more previous tuning jobs as a starting point. The results of previous tuning jobs are used to inform which combinations of hyperparameters to search over in the new tuning job. Hyperparameter tuning uses either Bayesian or random search to choose combinations of hyperparameter values from ranges that you specify. For more information, see cite5†Understand the hyperparameter tuning strategies available in Amazon SageMaker AI .
L7: Using information from previous hyperparameter tuning jobs can help increase the performance of the new hyperparameter tuning job by making the search for the best combination of hyperparameters more efficient.
L8: ###### Note
L9: 
L10: Warm start tuning jobs typically take longer to start than standard hyperparameter tuning jobs, because the results from the parent jobs have to be loaded before the job can start. The increased time depends on the total number of training jobs launched by the parent jobs.
L11: 
L12: Reasons to consider warm start include the following:
L13: 
L14:   * To gradually increase the number of training jobs over several tuning jobs based on results after each iteration.
L15:   * To tune a model using new data that you received.
L16: 
L17:   * To change hyperparameter ranges that you used in a previous tuning job, change static hyperparameters to tunable, or change tunable hyperparameters to static values.
L18: 
L19:   * You stopped a previous hyperparameter job early or it stopped unexpectedly.
L20: ###### Topics
L21: 
L22:   * cite1†Types of Warm Start Tuning Jobs L23: 
L24:   * cite2†Warm Start Tuning Restrictions L25: 
L26:   * cite3†Warm Start Tuning Sample Notebook L27: 
L28:   * cite4†Create a Warm Start Tuning Job L29: ## Types of Warm Start Tuning Jobs
L30: 
L31: There are two different types of warm start tuning jobs:
L32: 
L33: `IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM`
L34: The new hyperparameter tuning job uses the same input data and training image as the parent tuning jobs. You can change the hyperparameter ranges to search and the maximum number of training jobs that the hyperparameter tuning job launches. You can also change hyperparameters from tunable to static, and from static to tunable, but the total number of static plus tunable hyperparameters must remain the same as it is in all parent jobs.
L35: You cannot use a new version of the training algorithm, unless the changes in the new version do not affect the algorithm itself. For example, changes that improve logging or adding support for a different data format are allowed.
L36: Use identical data and algorithm when you use the same training data as you used in a previous hyperparameter tuning job, but you want to increase the total number of training jobs or change ranges or values of hyperparameters.
L37: When you run an warm start tuning job of type `IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM`, there is an additional field in the response to cite6†`DescribeHyperParameterTuningJob` named `OverallBestTrainingJob`. The value of this field is the cite7†TrainingJobSummary for the training job with the best objective metric value of all training jobs launched by this tuning job and all parent jobs specified for the warm start tuning job.
L38: 
L39: `TRANSFER_LEARNING`
L40: The new hyperparameter tuning job can include input data, hyperparameter ranges, maximum number of concurrent training jobs, and maximum number of training jobs that are different than those of its parent hyperparameter tuning jobs. You can also change hyperparameters from tunable to static, and from static to tunable, but the total number of static plus tunable hyperparameters must remain the same as it is in all parent jobs.
L41: The training algorithm image can also be a different version from the version used in the parent hyperparameter tuning job. When you use transfer learning, changes in the dataset or the algorithm that significantly affect the value of the objective metric might reduce the usefulness of using warm start tuning.
L42: ## Warm Start Tuning Restrictions
L43: 
L44: The following restrictions apply to all warm start tuning jobs:
L45: 
L46:   * A tuning job can have a maximum of 5 parent jobs, and all parent jobs must be in a terminal state (`Completed`, `Stopped`, or `Failed`) before you start the new tuning job.
L47: 
L48:   * The objective metric used in the new tuning job must be the same as the objective metric used in the parent jobs.
L49:   * The total number of static plus tunable hyperparameters must remain the same between parent jobs and the new tuning job. Because of this, if you think you might want to use a hyperparameter as tunable in a future warm start tuning job, you should add it as a static hyperparameter when you create a tuning job.
L50: 
L51:   * The type of each hyperparameter (continuous, integer, categorical) must not change between parent jobs and the new tuning job.
L52:   * The number of total changes from tunable hyperparameters in the parent jobs to static hyperparameters in the new tuning job, plus the number of changes in the values of static hyperparameters cannot be more than 10. For example, if the parent job has a tunable categorical hyperparameter with the possible values `red` and `blue`, you change that hyperparameter to static in the new tuning job, that counts as 2 changes against the allowed total of 10.
L53: If the same hyperparameter had a static value of `red` in the parent job, and you change the static value to `blue` in the new tuning job, it also counts as 2 changes.
L54:   * Warm start tuning is not recursive. For example, if you create `MyTuningJob3` as a warm start tuning job with `MyTuningJob2` as a parent job, and `MyTuningJob2` is itself an warm start tuning job with a parent job `MyTuningJob1`, the information that was learned when running `MyTuningJob1` is not used for `MyTuningJob3`. If you want to use the information from `MyTuningJob1`, you must explicitly add it as a parent for `MyTuningJob3`.
L55:   * The training jobs launched by every parent job in a warm start tuning job count against the 500 maximum training jobs for a tuning job.
L56: 
L57:   * Hyperparameter tuning jobs created before October 1, 2018 cannot be used as parent jobs for warm start tuning jobs.
L58: ## Warm Start Tuning Sample Notebook
L59: 
L60: For a sample notebook that shows how to use warm start tuning, see cite8†https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-sagemaker-examples/blob/master/hyperparameter_tuning/image_classification_warmstart/hpo_image_classification_warmstart.ipynb†github.com .
L61: 
L62: ## Create a Warm Start Tuning Job
L63: 
L64: You can use either the low-level AWS SDK for Python (Boto 3) or the high-level SageMaker AI Python SDK to create a warm start tuning job.
L65: ###### Topics
L66: 
L67:   * cite9†Create a Warm Start Tuning Job ( Low-level SageMaker AI API for Python (Boto 3)) L68: 
L69:   * cite10†Create a Warm Start Tuning Job (SageMaker AI Python SDK) L70: ### Create a Warm Start Tuning Job ( Low-level SageMaker AI API for Python (Boto 3))
L71: 
L72: To use warm start tuning, you specify the values of a cite11†`HyperParameterTuningJobWarmStartConfig` object, and pass that as the `WarmStartConfig` field in a call to cite12†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` .
L73: 
L74: The following code shows how to create a cite11†`HyperParameterTuningJobWarmStartConfig` object and pass it to cite12†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` job by using the low-level SageMaker AI API for Python (Boto 3).
L75: Create the `HyperParameterTuningJobWarmStartConfig` object:
L76: 
L77:     `warm_start_config = {
L78:               "ParentHyperParameterTuningJobs" : [
L79:               {"HyperParameterTuningJobName" : 'MyParentTuningJob'}
L80:               ],
L81:               "WarmStartType" : "IdenticalDataAndAlgorithm"
L82:     }`
L83: Create the warm start tuning job:
L84: 
L85:     `smclient = boto3.Session().client('sagemaker')
L86:     smclient.create_hyper_parameter_tuning_job(HyperParameterTuningJobName = 'MyWarmStartTuningJob',
L87:        HyperParameterTuningJobConfig = tuning_job_config, # See notebook for tuning configuration
L88:        TrainingJobDefinition = training_job_definition, # See notebook for job definition
L89:        WarmStartConfig = warm_start_config)`
L90: ### Create a Warm Start Tuning Job (SageMaker AI Python SDK)
L91: 
L92: To use the cite13†Amazon SageMaker Python SDK†sagemaker.readthedocs.io to run a warm start tuning job, you:
L93: 
L94:   * Specify the parent jobs and the warm start type by using a `WarmStartConfig` object.
L95: 
L96:   * Pass the `WarmStartConfig` object as the value of the `warm_start_config` argument of a cite14†HyperparameterTuner†sagemaker.readthedocs.io object.
L97: 
L98:   * Call the `tune` method of the `HyperparameterTuner` object.
L99: For more information about using the cite13†Amazon SageMaker Python SDK†sagemaker.readthedocs.io for hyperparameter tuning, see cite15†https://github.com/aws/sagemaker-python-sdk#sagemaker-automatic-model-tuning†github.com .
L100: This example uses an estimator that uses the cite16†Image Classification - MXNet algorithm for training. The following code sets the hyperparameter ranges that the warm start tuning job searches within to find the best combination of values. For information about setting hyperparameter ranges, see cite17†Define Hyperparameter Ranges .
L101: 
L102:     `hyperparameter_ranges = {'learning_rate': ContinuousParameter(0.0, 0.1),
L103:                              'momentum': ContinuousParameter(0.0, 0.99)}`
L104: The following code configures the warm start tuning job by creating a `WarmStartConfig` object.
L105: 
L106:     `from sagemaker.train.tuner import WarmStartTypes
L107:     from sagemaker.core.shapes import HyperParameterTuningJobWarmStartConfig
L108: 
L109:     parent_tuning_job_name = "MyParentTuningJob"
L110:     warm_start_config = HyperParameterTuningJobWarmStartConfig(warm_start_type=WarmStartTypes.IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM, parents=[parent_tuning_job_name])`
L111: Now set the values for static hyperparameters, which are hyperparameters that keep the same value for every training job that the warm start tuning job launches. In the following code, `imageclassification` is a ModelTrainer that was created previously.
L112: 
L113:     `from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer
L114:     from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute
L115: 
L116:     imageclassification = ModelTrainer(
L117:         training_image=training_image,
L118:         role=role,
L119:         hyperparameters={
L120:             'num_layers': '18',
L121:             'image_shape': '3,224,224',
L122:             'num_classes': '257',
L123:             'num_training_samples': '15420',
L124:             'mini_batch_size': '128',
L125:             'epochs': '30',
L126:             'optimizer': 'sgd',
L127:             'top_k': '2',
L128:             'precision_dtype': 'float32',
L129:             'augmentation_type': 'crop',
L130:         },
L131:         compute=Compute(instance_type='ml.p3.8xlarge', instance_count=1),
L132:     )`
L133: Now create the `HyperparameterTuner` object and pass the `WarmStartConfig` object that you previously created as the `warm_start_config` argument.
L134: 
L135:     `tuner_warm_start = HyperparameterTuner(model_trainer=imageclassification,
L136:                                 objective_metric_name='validation:accuracy',

Define Hyperparameter Ranges - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/automatic-model-tuning-define-ranges.html)
citeturn98view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/automatic-model-tuning-define-ranges.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 166
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Define Hyperparameter Ranges - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Static hyperparameters cite2†Dynamic hyperparameters cite3†Autotune cite4†Hyperparameter scaling types L5: # Define Hyperparameter Ranges
L6: 
L7: This guide shows how to use SageMaker APIs to define hyperparameter ranges. It also provides a list of hyperparameter scaling types that you can use.
L8: Choosing hyperparameters and ranges significantly affects the performance of your tuning job. Hyperparameter tuning finds the best hyperparameter values for your model by searching over a cite5†range of values that you specify for each tunable hyperparameter. You can also specify up to 100 cite6†static hyperparameters that do not change over the course of the tuning job. You can use up to 100 hyperparameters in total (static + tunable).
L9: For guidance on choosing hyperparameters and ranges, see cite7†Best Practices for Hyperparameter Tuning . You can also use autotune to find optimal tuning job settings. For more information, see the following Autotune section.
L10: ###### Note
L11: 
L12: SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning (AMT) may add additional hyperparameters(s) that contribute to the limit of 100 total hyperparameters. Currently, to pass your objective metric to the tuning job for use during training, SageMaker AI adds `_tuning_objective_metric` automatically.
L13: ## Static hyperparameters
L14: 
L15: Use static hyperparameters for the following cases: For example, you can use AMT to tune your model using `param1` (a tunable parameter) and `param2` (a static parameter). If you do, then use a search space for `param1` that lies between two values, and pass `param2` as a static hyperparameter, as follows.
L16: 
L17:     `param1: ["range_min","range_max"]
L18:     param2: "static_value"`
L19: Static hyperparameters have the following structure:
L20: 
L21:     `"StaticHyperParameters": {
L22:         "objective" : "reg:squarederror",
L23:         "dropout_rate": "0.3"
L24:     }  `
L25: 
L26: You can use the Amazon SageMaker API to specify key value pairs in the cite6†StaticHyperParameters field of the `HyperParameterTrainingJobDefinition` parameter that you pass to the cite8†CreateHyperParameterTuningJob operation.
L27: ## Dynamic hyperparameters
L28: 
L29: You can use the SageMaker API to define cite5†hyperparameter ranges . Specify the names of hyperparameters and ranges of values in the `ParameterRanges` field of the `HyperParameterTuningJobConfig` parameter that you pass to the cite8†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` operation.
L30: 
L31: The `ParameterRanges` field has three subfields: categorical, integer, and continuous. You can define up to 30 total (categorical + integer + continuous) tunable hyperparameters to search over.
L32: ###### Note
L33: 
L34: Each categorical hyperparameter can have at most 30 different values.
L35: Dynamic hyperparameters have the following structure:
L36: 
L37:     `"ParameterRanges": {
L38:         "CategoricalParameterRanges": [
L39:             {
L40:                 "Name": "tree_method",
L41:                 "Values": ["auto", "exact", "approx", "hist"]
L42:             }
L43:         ],
L44:         "ContinuousParameterRanges": [
L45:             {
L46:                 "Name": "eta",
L47:                 "MaxValue" : "0.5",
L48:                 "MinValue": "0",
L49:                 "ScalingType": "Auto"
L50:             }
L51:         ],
L52:         "IntegerParameterRanges": [
L53:             {
L54:                 "Name": "max_depth",
L55:                 "MaxValue": "10",
L56:                 "MinValue": "1",
L57:                 "ScalingType": "Auto"
L58:             }
L59:         ]
L60:     }`
L61: If you create a tuning job with a `Grid` strategy, you can only specify categorical values. You don't need to provide the `MaxNumberofTrainingJobs`. This value is inferred from the total number of configurations that can be produced from your categorical parameters. If specified, the value of `MaxNumberOfTrainingJobs` should be equal to the total number of distinct categorical combinations possible.
L62: ## Autotune
L63: 
L64: To save time and resources searching for hyperparameter ranges, resources or objective metrics, autotune can automatically guess optimal values for some hyperparameter fields. Use autotune to find optimal values for the following fields:
L65: 
L66:   * cite9†ParameterRanges – The names and ranges of hyperparameters that a tuning job can optimize.
L67:   * cite10†ResourceLimits – The maximum resources to be used in a tuning job. These resources can include the maximum number of training jobs, maximum runtime of a tuning job, and the maximum number of training jobs that can be run at the same time.
L68: 
L69:   * cite11†TrainingJobEarlyStoppingType – A flag that stops a training job if a job is not significantly improving against an objective metric. Defaults to enabled. For more information, see cite12†Stop Training Jobs Early .
L70:   * cite13†RetryStrategy – The number of times to retry a training job. Non-zero values for `RetryStrategy` can increase the likelihood that your job will complete successfully.
L71: 
L72:   * cite14†Strategy – Specifies how hyperparameter tuning chooses the combinations of hyperparameter values to use for the training job that it launches.
L73: 
L74:   * cite15†ConvergenceDetected – A flag to indicate that Automatic Model Tuning (AMT) has detected model convergence.
L75: 
L76: To use autotune, do the following:
L77:   1. Specify the hyperparameter and an example value in the `AutoParameters` field of the cite16†ParameterRanges API.
L78: 
L79:   2. Enable autotune.
L80: 
L81: AMT will determine if your hyperparameters and example values are eligible for autotune. Hyperparameters that can be used in autotune are automatically assigned to the appropriate parameter range type. Then, AMT uses `ValueHint` to select an optimal range for you. You can use the `DescribeHyperParameterTrainingJob` API to view these ranges.
L82: The following example shows you how to configure a tuning job that uses autotune. In the configuration example, the hyperparameter `max_depth` has `ValueHint` containing an example value of `4`.
L83: 
L84:     `config = {
L85:         'Autotune': {'Mode': 'Enabled'},
L86:         'HyperParameterTuningJobName':'my-autotune-job',
L87:         'HyperParameterTuningJobConfig': {
L88:             'HyperParameterTuningJobObjective': {'Type': 'Minimize', 'MetricName': 'validation:rmse'},
L89:             'ResourceLimits': {'MaxNumberOfTrainingJobs': 5, 'MaxParallelTrainingJobs': 1},
L90:             'ParameterRanges': {
L91:                 'AutoParameters': [
L92:                     {'Name': 'max_depth', 'ValueHint': '4'}
L93:                 ]
L94:             }
L95:         },
L96:         'TrainingJobDefinition': {
L97:         .... }`
L98: Continuing the previous example, a tuning job is created after the previous configuration is included in a call to the `CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` API. Then, autotune converts the max_depth hyperparameter in AutoParameters to the hyperparameter `IntegerParameterRanges`. The following response from a `DescribeHyperParameterTrainingJob` API shows that the optimal `IntegerParameterRanges` for `max_depth` are between `2` and `8`.
L99: 
L100:     `{
L101:         'HyperParameterTuningJobName':'my_job',
L102:         'HyperParameterTuningJobConfig': {
L103:             'ParameterRanges': {
L104:                 'IntegerParameterRanges': [
L105:                     {'Name': 'max_depth', 'MinValue': '2', 'MaxValue': '8'},
L106:                 ],
L107:             }
L108:         },
L109:         'TrainingJobDefinition': {
L110:             ...
L111:         },
L112:         'Autotune': {'Mode': 'Enabled'}
L113: 
L114:     }`
L115: ## Hyperparameter scaling types
L116: 
L117: For integer and continuous hyperparameter ranges, you can choose the scale that you want hyperparameter tuning to use. For example, to search the range of values, you can specify a value for the `ScalingType` field of the hyperparameter range. You can choose from the following hyperparameter scaling types:
L118: 
L119: Auto
L120: 
L121: 
L122: SageMaker AI hyperparameter tuning chooses the best scale for the hyperparameter.
L123: 
L124: Linear
L125: Hyperparameter tuning searches the values in the hyperparameter range by using a linear scale. Typically, you choose this if the range of all values from the lowest to the highest is relatively small (within one order of magnitude). Uniformly searching values from the range provides a reasonable exploration of the entire range.
L126: 
L127: Logarithmic
L128: 
L129: 
L130: Hyperparameter tuning searches the values in the hyperparameter range by using a logarithmic scale.
L131: Logarithmic scaling works only for ranges that have values greater than 0.
L132: 
L133: Choose logarithmic scaling when you're searching a range that spans several orders of magnitude.
L134: For example, if you're tuning a cite17†Tune a linear learner model model, and you specify a range of values between .0001 and 1.0 for the `learning_rate` hyperparameter, consider the following: Searching uniformly on a logarithmic scale gives you a better sample of the entire range than searching on a linear scale would. This is because searching on a linear scale would, on average, devote 90 percent of your training budget to only the values between .1 and 1.0.
L135: As a result, that leaves only 10 percent of your training budget for the values between .0001 and .1.
L136: `ReverseLogarithmic`
L137: 
L138: 
L139: Hyperparameter tuning searches the values in the hyperparameter range by using a reverse logarithmic scale. Reverse logarithmic scaling is supported only for continuous hyperparameter ranges. It is not supported for integer hyperparameter ranges.
L140: 
L141: Choose reverse logarithmic scaling when you are searching a range that is highly sensitive to small changes that are very close to 1.
L142: 
L143: Reverse logarithmic scaling works only for ranges that are entirely within the range 0<=x<1.0.
L144: For an example notebook that uses hyperparameter scaling, see these cite18†Amazon SageMaker AI hyperparameter examples on GitHub†github.com .

citeturn99view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/k-nearest-neighbors.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 79
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the k-NN Algorithm cite2†Sample Notebooks cite3†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the k-NN Algorithm L5: # K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Algorithm
L6: Amazon SageMaker AI k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) algorithm is an index-based algorithm. It uses a non-parametric method for classification or regression. For classification problems, the algorithm queries the k points that are closest to the sample point and returns the most frequently used label of their class as the predicted label. For regression problems, the algorithm queries the k closest points to the sample point and returns the average of their feature values as the predicted value.
L7: Training with the k-NN algorithm has three steps: sampling, dimension reduction, and index building. Sampling reduces the size of the initial dataset so that it fits into memory. For dimension reduction, the algorithm decreases the feature dimension of the data to reduce the footprint of the k-NN model in memory and inference latency. We provide two methods of dimension reduction methods: random projection and the fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform.
L8: Typically, you use dimension reduction for high-dimensional (d >1000) datasets to avoid the “curse of dimensionality” that troubles the statistical analysis of data that becomes sparse as dimensionality increases. The main objective of k-NN's training is to construct the index. The index enables efficient lookups of distances between points whose values or class labels have not yet been determined and the k nearest points to use for inference.
L9: ###### Topics
L10: 
L11:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the k-NN Algorithm L12: 
L13:   * cite2†k-NN Sample Notebooks L14: 
L15:   * cite4†How the k-NN Algorithm Works L16: 
L17:   * cite3†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the k-NN Algorithm L18: 
L19:   * cite5†k-NN Hyperparameters L20: 
L21:   * cite6†Tune a k-NN Model L22: 
L23:   * cite7†Data Formats for k-NN Training Input L24: 
L25:   * cite8†k-NN Request and Response Formats L26: ## Input/Output Interface for the k-NN Algorithm
L27: 
L28: SageMaker AI k-NN supports train and test data channels.
L29: 
L30:   * Use a train channel for data that you want to sample and construct into the k-NN index.
L31: 
L32:   * Use a test channel to emit scores in log files. Scores are listed as one line per mini-batch: accuracy for `classifier`, mean-squared error (mse) for `regressor` for score.
L33: For training inputs, k-NN supports `text/csv` and `application/x-recordio-protobuf` data formats. For input type `text/csv`, the first `label_size` columns are interpreted as the label vector for that row. You can use either File mode or Pipe mode to train models on data that is formatted as `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` or as `CSV`.
L34: For inference inputs, k-NN supports the `application/json`, `application/x-recordio-protobuf`, and `text/csv` data formats. The `text/csv` format accepts a `label_size` and encoding parameter. It assumes a `label_size` of 0 and a UTF-8 encoding.
L35: For inference outputs, k-NN supports the `application/json` and `application/x-recordio-protobuf` data formats. These two data formats also support a verbose output mode. In verbose output mode, the API provides the search results with the distances vector sorted from smallest to largest, and corresponding elements in the labels vector.
L36: For batch transform, k-NN supports the `application/jsonlines` data format for both input and output. An example input is as follows:
L37: 
L38:     `content-type: application/jsonlines
L39: 
L40:     {"features": [1.5, 16.0, 14.0, 23.0]}
L41:     {"data": {"features": {"values": [1.5, 16.0, 14.0, 23.0]}}`
L42: 
L43: An example output is as follows:
L44: 
L45:     `accept: application/jsonlines
L46: 
L47:     {"predicted_label": 0.0}
L48:     {"predicted_label": 2.0}`
L49: For more information on input and output file formats, see cite7†Data Formats for k-NN Training Input for training, cite8†k-NN Request and Response Formats for inference, and the cite2†k-NN Sample Notebooks .
L50: ## k-NN Sample Notebooks
L51: 
L52: For a sample notebook that uses the SageMaker AI k-nearest neighbor algorithm to predict wilderness cover types from geological and forest service data, see the cite9†K-Nearest Neighbor Covertype†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io .
L53: Use a Jupyter notebook instance to run the example in SageMaker AI. To learn how to create and open a Jupyter notebook instance in SageMaker AI, see cite10†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances . Once you have created a notebook instance and opened it, select the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI example notebooks. Find K-Nearest Neighbor notebooks in the Introduction to Amazon algorithms section. To open a notebook, click on its Use tab and select Create copy.
L54: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the k-NN Algorithm
L55: 
L56: We recommend training on a CPU instance (such as ml.m5.2xlarge) or on a GPU instance. The k-NN algorithm supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 GPU instance families for training and inference.
L57: 
L58: Inference requests from CPUs generally have a lower average latency than requests from GPUs because there is a tax on CPU-to-GPU communication when you use GPU hardware. However, GPUs generally have higher throughput for larger batches.

L2: Custom entity recognition - Amazon Comprehend
L3: # Custom entity recognition
L4: 
L5: Custom entity recognition extends the capability of Amazon Comprehend by helping you identify your specific new entity types that are not in the preset cite1†generic entity types . This means that you can analyze documents and extract entities like product codes or business-specific entities that fit your particular needs.
L6: Building an accurate custom entity recognizer on your own can be a complex process, requiring preparation of large sets of manually annotated training documents and the selection of the right algorithms and parameters for model training. Amazon Comprehend helps to reduce the complexity by providing automatic annotation and model development to create a custom entity recognition model.
L7: Creating a custom entity recognition model is a more effective approach than using string matching or regular expressions to extract entities from documents. For example, to extract ENGINEER names in a document, it is difficult to enumerate all possible names. Additionally, without context, it is challenging to distinguish between ENGINEER names and ANALYST names. A custom entity recognition model can learn the context where those names are likely to appear.
L8: Additionally, string matching will not detect entities that have typos or follow new naming conventions, while this is possible using a custom model.
L9: You have two options for creating a custom model:
L10: 
L11:   1. Annotations – provide a data set containing annotated entities for model training.
L12: 
L13:   2. Entity lists (plaintext only) – provide a list of entities and their type label (such as `PRODUCT_CODES` and a set of unannotated documents containing those entities for model training.
L14: When you create a custom entity recognizer using annotated PDF files, you can use that recognizer with a variety of input file formats: plaintext, image files (JPG, PNG, TIFF), PDF files, and Word documents, with no pre-processing or doc flattening required. Amazon Comprehend doesn't support annotation of image files or Word documents.
L15: ###### Note
L16: 
L17: A custom entity recognizer using annotated PDF files supports English documents only.
L18: 
L19: You can train a model on up to 25 custom entities at once. For more details, see the cite2†Guidelines and quotas page .
L20: 
L21: After your model is trained, you can use the model for real-time entity detection and in entity detection jobs.

citeturn102view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 3 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-sentiment.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 59
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Sentiment - Amazon Comprehend
L3: # Sentiment
L4: 
L5: Use Amazon Comprehend to determine the sentiment of content in UTF-8 encoded text documents. For example, you can use sentiment analysis to determine the sentiments of comments on a blog posting to determine if your readers liked the post.
L6: 
L7: You can determine sentiment for documents in any of the primary languages supported by Amazon Comprehend. All documents in one job must be in the same language.
L8: 
L9: Sentiment determination returns the following values:
L10:   * Positive – The text expresses an overall positive sentiment.
L11: 
L12:   * Negative – The text expresses an overall negative sentiment.
L13: 
L14:   * Mixed – The text expresses both positive and negative sentiments.
L15: 
L16:   * Neutral – The text does not express either positive or negative sentiments.
L17: 
L18: You can use any of the following API operations to detect the sentiment of a document or a set of documents.
L19: 
L20:   * cite1†DetectSentiment L21: 
L22:   * cite2†BatchDetectSentiment L23: 
L24:   * cite3†StartSentimentDetectionJob L25: The operations return the most likely sentiment for the text and the scores for each of the sentiments. The score represents the likelihood that the sentiment was correctly detected. For example, in the example below it is 95 percent likely that the text has a `Positive` sentiment. There is a less than 1 percent likelihood that the text has a `Negative` sentiment. You can use the `SentimentScore` to determine if the accuracy of the detection meets the needs of your application.
L26: The `DetectSentiment` operation returns an object that contains the detected sentiment and a cite4†SentimentScore object. The `BatchDetectSentiment` operation returns a list of sentiments and `SentimentScore` objects, one for each document in the batch. The `StartSentimentDetectionJob` operation starts an asynchronous job that produces a file containing a list of sentiments and `SentimentScore` objects, one for each document in the job.
L27: The following example is the response from the `DetectSentiment` operation.
L28: 
L29:     `{
L30:     "SentimentScore": {
L31:             "Mixed": 0.030585512690246105,
L32:             "Positive": 0.94992071056365967,
L33:             "Neutral": 0.0141543131828308,
L34:             "Negative": 0.00893945890665054
L35:         },
L36:         "Sentiment": "POSITIVE",
L37:         "LanguageCode": "en"

citeturn204view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/custom-slot-types.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 49

L2: Custom slot type - Amazon Lex
L3: # Custom slot type
L4: For each intent, you can specify parameters that indicate the information that the intent needs to fulfill the user's request. These parameters, or slots, have a type. A slot type is a list of values that Amazon Lex V2 uses to train the machine learning model to recognize values for a slot. For example, you can define a slot type called `Genres` with values such as "comedy," "adventure," "documentary," and so on. You can define synonyms for a slot type value.
L5: For example, you can define the synonyms "funny" and "humorous" for the value "comedy."
L6: cite1†Image: Create a custom slot type. L7: You can configure the slot type to expand the slot values. Slot values will be used as training data and the model will resolve the slot to the value provided by the user if it is similar to the slot values and synonyms of those values. This is the default behavior. Amazon Lex V2 maintains a list of possible resolutions for a slot. Each entry in the list provides a resolved value that Amazon Lex V2 recognized as additional possibilities for the slot.
L8: A resolved value is the best effort to match the slot value. The list contains up to five values.
L9: Alternatively, you can configure the slot type to restrict resolution to the slot values. In this case, the model will resolve a slot value entered by the user to an existing slot value only if it is the same as that slot value or it is a synonym. For example, if the user enters "funny" it will resolve to the slot value "comedy."
L10: When the value entered by the user is a synonym of a slot type value, the model returns that slot type value as the first entry in the list of `resolvedValues`.
L11: For example, if the user enters "funny," the model populates the `originalValue` field with the value "funny" and the first entry in the resolvedValues field with "comedy." You can configure the `valueSelectionStrategy` when you create or update a slot type with the cite2†CreateSlotType operation so that the slot value is filled with the first value in the resolution list.
L12: Custom slot types support inputs using spelling styles. You can use the spell-by-letter and spell-by-word styles to help your customers enter letters. For more information, see cite3†Capturing slot values with spelling styles during the conversation .
L13: If you are using a Lambda function, the input event to the function includes a resolution list called `resolvedValues`. The following example shows the slot section of the input to a Lambda function:
L14: 
L15:     `
L16:        "slots": {
L17:           "MovieGenre": {
L18:              "value": {
L19:                 "originalValue": "funny",
L20:                 "interpretedValue": "comedy",
L21:                 "resolvedValues": [
L22:                    "comedy"
L23:                 ]
L24:              }
L25:           }
L26:        }`
L27: For each slot type, you can define a maximum of 10,000 values and synonyms. Each bot can have a total number of 50,000 slot type values and synonyms. For example, you can have 5 slot types, each with 5,000 values and 5,000 synonyms, or you can have 10 slot types, each with 2,500 values and 2,500 synonyms.
L28: A custom slot type should not have the same name as the built-in slot types. For example, a custom slot type should not be named with the reserved keywords of Date, Number, or Confirmation. These keywords are reserved for built-in slot types. For a list of all built-in slot types, see cite4†Built-in slot types .

L4: cite1†Custom vocabulary tables versus lists L5: # Custom vocabularies
L6: 
L7: Use custom vocabularies to improve transcription accuracy for one or more specific words. These are generally domain-specific terms, such as brand names and acronyms, proper nouns, and words that Amazon Transcribe isn't rendering correctly.
L8: 
L9: Custom vocabularies can be used with all supported languages. Note that only the characters listed in your language's cite2†character set can be used in a custom vocabulary.
L10: ###### Important
L11: 
L12: You are responsible for the integrity of your own data when you use Amazon Transcribe. Do not enter confidential information, personal information (PII), or protected health information (PHI) into a custom vocabulary.
L13: 
L14: Considerations when creating a custom vocabulary:
L15: 
L16:   * You can have up to 100 custom vocabulary files per AWS account
L17: 
L18:   * The size limit for each custom vocabulary file is 50 Kb
L19:   * If using the API to create your custom vocabulary, your vocabulary file must be in text (*.txt) format. If using the AWS Management Console, your vocabulary file can be in text (*.txt) format or comma-separated value (*.csv) format.
L20: 
L21:   * Each entry within a custom vocabulary cannot exceed 256 characters
L22: 
L23:   * To use a custom vocabulary, it must have been created in the same AWS Region as your transcription.
L24: ###### Tip
L25: 
L26: You can test your custom vocabulary using the AWS Management Console. Once your custom vocabulary is ready to use, log in to the AWS Management Console, select Real-time transcription, scroll to Customizations, toggle on Custom vocabulary, and select your custom vocabulary from the dropdown list. Then select start streaming. Speak some of the words in your custom vocabulary into your microphone to see if they render correctly.
L27: 
L28: ## Custom vocabulary tables versus lists
L29: ###### Important
L30: 
L31: Custom vocabularies in list format are being deprecated. If you're creating a new custom vocabulary, use the cite3†table format .
L32: 
L33: Tables give you more options for—and more control over—the input and output of words within your custom vocabulary. With tables, you must specify multiple categories (Phrase and DisplayAs), allowing you to fine-tune your output.
L34: Lists don't have additional options, so you can only type in entries as you want them to appear in your transcript, replacing all spaces with hyphens.
L35: 
L36: The AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, and AWS SDKs all use custom vocabulary tables in the same way; lists are used differently for each method and thus may require additional formatting for successful use between methods.
L37: 
L38: For more information, see cite3†Creating a custom vocabulary using a table and cite4†Creating a custom vocabulary using a list .
L39: To dive a little deeper and learn how to use Amazon Augmented AI with custom vocabularies, see:
