L2: DeepAR+ Algorithm - Amazon Forecast
L3: 
L4: cite1†How It Works cite2†Hyperparameters cite3†Model Tuning L5: # DeepAR+ Algorithm
L6: Amazon Forecast DeepAR+ is a supervised learning algorithm for forecasting scalar (one-dimensional) time series using recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Classical forecasting methods, such as autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) or exponential smoothing (ETS), fit a single model to each individual time series, and then use that model to extrapolate the time series into the future. In many applications, however, you have many similar time series across a set of cross-sectional units.
L7: These time-series groupings demand different products, server loads, and requests for web pages. In this case, it can be beneficial to train a single model jointly over all of the time series. DeepAR+ takes this approach. When your dataset contains hundreds of feature time series, the DeepAR+ algorithm outperforms the standard ARIMA and ETS methods. You can also use the trained model for generating forecasts for new time series that are similar to the ones it has been trained on.
L8: ###### Python notebooks
L9: 
L10: For a step-by-step guide on using the DeepAR+ algorithm, see cite4†Getting Started with DeepAR+†github.com .
L11: 
L12: ###### Topics
L13: 
L14:   * cite1†How DeepAR+ Works L15: 
L16:   * cite2†DeepAR+ Hyperparameters L17: 
L18:   * cite3†Tune DeepAR+ Models L19: ## How DeepAR+ Works
L20: During training, DeepAR+ uses a training dataset and an optional testing dataset. It uses the testing dataset to evaluate the trained model. In general, the training and testing datasets don't have to contain the same set of time series. You can use a model trained on a given training set to generate forecasts for the future of the time series in the training set, and for other time series. Both the training and the testing datasets consist of (preferably more than one) target time series.
L21: Optionally, they can be associated with a vector of feature time series and a vector of categorical features (for details, see cite5†DeepAR Input/Output Interface in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide). The following example shows how this works for an element of a training dataset indexed by `i`. The training dataset consists of a target time series, `z_{i,t}`, and two associated feature time series, `x_{i,1,t}` and `x_{i,2,t}`.
L22: cite6†Image: Image: DeepAR+ time-series data. L23: 
L24: The target time series might contain missing values (denoted in the graphs by breaks in the time series). DeepAR+ supports only feature time series that are known in the future. This allows you to run counterfactual "what-if" scenarios. For example, "What happens if I change the price of a product in some way?"
L25: Each target time series can also be associated with a number of categorical features. You can use these to encode that a time series belongs to certain groupings. Using categorical features allows the model to learn typical behavior for those groupings, which can increase accuracy. A model implements this by learning an embedding vector for each group that captures the common properties of all time series in the group.
L26: To facilitate learning time-dependent patterns, such as spikes during weekends, DeepAR+ automatically creates feature time series based on time-series granularity. For example, DeepAR+ creates two feature time series (day of the month and day of the year) at a weekly time-series frequency. It uses these derived feature time series along with the custom feature time series that you provide during training and inference.
L27: The following example shows two derived time-series features: `u_{i,1,t}` represents the hour of the day, and `u_{i,2,t}` the day of the week.
L28: cite7†Image: Image: DeepAR+ two derived time-series. L29: 
L30: DeepAR+ automatically includes these feature time series based on the data frequency and the size of training data. The following table lists the features that can be derived for each supported basic time frequency.
L31: Frequency of the Time Series  | Derived Features
L32: --- | ---
L33: Minute  | minute-of-hour, hour-of-day, day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L34: Hour  | hour-of-day, day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L35: Day  | day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L36: Week  | week-of-month, week-of-year
L37: Month  | month-of-year
L38: A DeepAR+ model is trained by randomly sampling several training examples from each of the time series in the training dataset. Each training example consists of a pair of adjacent context and prediction windows with fixed predefined lengths. The `context_length` hyperparameter controls how far in the past the network can see, and the `ForecastHorizon` parameter controls how far in the future predictions can be made.
L39: During training, Amazon Forecast ignores elements in the training dataset with time series shorter than the specified prediction length. The following example shows five samples, with a context length (highlighted in green) of 12 hours and a prediction length (highlighted in blue) of 6 hours, drawn from element `i`. For the sake of brevity, we've excluded the feature time series `x_{i,1,t}` and `u_{i,2,t}`.
L40: cite8†Image: Image: DeepAR+ sampled. L41: 
L42: To capture seasonality patterns, DeepAR+ also automatically feeds lagged (past period) values from the target time series. In our example with samples taken at an hourly frequency, for each time index `t = T`, the model exposes the `z_{i,t}` values which occurred approximately one, two, and three days in the past (highlighted in pink).
L43: 
L44: cite9†Image: Image: DeepAR+ lags. L45: For inference, the trained model takes as input the target time series, which might or might not have been used during training, and forecasts a probability distribution for the next `ForecastHorizon` values. Because DeepAR+ is trained on the entire dataset, the forecast takes into account learned patterns from similar time series.
L46: For information on the mathematics behind DeepAR+, see cite10†DeepAR: Probabilistic Forecasting with Autoregressive Recurrent Networks†arxiv.org on the Cornell University Library website.
L47: ## DeepAR+ Hyperparameters
L48: 
L49: The following table lists the hyperparameters that you can use in the DeepAR+ algorithm. Parameters in bold participate in hyperparameter optimization (HPO).
L50: Parameter Name  | Description
L51: --- | ---
L52: `context_length`  | The number of time points that the model reads in before making the prediction. The value for this parameter should be about the same as the `ForecastHorizon`. The model also receives lagged inputs from the target, so `context_length` can be much smaller than typical seasonalities. For example, a daily time series can have yearly seasonality. The model automatically includes a lag of one year, so the context length can be shorter than a year.
L53: The lag values that the model picks depend on the frequency of the time series. For example, lag values for daily frequency are: previous week, 2 weeks, 3 weeks, 4 weeks, and year.
L54: Valid values
L55:     Positive integers
L56: Typical values
L57:     ceil(0.1 * `ForecastHorizon`) to min(200, 10 * `ForecastHorizon`)
L58: Default value
L59:     2 * `ForecastHorizon`
L60: `epochs`  | The maximum number of passes to go over the training data. The optimal value depends on your data size and learning rate. Smaller datasets and lower learning rates both require more epochs, to achieve good results.
L61: Valid values
L62:     Positive integers
L63: Typical values
L64:     10 to 1000
L65: Default value
L66:     500
L67: `learning_rate`  | The learning rate used in training.
L68: 
L69: Valid values
L70:     Positive floating-point numbers
L71: Typical values
L72:     0.0001 to 0.1
L73: Default value
L74:     0.001
L75: `learning_rate_decay`  | The rate at which the learning rate decreases. At most, the learning rate is reduced `max_learning_rate_decays` times, then training stops. This parameter will be used only if `max_learning_rate_decays` is greater than 0.
L76: Valid values
L77:     Positive floating-point numbers
L78: Typical values
L79:     0.5 to 0.8 (inclusive)
L80: Default value
L81:     0.5
L82: `likelihood`  | The model generates a probabilistic forecast, and can provide quantiles of the distribution and return samples. Depending on your data, choose an appropriate likelihood (noise model) that is used for uncertainty estimates. Valid values
L83:   * `beta`: Use for real-valued targets between 0 and 1, inclusively.
L84:   * `deterministic-L1`: A loss function that does not estimate uncertainty and only learns a point forecast.
L85:   * `gaussian`: Use for real-valued data.
L86:   * `negative-binomial`: Use for count data (non-negative integers).
L87:   * `piecewise-linear`: Use for flexible distributions.
L88:   * `student-T`: Use this alternative for real-valued data for bursty data.
L89: Default value
L90:     `student-T`
L91: `max_learning_rate_decays`  | The maximum number of learning rate reductions that should occur.
L92: 
L93: Valid values
L94:     Positive integers
L95: Typical values
L96:     0 to 10
L97: Default value
L98:     0
L99: `num_averaged_models`  | In DeepAR+, a training trajectory can encounter multiple models. Each model might have different forecasting strengths and weaknesses. DeepAR+ can average the model behaviors to take advantage of the strengths of all models.
L100: Valid values
L101:     Positive integers
L102: Typical values
L103:     1 to 5 (inclusive)
L104: Default value
L105:     1
L106: `num_cells`  | The number of cells to use in each hidden layer of the RNN.
L107: 
L108: Valid values
L109:     Positive integers
L110: Typical values
L111:     30 to 100
L112: Default value
L113:     40
L114: `num_layers`  | The number of hidden layers in the RNN.
L115: 
L116: Valid values
L117:     Positive integers
L118: Typical values
L119:     1 to 4
L120: Default value
L121:     2
L122: ## Tune DeepAR+ Models
L123: 
L124: To tune Amazon Forecast DeepAR+ models, follow these recommendations for optimizing the training process and hardware configuration.
L125: ### Best Practices for Process Optimization
L126: 
L127: To achieve the best results, follow these recommendations:
L128: 
L129:   * Except when splitting the training and testing datasets, always provide entire time series for training and testing, and when calling the model for inference. Regardless of how you set `context_length`, don't divide the time series or provide only a part of it. The model will use data points further back than `context_length` for the lagged values feature.
L130:   * For model tuning, you can split the dataset into training and testing datasets. In a typical evaluation scenario, you should test the model on the same time series used in training, but on the future `ForecastHorizon` time points immediately after the last time point visible during training.
L131: To create training and testing datasets that satisfy these criteria, use the entire dataset (all of the time series) as a testing dataset and remove the last `ForecastHorizon` points from each time series for training. This way, during training, the model doesn't see the target values for time points on which it is evaluated during testing. In the test phase, the last `ForecastHorizon` points of each time series in the testing dataset are withheld and a prediction is generated.
L132: The forecast is then compared with the actual values for the last `ForecastHorizon` points. You can create more complex evaluations by repeating time series multiple times in the testing dataset, but cutting them off at different end points. This produces accuracy metrics that are averaged over multiple forecasts from different time points.
L133:   * Avoid using very large values (> 400) for the `ForecastHorizon` because this slows down the model and makes it less accurate. If you want to forecast further into the future, consider aggregating to a higher frequency. For example, use `5min` instead of `1min`.
L134: 
L135:   * Because of lags, the model can look further back than `context_length`. Therefore, you don't have to set this parameter to a large value. A good starting point for this parameter is the same value as the `ForecastHorizon`.
L136:   * Train DeepAR+ models with as many time series as are available. Although a DeepAR+ model trained on a single time series might already work well, standard forecasting methods such as ARIMA or ETS might be more accurate and are more tailored to this use case. DeepAR+ starts to outperform the standard methods when your dataset contains hundreds of feature time series. Currently, DeepAR+ requires that the total number of observations available, across all training time series, is at least 300.

citeturn125view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/forecast/latest/dg/aws-forecast-algo-cnnqr.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 157
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: CNN-QR Algorithm - Amazon Forecast
L3: 
L4: cite1†Getting Started cite2†How It Works cite3†Related Data cite4†Hyperparameters cite5†Tips and Best Practices L5: # CNN-QR Algorithm
L6: 
L7: Amazon Forecast CNN-QR, Convolutional Neural Network - Quantile Regression, is a proprietary machine learning algorithm for forecasting scalar (one-dimensional) time series using causal convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This supervised learning algorithm trains one global model from a large collection of time series and uses a quantile decoder to make probabilistic predictions.
L8: ###### Topics
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†Getting Started with CNN-QR L11: 
L12:   * cite2†How CNN-QR Works L13: 
L14:   * cite3†Using Related Data with CNN-QR L15: 
L16:   * cite4†CNN-QR Hyperparameters L17: 
L18:   * cite5†Tips and Best Practices L19: ## Getting Started with CNN-QR
L20: 
L21: You can train a predictor with CNN-QR in two ways:
L22: 
L23:   1. Manually selecting the CNN-QR algorithm.
L24: 
L25:   2. Choosing AutoML (CNN-QR is part of AutoML).
L26: 
L27: If you are unsure of which algorithm to use, we recommend selecting AutoML, and Forecast will select CNN-QR if it is the most accurate algorithm for your data. To see if CNN-QR was selected as the most accurate model, either use the cite6†DescribePredictor API or choose the predictor name in the console.
L28: Here are some key use cases for CNN-QR:
L29: 
L30:   * Forecast with large and complex datasets - CNN-QR works best when trained with large and complex datasets. The neural network can learn across many datasets, which is useful when you have related time series and item metadata.
L31:   * Forecast with historical related time series - CNN-QR does not require related time series to contain data points within the forecast horizon. This added flexibility allows you to include a broader range of related time series and item meta data, such as item price, events, web metrics, and product categories.
L32: ## How CNN-QR Works
L33: 
L34: CNN-QR is a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model for probabilistic forecasting that tests how well a prediction reconstructs the decoding sequence, conditioned on the encoding sequence.
L35: The algorithm allows for different features in the encoding and the decoding sequences, so you can use a related time series in the encoder, and omit it from the decoder (and vice versa). By default, related time series with data points in the forecast horizon will be included in both the encoder and decoder. Related time series without data points in the forecast horizon will only be included in the encoder.
L36: CNN-QR performs quantile regression with a hierarchical causal CNN serving as a learnable feature extractor.
L37: To facilitate learning time-dependent patterns, such as spikes during weekends, CNN-QR automatically creates feature time series based on time-series granularity. For example, CNN-QR creates two feature time series (day-of-month and day-of-year) at a weekly time-series frequency. The algorithm uses these derived feature time series along with the custom feature time series provided during training and inference.
L38: The following example shows a target time series, `z_{i,t}`, and two derived time-series features: `u_{i,1,t}` represents the hour of the day, and `u_{i,2,t}` represents the day of the week.
L39: cite7†Image: Image: CNN-QR with derived features for time frequencies. L40: 
L41: CNN-QR automatically includes these feature time series based on the data frequency and the size of training data. The following table lists the features that can be derived for each supported basic time frequency.
L42: Frequency of the Time Series  | Derived Features
L43: --- | ---
L44: Minute  | minute-of-hour, hour-of-day, day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L45: Hour  | hour-of-day, day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L46: Day  | day-of-week, day-of-month, day-of-year
L47: Week  | week-of-month, week-of-year
L48: Month  | month-of-year
L49: During training, each time series in the training dataset consists of a pair of adjacent context and forecast windows with fixed predefined lengths. This is shown in the figure below, where the context window is represented in green, and the forecast window is represented in blue.
L50: You can use a model trained on a given training set to generate predictions for time series in the training set, and for other time series. The training dataset consists of a target time series, which may be associated with a list of related time series and item metadata.
L51: The figure below shows how this works for an element of a training dataset indexed by `i`. The training dataset consists of a target time series, `z_{i,t}`, and two associated related time series, `x_{i,1,t}` and `x_{i,2,t}`. The first related time series, `x_{i,1,t}`, is a forward-looking time series, and the second, `x_{i,2,t}`, is a historical time series.
L52: 
L53: cite8†Image: Image: CNN-QR with historical and future-looking related time series L54: CNN-QR learns across the target time series, `z_{i,t}`, and the related time series, `x_{i,1,t}` and `x_{i,2,t}`, to generate predictions in the forecast window, represented by the orange line.
L55: ## Using Related Data with CNN-QR
L56: 
L57: CNNQR supports both historical and forward looking related time series datasets. If you provide a forward looking related time series dataset, any missing value will be filled using the cite9†future filling method . For more information on historical and forward-looking related time series, see cite10†Using Related Time Series Datasets .
L58: You can also use item metadata datasets with CNN-QR. These are datasets with static information on the items in your target time series. Item metadata is especially useful for coldstart forecasting scenarios where there is little to no historical data. For more information on item metadata, see cite11†Item Metadata. L59: ## CNN-QR Hyperparameters
L60: 
L61: Amazon Forecast optimizes CNN-QR models on selected hyperparameters. When manually selecting CNN-QR, you have the option to pass in training parameters for these hyperparameters. The following table lists the tunable hyperparameters of the CNN-QR algorithm.
L62: 
L63: Parameter Name  | Values  | Description
L64: --- | --- | ---
L65: `context_length`  |
L66: Valid values
L67:     Positive Integers
L68: Valid range
L69:     10 to 500
L70: Typical values
L71:     2 * `ForecastHorizon` to 12 * `ForecastHorizon`
L72: HPO tunable
L73:     Yes
L74:  | The number of time points that the model reads before making predictions. Typically, CNN-QR has larger values for `context_length` than DeepAR+ because CNN-QR does not use lags to look at further historical data. If the value for `context_length` is outside of a predefined range, CNN-QR will automatically set the default `context_length` to an appropriate value.
L75: `use_related_data`  |
L76: Valid values
L77:     `ALL` `NONE` `HISTORICAL` `FORWARD_LOOKING`
L78: Default value
L79:     `ALL`
L80: HPO tunable
L81:     Yes
L82:  | Determines which kinds of related time series data to include in the model. Choose one of four options:
L83:   * `ALL`: Include all provided related time series.
L84:   * `NONE`: Exclude all provided related time series.
L85:   * `HISTORICAL`: Include only related time series that do not extend into the forecast horizon.
L86:   * `FORWARD_LOOKING`: Include only related time series that do extend into the forecast horizon.
L87: `HISTORICAL` includes all historical related time series, and `FORWARD_LOOKING` includes all forward-looking related time series. You cannot choose a subset of `HISTORICAL` or `FORWARD_LOOKING` related time series.
L88: `use_item_metadata`  |
L89: Valid values
L90:     `ALL` `NONE`
L91: Default value
L92:     `ALL`
L93: HPO tunable
L94:     Yes
L95:  | Determines whether the model includes item metadata. Choose one of two options:
L96: 
L97:   * `ALL`: Include all provided item metadata.
L98:   * `NONE`: Exlude all provided item metadata.
L99: `use_item_metadata` includes either all provided item metadata or none. You cannot choose a subset of item metadata.
L100: `epochs`  |
L101: Valid values
L102:     Positive Integers
L103: Typical values
L104:     10 to 1000
L105: Default value
L106:     100
L107: HPO tunable
L108:     No
L109:  | The maximum number of complete passes through the training data. Smaller datasets require more epochs. For large values of `ForecastHorizon` and `context_length`, consider decreasing epochs to improve the training time.
L110: ### Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO)
L111: 
L112: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is the task of selecting the optimal hyperparameter values for a specific learning objective. With Forecast, you can automate this process in two ways:
L113: 
L114:   1. Choosing AutoML, and HPO will automatically run for CNN-QR.
L115: 
L116:   2. Manually selecting CNN-QR and setting `PerformHPO = TRUE`.
L117: Additional related time series and item metadata does not always improve the accuracy of your CNN-QR model. When you run AutoML or enable HPO, CNN-QR tests the accuracy of your model with and without the provided related time series and item metadata, and selects the model with the highest accuracy.
L118: 
L119: Amazon Forecast automatically optimizes the following three hyperparameters during HPO and provides you with the final trained values:
L120:   * context_length - determines how far into the past the network can see. The HPO process automatically sets a value for `context_length` that maximizes model accuracy, while taking training time into account.
L121: 
L122:   * use_related_data - determines which forms of related time series data to include in your model. The HPO process automatically checks whether your related time series data improves the model, and selects the optimal setting.
L123:   * use_item_metadata - determines whether to include item metadata in your model. The HPO process automatically checks whether your item metadata improves the model, and chooses the optimal setting.
L124: ###### Note
L125: 
L126: If `use_related_data` is set to `NONE` or `HISTORICAL` when the `Holiday` supplementary feature is selected, this means that including holiday data does not improve model accuracy.
L127: 
L128: You can set the HPO configuration for the `context_length` hyperparameter if you set `PerformHPO = TRUE` during manual selection. However, you cannot alter any aspect of the HPO configuration if you choose AutoML. For more information on HPO configuration, refer to the cite12†IntergerParameterRange API.
L129: ## Tips and Best Practices
L130: 
L131: Avoid large values for ForecastHorizon - Using values over 100 for the `ForecastHorizon` will increase training time and can reduce model accuracy. If you want to forecast further into the future, consider aggregating to a higher frequency. For example, use `5min` instead of `1min`.
L132: 
L133: CNNs allow for a higher context length - With CNN-QR, you can set the `context_length` slightly higher than that for DeepAR+, as CNNs are generally more efficient than RNNs.
L134: Feature engineering of related data - Experiment with different combinations of related time series and item metadata when training your model, and assess whether the additional information improves accuracy. Different combinations and transformations of related time series and item metadata will deliver different results.
L135: CNN-QR does not forecast at the mean quantile – When you set `ForecastTypes` to `mean` with the cite13†CreateForecast API, forecasts will instead be generated at the median quantile (`0.5` or `P50`).

citeturn128view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/forecast/latest/dg/howitworks-missing-values.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 108
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Handling Missing Values - Amazon Forecast
L3: 
L4: cite1†Choosing Filling Logic cite2†Target Time Series and Related Time Series Filling Logic cite3†Missing Value Syntax L5: # Handling Missing Values
L6: A common issue in time-series forecasting data is the presence of missing values. Your data might contain missing values for a number of reasons, including measurement failures, formatting problems, human errors, or a lack of information to record. For instance, if you're forecasting product demand for a retail store and an item is sold out or unavailable, there would be no sales data to record while that item is out of stock.
L7: If prevalent enough, missing values can significantly impact a model's accuracy.
L8: Amazon Forecast provides a number of filling methods to handle missing values in your target time series and related time series datasets. Filling is the process of adding standardized values to missing entries in your dataset.
L9: 
L10: Forecast supports the following filling methods:
L11: 
L12:   * Middle filling – Fills any missing values between the item start and item end date of a data set.
L13: 
L14:   * Back filling – Fills any missing values between the last recorded data point and global end date of a dataset.
L15:   * Future filling (related time series only) – Fills any missing values between the global end date and the end of the forecast horizon.
L16: 
L17: The following image provides a visual representation of different filling methods.
L18: 
L19: cite4†Image: Timeline showing three items with front fill, middle fill, back fill, and future fill periods between global start and end dates. L20: ## Choosing Filling Logic
L21: When choosing a filling logic, you should consider how the logic will be interpreted by your model. For instance, in a retail scenario, recording 0 sales of an available item is different from recording 0 sales of an unavailable item, as the latter does not imply a lack of customer interest in the item.
L22: Because of this, `0` filling in the target time series might cause the predictor to be under-biased in its predictions, while `NaN` filling might ignore actual occurrences of 0 available items being sold and cause the predictor to be over-biased.
L23: The following time-series graphs illustrate how choosing the wrong filling value can significantly affect the accuracy of your model. Graphs A and B plot the demand for an item that is partially out-of-stock, with the black lines representing actual sales data. Missing values in A1 are filled with `0`, leading to relatively under-biased predictions (represented by the dotted lines) in A2. Similarly, missing values in B1 are filled with `NaN`, which leads to predictions that are more exact in B2.
L24: cite5†Image: Two time-series graphs comparing zero-filled versus NaN-filled missing values and their predictions. L25: 
L26: For a list of supported filling logic, see the following section.
L27: ## Target Time Series and Related Time Series Filling Logic
L28: 
L29: You can perform filling on both target time series and related time series datasets. Each dataset type has different filling guidelines and restrictions.
L30: 
L31: Filling Guidelines
L32: Dataset type  | Filling by default?  | Supported filling methods  | Default filling logic  | Accepted filling logic
L33: --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L34: Target time series  | Yes  | Middle and back filling  | 0  |
L35:   * `zero` - 0 filling.
L36:   * `value` - an integer or float number.
L37:   * `nan` - not a number.
L38:   * `mean` - the mean value from the data series.
L39:   * `median` - the median value from the data series.
L40:   * `min` - the minimum value from the data series.
L41:   * `max` - the maximum value from the data series.
L42: Related time series  | No  | Middle, back, and future filling  | No default  |
L43:   * `zero` - 0 filling.
L44:   * `value` - an integer or float value.
L45:   * `mean` - the mean value from the data series.
L46:   * `median` - the median value from the data series.
L47:   * `min` - the minimum value from the data series.
L48:   * `max` - the maximum value from the data series.
L49: ###### Important
L50: 
L51: For both target and related time series datasets, `mean`, `median`, `min`, and `max` are calculated based on a rolling window of the 64 most recent data entries before the missing values.
L52: ## Missing Value Syntax
L53: 
L54: To perform missing value filling, specify the types of filling to implement when you call the cite6†CreatePredictor operation. Filling logic is specified in cite7†FeaturizationMethod objects.
L55: 
L56: The following excerpt demonstrates a correctly formatted `FeaturizationMethod` object for a target time series attribute and related time series attribute (`target_value` and `price` respectively).
L57: To set a filling method to a specific value, set the fill parameter to `value` and define the value in a corresponding `_value` parameter. As shown below, backfilling for the related time series is set to a value of 2 with the following: `"backfill": "value"` and `"backfill_value":"2"`.
L58: 
L59:     `[
L60:         {
L61:             "AttributeName": "target_value",
L62:             "FeaturizationPipeline": [
L63:                 {
L64:                     "FeaturizationMethodName": "filling",
L65:                     "FeaturizationMethodParameters": {
L66:                         "aggregation": "sum",
L67:                         "middlefill": "zero",
L68:                         "backfill": "zero"
L69:                     }
L70:                 }
L71:             ]
L72:         },
L73:         {
L74:             "AttributeName": "price",
L75:             "FeaturizationPipeline": [
L76:                 {
L77:                     "FeaturizationMethodName": "filling",
L78:                     "FeaturizationMethodParameters": {
L79:                         "middlefill": "median",
L80:                         "backfill": "value",
L81:                         "backfill_value": "2",
L82:                         "futurefill": "max"
L83:                         }
L84:                 }
L85:             ]
L86:         }
L87:     ]`

L2: Perform machine learning inference - AWS IoT Greengrass
L3: 
L4: cite1†How AWS IoT Greengrass ML inference works cite2†What's different in AWS IoT Greengrass Version 2? cite3†Requirements cite4†Supported model sources cite5†Supported runtimes cite6†Machine learning components L5: # Perform machine learning inference
L6: 
L7: With AWS IoT Greengrass, you can perform machine learning (ML) inference on your edge devices on locally generated data using cloud-trained models. You benefit from the low latency and cost savings of running local inference, yet still take advantage of cloud computing power for training models and complex processing.
L8: AWS IoT Greengrass makes the steps required to perform inference more efficient. You can train your inference models anywhere and deploy them locally as machine learning components. For example, you can build and train deep-learning models in cite7†Amazon SageMaker AI†console.aws.amazon.com . Then, you can store these models in an cite8†Amazon S3†console.aws.amazon.com bucket, so you can use these models as artifacts in your components to perform inference on your core devices.
L9: ###### Topics
L10: 
L11:   * cite1†How AWS IoT Greengrass ML inference works L12: 
L13:   * cite2†What's different in AWS IoT Greengrass Version 2? L14: 
L15:   * cite3†Requirements L16: 
L17:   * cite4†Supported model sources L18: 
L19:   * cite5†Supported machine learning runtimes L20: 
L21:   * cite6†AWS-provided machine learning components L22: 
L23:   * cite9†Use Amazon SageMaker AI Edge Manager on Greengrass core devices L24: 
L25:   * cite10†Customize your machine learning components L26: 
L27:   * cite11†Troubleshooting machine learning inference L28: ## How AWS IoT Greengrass ML inference works
L29: 
L30: AWS provides cite6†machine learning components that you can use to create one-step deployments to perform machine learning inference on your device. You can also use these components as templates to create custom components to meet your specific requirements.
L31: 
L32: AWS provides the following categories of machine learning components:
L33: 
L34:   * Model component—Contains machine learning models as Greengrass artifacts.
L35:   * Runtime component—Contains the script that installs the machine learning framework and its dependencies on the Greengrass core device.
L36: 
L37:   * Inference component—Contains the inference code and includes component dependencies to install the machine learning framework and download pre-trained machine learning models.
L38: Each deployment that you create to perform machine learning inference consists of at least one component that runs your inference application, installs the machine learning framework, and downloads your machine learning models. To perform sample inference with AWS-provided components, you deploy an inference component to your core device, which automatically includes the corresponding model and runtime components as dependencies.
L39: To customize your deployments, you can plug in or swap out the sample model components with custom model components, or you can use the component recipes for the AWS-provided components as templates to create your own custom inference, model, and runtime components.
L40: To perform machine learning inference by using custom components:
L41: 
L42:   1. Create a model component. This component contains the machine learning models that you want to use to perform inference. AWS provides sample pre-trained DLR and TensorFlow Lite models. To use a custom model, create your own model component.
L43:   2. Create a runtime component. This component contains the scripts required to install the machine learning runtime for your models. AWS provides sample runtime components for cite12†Deep Learning Runtime†github.com (DLR) and cite13†TensorFlow Lite†www.tensorflow.org . To use other runtimes with your custom models and inference code, create your own runtime components.
L44:   3. Create an inference component. This component contains your inference code, and includes your model and runtime components as dependencies. AWS provides sample inference components for image classification and object detection using DLR and TensorFlow Lite. To perform other types of inference, or to use custom models and runtimes, create your own inference component.
L45:   4. Deploy the inference component. When you deploy this component, AWS IoT Greengrass also automatically deploys the model and runtime component dependencies.
L46: 
L47: To get started with AWS-provided components, see cite14†Tutorial: Perform sample image classification inference using TensorFlow Lite .
L48: 
L49: For information about creating custom machine learning components, see cite10†Customize your machine learning components .
L50: ## What's different in AWS IoT Greengrass Version 2?
L51: 
L52: AWS IoT Greengrass consolidates functional units for machine learning—such as models, runtimes, and inference code— into components that enable you to use a one-step process to install the machine learning runtime, download your trained models, and perform inference on your device.
L53: By using the AWS-provided machine learning components, you have the flexibility to start performing machine learning inference with sample inference code and pre-trained models. You can plug in custom model components to use your own custom-trained models with the inference and runtime components that AWS provides. For a completely customized machine learning solution, you can use the public components as templates to create custom components and use any runtime, model, or inference type that you want.
L54: ## Requirements
L55: 
L56: To create and use machine learning components, you must have the following:
L57: 
L58:   * A Greengrass core device. If you don't have one, see cite15†Tutorial: Getting started with AWS IoT Greengrass V2 .
L59: 
L60:   * Minimum 500 MB local storage space to use AWS-provided sample machine learning components.
L61: ## Supported model sources
L62: 
L63: AWS IoT Greengrass supports using custom-trained machine learning models that are stored in Amazon S3. You can also use Amazon SageMaker AI edge packaging jobs to directly create model components for your SageMaker AI Neo-compiled models. For information about using SageMaker AI Edge Manager with AWS IoT Greengrass, see cite9†Use Amazon SageMaker AI Edge Manager on Greengrass core devices .
L64: 
L65: The S3 buckets that contain your models must meet the following requirements:
L66:   * They must not be encrypted using SSE-C. For buckets that use server-side encryption, AWS IoT Greengrass machine learning inference currently supports the SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS encryption options only. For more information about server-side encryption options, see cite16†Protecting data using server-side encryption in the Amazon Simple Storage Service User Guide.
L67:   * Their names must not include periods (`.`). For more information, see the rule about using virtual hosted-style buckets with SSL in cite17†Rules for bucket naming in the Amazon Simple Storage Service User Guide.
L68: 
L69:   * The S3 buckets that store your model sources must be in the same AWS account and AWS Region as your machine learning components.
L70:   * AWS IoT Greengrass must have `read` permission to the model source. To enable AWS IoT Greengrass to access the S3 buckets, the cite18†Greengrass device role must allow the `s3:GetObject` action. For more information about the device role, see cite18†Authorize core devices to interact with AWS services .
L71: ## Supported machine learning runtimes
L72: 
L73: AWS IoT Greengrass enables you to create custom components to use any machine learning runtime of your choice to perform machine learning inference with your custom-trained models. For information about creating custom machine learning components, see cite10†Customize your machine learning components .
L74: To make the process of getting started with machine learning more efficient, AWS IoT Greengrass provides sample inference, model, and runtime components that use the following machine learning runtimes:
L75: 
L76:   * cite12†Deep Learning Runtime†github.com (DLR) v1.6.0 and v1.3.0
L77: 
L78:   * cite13†TensorFlow Lite†www.tensorflow.org v2.5.0
L79: ## AWS-provided machine learning components
L80: 
L81: The following table lists the AWS-provided components used for machine learning.

L83:

Because of this dependency, you need to update these components when you update the Greengrass nucleus to a new minor version. For information about the specific versions of the nucleus that each component depends on, see the corresponding component topic. For more information about updating the nucleus, see cite19†Update the AWS IoT Greengrass Core software (OTA) .

L6: 
L7: Snowball Edge is a device with on-board storage and compute power for select AWS capabilities. Snowball Edge can process data locally, run edge-computing workloads, and transfer data to or from the AWS Cloud.
L8: 
L9: Each Snowball Edge device can transport data at speeds faster than the internet. This transport is done by shipping the data in the devices through a regional carrier. The appliances are rugged, complete with E Ink shipping labels.
L10: Snowball Edge devices have two options for device configurations—Storage Optimized 210 TB and Compute Optimized. When this guide refers to Snowball Edge devices, it's referring to all options of the device. When specific information applies only to one or more optional configurations of devices, it is called out specifically. For more information, see cite7†Snowball Edge device configurations .

L27:   * cite9†Prerequisites for using Snowball Edge L28: ## Snowball Edge features
L29: 
L30: Snowball Edge devices have the following features:
L31: 
L32:   * Large amounts of storage capacity or compute functionality for devices. This depends on the options you choose when you create your job.
L33: 
L34:   * Network adapters with transfer speeds of up to 100 Gbit/second.
L35: 
L36:   * Encryption is enforced, protecting your data at rest and in physical transit.
L37:   * You can import or export data between your local environments and Amazon S3, and physically transport the data with one or more devices without using the internet.
L38: 
L39:   * Snowball Edge devices are their own rugged box. The built-in E Ink display changes to show your shipping label when the device is ready to ship.
L40: 
L41:   * Snowball Edge devices come with an on-board LCD display that can be used to manage network connections and get service status information.
L42:   * You can cluster Snowball Edge devices for local storage and compute jobs to achieve data durability across 3 to 16 devices and locally grow or shrink storage on demand.
L43: 
L44:   * You can use Amazon EKS Anywhere on Snowball Edge devices for Kubernetes workloads.
L45: 
L46:   * Snowball Edge devices have Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2 compatible endpoints available, enabling programmatic use cases.
L47:   * Snowball Edge devices support the new `sbe1`, `sbe-c`, and `sbe-g` instance types, which you can use to run compute instances on the device using Amazon Machine Images (AMIs).
L48: 
L49:   * Snowball Edge supports these data transfer protocols for data migration:
L50: 
L51:     * NFSv3
L52: 
L53:     * NFSv4
L54: 
L55:     * NFSv4.1
L56: 
L57:     * Amazon S3 over HTTP or HTTPS (via API compatible with AWS CLI version 1.16.14 and earlier)
L58: ## Services related to Snowball Edge
L59: 
L60: You can use an AWS Snowball Edge device with the following related AWS services:
L61:   * Amazon S3 adapter — Use for programmatic data transfer in to and out of AWS using the Amazon S3 API for Snowball Edge, which supports a subset of Amazon S3 API operations. In this role, data is transferred to the Snow device by AWS on your behalf and the device is shipped to you (for an export job), or AWS ships an empty Snow device to you and you transfer data from your on-premises sources to the device and ship it back to AWS (for an import job)"
L62:   * Amazon S3 compatible storage on Snowball Edge — Use to support the data needs of compute services such as Amazon EC2, Amazon EKS Anywhere on Snow, and others. This feature is available on Snowball Edge devices and provides an expanded Amazon S3 API set and features such as increased resiliency with flexible cluster setup for 3 to 16 nodes, local bucket management, and local notifications.
L63:   * Amazon EC2 – Run compute instances on a Snowball Edge device using the Amazon EC2 compatible endpoint, which supports a subset of the Amazon EC2 API operations. For more information about using Amazon EC2 in AWS, see cite10†Getting started with Amazon EC2 Linux instances .
L64: 
L65:   * Amazon EKS Anywhere on Snow – Create and operate Kubernetes clusters on Snowball Edge devices. See cite11†Using Amazon EKS Anywhere on AWS Snow .
L66:   * AWS Lambda powered by AWS IoT Greengrass – Invoke Lambda functions based on Amazon S3 compatible storage on Snowball Edge storage actions made on an AWS Snowball Edge device. For more information about using Lambda, see cite12†Using AWS Lambda with an AWS Snowball Edge and the cite13†AWS Lambda Developer Guide .
L67: 
L68:   * Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – Provide block-level storage volumes for use with EC2-compatible instances. For more information, see cite14†Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) .
L69:   * AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) – Use this service to securely control access to AWS resources. For more information, see cite15†What is IAM? L70: 
L71:   * AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) – Request temporary, limited-privilege credentials for IAM users or for users that you authenticate (federated users). For more information, see cite16†Temporary security credentials in IAM .
L72:   * Amazon EC2 Systems Manager – Use this service to view and control your infrastructure on AWS. For more information, see cite17†What is AWS Systems Manager? L73: ## Accessing the Snowball Edge service
L74: 
L75: You can use the cite18†AWS Snow Family Management Console†console.aws.amazon.com or the job management API to create and manage jobs. For more information about using the cite18†AWS Snow Family Management Console†console.aws.amazon.com , see cite19†Getting started with Snowball Edge . For information about the job management API, see cite20†Job Management API Reference for Snowball Edge .
L76: ### Accessing an AWS Snowball Edge device
L77: 
L78: After your Snowball Edge device is onsite, you can configure it with an IP address using the LCD screen then you can unlock the device using the Snowball Edge client or AWS OpsHub. Then, you run can perform data transfer or edge compute tasks. For more information, see cite21†Receiving the Snowball Edge .
L79: ## Pricing for the Snowball Edge
L80: 
L81: For information about the pricing and fees associated with the service and its devices, see cite22†AWS Snowball Edge Pricing.†aws.amazon.com L82: ## AWS monitoring of Snowball Edge
L83: 
L84: AWS will monitor the Snow device and may collect metrics and usage information when the Snow device is connected to an AWS Region. If the Snow device is not connected to the AWS Region, then AWS will not monitor the Snow device.
L85: If AWS detects an irreparable issue, and there is a need to replace physical equipment, AWS will notify you. You can then place a replacement job that we will ship to your site. There is no additional charge for this, as Snow device monitoring is included as part of the Snow device service fee.
L86: ## Resources for first-time AWS Snowball Edge users
L87: 
L88: If you are a first-time user of the AWS Snowball Edge service, we recommend that you read the following sections in order:
L89: 
L90:   1. For information about device types and options, see cite8†AWS Snowball Edge device hardware information .
L91: 
L92:   2. To learn more about the types of jobs, see cite23†Understanding Snowball Edge jobs .

L95:   4. When you're ready to get started, see cite19†Getting started with Snowball Edge .
L96: 
L97:   5. For information about using compute instances on a device, see cite25†Using Amazon EC2-compatible compute instances on Snowball Edge .

L2: Pre-training Bias Metrics - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: # Pre-training Bias Metrics
L5: ###### Note
L6: 
L7: Amazon SageMaker Clarify is no longer open to new customers. Existing customers can continue to use the service as normal. AWS continues to invest in security and availability improvements for Clarify, but we do not plan to introduce new features. For more information, see cite1†Clarify availability change .
L8: Measuring bias in ML models is a first step to mitigating bias. Each measure of bias corresponds to a different notion of fairness. Even considering simple concepts of fairness leads to many different measures applicable in various contexts. For example, consider fairness with respect to age, and, for simplicity, that middle-aged and rest of the age groups are the two relevant demographics, referred to as facets.
L9: In the case of an ML model for lending, we may want small business loans to be issued to equal numbers of both demographics. Or, when processing job applicants, we may want to see equal numbers of members of each demographic hired. However, this approach may assume that equal numbers of both age groups apply to these jobs, so we may want to condition on the number that apply. Further, we may want to consider not whether equal numbers apply, but whether we have equal numbers of qualified applicants.
L10: Or, we may consider fairness to be an equal acceptance rate of qualified applicants across both age demographics, or, an equal rejection rate of applicants, or both. You might use datasets with different proportions of data on the attributes of interest. This imbalance can conflate the bias measure you choose. The models might be more accurate in classifying one facet than in the other. Thus, you need to choose bias metrics that are conceptually appropriate for the application and the situation.
L11: We use the following notation to discuss the bias metrics. The conceptual model described here is for binary classification, where events are labeled as having only two possible outcomes in their sample space, referred to as positive (with value 1) and negative (with value 0). This framework is usually extensible to multicategory classification in a straightforward way or to cases involving continuous valued outcomes when needed.
L12: In the binary classification case, positive and negative labels are assigned to outcomes recorded in a raw dataset for a favored facet a and for a disfavored facet d. These labels y are referred to as observed labels to distinguish them from the predicted labels y' that are assigned by a machine learning model during the training or inferences stages of the ML lifecycle. These labels are used to define probability distributions P_{a}(y) and P_{d}(y) for their respective facet outcomes.
L13:   * labels:
L14: 
L15:     * y represents the n observed labels for event outcomes in a training dataset.
L16: 
L17:     * y' represents the predicted labels for the n observed labels in the dataset by a trained model.
L18: 
L19:   * outcomes:
L20: 
L21:     * A positive outcome (with value 1) for a sample, such as an application acceptance.
L22: 
L23:       * n^{(1)} is the number of observed labels for positive outcomes (acceptances).
L24: 
L25:       * n'^{(1)} is the number of predicted labels for positive outcomes (acceptances).
L26:     * A negative outcome (with value 0) for a sample, such as an application rejection.
L27: 
L28:       * n^{(0)} is the number of observed labels for negative outcomes (rejections).
L29: 
L30:       * n'^{(0)} is the number of predicted labels for negative outcomes (rejections).
L31: 
L32:   * facet values:
L33: 
L34:     * facet a – The feature value that defines a demographic that bias favors.
L35:       * n_{a} is the number of observed labels for the favored facet value: n_{a} = n_{a}^{(1)} + n_{a}^{(0)} the sum of the positive and negative observed labels for the value facet a.
L36: 
L37:       * n'_{a} is the number of predicted labels for the favored facet value: n'_{a} = n'_{a}^{(1)} + n'_{a}^{(0)} the sum of the positive and negative predicted outcome labels for the facet value a. Note that n'_{a} = n_{a}.
L38: 
L39:     * facet d – The feature value that defines a demographic that bias disfavors.
L40:       * n_{d} is the number of observed labels for the disfavored facet value: n_{d} = n_{d}^{(1)} + n_{d}^{(0)} the sum of the positive and negative observed labels for the facet value d.
L41: 
L42:       * n'_{d} is the number of predicted labels for the disfavored facet value: n'_{d} = n'_{d}^{(1)} + n'_{d}^{(0)} the sum of the positive and negative predicted labels for the facet value d. Note that n'_{d} = n_{d}.
L43: 
L44:   * probability distributions for outcomes of the labeled facet data outcomes:
L45:     * P_{a}(y) is the probability distribution of the observed labels for facet a. For binary labeled data, this distribution is given by the ratio of the number of samples in facet a labeled with positive outcomes to the total number, P_{a}(y^{1}) = n_{a}^{(1)}/ n_{a}, and the ratio of the number of samples with negative outcomes to the total number, P_{a}(y^{0}) = n_{a}^{(0)}/ n_{a}.
L46:     * P_{d}(y) is the probability distribution of the observed labels for facet d. For binary labeled data, this distribution is given by the number of samples in facet d labeled with positive outcomes to the total number, P_{d}(y^{1}) = n_{d}^{(1)}/ n_{d}, and the ratio of the number of samples with negative outcomes to the total number, P_{d}(y^{0}) = n_{d}^{(0)}/ n_{d}.
L47: Models trained on data biased by demographic disparities might learn and even exacerbate them. To identify bias in the data before expending resources to train models on it, SageMaker Clarify provides data bias metrics that you can compute on raw datasets before training. All of the pretraining metrics are model-agnostic because they do not depend on model outputs and so are valid for any model. The first bias metric examines facet imbalance, but not outcomes.
L48: It determines the extent to which the amount of training data is representative across different facets, as desired for the application. The remaining bias metrics compare the distribution of outcome labels in various ways for facets a and d in the data. The metrics that range over negative values can detect negative bias. The following table contains a cheat sheet for quick guidance and links to the pretraining bias metrics.
L49: Pre-training Bias Metrics
L50: 
L51: Bias metric  | Description  | Example question  | Interpreting metric values
L52: --- | --- | --- | ---
L53: cite2†Class Imbalance (CI) | Measures the imbalance in the number of members between different facet values.  | Could there be age-based biases due to not having enough data for the demographic outside a middle-aged facet?  | Normalized range: [-1,+1] Interpretation:
L54:   * Positive values indicate the facet a has more training samples in the dataset.
L55:   * Values near zero indicate the facets are balanced in the number of training samples in the dataset.
L56:   * Negative values indicate the facet d has more training samples in the dataset.
L57: cite3†Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL) | Measures the imbalance of positive outcomes between different facet values.  | Could there be age-based biases in ML predictions due to biased labeling of facet values in the data?  | Range for normalized binary & multicategory facet labels: [-1,+1] Range for continuous labels: (-∞, +∞) Interpretation:
L58:   * Positive values indicate facet a has a higher proportion of positive outcomes.
L59:   * Values near zero indicate a more equal proportion of positive outcomes between facets.
L60:   * Negative values indicate facet d has a higher proportion of positive outcomes.
L61: cite4†Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL) | Measures how much the outcome distributions of different facets diverge from each other entropically.  | How different are the distributions for loan application outcomes for different demographic groups?  | Range for binary, multicategory, continuous: [0, +∞) Interpretation:
L62:   * Values near zero indicate the labels are similarly distributed.
L63:   * Positive values indicate the label distributions diverge, the more positive the larger the divergence.
L64: cite5†Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JS) | Measures how much the outcome distributions of different facets diverge from each other entropically.  | How different are the distributions for loan application outcomes for different demographic groups?  | Range for binary, multicategory, continuous: [0, +∞) Interpretation:
L65:   * Values near zero indicate the labels are similarly distributed.
L66:   * Positive values indicate the label distributions diverge, the more positive the larger the divergence.
L67: cite6†Lp-norm (LP) | Measures a p-norm difference between distinct demographic distributions of the outcomes associated with different facets in a dataset.  | How different are the distributions for loan application outcomes for different demographics?  | Range for binary, multicategory, continuous: [0, +∞) Interpretation:
L68:   * Values near zero indicate the labels are similarly distributed.
L69:   * Positive values indicate the label distributions diverge, the more positive the larger the divergence.
L70: cite7†Total Variation Distance (TVD) | Measures half of the L_{1}-norm difference between distinct demographic distributions of the outcomes associated with different facets in a dataset.  | How different are the distributions for loan application outcomes for different demographics?  | Range for binary, multicategory, and continuous outcomes: [0, +∞)
L71:   * Values near zero indicates the labels are similarly distributed.
L72:   * Positive values indicates the label distributions diverge, the more positive the larger the divergence.
L73: cite8†Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) | Measures maximum divergence between outcomes in distributions for different facets in a dataset.  | Which college application outcomes manifest the greatest disparities by demographic group?  | Range of KS values for binary, multicategory, and continuous outcomes: [0,+1]
L74:   * Values near zero indicate the labels were evenly distributed between facets in all outcome categories.
L75:   * Values near one indicate the labels for one category were all in one facet, so very imbalanced.
L76:   * Intermittent values indicate relative degrees of maximum label imbalance.
L77: cite9†Conditional Demographic Disparity (CDD) | Measures the disparity of outcomes between different facets as a whole, but also by subgroups.  | Do some groups have a larger proportion of rejections for college admission outcomes than their proportion of acceptances?  | Range of CDD: [-1, +1]
L78:   * Positive values indicate a outcomes where facet d is rejected more than accepted.
L79:   * Near zero indicates no demographic disparity on average.
L80:   * Negative values indicate a outcomes where facet a is rejected more than accepted.
L81: 
L82: For additional information about bias metrics, see cite10†Fairness Measures for Machine Learning in Finance†pages.awscloud.com .

L6: # What is AWS DataSync?
L7: 
L8: AWS DataSync is a secure, reliable, high‐speed file transfer service that helps you quickly and easily transfer your file or object data to, from, and between AWS storage services.
L9: ###### On-premises storage transfers
L10: 
L11: DataSync works with the following on-premises storage systems:
L12: 
L13:   * cite4†Network File System (NFS) L14: 
L15:   * cite5†Server Message Block (SMB) L16: 
L17:   * cite6†Hadoop Distributed File Systems (HDFS) L18: 
L19:   * cite7†Object storage L20: ###### AWS storage transfers
L21: 
L22: DataSync works with the following AWS storage services:
L23: 
L24:   * cite8†Amazon S3 L25: 
L26:   * cite9†Amazon EFS L27: 
L28:   * cite10†Amazon FSx for Windows File Server L29: 
L30:   * cite11†Amazon FSx for Lustre L31: 
L32:   * cite12†Amazon FSx for OpenZFS L33: 
L34:   * cite13†Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP L35: ###### Other cloud storage transfers
L36: 
L37: DataSync works with the following storage services in other clouds:
L38: 
L39:   * cite14†Google Cloud Storage L40: 
L41:   * cite15†Microsoft Azure Blob Storage L42: 
L43:   * cite16†Microsoft Azure Files L44: 
L45:   * cite17†Wasabi Cloud Storage L46: 
L47:   * cite17†DigitalOcean Spaces L48: 
L49:   * cite17†Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Object Storage L50: 
L51:   * cite17†Cloudflare R2 Storage L52: 
L53:   * cite17†Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage L54: 
L55:   * cite17†NAVER Cloud Object Storage L56: 
L57:   * cite17†Alibaba Cloud Object Storage Service L58: 
L59:   * cite17†IBM Cloud Object Storage L60:   * cite17†Seagate Lyve Cloud L61: ## Use cases
L62: 
L63: These are some of the main use cases for DataSync:
L64: 
L65:   * Migrate data – Transfer active datasets rapidly over the network into AWS storage services. DataSync includes automatic encryption and data integrity validation to help make sure that your data arrives securely, intact, and ready to use.
L66:   * Archive cold data – Move cold data stored in on-premises storage directly to durable and secure long-term storage classes such as S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Doing so can free up on-premises storage capacity and help you shut down legacy systems.
L67: 
L68:   * Replicate data – Copy data into most Amazon S3 storage classes, choosing the most cost-effective one for your needs. You can also send data to Amazon EFS or Amazon FSx for a standby file system.
L69:   * Transfer data for timely in-cloud processing – Transfer data in or out of AWS for processing. This approach can speed up critical hybrid cloud workflows across many industries. These include machine learning in the life-sciences industry, video production in media and entertainment, big-data analytics in financial services, and seismic research in the oil and gas industry.
L70: ## Benefits
L71: 
L72: By using DataSync, you can get the following benefits:
L73: 
L74:   * Automate data movement – DataSync makes it easier to transfer data over the network between storage systems and services. DataSync automates both the management of data-transfer processes and the infrastructure required for high performance and secure data transfers.
L75:   * Transfer data securely – DataSync provides end-to-end security, including encryption and data integrity validation, to help ensure that your data arrives securely, intact, and ready to use. DataSync accesses your AWS storage through built-in AWS security mechanisms, such as AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
L76: It also supports virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, giving you the option to transfer data without traversing the public internet and further increasing the security of data copied online.
L77:   * Move data faster – DataSync uses a purpose-built network protocol and a parallel, multi-threaded architecture to accelerate your transfers. This approach speeds up migrations, recurring data-processing workflows for analytics and machine learning, and data-protection processes.
L78: ## Additional resources
L79: 
L80: We recommend that you read the following:
L81: 
L82:   * cite18†DataSync resources†aws.amazon.com – Includes blogs, videos, and other training materials
L83: 
L84:   * cite19†AWS re:Post†repost.aws – See the latest discussion around DataSync

Video playback with HLS - Amazon Kinesis Video Streams (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kinesisvideostreams/latest/dg/hls-playback.html)
citeturn132view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kinesisvideostreams/latest/dg/hls-playback.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 322
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Video playback with HLS - Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
L3: 
L4: cite1†Use the AWS CLI to retrieve an HLS streaming session URL cite2†Example: Use HLS in HTML and JavaScript cite3†Troubleshooting HLS issues L5: # Video playback with HLS
L6: 
L7: cite4†HTTP Live Streaming (HLS)†en.wikipedia.org is an industry standard HTTP-based media streaming communications protocol. You can use HLS to view a Kinesis video stream, either for live playback or to view archived video.
L8: You can use HLS for live playback. Latency is typically between 3–5 seconds, but it can be between 1–10 seconds, depending on the use case, player, and network conditions. You can use a third-party player (such as cite5†Video.js†github.com or cite6†Google Shaka Player†github.com ) to display the video stream by providing the HLS streaming session URL, either programmatically or manually.
L9: You can also play back video by entering the HLS streaming session URL in the Location bar of the cite7†Apple Safari†www.apple.com or cite8†Microsoft Edge†www.microsoft.com browsers.
L10: To view a Kinesis video stream using HLS, first create a streaming session using cite9†GetHLSStreamingSessionURL . This action returns a URL (containing a session token) for accessing the HLS session. You can then use the URL in a media player or a standalone application to display the stream.
L11: ###### Important
L12: 
L13: Not all media sent to Kinesis Video Streams can be played back through HLS. See cite10†GetHLSStreamingSessionURL for specific uploading requirements.
L14: 
L15: ###### Topics
L16: 
L17:   * cite1†Use the AWS CLI to retrieve an HLS streaming session URL L18: 
L19:   * cite2†Example: Use HLS in HTML and JavaScript L20: 
L21:   * cite3†Troubleshooting HLS issues L22: ## Use the AWS CLI to retrieve an HLS streaming session URL
L23: 
L24: The following procedure demonstrates how to use the AWS CLI to generate an HLS streaming session URL for a Kinesis video stream.
L25: 
L26: For installation instructions, see the cite11†AWS Command Line Interface User Guide . After installation, cite12†configure the AWS CLI with credentials and region.
L27: 
L28: Alternatively, open the AWS CloudShell terminal, which has the AWS CLI installed and configured. See the cite13†AWS CloudShell User Guide for more information.
L29: ###### Retrieve the HLS URL endpoint for your Kinesis video stream.
L30: 
L31:   1. Type the following into the terminal:
L32: 
L33:     `aws kinesisvideo get-data-endpoint \
L34:       --api-name GET_HLS_STREAMING_SESSION_URL \
L35:       --stream-name `YourStreamName``
L36: 
L37: You'll receive a response that looks like this:
L38: 
L39:     `{
L40:         "DataEndpoint": "https://b-`1234abcd`.kinesisvideo.`aws-region`.amazonaws.com"
L41:     }`
L42: 
L43:   2. Make the HLS streaming session URL request to that returned endpoint.
L44: 
L45: Live
L46: For live playback, the HLS media playlist is continually updated with the latest media as it becomes available. When you play this type of session in a media player, the user interface typically displays a "live" notification, with no scrubber control for choosing the position in the playback window to display.
L47: Make sure that you are uploading media to this stream when you run this command.
L48: 
L49:     `aws kinesis-video-archived-media get-hls-streaming-session-url \
L50:       --endpoint-url https://b-`1234abcd`.kinesisvideo.`aws-region`.amazonaws.com \
L51:       --stream-name `YourStreamName` \
L52:       --playback-mode LIVE`
L53: 
L54: Live replay
L55: For live replay, playback starts from a specified start time. The HLS media playlist is also continually updated with the latest media as it becomes available. The session will continue to include newly ingested media until the session expires, or until the specified end time, whichever comes first. This mode is useful to be able to start playback from when an event is detected and continue live streaming media that has not yet been ingested as of the time of the session creation.
L56: Determine a start timestamp.
L57: 
L58: For this example, we use the Unix Epoch time in seconds format. Refer to the cite14†Timestamps section in the AWS Command Line Interface User Guide for more information on timestamp formatting.
L59: 
L60: See cite15†UnixTime.org†unixtime.org for a conversion tool.
L61: 
L62:      * 1708471800 is equal to February 20, 2024 3:30:00 PM GMT-08:00
L63: 
L64: In this example, we don't specify an end timestamp, meaning that the session will continue to include newly ingested media until the session expires.
L65: Invoke the `GetHLSStreamingSessionURL` API with `LIVE_REPLAY` playback mode and an cite16†HLS Fragment Selector specified.
L66: 
L67:     `aws kinesis-video-archived-media get-hls-streaming-session-url \
L68:       --endpoint-url https://b-`1234abcd`.kinesisvideo.`aws-region`.amazonaws.com \
L69:       --stream-name `YourStreamName` \
L70:       --playback-mode LIVE_REPLAY \
L71:       --hls-fragment-selector \
L72:         "FragmentSelectorType=SERVER_TIMESTAMP,TimestampRange={StartTimestamp=`1708471800`}"`
L73: 
L74: On-demand
L75: For on demand playback, the HLS media playlist contains the media specified by the HLS fragment selector. When this type of session is played in a media player, the user interface typically displays a scrubber control for choosing the position in the playback window to display.
L76: 
L77: To create a URL for a certain section of stream, first determine start and end timestamps.
L78: For this example, we use the Unix Epoch time in seconds format. Refer to the cite14†Timestamps section in the AWS Command Line Interface User Guide for more information on timestamp formatting.
L79: 
L80: See cite15†UnixTime.org†unixtime.org for a conversion tool.
L81: 
L82:      * 1708471800 is equal to February 20, 2024 3:30:00 PM GMT-08:00
L83: 
L84:      * 1708471860 is equal to February 20, 2024 3:31:00 PM GMT-08:00
L85: Invoke the `GetHLSStreamingSessionURL` API with `ON_DEMAND` playback mode and an cite16†HLS Fragment Selector specified.
L86: 
L87:     `aws kinesis-video-archived-media get-hls-streaming-session-url \
L88:       --endpoint-url https://b-`1234abcd`.kinesisvideo.`aws-region`.amazonaws.com \
L89:       --stream-name `YourStreamName` \
L90:       --playback-mode ON_DEMAND \
L91:       --hls-fragment-selector \
L92:         "FragmentSelectorType=SERVER_TIMESTAMP,TimestampRange={StartTimestamp=`1708471800`,EndTimestamp=`1708471860`}" `
L93: ###### Note
L94: 
L95: The timestamps must be within 24-hours of each other, as mentioned in the cite17†HLSTimestampRange documentation.
L96: 
L97: You'll receive a response that looks like this:
L98: 
L99:     `{
L100:         "HLSStreamingSessionURL": "https://b-`1234abcd`.kinesisvideo.`aws-region`.amazonaws.com/hls/v1/getHLSMasterPlaylist.m3u8?SessionToken=`CiAz...DkRE6M`~"
L101:     }`
L102: ###### Important
L103: 
L104: Don't share or store this token where an unauthorized entity could access it. The token provides access to the content of the stream. Safeguard the token with the same measures that you would use with your AWS credentials.
L105: 
L106: You can use this URL and any HLS player to view the HLS stream.
L107: 
L108: For example, use VLC media player.
L109: 
L110: You can also play the HLS Stream by entering the HLS streaming session URL in the Location bar of the Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge browsers.
L111: ## Example: Use HLS in HTML and JavaScript
L112: 
L113: The following example shows how to use the AWS SDK for JavaScript v2 to retrieve an HLS streaming session for a Kinesis video stream and play it back in a web page. The example shows how to play back video in the following players:
L114: 
L115:   * cite5†Video.js†github.com L116: 
L117:   * cite6†Google Shaka Player†github.com L118: 
L119:   * cite18†hls.js†github.com L120: View the cite19†complete example code†github.com and cite20†hosted web page†aws-samples.github.io in GitHub. This static webpage simplifies testing and experimenting with HLS and MPEG-DASH output from Amazon Kinesis video stream. The example page provides input fields for the following parameters:
L121: 
L122:   * AWS Region: The Region where your Kinesis video stream is located
L123: 
L124:   * Stream name: The name of your Kinesis video stream
L125: 
L126:   * Playback mode: The HLS playback mode (LIVE, LIVE_REPLAY, or ON_DEMAND)
L127:   * Fragment selector type: The method used to select fragments (SERVER_TIMESTAMP or PRODUCER_TIMESTAMP)
L128: 
L129:   * Fragment number: The starting fragment number (when applicable)
L130: 
L131:   * Container format: The format of the media container (FRAGMENTED_MP4 or MPEG_TS)
L132: 
L133: The application retrieves these values from the input boxes on the HTML page and uses them to construct the request for an HLS streaming session that displays on the page.
L134: ###### Code walk through topics:
L135: 
L136:   * cite21†Import the AWS SDK for JavaScript for browsers L137: 
L138:   * cite22†Set up the Kinesis Video Streams client L139: 
L140:   * cite23†Retrieve the endpoint for HLS playback L141: 
L142:   * cite24†Set up the Kinesis Video Streams archived media client L143: 
L144:   * cite25†Retrieve the HLS streaming session URL L145: 
L146:   * cite26†Display the HLS stream on the web page L147: ### Import the AWS SDK for JavaScript for browsers
L148: 
L149: In the web page, include the following script tag to import the AWS SDK for JavaScript v2 into the project.
L150: 
L151:     `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/aws-sdk/2.490.0/aws-sdk.min.js"></script>`
L152: 
L153: For more information, refer to the cite27†AWS SDK for JavaScript documentation.
L154: ### Set up the Kinesis Video Streams client
L155: 
L156: To access streaming video with HLS, first create and configure the Kinesis Video Streams client. See cite28†Setting Credentials in a Web Browser for other authentication methods.
L157: 
L158:     `const clientConfig = {
L159:         accessKeyId: '`YourAccessKey`',
L160:         secretAccessKey: '`YourSecretKey`',
L161:         region: '`us-west-2`'
L162:     };
L163:     const kinesisVideoClient = new AWS.KinesisVideo(clientConfig);`
L164: The application retrieves the necessary values from input boxes on the HTML page.
L165: ### Retrieve the endpoint for HLS playback
L166: 
L167: Use the Kinesis Video Streams client to invoke the cite29†GetDataEndpoint API to retrieve the endpoint.
L168: 
L169:     `const getDataEndpointOptions = {
L170:         StreamName: '`YourStreamName`',
L171:         APIName: 'GET_HLS_STREAMING_SESSION_URL'
L172:     };
L173:     const getDataEndpointResponse = await kinesisVideoClient
L174:         .getDataEndpoint(getDataEndpointOptions)
L175:         .promise();
L176:     const hlsDataEndpoint = getDataEndpointResponse.DataEndpoint;`
L177: This code stores the endpoint in the `hlsDataEndpoint` variable.
L178: ### Set up the Kinesis Video Streams archived media client
L179: In the client configuration for the Kinesis Video Streams archived media client, specify the endpoint that you obtained in the previous step.
L180: 
L181:     `const archivedMediaClientConfig = {
L182:         accessKeyId: '`YourAccessKey'`,
L183:         secretAccessKey: '`YourSecretKey'`,
L184:         region: '`us-west-2`',
L185:         endpoint: hlsDataEndpoint
L186:     };
L187:     const kinesisVideoArchivedMediaClient = new AWS.KinesisVideoArchivedMedia(archivedMediaClientConfig);  `
L188: ### Retrieve the HLS streaming session URL
L189: Use the Kinesis Video Streams archived media client to invoke the cite10†GetHLSStreamingSessionURL API to retrieve the HLS playback URL.
L190: 
L191:     `const getHLSStreamingSessionURLOptions = {
L192:         StreamName: '`YourStreamName`',
L193:         PlaybackMode: 'LIVE'
L194:     };
L195:     const getHLSStreamingSessionURLResponse = await kinesisVideoArchivedMediaClient
L196:         .getHLSStreamingSessionURL(getHLSStreamingSessionURLOptions)
L197:         .promise();
L198:     const hlsUrl = getHLSStreamingSessionURLResponse.HLSStreamingSessionURL;`
L199: ### Display the HLS stream on the web page
L200: 
L201: When you have the HLS streaming session URL, provide it to the video player. The method for providing the URL to the video player is specific to the player used.
L202: 
L203: Video.js
L204: Do the following to import cite5†Video.js†github.com and its CSS classes into our browser script:
L205: 
L206:     `<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://vjs.zencdn.net/6.6.3/video-js.css">
L207:     <script src="https://vjs.zencdn.net/6.6.3/video.js"></script>
