L21: ###### Tip
L22: 
L23: To learn best practices for distributed computing of machine learning (ML) training and processing jobs in general, see cite9†Distributed computing with SageMaker AI best practices .
L24: ## Use Amazon SageMaker Processing Sample Notebooks
L25: 
L26: We provide two sample Jupyter notebooks that show how to perform data preprocessing, model evaluation, or both.
L27: For a sample notebook that shows how to run scikit-learn scripts to perform data preprocessing and model training and evaluation with the SageMaker Python SDK for Processing, see cite10†scikit-learn Processing†github.com . This notebook also shows how to use your own custom container to run processing workloads with your Python libraries and other specific dependencies.
L28: For a sample notebook that shows how to use Amazon SageMaker Processing to perform distributed data preprocessing with Spark, see cite11†Distributed Processing (Spark)†github.com . This notebook also shows how to train a regression model using XGBoost on the preprocessed dataset.
L29: For instructions on how to create and access Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run these samples in SageMaker AI, see cite12†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances . After you have created a notebook instance and opened it, choose the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI samples. To open a notebook, choose its Use tab and choose Create copy.
L30: ## Monitor Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics
L31: 
L32: Amazon SageMaker Processing provides Amazon CloudWatch logs and metrics to monitor processing jobs. CloudWatch provides CPU, GPU, memory, GPU memory, and disk metrics, and event logging. For more information, see cite13†Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and cite14†CloudWatch Logs for Amazon SageMaker AI .

L11: Experiments Classic automatically tracks the inputs, parameters, configurations, and results of your iterations as runs. You can assign, group, and organize these runs into experiments. L12: SageMaker Experiments tracks all of the steps and artifacts that went into creating a model, and you can quickly revisit the origins of a model when you are troubleshooting issues in production, or auditing your models for compliance verifications.

L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the IP Insights Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the IP Insights Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # IP Insights
L6: Amazon SageMaker AI IP Insights is an unsupervised learning algorithm that learns the usage patterns for IPv4 addresses. It is designed to capture associations between IPv4 addresses and various entities, such as user IDs or account numbers. You can use it to identify a user attempting to log into a web service from an anomalous IP address, for example. Or you can use it to identify an account that is attempting to create computing resources from an unusual IP address.
L7: Trained IP Insight models can be hosted at an endpoint for making real-time predictions or used for processing batch transforms.
L8: SageMaker AI IP insights ingests historical data as (entity, IPv4 Address) pairs and learns the IP usage patterns of each entity. When queried with an (entity, IPv4 Address) event, a SageMaker AI IP Insights model returns a score that infers how anomalous the pattern of the event is. For example, when a user attempts to log in from an IP address, if the IP Insights score is high enough, a web login server might decide to trigger a multi-factor authentication system.
L9: In more advanced solutions, you can feed the IP Insights score into another machine learning model. For example, you can combine the IP Insight score with other features to rank the findings of another security system, such as those from cite4†Amazon GuardDuty .
L10: The SageMaker AI IP Insights algorithm can also learn vector representations of IP addresses, known as embeddings. You can use vector-encoded embeddings as features in downstream machine learning tasks that use the information observed in the IP addresses. For example, you can use them in tasks such as measuring similarities between IP addresses in clustering and visualization tasks.

L25:   * cite8†IP Insights Data Formats L26: ## Input/Output Interface for the IP Insights Algorithm
L27: 
L28: Training and Validation
L29: The SageMaker AI IP Insights algorithm supports training and validation data channels. It uses the optional validation channel to compute an area-under-curve (AUC) score on a predefined negative sampling strategy. The AUC metric validates how well the model discriminates between positive and negative samples. Training and validation data content types need to be in `text/csv` format. The first column of the CSV data is an opaque string that provides a unique identifier for the entity.
L30: The second column is an IPv4 address in decimal-dot notation. IP Insights currently supports only File mode. For more information and some examples, see cite9†IP Insights Training Data Formats .
L31: Inference
L32: For inference, IP Insights supports `text/csv`, `application/json`, and `application/jsonlines` data content types. For more information about the common data formats for inference provided by SageMaker AI, see cite10†Common data formats for inference . IP Insights inference returns output formatted as either `application/json` or `application/jsonlines`. Each record in the output data contains the corresponding `dot_product` (or compatibility score) for each input data point.
L33: For more information and some examples, see cite11†IP Insights Inference Data Formats .
L34: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the IP Insights Algorithm
L35: 
L36: The SageMaker AI IP Insights algorithm can run on both GPU and CPU instances. For training jobs, we recommend using GPU instances. However, for certain workloads with large training datasets, distributed CPU instances might reduce training costs. For inference, we recommend using CPU instances. IP Insights supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 GPU families.
L37: ### GPU Instances for the IP Insights Algorithm
L38: IP Insights supports all available GPUs. If you need to speed up training, we recommend starting with a single GPU instance, such as ml.p3.2xlarge, and then moving to a multi-GPU environment, such as ml.p3.8xlarge and ml.p3.16xlarge. Multi-GPUs automatically divide the mini batches of training data across themselves. If you switch from a single GPU to multiple GPUs, the `mini_batch_size` is divided equally into the number of GPUs used.
L39: You may want to increase the value of the `mini_batch_size` to compensate for this.
L40: ### CPU Instances for the IP Insights Algorithm
L41: The type of CPU instance that we recommend depends largely on the instance's available memory and the model size. The model size is determined by two hyperparameters: `vector_dim` and `num_entity_vectors`. The maximum supported model size is 8 GB. The following table lists typical EC2 instance types that you would deploy based on these input parameters for various model sizes.
L42: In Table 1, the value for `vector_dim` in the first column range from 32 to 2048 and the values for `num_entity_vectors` in the first row range from 10,000 to 50,000,000.

L4: cite1†Schedule a Pipeline with Amazon EventBridge cite2†Schedule a pipeline with the SageMaker Python SDK L5: # Schedule Pipeline Runs
L6: You can schedule your Amazon SageMaker Pipelines executions using cite3†Amazon EventBridge . Amazon SageMaker Pipelines is supported as a target in cite3†Amazon EventBridge . This allows you to initiate the execution of your model building pipeline based on any event in your event bus. With EventBridge, you can automate your pipeline executions and respond automatically to events such as training job or endpoint status changes.
L7: Events include a new file being uploaded to your Amazon S3 bucket, a change in status of your Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint due to drift, and Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) topics.
L8: The following Pipelines actions can be automatically initiated:
L9: 
L10:   * `StartPipelineExecution`
L11: 
L12: For more information on scheduling SageMaker AI jobs, see cite4†Automating SageMaker AI with Amazon EventBridge. L13: ###### Topics
L14: 
L15:   * cite1†Schedule a Pipeline with Amazon EventBridge L16: 
L17:   * cite2†Schedule a pipeline with the SageMaker Python SDK L18: ## Schedule a Pipeline with Amazon EventBridge
L19: 
L20: To start a pipeline execution with Amazon CloudWatch Events, you must create an EventBridge cite5†rule . When you create a rule for events, you specify a target action to take when EventBridge receives an event that matches the rule. When an event matches the rule, EventBridge sends the event to the specified target and initiates the action defined in the rule.
L21: The following tutorials show how to schedule a pipeline execution with EventBridge using the EventBridge console or the AWS CLI.
L22: ### Prerequisites
L23: 
L24:   * A role that EventBridge can assume with the `SageMaker::StartPipelineExecution` permission. This role can be created automatically if you create a rule from the EventBridge console; otherwise, you need to create this role yourself. For information on creating a SageMaker AI role, see cite6†SageMaker Roles .
L25: 
L26:   * An Amazon SageMaker AI Pipeline to schedule. To create an Amazon SageMaker AI Pipeline, see cite7†Define a Pipeline .
L27: ### Create an EventBridge rule using the EventBridge console
L28: 
L29: The following procedure shows how to create an EventBridge rule using the EventBridge console.
L30: 
L31:   1. Navigate to the cite8†EventBridge console†console.aws.amazon.com .
L32: 
L33:   2. Select Rules on the left hand side.
L34: 
L35:   3. Select `Create Rule`.
L36: 
L37:   4. Enter a name and description for your rule.
L38: 
L39:   5. Select how you want to initiate this rule. You have the following choices for your rule:
L40:      * Event pattern: Your rule is initiated when an event matching the pattern occurs. You can choose a predefined pattern that matches a certain type of event, or you can create a custom pattern. If you select a predefined pattern, you can edit the pattern to customize it. For more information on Event patterns, see cite9†Event Patterns in CloudWatch Events .
L41:      * Schedule: Your rule is initiated regularly on a specified schedule. You can use a fixed-rate schedule that initiates regularly for a specified number of minutes, hour, or weeks. You can also use a cite10†cron expression to create a more fine-grained schedule, such as “the first Monday of each month at 8am.” Schedule is not supported on a custom or partner event bus.
L42: 
L43:   6. Select your desired Event bus.
L44:   7. Select the target(s) to invoke when an event matches your event pattern or when the schedule is initiated. You can add up to 5 targets per rule. Select `SageMaker Pipeline` in the target dropdown list.
L45: 
L46:   8. Select the pipeline you want to initiate from the pipeline dropdown list.
L47:   9. Add parameters to pass to your pipeline execution using a name and value pair. Parameter values can be static or dynamic. For more information on Amazon SageMaker AI Pipeline parameters, see cite11†AWS::Events::Rule SagemakerPipelineParameters .
L48:      * Static values are passed to the pipeline execution every time the pipeline is initiated. For example, if `{"Name": "Instance_type", "Value": "ml.4xlarge"}` is specified in the parameter list, then it is passed as a parameter in `StartPipelineExecutionRequest` every time EventBridge initiates the pipeline.
L49: 
L50:      * Dynamic values are specified using a JSON path. EventBridge parses the value from an event payload, then passes it to the pipeline execution. For example: `$.detail.param.value`
L51:   10. Select the role to use for this rule. You can either use an existing role or create a new one.
L52: 
L53:   11. (Optional) Add tags.
L54: 
L55:   12. Select `Create` to finalize your rule.
L56: 
L57: Your rule is now in effect and ready to initiate your pipeline executions.
L58: ### Create an EventBridge rule using the cite12†AWS CLI L59: 
L60: The following procedure shows how to create an EventBridge rule using the AWS CLI.
L61: 
L62:   1. Create a rule to be initiated. When creating an EventBridge rule using the AWS CLI, you have two options for how your rule is initiated, event pattern and schedule.
L63:      * Event pattern: Your rule is initiated when an event matching the pattern occurs. You can choose a predefined pattern that matches a certain type of event, or you can create a custom pattern. If you select a predefined pattern, you can edit the pattern to customize it.  You can create a rule with event pattern using the following command:
L64:         `aws events put-rule --name `<RULE_NAME>` ----event-pattern `<YOUR_EVENT_PATTERN>` --description `<RULE_DESCRIPTION>` --role-arn `<ROLE_TO_EXECUTE_PIPELINE>` --tags `<TAGS>``
L65:      * Schedule: Your rule is initiated regularly on a specified schedule. You can use a fixed-rate schedule that initiates regularly for a specified number of minutes, hour, or weeks. You can also use a cron expression to create a more fine-grained schedule, such as “the first Monday of each month at 8am.” Schedule is not supported on a custom or partner event bus. You can create a rule with schedule using the following command:
L66:         `aws events put-rule --name `<RULE_NAME>` --schedule-expression `<YOUR_CRON_EXPRESSION>` --description `<RULE_DESCRIPTION>` --role-arn `<ROLE_TO_EXECUTE_PIPELINE>` --tags `<TAGS>``
L67:   2. Add target(s) to invoke when an event matches your event pattern or when the schedule is initiated. You can add up to 5 targets per rule.  For each target, you must specify:
L68: 
L69:      * ARN: The resource ARN of your pipeline.
L70: 
L71:      * Role ARN: The ARN of the role EventBridge should assume to execute the pipeline.
L72: 
L73:      * Parameters:  Amazon SageMaker AI pipeline parameters to pass.
L74:   3. Run the following command to pass a Amazon SageMaker AI pipeline as a target to your rule using cite13†put-targets :
L75: 
L76:     `aws events put-targets --rule `<RULE_NAME>` --event-bus-name `<EVENT_BUS_NAME>` --targets "[{\"Id\": `<ID>`, \"Arn\": `<RESOURCE_ARN>`, \"RoleArn\": `<ROLE_ARN>`, \"SageMakerPipelineParameter\": { \"SageMakerParameterList\": [{\"Name\": `<NAME>`, \"Value\": `<VALUE>`}]} }]"] `
L77: ## Schedule a pipeline with the SageMaker Python SDK
L78: 
L79: The following sections show you how to set up permissions to access EventBridge resources and create your pipeline schedule using the SageMaker Python SDK.
L80: ### Required permissions
L81: 
L82: You need to have necessary permissions to use the pipeline scheduler. Complete the following steps to set up your permissions:
L83: 
L84:   1. Attach the following minimum privilege policy to the IAM role used to create the pipeline triggers, or use the AWS managed policy `AmazonEventBridgeSchedulerFullAccess`.
L85: 
L86: JSON
L87: 
L88: 
L89:     ``{
L90:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L91:         "Statement":
L92:         [
L93:             {
L94:                 "Action":
L95:                 [
L96:                     "scheduler:ListSchedules",
L97:                     "scheduler:GetSchedule",
L98:                     "scheduler:CreateSchedule",
L99:                     "scheduler:UpdateSchedule",
L100:                     "scheduler:DeleteSchedule"
L101:                 ],
L102:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L103:                 "Resource":
L104:                 [
L105:                     "*"
L106:                 ]
L107:             },
L108:             {
L109:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L110:                 "Action": "iam:PassRole",
L111:                 "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/*",
L112:                 "Condition": {
L113:                     "StringLike": {
L114:                         "iam:PassedToService": "scheduler.amazonaws.com"
L115:                     }
L116:                 }
L117:             }
L118:         ]
L119:     }`
L120:     `
L121:   2. Establish a trust relationship with EventBridge by adding the service principal `scheduler.amazonaws.com` to this role’s trust policy. Make sure you attach the following trust policy to the execution role if you launch the notebook in SageMaker Studio.
L122: 
L123: JSON
L124: 
L125: 
L126:     ``{
L127:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L128:         "Statement": [
L129:             {
L130:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L131:                 "Principal": {
L132:                     "Service": [
L133:                         "scheduler.amazonaws.com",
L134:                         "sagemaker.amazonaws.com"
L135:                     ]
L136:                 },
L137:             "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
L138:             }
L139:         ]
L140:     }`
L141:     `
L142: ### Create a pipeline schedule
L143: Using the `PipelineSchedule` constructor, you can schedule a pipeline to run once or at a predetermined interval. A pipeline schedule must be of the type `at`, `rate`, or `cron`. This set of scheduling types is an extension of the cite14†EventBridge scheduling options . For more information about how to use the `PipelineSchedule` class, see cite15†sagemaker.workflow.triggers.PipelineSchedule†sagemaker.readthedocs.io . The following example demonstrates how to create each scheduling type with `PipelineSchedule`.
L144: 
L145:     `from sagemaker.workflow.triggers import PipelineSchedule
L146: 
L147:     # schedules a pipeline run for 12/13/2023 at time 10:15:20 UTC
L148:     my_datetime_schedule = PipelineSchedule(
L149:         name="`<schedule-name>`",
L150:         at=datetime(2023, 12, 13, 10, 15, 20)
L151:     )
L152: 
L153:     # schedules a pipeline run every 5 minutes
L154:     my_rate_schedule = PipelineSchedule(
L155:         name="`<schedule-name>`",
L156:         rate=(5, "minutes")
L157:     )
L158:     # schedules a pipeline run at 10:15am UTC on the last Friday of each month during the years 2022 to 2023
L159:     my_cron_schedule = PipelineSchedule(
L160:         name="`<schedule-name>`",
L161:         cron="15 10 ? * 6L 2022-2023"
L162:     )`
L163: ###### Note
L164: 
L165: If you create a one-time schedule and need to access the current time, use `datetime.utcnow()` instead of `datetime.now()`. The latter does not store the current zone context and results in an incorrect time passed to EventBridge.
L166: ### Attach the trigger to your pipeline
L167: To attach your `PipelineSchedule` to your pipeline, invoke the `put_triggers` call on your created pipeline object with a list of triggers. If you get a response ARN, you successfully created the schedule in your account and EventBridge begins to invoke the target pipeline at the time or rate specified. You must specify a role with correct permissions to attach triggers to a parent pipeline.
L168: If you don't provide one, Pipelines fetches the default role used to create the pipeline from the cite16†configuration file .
L169: The following example demonstrates how to attach a schedule to a pipeline.
L170: 
L171:     `scheduled_pipeline = Pipeline(
L172:         name="`<pipeline-name>`",
L173:         steps=[...],
L174:         sagemaker_session=`<sagemaker-session>`,
L175:     )
L176:     custom_schedule = PipelineSchedule(
L177:         name="`<schedule-name>`",
L178:         at=datetime(year=2023, month=12, date=25, hour=10, minute=30, second=30)
L179:     )
L180:     scheduled_pipeline.put_triggers(triggers=[custom_schedule], role_arn=`<role>`)`
L181: ### Describe current triggers
L182: 
L183: To retrieve information about your created pipeline triggers, you can invoke the `describe_trigger()` API with the trigger name. This command returns details about the created schedule expression such as its start time, enabled state, and other useful information. The following snippet shows a sample invocation:
L184: 
L185:     `scheduled_pipeline.describe_trigger(name="`<schedule-name>`")`
L186: ### Cleanup trigger resources
L187: 
L188: Before you delete your pipeline, clean up existing triggers to avoid a resource leak in your account. You should delete the triggers before destroying the parent pipeline. You can delete your triggers by passing a list of trigger names to the `delete_triggers` API. The following snippet demonstrates how to delete triggers.
L189: 
L190:     `pipeline.delete_triggers(trigger_names=["`<schedule-name>`"])`
L191: ###### Note
L192: 
L193: Be aware of the following limitations when you delete your triggers:
L194: 
L195:   * The option to delete the triggers by specifying trigger names is only available in the SageMaker Python SDK. Deleting the pipeline in the CLI or a `DeletePipeline` API call does not delete your triggers. As a result, the triggers become orphaned and SageMaker AI attempts to start a run for a non-existent pipeline.
L196:   * Also, if you are using another notebook session or already deleted the pipeline target, clean up orphaned schedules through the scheduler cite17†CLI†awscli.amazonaws.com or EventBridge console.

L6: # Testing models with shadow variants
L7: 
L8: You can use SageMaker AI Model Shadow Deployments to create long running shadow variants to validate any new candidate component of your model serving stack before promoting it to production. The following diagram shows how shadow variants work in more detail.

L13: The following code example shows how you can programmatically deploy shadow variants. Replace the `user placeholder text` in the example with your own information.

L18:

L28:     model_name2 = "`name-of-your-second-model`"

L37:             }

L3: # Pipelines
L4: 
L5: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines is a purpose-built workflow orchestration service to automate machine learning (ML) development.
L6: 
L7: Pipelines provide the following advantages over other AWS workflow offerings:
L8: Auto-scaling serverless infrastructure You don't need to manage the underlying orchestration infrastructure to run Pipelines, which allows you to focus on core ML tasks. SageMaker AI automatically provisions, scales, and shuts down the pipeline orchestration compute resources as your ML workload demands.
L9: Intuitive user experience Pipelines can be created and managed through your interface of choice: visual editor, SDK, APIs, or JSON. You can drag-and-drop the various ML steps to author your pipelines in the Amazon SageMaker Studio visual interface. The following screenshot shows the Studio visual editor for pipelines.
L10: 
L11: cite1†Image: Screenshot of the visual drag-and-drop interface for Pipelines in Studio. L12: If you prefer managing your ML workflows programmatically, the SageMaker Python SDK offers advanced orchestration features. For more information, see cite2†Amazon SageMaker Pipelines†sagemaker.readthedocs.io in the SageMaker Python SDK documentation.
L13: AWS integrations Pipelines provide seamless integration with all SageMaker AI features and other AWS services to automate data processing, model training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring jobs. You can incorporate the SageMaker AI features in your Pipelines and navigate across them using deep links to create, monitor, and debug your ML workflows at scale.
L14: Reduced costs With Pipelines, you only pay for the SageMaker Studio environment and the underlying jobs that are orchestrated by Pipelines (for example, SageMaker Training, SageMaker Processing, SageMaker AI Inference, and Amazon S3 data storage).
L15: Auditability and lineage tracking With Pipelines, you can track the history of pipeline updates and executions using built-in versioning. Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking helps you analyze the data sources and data consumers in the end-to-end ML development lifecycle.

L4: cite1†Program your Apache Flink application cite2†Create your Managed Service for Apache Flink application L5: # Managed Service for Apache Flink: How it works
L6: 
L7: Managed Service for Apache Flink is a fully managed Amazon service that lets you use an Apache Flink application to process streaming data. First, you program your Apache Flink application, and then you create your Managed Service for Apache Flink application.
L8: ## Program your Apache Flink application
L9: 
L10: An Apache Flink application is a Java or Scala application that is created with the Apache Flink framework. You author and build your Apache Flink application locally.
L11: 
L12: Applications primarily use either the cite3†DataStream API†nightlies.apache.org or the cite4†Table API†nightlies.apache.org . The other Apache Flink APIs are also available for you to use, but they are less commonly used in building streaming applications.
L13: 
L14: The features of the two APIs are as follows:
L15: ### DataStream API
L16: 
L17: The Apache Flink DataStream API programming model is based on two components:
L18: 
L19:   * Data stream: The structured representation of a continuous flow of data records.
L20: 
L21:   * Transformation operator: Takes one or more data streams as input, and produces one or more data streams as output.
L22: 
L23: Applications created with the DataStream API do the following:
L24: 
L25:   * Read data from a Data Source (such as a Kinesis stream or Amazon MSK topic).
L26:   * Apply transformations to the data, such as filtering, aggregation, or enrichment.
L27: 
L28:   * Write the transformed data to a Data Sink.
L29: 
L30: Applications that use the DataStream API can be written in Java or Scala, and can read from a Kinesis data stream, a Amazon MSK topic, or a custom source.
L31: 
L32: Your application processes data by using a connector. Apache Flink uses the following types of connectors:
L33: 
L34:   * Source: A connector used to read external data.
L35: 
L36:   * Sink: A connector used to write to external locations.
L37:   * Operator: A connector used to process data within the application.
L38: 
L39: A typical application consists of at least one data stream with a source, a data stream with one or more operators, and at least one data sink.
L40: 
L41: For more information about using the DataStream API, see cite5†Review DataStream API components .
L42: ### Table API
L43: 
L44: The Apache Flink Table API programming model is based on the following components:
L45: 
L46:   * Table Environment: An interface to underlying data that you use to create and host one or more tables.
L47: 
L48:   * Table: An object providing access to a SQL table or view.
L49: 
L50:   * Table Source: Used to read data from an external source, such as an Amazon MSK topic.
L51: 
L52:   * Table Function: A SQL query or API call used to transform data.
L53:   * Table Sink: Used to write data to an external location, such as an Amazon S3 bucket.
L54: 
L55: Applications created with the Table API do the following:
L56: 
L57:   * Create a `TableEnvironment` by connecting to a `Table Source`.
L58: 
L59:   * Create a table in the `TableEnvironment` using either SQL queries or Table API functions.
L60: 
L61:   * Run a query on the table using either Table API or SQL
L62: 
L63:   * Apply transformations on the results of the query using Table Functions or SQL queries.
L64:   * Write the query or function results to a `Table Sink`.
L65: 
L66: Applications that use the Table API can be written in Java or Scala, and can query data using either API calls or SQL queries.
L67: 
L68: For more information about using the Table API, see cite6†Review Table API components .
L69: ## Create your Managed Service for Apache Flink application
L70: 
L71: Managed Service for Apache Flink is an AWS service that creates an environment for hosting your Apache Flink application and provides it with the following settings::
L72: 
L73:   * cite7†Use runtime properties : Parameters that you can provide to your application. You can change these parameters without recompiling your application code.
L74: 
L75:   * cite8†Implement fault tolerance : How your application recovers from interrupts and restarts.
L76:   * cite9†Logging and monitoring in Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink : How your application logs events to CloudWatch Logs.
L77: 
L78:   * cite10†Implement application scaling : How your application provisions computing resources.
L79: 
L80: You create your Managed Service for Apache Flink application using either the console or the AWS CLI. To get started creating a Managed Service for Apache Flink application, see cite11†Tutorial: Get started using the DataStream API in Managed Service for Apache Flink .

L2: Run a custom load test - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Create a load test job cite2†Get your load test results L5: # Run a custom load test
L6: 
L7: Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender load tests conduct extensive benchmarks based on production requirements for latency and throughput, custom traffic patterns, and either serverless endpoints or real-time instances (up to 10) that you select.
L8: 
L9: The following sections demonstrate how to create, describe, and stop a load test programmatically using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) and the AWS CLI, or interactively using Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic or the SageMaker AI console.
L10: ## Create a load test job
L11: 
L12: Create a load test programmatically using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3), with the AWS CLI, or interactively using Studio Classic or the SageMaker AI console. As with Inference Recommender inference recommendations, specify a job name for your load test, an AWS IAM role ARN, an input configuration, and your model package ARN from when you registered your model with the model registry. Load tests require that you also specify a traffic pattern and stopping conditions.
L13: AWS SDK for Python (Boto3)
L14: 
L15: 
L16: Use the `CreateInferenceRecommendationsJob` API to create an Inference Recommender load test. Specify `Advanced` for the `JobType` field and provide:
L17: 
L18:   * A job name for your load test (`JobName`). The job name must be unique within your AWS Region and within your AWS account.
L19: 
L20:   * The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of an IAM role that enables Inference Recommender to perform tasks on your behalf. Define this for the `RoleArn` field.
L21:   * An endpoint configuration dictionary (`InputConfig`) where you specify the following:
L22: 
L23:     * For `TrafficPattern`, specify either the phases or stairs traffic pattern. With the phases traffic pattern, new users spawn every minute at the rate you specify. With the stairs traffic pattern, new users spawn at timed intervals (or steps) at a rate you specify. Choose one of the following:
L24:       * For `TrafficType`, specify `PHASES`. Then, for the `Phases` array, specify the `InitialNumberOfUsers` (how many concurrent users to start with, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 3), `SpawnRate` (the number of users to be spawned in a minute for a specific phase of load testing, with a minimum of 0 and maximum of 3), and `DurationInSeconds` (how long the traffic phase should be, with a minimum of 120 and maximum of 3600).
L25:       * For `TrafficType`, specify `STAIRS`. Then, for the `Stairs` array, specify the `DurationInSeconds` (how long the traffic phase should be, with a minimum of 120 and maximum of 3600), `NumberOfSteps` (how many intervals are used during the phase), and `UsersPerStep` (how many users are added during each interval). Note that the length of each step is the value of `DurationInSeconds / NumberOfSteps`.
L26: For example, if your `DurationInSeconds` is `600` and you specify `5` steps, then each step is 120 seconds long.
L27: ###### Note
L28: 
L29: A user is defined as a system-generated actor that runs in a loop and invokes requests to an endpoint as part of Inference Recommender. For a typical XGBoost container running on an `ml.c5.large` instance, endpoints can reach 30,000 invocations per minute (500 tps) with just 15-20 users.
L30:     * For `ResourceLimit`, specify `MaxNumberOfTests` (the maximum number of benchmarking load tests for an Inference Recommender job, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10) and `MaxParallelOfTests` (the maximum number of parallel benchmarking load tests for an Inference Recommender job, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10).
L31: 
L32:     * For `EndpointConfigurations`, you can specify one of the following:
L33:       * The `InstanceType` field, where you specify the instance type on which you want to run your load tests.
L34: 
L35:       * The `ServerlessConfig`, in which you specify your ideal values for `MaxConcurrency` and `MemorySizeInMB` for a serverless endpoint. For more information, see the cite3†Serverless Inference documentation .
L36:   * A stopping conditions dictionary (`StoppingConditions`), where if any of the conditions are met, the Inference Recommender job stops. For this example, specify the following fields in the dictionary:
L37: 
L38:     * For `MaxInvocations`, specify the maximum number of requests per minute expected for the endpoint, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 30,000.
L39:     * For `ModelLatencyThresholds`, specify `Percentile` (the model latency percentile threshold) and `ValueInMilliseconds` (the model latency percentile value in milliseconds).
L40:     * (Optional) For `FlatInvocations`, you can specify whether to continue the load test when the TPS (invocations per minute) rate flattens. A flattened TPS rate usually means that the endpoint has reached capacity. However, you might want to continue monitoring the endpoint under full capacity conditions. To continue the load test when this happens, specify this value as `Continue`. Otherwise, the default value is `Stop`.
L41: 
L42:     `# Create a low-level SageMaker service client.
L43:     import boto3
L44:     aws_region=`<INSERT>`
L45:     sagemaker_client=boto3.client('sagemaker', region=aws_region)
L46: 
L47:     # Provide a name to your recommendation based on load testing
L48:     load_test_job_name=`"<INSERT>"`
L49: 
L50:     # Provide the name of the sagemaker instance type
L51:     instance_type=`"<INSERT>"`
L52: 
L53:     # Provide the IAM Role that gives SageMaker permission to access AWS services
L54:     role_arn='arn:aws:iam::`<account>:role/*`'
L55:     # Provide your model package ARN that was created when you registered your
L56:     # model with Model Registry

L122: Use the `create-inference-recommendations-job` API to create an Inference Recommender load test. Specify `Advanced` for the `JobType` field and provide:
L123: 
L124:   * A job name for your load test (`job-name`). The job name must be unique within your AWS Region and within your AWS account.
L125:   * The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of an IAM role that enables Inference Recommender to perform tasks on your behalf. Define this for the `role-arn` field.
L126: 
L127:   * An endpoint configuration dictionary (`input-config`) where you specify the following:
L128:     * For `TrafficPattern`, specify either the phases or stairs traffic pattern. With the phases traffic pattern, new users spawn every minute at the rate you specify. With the stairs traffic pattern, new users spawn at timed intervals (or steps) at a rate you specify. Choose one of the following:
L129:       * For `TrafficType`, specify `PHASES`. Then, for the `Phases` array, specify the `InitialNumberOfUsers` (how many concurrent users to start with, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 3), `SpawnRate` (the number of users to be spawned in a minute for a specific phase of load testing, with a minimum of 0 and maximum of 3), and `DurationInSeconds` (how long the traffic phase should be, with a minimum of 120 and maximum of 3600).
L130:       * For `TrafficType`, specify `STAIRS`. Then, for the `Stairs` array, specify the `DurationInSeconds` (how long the traffic phase should be, with a minimum of 120 and maximum of 3600), `NumberOfSteps` (how many intervals are used during the phase), and `UsersPerStep` (how many users are added during each interval). Note that the length of each step is the value of `DurationInSeconds / NumberOfSteps`.
L131: For example, if your `DurationInSeconds` is `600` and you specify `5` steps, then each step is 120 seconds long.
L132: ###### Note
L133: 
L134: A user is defined as a system-generated actor that runs in a loop and invokes requests to an endpoint as part of Inference Recommender. For a typical XGBoost container running on an `ml.c5.large` instance, endpoints can reach 30,000 invocations per minute (500 tps) with just 15-20 users.
L135:     * For `ResourceLimit`, specify `MaxNumberOfTests` (the maximum number of benchmarking load tests for an Inference Recommender job, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10) and `MaxParallelOfTests` (the maximum number of parallel benchmarking load tests for an Inference Recommender job, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10).
L136: 
L137:     * For `EndpointConfigurations`, you can specify one of the following:
L138:       * The `InstanceType` field, where you specify the instance type on which you want to run your load tests.
L139: 
L140:       * The `ServerlessConfig`, in which you specify your ideal values for `MaxConcurrency` and `MemorySizeInMB` for a serverless endpoint.
L141: 
L142:   * A stopping conditions dictionary (`stopping-conditions`), where if any of the conditions are met, the Inference Recommender job stops. For this example, specify the following fields in the dictionary:
L143:     * For `MaxInvocations`, specify the maximum number of requests per minute expected for the endpoint, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 30,000.
L144: 
L145:     * For `ModelLatencyThresholds`, specify `Percentile` (the model latency percentile threshold) and `ValueInMilliseconds` (the model latency percentile value in milliseconds).
L146:     * (Optional) For `FlatInvocations`, you can specify whether to continue the load test when the TPS (invocations per minute) rate flattens. A flattened TPS rate usually means that the endpoint has reached capacity. However, you might want to continue monitoring the endpoint under full capacity conditions. To continue the load test when this happens, specify this value as `Continue`. Otherwise, the default value is `Stop`.

L208: Create a load test with Studio Classic.
L209: 
L210:   1. In your Studio Classic application, choose the home icon ( cite5†Image: Menu icon. ).
L211: 
L212:   2. In the left sidebar of Studio Classic, choose Deployments.
L213: 
L214:   3. Choose Inference recommender from the dropdown list.
L215: 
L216:   4. Choose Create inference recommender job. A new tab titled Create inference recommender job opens.
L217:   5. Select the name of your model group from the dropdown Model group field. The list includes all the model groups registered with the model registry in your account, including models registered outside of Studio Classic.
L218: 
L219:   6. Select a model version from the dropdown Model version field.
L220: 
L221:   7. Choose Continue.
L222: 
L223:   8. Provide a name for the job in the Name field.
L224: 
L225:   9. (Optional) Provide a description of your job in the Description field.
L226:   10. Choose an IAM role that grants Inference Recommender permission to access AWS services. You can create a role and attach the `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess` IAM managed policy to accomplish this, or you can let Studio Classic create a role for you.
L227: 
L228:   11. Choose Stopping Conditions to expand the available input fields. Provide a set of conditions for stopping a deployment recommendation.
L229:     1. Specify the maximum number of requests per minute expected for the endpoint in the Max Invocations Per Minute field.
L230:     2. Specify the model latency threshold in microseconds in the Model Latency Threshold field. The Model Latency Threshold depicts the interval of time taken by a model to respond as viewed from Inference Recommender. The interval includes the local communication time taken to send the request and to fetch the response from the model container and the time taken to complete the inference in the container.
L231: 
L232:   12. Choose Traffic Pattern to expand the available input fields.
L233:     1. Set the initial number of virtual users by specifying an integer in the Initial Number of Users field.
L234: 
L235:     2. Provide an integer number for the Spawn Rate field. The spawn rate sets the number of users created per second.
L236: 
L237:     3. Set the duration for the phase in seconds by specifying an integer in the Duration field.
L238: 
L239:     4. (Optional) Add additional traffic patterns. To do so, choose Add.
L240:   13. Choose the Additional setting to reveal the Max test duration field. Specify, in seconds, the maximum time a test can take during a job. New jobs are not scheduled after the defined duration. This helps ensure jobs that are in progress are not stopped and that you only view completed jobs.
L241: 
L242:   14. Choose Continue.
L243: 
L244:   15. Choose Selected Instances.
L245: 
L246:   16. In the Instances for benchmarking field, choose Add instances to test. Select up to 10 instances for Inference Recommender to use for load testing.
L247:   17. Choose Additional settings.
L248: 
L249:     1. Provide an integer that sets an upper limit on the number of tests a job can make for the Max number of tests field. Note that each endpoint configuration results in a new load test.
L250: 
L251:     2. Provide an integer for the Max parallel test field. This setting defines an upper limit on the number of load tests that can run in parallel.
L252: 
L253:   18. Choose Submit.
L254: 
L255: The load test can take up to 2 hours.

L258: Do not close this tab. If you close this tab, you cancel the Inference Recommender load test job.

L4: cite1†Lake Formation features cite2†Getting started with Lake Formation L5: # What is AWS Lake Formation?
L6: 
L7: Welcome to the AWS Lake Formation Developer Guide.
L8: 
L9: AWS Lake Formation helps you centrally govern, secure, and globally share data for analytics and machine learning. With Lake Formation, you can manage fine-grained access control for your data lake data on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and its metadata in AWS Glue Data Catalog.
L10: Lake Formation provides its own permissions model that augments the IAM permissions model. Lake Formation permissions model enables fine-grained access to data stored in data lakes as well as external data sources such as Amazon Redshift data warehouses, Amazon DynamoDB databases, and third-party data sources through a simple grant or revoke mechanism, much like a relational database management system (RDBMS).
L11: Lake Formation permissions are enforced using granular controls at the column, row, and cell-levels across AWS analytics and machine learning services, including Amazon Athena, Amazon Quick, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue.
L12: With Lake Formation hybrid access mode for AWS Glue Data Catalog (Data Catalog), you can secure and access the cataloged data using both Lake Formation permissions and IAM permissions policies for Amazon S3 and AWS Glue actions. With hybrid access mode, data administrators can onboard Lake Formation permissions selectively and incrementally, focusing on one data lake use case at a time.
L13: Lake Formation also allows you to share data internally and externally across multiple AWS accounts, AWS organizations or directly with IAM principals in another account providing fine-grained access to the Data Catalog metadata and underlying data.

L16:   * cite1†Lake Formation features L17: 
L18:   * cite3†AWS Lake Formation: How it works L19: 
L20:   * cite4†Lake Formation components L21: 
L22:   * cite5†Lake Formation terminology L23: 
L24:   * cite6†AWS service integrations with Lake Formation L25: 
L26:   * cite7†Additional Lake Formation resources L27: 
L28:   * cite2†Getting started with Lake Formation L29: ## Lake Formation features
L30: 
L31: Lake Formation helps you break down data silos and combine different types of structured and unstructured data into a centralized repository. First, identify existing data stores in Amazon S3 or relational and NoSQL databases, and move the data into your data lake. Then crawl, catalog, and prepare the data for analytics. Next, provide your users with secure self-service access to the data through their choice of analytics services.
L32: You can use Lake Formation console to create multi-level federated catalogs in the Data Catalog, and unify data across Amazon S3 data lakes and Amazon Redshift data warehouses. You can also integrate data from your operational databases such as Amazon DynamoDB, and third-party data sources such as Google BigQuery, MySQL, among others. The Data Catalog provides a centralized metadata repository that makes managing and discovering data across disparate systems easier.
L33: For more information, see cite8†Bringing your data into the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L34: ###### Topics
L35: 
L36:   * cite9†Data ingestion and management L37: 
L38:   * cite10†Security management L39: 
L40:   * cite11†Bring your data into the Data Catalog L41: 
L42: ### Data ingestion and management
L43: ###### Import data from databases already in AWS
L44: Once you specify where your existing databases are and provide your access credentials, Lake Formation reads the data and its metadata (schema) to understand the contents of the data source. It then imports the data to your new data lake and records the metadata in a central catalog. With Lake Formation, you can import data from MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MariaDB, and Oracle databases running in Amazon RDS or hosted in Amazon EC2. Both bulk and incremental data loading are supported.
L45: ###### Import data from other external sources
L46: 
L47: You can use Lake Formation to move data from on-premises databases by connecting with Java Database Connectivity (JDBC). Identify your target sources and provide access credentials in the console, and Lake Formation reads and loads your data into the data lake. To import data from databases other than the ones listed above, you can create custom ETL jobs with AWS Glue.
L48: ###### Catalog and label your data
L49: 
L50: You can use AWS Glue crawlers to read your data in Amazon S3 and extract database and table schema and store that data in a searchable Data Catalog. Then, use Lake Formation cite12†Lake Formation tag-based access control (TBAC) to manage permissions on databases, tables, and columns. For more information about adding tables to the Data Catalog, see cite13†Creating objects in the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L51: 
L52: ### Security management
L53: ###### Define and manage access controls
L54: Lake Formation provides a single place to manage access controls for data in your data lake. You can define security policies that restrict access to data at the database, table, column, row, and cell levels. These policies apply to IAM users and roles, and to users and groups when federating through an external identity provider. You can use fine-grained controls to access data secured by Lake Formation within Amazon Redshift Spectrum, Athena, AWS Glue ETL, and Amazon EMR for Apache Spark.
L55: Whenever you create IAM identities, make sure to follow IAM best practices. For more information, see cite14†Security best practices in the IAM User Guide.
L56: ###### Hybrid access mode
L57: 
L58: Lake Formation hybrid access mode provides the flexibility to selectively enable Lake Formation permissions for databases and tables in your Data Catalog. With hybrid access mode, you now have an incremental path that allows you to set Lake Formation permissions for a specific set of users without interrupting the permission policies of other existing users or workloads. For more information, see cite15†Hybrid access mode .
L59: ###### Implement audit logging
L60: Lake Formation provides comprehensive audit logs with CloudTrail to monitor access and show compliance with centrally defined policies. You can audit data access history across analytics and machine learning services that read the data in your data lake via Lake Formation. This lets you see which users or roles have attempted to access what data, with which services, and when. You can access audit logs in the same way you access any other CloudTrail logs using the CloudTrail APIs and console.
L61: For more information about CloudTrail logs see cite16†Logging AWS Lake Formation API calls using AWS CloudTrail .
L62: ###### Row and cell-level security
L63: 
L64: Lake Formation provides data filters that allow you to restrict access to a combination of columns and rows. Use row and cell-level security to protect sensitive data like Personal Identifiable Information (PII). For more information about row-level security, see cite17†Data filtering and cell-level security in Lake Formation .
L65: ###### Tag-based access control
L66: Use Lake Formation cite12†attribute-based access control to manage hundreds or even thousands of data permissions by creating custom labels called LF-Tags. You can now define LF-Tags and attach them to databases, tables, or columns. Then, share controlled access across analytic, machine learning (ML), and extract, transform, and load (ETL) services for consumption.
L67: LF-Tags make sure that data governance can be scaled easily by replacing the policy definitions of thousands of resources with a few logical tags. Lake Formation provides a text-based search over this metadata, so your users can quickly find the data they need to analyze.
L68: ###### Attribute-based access control
L69: Use cite18†attribute-based access control to grant access on Data Catalog objects. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) is an authorization strategy that defines permissions based on attributes. AWS calls these attributes tags. You can use ABAC to grant access to principals within the same account or in another account on the Data Catalog resources. Any IAM principal with matching IAM tag or session tag keys and values gains access to the resource.
L70: You must have grantable permissions on the resources to make these grants.
L71: ###### Cross account access
L72: 
L73: Lake Formation permission management capabilities simplify securing and managing distributed data lakes across multiple AWS accounts through a centralized approach, providing fine-grained access control to the Data Catalog and Amazon S3 locations. For more information, see cite19†Cross-account data sharing in Lake Formation .
L74: ### Bring your data into the Data Catalog
L75: 
L76: The federation capability allows you to create federated catalogs and set up permissions on datasets stored in different data sources like Amazon Redshift without migrating data or metadata into Amazon S3 or AWS Glue Data Catalog. You can use the following methods to bring data and manage permissions on external datasets in Lake Formation:
L77: 
L78: For more information, see cite8†Bringing your data into the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L79:   * Bringing data in Amazon Redshift data warehouses into the AWS Glue Data Catalog – Register an existing cite20†Amazon Redshift namespace or a cluster with the Data Catalog, and create a multi-level federated catalog in the Data Catalog.
L80: 
L81: You can access your data using any query engine compatible with Apache Iceberg REST catalog OpenAPI specification, such as Amazon EMR Serverless, and Amazon Athena.
L82: 
L83: For more information, see cite21†Bringing Amazon Redshift data into the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L84:   * Federating into the Data Catalog from external data sources – Connect the Data Catalog to external data sources using AWS Glue connections, and create federated catalogs to centrally manage access permissions on datasets using Lake Formation. No migration of metadata into the Data Catalog is necessary.
L85: 
L86: For more information, see cite22†Federating into external data sources in the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L87:   * Integrating Amazon S3 Table Buckets with Data Catalog – You can publish and catalog Amazon S3 Tables as Data Catalog objects and register the catalog as a Lake Formation data location from Lake Formation console or using AWS Glue APIs.
L88: 
L89: For more information, see cite23†Amazon S3 Tables integration with AWS Glue Data Catalog and AWS Lake Formation .
L90:   * Create catalogs to manage Amazon Redshift tables in the Data Catalog – You may not have an Amazon Redshift producer cluster or an Amazon Redshift datashare available today, but want to create and manage Amazon Redshift tables using Data Catalog. You can get started by creating an AWS Glue managed catalog using the `glue:CreateCatalog` API or the AWS Lake Formation console by setting the catalog type as `Managed` and `Catalog source` as Redshift.
L91: For more information, see cite24†Creating an Amazon Redshift managed catalog in the AWS Glue Data Catalog .
L92: 
L93:   * Integrating Lake Formation with Amazon Redshift data sharing – Use Lake Formation to centrally manage database, table, column, and row-level access permissions of cite20†Amazon Redshift datashares and restrict user access to objects within a datashare.
L94:   * Connecting Data Catalog to external metastores – Connect AWS Glue Data Catalog to external metastores to manage access permissions on data sets in Amazon S3 using Lake Formation. No migration of metadata into the Data Catalog is necessary.
L95: 
L96: For more information, see cite25†Managing permissions on datasets that use external metastores .
L97:   * Integrating Lake Formation with AWS Data Exchange – Lake Formation supports licensing access to your data through AWS Data Exchange. If you're interested in licensing your Lake Formation data, see cite26†What is AWS Data Exchange in the AWS Data Exchange User Guide.
L98: ## Getting started with Lake Formation
L99: 
L100: We recommend that you start with the following sections:
L101: 
L102:   * cite3†AWS Lake Formation: How it works — Learn about essential terminology and how the various components interact.

L104:   * cite27†Getting started with Lake Formation — Get information about prerequisites, and complete important setup tasks.

L106:   * cite28†AWS Lake Formation tutorials — Follow step-by-step tutorials to learn how to use Lake Formation.
L107:   * cite29†Security in AWS Lake Formation — Understand how you can help secure access to data in Lake Formation.

L6: # Firehose
L7: 
L8: The Firehose(`firehose`) action sends data from an MQTT message to an Amazon Data Firehose stream.
L9: ## Requirements
L10: 
L11: This rule action has the following requirements:
L12: 
L13:   * An IAM role that AWS IoT can assume to perform the `firehose:PutRecord` operation. For more information, see cite5†Granting an AWS IoT rule the access it requires .
L14: 
L15: In the AWS IoT console, you can choose or create a role to allow AWS IoT to perform this rule action.
L16:   * If you use Firehose to send data to an Amazon S3 bucket, and you use an AWS KMS customer managed AWS KMS key to encrypt data at rest in Amazon S3, Firehose must have access to your bucket and permission to use the AWS KMS key on the caller's behalf. For more information, see cite6†Grant Firehose access to an Amazon S3 destination in the Amazon Data Firehose Developer Guide.
L17: ## Parameters
L18: 
L19: When you create an AWS IoT rule with this action, you must specify the following information:
L20: 
L21: `batchMode`
L22: 
L23: 
L24: (Optional) Whether to deliver the Firehose stream as a batch by using cite7†`PutRecordBatch` . The default value is `false`.
L25: 
L26: When `batchMode` is `true` and the rule's SQL statement evaluates to an Array, each Array element forms one record in the `PutRecordBatch` request. The resulting array can't have more than 500 records.
L27: 
L28: Supports cite8†substitution templates : No
L29: `deliveryStreamName`
L30: 
L31: 
L32: The Firehose stream to which to write the message data.
L33: 
L34: Supports cite8†substitution templates : API and AWS CLI only
L35: 
L36: `separator`
L37: 
L38: 
L39: (Optional) A character separator that is used to separate records written to the Firehose stream. If you omit this parameter, the stream uses no separator. Valid values: `,` (comma), `\t` (tab), `\n` (newline), `\r\n` (Windows newline).
L40: 
L41: Supports cite8†substitution templates : No
L42: 
L43: `roleArn`
L44: The IAM role that allows access to the Firehose stream. For more information, see cite1†Requirements .
L45: 
L46: Supports cite8†substitution templates : No
L47: ## Examples
L48: The following JSON example defines a Firehose action in an AWS IoT rule.
L49: 
L50:     `{
L51:         "topicRulePayload": {
L52:             "sql": "SELECT * FROM 'some/topic'",
L53:             "ruleDisabled": false,
L54:             "awsIotSqlVersion": "2016-03-23",
L55:             "actions": [
L56:                 {
L57:                     "firehose": {
L58:                         "deliveryStreamName": "my_firehose_stream",
L59:                         "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/aws_iot_firehose"
L60:                     }
L61:                 }
L62:             ]
L63:         }
L64:     }
L65:     `
L66: The following JSON example defines a Firehose action with substitution templates in an AWS IoT rule.
L67: 
L68:     `{
L69:         "topicRulePayload": {
L70:             "sql": "SELECT * FROM 'some/topic'",
L71:             "ruleDisabled": false,
L72:             "awsIotSqlVersion": "2016-03-23",
L73:             "actions": [
L74:                 {
L75:                     "firehose": {
L76:                         "deliveryStreamName": "${topic()}",
L77:                         "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/aws_iot_firehose"
L78:                     }
L79:                 }
L80:             ]
L81:         }
L82:     }`

L6: 
L7: Creates a URL for a specified UserProfile in a Domain. When accessed in a web browser, the user will be automatically signed in to the domain, and granted access to all of the Apps and files associated with the Domain's Amazon Elastic File System volume. This operation can only be called when the authentication mode equals IAM.
L8: The IAM role or user passed to this API defines the permissions to access the app. Once the presigned URL is created, no additional permission is required to access this URL. IAM authorization policies for this API are also enforced for every HTTP request and WebSocket frame that attempts to connect to the app.
L9: You can restrict access to this API and to the URL that it returns to a list of IP addresses, Amazon VPCs or Amazon VPC Endpoints that you specify. For more information, see cite7†Connect to Amazon SageMaker AI Studio Through an Interface VPC Endpoint .

L11: 
L12:   * The URL that you get from a call to `CreatePresignedDomainUrl` has a default timeout of 5 minutes. You can configure this value using `ExpiresInSeconds`. If you try to use the URL after the timeout limit expires, you are directed to the AWS console sign-in page.

L3: 
L4: cite1†Development environment L5: 
L6: # Developing scripts using development endpoints
L7: ###### Note
L8: 
L9: Development Endpoints are only supported for versions of AWS Glue prior to 2.0. For an interactive environment where you can author and test ETL scripts, use cite2†Notebooks on AWS Glue Studio .
L10: 
L11: AWS Glue can create an environment—known as a development endpoint—that you can use to iteratively develop and test your extract, transform, and load (ETL) scripts. You can create, edit, and delete development endpoints using the AWS Glue console or API.
L12: ## Managing your development environment
L13: 
L14: When you create a development endpoint, you provide configuration values to provision the development environment. These values tell AWS Glue how to set up the network so that you can access the endpoint securely and the endpoint can access your data stores.
L15: You can then create a notebook that connects to the endpoint, and use your notebook to author and test your ETL script. When you're satisfied with the results of your development process, you can create an ETL job that runs your script. With this process, you can add functions and debug your scripts in an interactive manner.
L16:

citeturn155view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/aws-glue-programming-etl-connect-jdbc-home.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 272
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: JDBC connections - AWS Glue
L3: 
L4: cite1†JDBC connection parameters cite2†Use sampleQuery cite3†Use custom JDBC driver L5: # JDBC connections
L6: 
L7: Certain, typically relational, database types support connecting through the JDBC standard. For more information about JDBC, see the cite4†Java JDBC API†docs.oracle.com documentation. AWS Glue natively supports connecting to certain databases through their JDBC connectors - the JDBC libraries are provided in AWS Glue Spark jobs. When connecting to these database types using AWS Glue libraries, you have access to a standard set of options.
L8: The JDBC connectionType values include the following:
L9: 
L10:   * `"connectionType": "sqlserver"`: Designates a connection to a Microsoft SQL Server database.
L11: 
L12:   * `"connectionType": "mysql"`: Designates a connection to a MySQL database.
L13: 
L14:   * `"connectionType": "oracle"`: Designates a connection to an Oracle database.
L15: 
L16:   * `"connectionType": "postgresql"`: Designates a connection to a PostgreSQL database.
L17:   * `"connectionType": "redshift"`: Designates a connection to an Amazon Redshift database. For more information, see cite5†Redshift connections .
L18: 
L19: The following table lists the JDBC driver versions that AWS Glue supports.
L20: Product  | JDBC driver versions for Glue 5.1  | JDBC driver versions for Glue 5.0  | JDBC driver versions for Glue 4.0  | JDBC driver versions for Glue 3.0  | JDBC driver versions for Glue 0.9, 1.0, 2.0
L21: --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L22: Microsoft SQL Server  | 10.2.0  | 10.2.0  | 9.4.0  | 7.x  | 6.x
L23: MySQL  | 8.0.33  | 8.0.33  | 8.0.23  | 8.0.23  | 5.1
L24: Oracle Database  | 23.3.0.23.09  | 23.3.0.23.09  | 21.7  | 21.1  | 11.2
L25: PostgreSQL  | 42.7.3  | 42.7.3  | 42.3.6  | 42.2.18  | 42.1.x
L26: Amazon Redshift *  | redshift-jdbc42-2.1.0.29  | redshift-jdbc42-2.1.0.29  | redshift-jdbc42-2.1.0.16  | redshift-jdbc41-1.2.12.1017  | redshift-jdbc41-1.2.12.1017
L27: * For the Amazon Redshift connection type, all other option name/value pairs that are included in connection options for a JDBC connection, including formatting options, are passed directly to the underlying SparkSQL DataSource. In AWS Glue with Spark jobs in AWS Glue 4.0 and later versions, the AWS Glue native connector for Amazon Redshift uses the Amazon Redshift integration for Apache Spark. For more information see cite6†Amazon Redshift integration for Apache Spark .
L28: In previous versions, see cite7†Amazon Redshift data source for Spark†github.com .
L29: To configure your Amazon VPC to connect to Amazon RDS data stores using JDBC, refer to cite8†Setting up Amazon VPC for JDBC connections to Amazon RDS data stores from AWS Glue .
L30: ###### Note
L31: 
L32: AWS Glue jobs are only associated with one subnet during a run. This may impact your ability to connect to multiple data sources through the same job. This behavior is not limited to JDBC sources.
L33: 
L34: ###### Topics
L35: 
L36:   * cite1†JDBC connection option reference L37: 
L38:   * cite2†Use sampleQuery L39: 
L40:   * cite3†Use custom JDBC driver L41: 
L42:   * cite9†Reading from JDBC tables in parallel L43: 
L44:   * cite8†Setting up Amazon VPC for JDBC connections to Amazon RDS data stores from AWS Glue L45: ## JDBC connection option reference
L46: 
L47: If you already have a JDBC AWS Glue connection defined, you can reuse the configuration properties defined in it, such as: url, user and password; so you don't have to specify them in the code as connection options. This feature is available in AWS Glue 3.0 and later versions. To do so, use the following connection properties:
L48: 
L49:   * `"useConnectionProperties"`: Set it to "true" to indicate you want to use the configuration from a connection.
L50:   * `"connectionName"`: Enter the connection name to retrieve the configuration from, the connection must be defined in the same region as the job.
L51: 
L52: Use these connection options with JDBC connections:
L53: 
L54:   * `"url"`: (Required) The JDBC URL for the database.
L55: 
L56:   * `"dbtable"`: (Required) The database table to read from. For JDBC data stores that support schemas within a database, specify `schema.table-name`. If a schema is not provided, then the default "public" schema is used.
L57:   * `"user"`: (Required) The user name to use when connecting.
L58: 
L59:   * `"password"`: (Required) The password to use when connecting.
L60: 
L61:   * (Optional) The following options allow you to supply a custom JDBC driver. Use these options if you must use a driver that AWS Glue does not natively support.
L62: ETL jobs can use different JDBC driver versions for the data source and target, even if the source and target are the same database product. This allows you to migrate data between source and target databases with different versions. To use these options, you must first upload the JAR file of the JDBC driver to Amazon S3.
L63: 
L64:     * `"customJdbcDriverS3Path"`: The Amazon S3 path of the custom JDBC driver.
L65: 
L66:     * `"customJdbcDriverClassName"`: The class name of JDBC driver.
L67:   * `"bulkSize"`: (Optional) Used to configure parallel inserts for speeding up bulk loads into JDBC targets. Specify an integer value for the degree of parallelism to use when writing or inserting data. This option is helpful for improving the performance of writes into databases such as the Arch User Repository (AUR).
L68:   * `"hashfield"` (Optional) A string, used to specify the name of a column in the JDBC table to be used to divide the data into partitions when reading from JDBC tables in parallel. Provide "hashfield" OR "hashexpression". For more information, see cite9†Reading from JDBC tables in parallel .
L69:   * `"hashexpression"` (Optional) A SQL select clause returning a whole number. Used to divide the data in a JDBC table into partitions when reading from JDBC tables in parallel. Provide "hashfield" OR "hashexpression". For more information, see cite9†Reading from JDBC tables in parallel .
L70:   * `"hashpartitions"` (Optional) A positive integer. Used to specify the number of parallel reads of the JDBC table when reading from JDBC tables in parallel. Default: 7. For more information, see cite9†Reading from JDBC tables in parallel .
L71:   * `"sampleQuery"`: (Optional) A custom SQL query statement. Used to specify a subset of information in a table to retrieve a sample of the table contents. When configured without regard to your data, it can be less efficient than DynamicFrame methods, causing timeouts or out of memory errors. For more information, see cite2†Use sampleQuery .
L72:   * `"enablePartitioningForSampleQuery"`: (Optional) A boolean. Default: false. Used to enable reading from JDBC tables in parallel when specifying `sampleQuery`. If set to true, `sampleQuery` must end with "where" or "and" for AWS Glue to append partitioning conditions. For more information, see cite2†Use sampleQuery .
L73:   * `"sampleSize"`: (Optional) A positive integer. Limits the number of rows returned by the sample query. Works only when `enablePartitioningForSampleQuery` is true. If partitioning is not enabled, you should instead directly add `"limit x"` in the `sampleQuery` to limit the size. For more information, see cite2†Use sampleQuery .
L74: ## Use sampleQuery
L75: 
L76: This section explains how to use `sampleQuery`, `sampleSize` and `enablePartitioningForSampleQuery`.
L77: `sampleQuery` can be an efficient way to sample a few rows of your dataset. By default, the query is run by a single executor. When configured without regard to your data, it can be less efficient than DynamicFrame methods, causing timeouts or out of memory errors. Running SQL on the underlying database as part of your ETL pipeline is generally only needed for performance purposes. If you are trying to preview a few rows of your dataset, consider using cite10†show .
L78: If you are trying to transform your dataset using SQL, consider using cite11†toDF to define a SparkSQL transform against your data in a DataFrame form.
L79: While your query may manipulate a variety of tables, `dbtable` remains required.
L80: 
L81: Using sampleQuery to retrieve a sample of your table
L82: 
L83: When using default sampleQuery behavior to retrieve a sample of your data, AWS Glue does not expect substantial throughput, so it runs your query on a single executor. In order to limit the data you provide and not cause performance problems, we suggest you provide SQL with a `LIMIT` clause.
L84: ###### Example Use sampleQuery without partitioning
L85: The following code example shows how to use `sampleQuery` without partitioning.
L86: 
L87:     `//A full sql query statement.
L88:     val query = "select name from `$tableName` where age > 0 limit 1"
L89:     val connectionOptions = JsonOptions(Map(
L90:         "url" -> url,
L91:         "dbtable" -> tableName,
L92:         "user" -> user,
L93:         "password" -> password,
L94:         "sampleQuery" -> query ))
L95:     val dyf = glueContext.getSource("mysql", connectionOptions)
L96:               .getDynamicFrame()`
L97: Using sampleQuery against larger datasets
L98: 
L99: If you're reading a large dataset, you might need to enable JDBC partitioning to query a table in parallel. For more information, see cite9†Reading from JDBC tables in parallel . To use `sampleQuery` with JDBC partitioning, set `enablePartitioningForSampleQuery` to true. Enabling this feature requires you to make some changes to your `sampleQuery`.
L100: When using JDBC partitioning with `sampleQuery`, your query must end with "where" or "and" for AWS Glue to append partitioning conditions.
L101: 
L102: If you would like to limit the results of your sampleQuery when reading from JDBC tables in parallel, set the `"sampleSize"` parameter rather than specifying a `LIMIT` clause.
L103: ###### Example Use sampleQuery with JDBC partitioning
L104: The following code example shows how to use `sampleQuery` with JDBC partitioning.
L105: 
L106:     `//note that the query should end with "where" or "and" if use with JDBC partitioning.
L107:     val query = "select name from `$tableName` where age > 0 and"
L108: 
L109:     //Enable JDBC partitioning by setting hashfield.
L110:     //to use sampleQuery with partitioning, set enablePartitioningForSampleQuery.
L111:     //use sampleSize to limit the size of returned data.
L112:     val connectionOptions = JsonOptions(Map(
L113:         "url" -> url,
L114:         "dbtable" -> tableName,
L115:         "user" -> user,
L116:         "password" -> password,
L117:         "hashfield" -> primaryKey,
L118:         "sampleQuery" -> query,
L119:         "enablePartitioningForSampleQuery" -> true,
L120:         "sampleSize" -> "1" ))
L121:     val dyf = glueContext.getSource("mysql", connectionOptions)
L122:               .getDynamicFrame()`
L123: Notes and Restrictions:
L124: 
L125: Sample queries cannot be used together with job bookmarks. The bookmark state will be ignored when configuration for both are provided.
L126: ## Use custom JDBC driver
L127: 
L128: The following code examples show how to read from and write to JDBC databases with custom JDBC drivers. They demonstrate reading from one version of a database product, and writing to a later version of the same product.
L129: Python
L130: 
L131: 
L132:     `import sys
L133:     from awsglue.transforms import *
L134:     from awsglue.utils import getResolvedOptions
L135:     from pyspark.context import SparkContext, SparkConf
L136:     from awsglue.context import GlueContext
L137:     from awsglue.job import Job
L138:     import time
L139:     from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, IntegerType, StringType
L140: 
L141:     sc = SparkContext()
L142:     glueContext = GlueContext(sc)
L143:     spark = glueContext.spark_session
L144: 
L145:     # Construct JDBC connection options
L146:     connection_mysql5_options = {
L147:         "url": "jdbc:mysql://<jdbc-host-name>:3306/db",
L148:         "dbtable": "test",
L149:         "user": "admin",
L150:         "password": "pwd"}
L151: 
L152:     connection_mysql8_options = {
L153:         "url": "jdbc:mysql://<jdbc-host-name>:3306/db",
L154:         "dbtable": "test",
L155:         "user": "admin",
L156:         "password": "pwd",
L157:         "customJdbcDriverS3Path": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/mysql-connector-java-8.0.17.jar",
L158:         "customJdbcDriverClassName": "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"}
L159:     connection_oracle11_options = {
L160:         "url": "jdbc:oracle:thin:@//<jdbc-host-name>:1521/ORCL",
L161:         "dbtable": "test",
L162:         "user": "admin",
L163:         "password": "pwd"}
L164: 
L165:     connection_oracle18_options = {
L166:         "url": "jdbc:oracle:thin:@//<jdbc-host-name>:1521/ORCL",
L167:         "dbtable": "test",
L168:         "user": "admin",
L169:         "password": "pwd",
L170:         "customJdbcDriverS3Path": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/ojdbc10.jar",
L171:         "customJdbcDriverClassName": "oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver"}
L172:     # Read from JDBC databases with custom driver
L173:     df_mysql8 = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_options(connection_type="mysql",
L174:                                                               connection_options=connection_mysql8_options)
L175: 
L176:     # Read DynamicFrame from MySQL 5 and write to MySQL 8
L177:     df_mysql5 = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_options(connection_type="mysql",
L178:                                                               connection_options=connection_mysql5_options)
L179:     glueContext.write_from_options(frame_or_dfc=df_mysql5, connection_type="mysql",
L180:                                    connection_options=connection_mysql8_options)
L181: 
L182:     # Read DynamicFrame from Oracle 11 and write to Oracle 18
L183:     df_oracle11 = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_options(connection_type="oracle",
L184:                                                                 connection_options=connection_oracle11_options)
L185:     glueContext.write_from_options(frame_or_dfc=df_oracle11, connection_type="oracle",
L186:                                    connection_options=connection_oracle18_options)
L187: 
L188:     `
L189: Scala
L190: 
L191: 
L192:     `import com.amazonaws.services.glue.GlueContext
L193:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.MappingSpec
L194:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.errors.CallSite
L195:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.util.GlueArgParser
L196:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.util.Job
L197:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.util.JsonOptions
L198:     import com.amazonaws.services.glue.DynamicFrame
L199:     import org.apache.spark.SparkContext
L200:     import scala.collection.JavaConverters._
L201: 
L202: 
L203:     object GlueApp {
L204:       val MYSQL_5_URI: String = "jdbc:mysql://<jdbc-host-name>:3306/db"
L205:       val MYSQL_8_URI: String = "jdbc:mysql://<jdbc-host-name>:3306/db"
L206:       val ORACLE_11_URI: String = "jdbc:oracle:thin:@//<jdbc-host-name>:1521/ORCL"
L207:       val ORACLE_18_URI: String = "jdbc:oracle:thin:@//<jdbc-host-name>:1521/ORCL"
L208: 
L209:       // Construct JDBC connection options
L210:       lazy val mysql5JsonOption = jsonOptions(MYSQL_5_URI)
L211:       lazy val mysql8JsonOption = customJDBCDriverJsonOptions(MYSQL_8_URI, "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/mysql-connector-java-8.0.17.jar", "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")
L212:       lazy val oracle11JsonOption = jsonOptions(ORACLE_11_URI)
L213:       lazy val oracle18JsonOption = customJDBCDriverJsonOptions(ORACLE_18_URI, "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/ojdbc10.jar", "oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver")
L214: 
L215:       def main(sysArgs: Array[String]): Unit = {
L216:         val spark: SparkContext = new SparkContext()
L217:         val glueContext: GlueContext = new GlueContext(spark)
L218:         val args = GlueArgParser.getResolvedOptions(sysArgs, Seq("JOB_NAME").toArray)
L219:         Job.init(args("JOB_NAME"), glueContext, args.asJava)
L220: 
L221:         // Read from JDBC database with custom driver
L222:         val df_mysql8: DynamicFrame = glueContext.getSource("mysql", mysql8JsonOption).getDynamicFrame()
L223: 
L224:         // Read DynamicFrame from MySQL 5 and write to MySQL 8
L225:         val df_mysql5: DynamicFrame = glueContext.getSource("mysql", mysql5JsonOption).getDynamicFrame()
L226:         glueContext.getSink("mysql", mysql8JsonOption).writeDynamicFrame(df_mysql5)
L227: 
L228:         // Read DynamicFrame from Oracle 11 and write to Oracle 18
L229:         val df_oracle11: DynamicFrame = glueContext.getSource("oracle", oracle11JsonOption).getDynamicFrame()
L230:         glueContext.getSink("oracle", oracle18JsonOption).writeDynamicFrame(df_oracle11)
L231: 
L232:         Job.commit()
L233:       }
L234:       private def jsonOptions(url: String): JsonOptions = {
L235:         new JsonOptions(
L236:           s"""{"url": "${url}",
L237:              |"dbtable":"test",
L238:              |"user": "admin",
L239:              |"password": "pwd"}""".stripMargin)
L240:       }
L241: 
L242:       private def customJDBCDriverJsonOptions(url: String, customJdbcDriverS3Path: String, customJdbcDriverClassName: String): JsonOptions = {
L243:         new JsonOptions(
L244:           s"""{"url": "${url}",
L245:              |"dbtable":"test",
L246:              |"user": "admin",
L247:              |"password": "pwd",
L248:              |"customJdbcDriverS3Path": "${customJdbcDriverS3Path}",
L249:              |"customJdbcDriverClassName" : "${customJdbcDriverClassName}"}""".stripMargin)
L250:       }
L251:     }`
