L35: By “group by” we are referring to a process involving one or more of the following steps:
L36: 
L37:   * Splitting the data into groups based on some criteria.
L38: 
L39:   * Applying a function to each group independently.
L40: 
L41:   * Combining the results into a data structure.
L42: 
L43: Out of these, the split step is the most straightforward. In the apply step, we might wish to do one of the following:
L44: 
L45:   * Aggregation: compute a summary statistic (or statistics) for each group. Some examples:
L46: >     * Compute group sums or means.
L47: >
L48: >     * Compute group sizes / counts.
L49: 
L50:   * Transformation: perform some group-specific computations and return a like-indexed object. Some examples:
L51: 
L52: >     * Standardize data (zscore) within a group.
L53: >
L54: >     * Filling NAs within groups with a value derived from each group.
L55: 
L56:   * Filtration: discard some groups, according to a group-wise computation that evaluates to True or False. Some examples:
L57: >     * Discard data that belong to groups with only a few members.
L58: >
L59: >     * Filter out data based on the group sum or mean.
L60: 
L61: Many of these operations are defined on GroupBy objects. These operations are similar to those of the cite31†aggregating API , cite32†window API , and cite33†resample API .
L62: It is possible that a given operation does not fall into one of these categories or is some combination of them. In such a case, it may be possible to compute the operation using GroupBy’s `apply` method. This method will examine the results of the apply step and try to sensibly combine them into a single result if it doesn’t fit into either of the above three categories.
L63: 
L64: Note
L65: An operation that is split into multiple steps using built-in GroupBy operations will be more efficient than using the `apply` method with a user-defined Python function.
L66: 
L67: The name GroupBy should be quite familiar to those who have used a SQL-based tool (or `itertools`), in which you can write code like:
L68: 
L69:     SELECT Column1, Column2, mean(Column3), sum(Column4)
L70:     FROM SomeTable
L71:     GROUP BY Column1, Column2
L72: We aim to make operations like this natural and easy to express using pandas. We’ll address each area of GroupBy functionality, then provide some non-trivial examples / use cases.
L73: 
L74: See the cite34†cookbook for some advanced strategies.
L75: ## Splitting an object into groupscite35†# L76: The abstract definition of grouping is to provide a mapping of labels to group names. To create a GroupBy object (more on what the GroupBy object is later), you may do the following:
L77: 
L78:     In [1]: speeds = pd.DataFrame(
L79:        ...:     [
L80:        ...:         ("bird", "Falconiformes", 389.0),
L81:        ...:         ("bird", "Psittaciformes", 24.0),
L82:        ...:         ("mammal", "Carnivora", 80.2),
L83:        ...:         ("mammal", "Primates", np.nan),
L84:        ...:         ("mammal", "Carnivora", 58),
L85:        ...:     ],
L86:        ...:     index=["falcon", "parrot", "lion", "monkey", "leopard"],
L87:        ...:     columns=("class", "order", "max_speed"),
L88:        ...: )
L89:        ...:
L90: 
L91:     In [2]: speeds
L92:     Out[2]:
L93:               class           order  max_speed
L94:     falcon     bird   Falconiformes      389.0
L95:     parrot     bird  Psittaciformes       24.0
L96:     lion     mammal       Carnivora       80.2
L97:     monkey   mammal        Primates        NaN
L98:     leopard  mammal       Carnivora       58.0
L99:     In [3]: grouped = speeds.groupby("class")
L100: 
L101:     In [4]: grouped = speeds.groupby(["class", "order"])
L102: The mapping can be specified many different ways:
L103: 
L104:   * A Python function, to be called on each of the index labels.
L105: 
L106:   * A list or NumPy array of the same length as the index.
L107: 
L108:   * A dict or `Series`, providing a `label -> group name` mapping.
L109: 
L110:   * For `DataFrame` objects, a string indicating either a column name or an index level name to be used to group.
L111: 
L112:   * A list of any of the above things.
L113: 
L114: Collectively we refer to the grouping objects as the keys. For example, consider the following `DataFrame`:
L115: Note
L116: A string passed to `groupby` may refer to either a column or an index level. If a string matches both a column name and an index level name, a `ValueError` will be raised.
L117: 
L118:     In [5]: df = pd.DataFrame(
L119:        ...:     {
L120:        ...:         "A": ["foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "foo"],
L121:        ...:         "B": ["one", "one", "two", "three", "two", "two", "one", "three"],
L122:        ...:         "C": np.random.randn(8),
L123:        ...:         "D": np.random.randn(8),
L124:        ...:     }
L125:        ...: )
L126:        ...:
L127: 
L128:     In [6]: df
L129:     Out[6]:
L130:          A      B         C         D
L131:     0  foo    one  0.469112 -0.861849
L132:     1  bar    one -0.282863 -2.104569
L133:     2  foo    two -1.509059 -0.494929
L134:     3  bar  three -1.135632  1.071804
L135:     4  foo    two  1.212112  0.721555
L136:     5  bar    two -0.173215 -0.706771
L137:     6  foo    one  0.119209 -1.039575
L138:     7  foo  three -1.044236  0.271860
L139: On a DataFrame, we obtain a GroupBy object by calling cite36†`groupby()` . This method returns a `pandas.api.typing.DataFrameGroupBy` instance. We could naturally group by either the `A` or `B` columns, or both:
L140: 
L141:     In [7]: grouped = df.groupby("A")
L142: 
L143:     In [8]: grouped = df.groupby("B")
L144: 
L145:     In [9]: grouped = df.groupby(["A", "B"])
L146: 
L147: 
L148: Note
L149: 
L150: `df.groupby('A')` is just syntactic sugar for `df.groupby(df['A'])`.
L151: DataFrame groupby always operates along axis 0 (rows). To split by columns, first do a transpose:
L152: 
L153:     In [10]: def get_letter_type(letter):
L154:        ....:     if letter.lower() in 'aeiou':
L155:        ....:         return 'vowel'
L156:        ....:     else:
L157:        ....:         return 'consonant'
L158:        ....:
L159: 
L160:     In [11]: grouped = df.T.groupby(get_letter_type)
L161: pandas cite37†`Index` objects support duplicate values. If a non-unique index is used as the group key in a groupby operation, all values for the same index value will be considered to be in one group and thus the output of aggregation functions will only contain unique index values:
L162: 
L163:     In [12]: index = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]
L164: 
L165:     In [13]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 30], index=index)
L166: 
L167:     In [14]: s
L168:     Out[14]:
L169:     1     1
L170:     2     2
L171:     3     3
L172:     1    10
L173:     2    20
L174:     3    30
L175:     dtype: int64
L176: 
L177:     In [15]: grouped = s.groupby(level=0)
L178: 
L179:     In [16]: grouped.first()
L180:     Out[16]:
L181:     1    1
L182:     2    2
L183:     3    3
L184:     dtype: int64
L185: 
L186:     In [17]: grouped.last()
L187:     Out[17]:
L188:     1    10
L189:     2    20
L190:     3    30
L191:     dtype: int64
L192: 
L193:     In [18]: grouped.sum()
L194:     Out[18]:
L195:     1    11
L196:     2    22
L197:     3    33
L198:     dtype: int64
L199: Note that no splitting occurs until it’s needed. Creating the GroupBy object only verifies that you’ve passed a valid mapping.
L200: 
L201: Note
L202: 
L203: Many kinds of complicated data manipulations can be expressed in terms of GroupBy operations (though it can’t be guaranteed to be the most efficient implementation). You can get quite creative with the label mapping functions.
L204: ### GroupBy sortingcite38†# L205: By default the group keys are sorted during the `groupby` operation. You may however pass `sort=False` for potential speedups. With `sort=False` the order among group-keys follows the order of appearance of the keys in the original dataframe:
L206: 
L207:     In [19]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({"X": ["B", "B", "A", "A"], "Y": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
L208: 
L209:     In [20]: df2.groupby(["X"]).sum()
L210:     Out[20]:
L211:        Y
L212:     X
L213:     A  7
L214:     B  3
L215: 
L216:     In [21]: df2.groupby(["X"], sort=False).sum()
L217:     Out[21]:
L218:        Y
L219:     X
L220:     B  3
L221:     A  7
L222: Note that `groupby` will preserve the order in which observations are sorted within each group. For example, the groups created by `groupby()` below are in the order they appeared in the original `DataFrame`:
L223: 
L224:     In [22]: df3 = pd.DataFrame({"X": ["A", "B", "A", "B"], "Y": [1, 4, 3, 2]})
L225: 
L226:     In [23]: df3.groupby("X").get_group("A")
L227:     Out[23]:
L228:        X  Y
L229:     0  A  1
L230:     2  A  3
L231: 
L232:     In [24]: df3.groupby(["X"]).get_group(("B",))
L233:     Out[24]:
L234:        X  Y
L235:     1  B  4
L236:     3  B  2
L237: #### GroupBy dropnacite39†# L238: By default `NA` values are excluded from group keys during the `groupby` operation. However, in case you want to include `NA` values in group keys, you could pass `dropna=False` to achieve it.
L239: 
L240:     In [25]: df_list = [[1, 2, 3], [1, None, 4], [2, 1, 3], [1, 2, 2]]
L241: 
L242:     In [26]: df_dropna = pd.DataFrame(df_list, columns=["a", "b", "c"])
L243: 
L244:     In [27]: df_dropna
L245:     Out[27]:
L246:        a    b  c
L247:     0  1  2.0  3
L248:     1  1  NaN  4
L249:     2  2  1.0  3
L250:     3  1  2.0  2
L251:     # Default ``dropna`` is set to True, which will exclude NaNs in keys
L252:     In [28]: df_dropna.groupby(by=["b"], dropna=True).sum()
L253:     Out[28]:
L254:          a  c
L255:     b
L256:     1.0  2  3
L257:     2.0  2  5
L258: 
L259:     # In order to allow NaN in keys, set ``dropna`` to False
L260:     In [29]: df_dropna.groupby(by=["b"], dropna=False).sum()
L261:     Out[29]:
L262:          a  c
L263:     b
L264:     1.0  2  3
L265:     2.0  2  5
L266:     NaN  1  4
L267: The default setting of `dropna` argument is `True` which means `NA` are not included in group keys.
L268: ### GroupBy object attributescite40†# L269: 
L270: The `groups` attribute of a GroupBy object is a dictionary that maps each unique group key to the index labels belonging to that group. In the above example:
L271: 
L272:     In [30]: df.groupby("A").groups
L273:     Out[30]: {'bar': [1, 3, 5], 'foo': [0, 2, 4, 6, 7]}
L274: 
L275:     In [31]: df.T.groupby(get_letter_type).groups
L276:     Out[31]: {'consonant': ['B', 'C', 'D'], 'vowel': ['A']}
L277: Calling the standard Python `len` function on the GroupBy object returns the number of groups, which is the same as the length of the `groups` dictionary:
L278: 
L279:     In [32]: grouped = df.groupby(["A", "B"])
L280: 
L281:     In [33]: grouped.groups
L282:     Out[33]:
L283:     {('bar', 'one'): RangeIndex(start=1, stop=2, step=1),
L284:      ('bar', 'three'): RangeIndex(start=3, stop=4, step=1),
L285:      ('bar', 'two'): RangeIndex(start=5, stop=6, step=1),
L286:      ('foo', 'one'): RangeIndex(start=0, stop=12, step=6),
L287:      ('foo', 'three'): RangeIndex(start=7, stop=8, step=1),
L288:      ('foo', 'two'): RangeIndex(start=2, stop=6, step=2)}
L289: 
L290:     In [34]: len(grouped)
L291:     Out[34]: 6
L292: `GroupBy` will tab complete column names, GroupBy operations, and other attributes:
L293: 
L294:     In [35]: n = 10
L295: 
L296:     In [36]: weight = np.random.normal(166, 20, size=n)
L297: 
L298:     In [37]: height = np.random.normal(60, 10, size=n)
L299: 
L300:     In [38]: time = pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=n)
L301: 
L302:     In [39]: gender = np.random.choice(["male", "female"], size=n)
L303: 
L304:     In [40]: df = pd.DataFrame(
L305:        ....:     {"height": height, "weight": weight, "gender": gender}, index=time
L306:        ....: )
L307:        ....:
L308: 
L309:     In [41]: df
L310:     Out[41]:
L311:                    height      weight  gender
L312:     2000-01-01  42.849980  157.500553    male
L313:     2000-01-02  49.607315  177.340407    male
L314:     2000-01-03  56.293531  171.524640    male
L315:     2000-01-04  48.421077  144.251986  female
L316:     2000-01-05  46.556882  152.526206    male
L317:     2000-01-06  68.448851  168.272968  female
L318:     2000-01-07  70.757698  136.431469    male
L319:     2000-01-08  58.909500  176.499753  female
L320:     2000-01-09  76.435631  174.094104  female
L321:     2000-01-10  45.306120  177.540920    male
L322: 
L323:     In [42]: gb = df.groupby("gender")
L324: 
L325: 
L326:     In [43]: gb.<TAB>  # noqa: E225, E999
L327:     gb.agg        gb.boxplot    gb.cummin     gb.describe   gb.filter     gb.get_group  gb.height     gb.last       gb.median     gb.ngroups    gb.plot       gb.rank       gb.std        gb.transform
L328:     gb.aggregate  gb.count      gb.cumprod    gb.dtype      gb.first      gb.groups     gb.hist       gb.max        gb.min        gb.nth        gb.prod       gb.resample   gb.sum        gb.var
L329:     gb.apply      gb.cummax     gb.cumsum     gb.gender     gb.head       gb.indices    gb.mean       gb.name       gb.ohlc       gb.quantile   gb.size       gb.tail       gb.weight
L330: ### GroupBy with MultiIndexcite41†# L331: 
L332: With cite42†hierarchically-indexed data , it’s quite natural to group by one of the levels of the hierarchy.
L333: Let’s create a Series with a two-level `MultiIndex`.
L334: 
L335:     In [44]: arrays = [
L336:        ....:     ["bar", "bar", "baz", "baz", "foo", "foo", "qux", "qux"],
L337:        ....:     ["one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two"],
L338:        ....: ]
L339:        ....:
L340: 
L341:     In [45]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=["first", "second"])
L342: 
L343:     In [46]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(8), index=index)
L344: 
L345:     In [47]: s
L346:     Out[47]:
L347:     first  second
L348:     bar    one      -0.919854
L349:            two      -0.042379
L350:     baz    one       1.247642
L351:            two      -0.009920
L352:     foo    one       0.290213
L353:            two       0.495767
L354:     qux    one       0.362949
L355:            two       1.548106
L356:     dtype: float64
L357: We can then group by one of the levels in `s`.
L358: 
L359:     In [48]: grouped = s.groupby(level=0)
L360: 
L361:     In [49]: grouped.sum()
L362:     Out[49]:
L363:     first
L364:     bar   -0.962232
L365:     baz    1.237723
L366:     foo    0.785980
L367:     qux    1.911055
L368:     dtype: float64
L369: 
L370: 
L371: If the MultiIndex has names specified, these can be passed instead of the level number:
L372: 
L373:     In [50]: s.groupby(level="second").sum()
L374:     Out[50]:
L375:     second
L376:     one    0.980950
L377:     two    1.991575
L378:     dtype: float64
L379: Grouping with multiple levels is supported.
L380: 
L381:     In [51]: arrays = [
L382:        ....:     ["bar", "bar", "baz", "baz", "foo", "foo", "qux", "qux"],
L383:        ....:     ["doo", "doo", "bee", "bee", "bop", "bop", "bop", "bop"],
L384:        ....:     ["one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two"],
L385:        ....: ]
L386:        ....:
L387: 
L388:     In [52]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=["first", "second", "third"])
L389: 
L390:     In [53]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(8), index=index)
L391: 
L392:     In [54]: s
L393:     Out[54]:
L394:     first  second  third
L395:     bar    doo     one     -1.131345
L396:                    two     -0.089329
L397:     baz    bee     one      0.337863
L398:                    two     -0.945867
L399:     foo    bop     one     -0.932132
L400:                    two      1.956030
L401:     qux    bop     one      0.017587
L402:                    two     -0.016692
L403:     dtype: float64
L404: 
L405:     In [55]: s.groupby(level=["first", "second"]).sum()
L406:     Out[55]:
L407:     first  second
L408:     bar    doo      -1.220674
L409:     baz    bee      -0.608004
L410:     foo    bop       1.023898
L411:     qux    bop       0.000895
L412:     dtype: float64
L413: Index level names may be supplied as keys.
L414: 
L415:     In [56]: s.groupby(["first", "second"]).sum()
L416:     Out[56]:
L417:     first  second
L418:     bar    doo      -1.220674
L419:     baz    bee      -0.608004
L420:     foo    bop       1.023898
L421:     qux    bop       0.000895
L422:     dtype: float64
L423: 
L424: 
L425: More on the `sum` function and aggregation later.
L426: ### Grouping DataFrame with Index levels and columnscite43†# L427: 
L428: A DataFrame may be grouped by a combination of columns and index levels. You can specify both column and index names, or use a cite44†`Grouper` .
L429: Let’s first create a DataFrame with a MultiIndex:
L430: 
L431:     In [57]: arrays = [
L432:        ....:     ["bar", "bar", "baz", "baz", "foo", "foo", "qux", "qux"],
L433:        ....:     ["one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two"],
L434:        ....: ]
L435:        ....:
L436: 
L437:     In [58]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=["first", "second"])
L438: 
L439:     In [59]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3], "B": np.arange(8)}, index=index)
L440: 
L441:     In [60]: df
L442:     Out[60]:
L443:                   A  B
L444:     first second
L445:     bar   one     1  0
L446:           two     1  1
L447:     baz   one     1  2
L448:           two     1  3
L449:     foo   one     2  4
L450:           two     2  5
L451:     qux   one     3  6
L452:           two     3  7
L453: Then we group `df` by the `second` index level and the `A` column.
L454: 
L455:     In [61]: df.groupby([pd.Grouper(level=1), "A"]).sum()
L456:     Out[61]:
L457:               B
L458:     second A
L459:     one    1  2
L460:            2  4
L461:            3  6
L462:     two    1  4
L463:            2  5
L464:            3  7
L465: Index levels may also be specified by name.
L466: 
L467:     In [62]: df.groupby([pd.Grouper(level="second"), "A"]).sum()
L468:     Out[62]:
L469:               B
L470:     second A
L471:     one    1  2
L472:            2  4
L473:            3  6
L474:     two    1  4
L475:            2  5
L476:            3  7
L477: Index level names may be specified as keys directly to `groupby`.
L478: 
L479:     In [63]: df.groupby(["second", "A"]).sum()
L480:     Out[63]:
L481:               B
L482:     second A
L483:     one    1  2
L484:            2  4
L485:            3  6
L486:     two    1  4
L487:            2  5
L488:            3  7
L489: ### DataFrame column selection in GroupBycite45†# L490: Once you have created the GroupBy object from a DataFrame, you might want to do something different for each of the columns. Thus, by using `[]` on the GroupBy object in a similar way as the one used to get a column from a DataFrame, you can do:
L491: 
L492:     In [64]: df = pd.DataFrame(
L493:        ....:     {
L494:        ....:         "A": ["foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "foo"],
L495:        ....:         "B": ["one", "one", "two", "three", "two", "two", "one", "three"],
L496:        ....:         "C": np.random.randn(8),
L497:        ....:         "D": np.random.randn(8),
L498:        ....:     }
L499:        ....: )
L500:        ....:
L501: 
L502:     In [65]: df
L503:     Out[65]:
L504:          A      B         C         D
L505:     0  foo    one -0.575247  1.346061
L506:     1  bar    one  0.254161  1.511763
L507:     2  foo    two -1.143704  1.627081
L508:     3  bar  three  0.215897 -0.990582
L509:     4  foo    two  1.193555 -0.441652
L510:     5  bar    two -0.077118  1.211526
L511:     6  foo    one -0.408530  0.268520
L512:     7  foo  three -0.862495  0.024580
L513: 
L514:     In [66]: grouped = df.groupby(["A"])
L515: 
L516:     In [67]: grouped_C = grouped["C"]
L517: 
L518:     In [68]: grouped_D = grouped["D"]
L519: This is mainly syntactic sugar for the alternative, which is much more verbose:
L520: 
L521:     In [69]: df["C"].groupby(df["A"])
L522:     Out[69]: <pandas.api.typing.SeriesGroupBy object at 0x7ff6138b2390>
L523: 
L524: 
L525: Additionally, this method avoids recomputing the internal grouping information derived from the passed key.
L526: You can also include the grouping columns if you want to operate on them.
L527: 
L528:     In [70]: grouped[["A", "B"]].sum()
L529:     Out[70]:
L530:                        A                  B
L531:     A
L532:     bar        barbarbar        onethreetwo
L533:     foo  foofoofoofoofoo  onetwotwoonethree
L534: 
L535: 
L536: Note
L537: The `groupby` operation in pandas drops the `name` field of the columns Index object after the operation. This change ensures consistency in syntax between different column selection methods within groupby operations.
L538: ## Iterating through groupscite46†# L539: With the GroupBy object in hand, iterating through the grouped data is very natural and functions similarly to cite47†`itertools.groupby()`†docs.python.org :
L540: 
L541:     In [71]: grouped = df.groupby('A')
L542: 
L543:     In [72]: for name, group in grouped:
L544:        ....:     print(name)
L545:        ....:     print(group)
L546:        ....:
L547:     bar
L548:          A      B         C         D
L549:     1  bar    one  0.254161  1.511763
L550:     3  bar  three  0.215897 -0.990582
L551:     5  bar    two -0.077118  1.211526
L552:     foo
L553:          A      B         C         D
L554:     0  foo    one -0.575247  1.346061
L555:     2  foo    two -1.143704  1.627081
L556:     4  foo    two  1.193555 -0.441652
L557:     6  foo    one -0.408530  0.268520
L558:     7  foo  three -0.862495  0.024580
L559: In the case of grouping by multiple keys, the group name will be a tuple:
L560: 
L561:     In [73]: for name, group in df.groupby(['A', 'B']):
L562:        ....:     print(name)
L563:        ....:     print(group)
L564:        ....:
L565:     ('bar', 'one')

L29: scipy.stats.poisson = <scipy.stats._discrete_distns.poisson_gen object>cite20†[source]†github.com cite21†# L30: 
L31: 
L32: A Poisson discrete random variable.
L33: 
L34: As an instance of the cite22†`rv_discrete` class, cite21†`poisson` object inherits from it a collection of generic methods (see below for the full list), and completes them with details specific for this particular distribution.
L35: 
L36: Methods
L37: rvs(mu, loc=0, size=1, random_state=None)  | Random variates.
L38: pmf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Probability mass function.
L39: logpmf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Log of the probability mass function.
L40: cdf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Cumulative distribution function.
L41: logcdf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Log of the cumulative distribution function.
L42: sf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Survival function (also defined as `1 - cdf`, but sf is sometimes more accurate).
L43: logsf(k, mu, loc=0)  | Log of the survival function.
L44: ppf(q, mu, loc=0)  | Percent point function (inverse of `cdf` — percentiles).
L45: isf(q, mu, loc=0)  | Inverse survival function (inverse of `sf`).
L46: stats(mu, loc=0, moments=’mv’)  | Mean(‘m’), variance(‘v’), skew(‘s’), and/or kurtosis(‘k’).
L47: entropy(mu, loc=0)  | (Differential) entropy of the RV.
L48: expect(func, args=(mu,), loc=0, lb=None, ub=None, conditional=False)  | Expected value of a function (of one argument) with respect to the distribution.
L49: median(mu, loc=0)  | Median of the distribution.
L50: mean(mu, loc=0)  | Mean of the distribution.
L51: var(mu, loc=0)  | Variance of the distribution.
L52: std(mu, loc=0)  | Standard deviation of the distribution.
L53: interval(confidence, mu, loc=0)  | Confidence interval with equal areas around the median.
L54: Notes
L55: 
L56: The probability mass function for cite21†`poisson` is:
L57: 
L58: \[f(k) = \exp(-\mu) \frac{\mu^k}{k!}\]
L59: 
L60: for \(k \ge 0\).
L61: 
L62: cite21†`poisson` takes \(\mu \geq 0\) as shape parameter. When \(\mu = 0\), the `pmf` method returns `1.0` at quantile \(k = 0\).
L63: 
L64: The probability mass function above is defined in the “standardized” form. To shift distribution use the `loc` parameter. Specifically, `poisson.pmf(k, mu, loc)` is identically equivalent to `poisson.pmf(k - loc, mu)`.
L65: 
L66: Examples
L67: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L68: 
L69:     >>> import numpy as np
L70:     >>> from scipy.stats import poisson
L71:     >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
L72:     >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
L73: 
L74: 
L75: Get the support:
L76: 
L77:     >>> mu = 0.6
L78:     >>> lb, ub = poisson.support(mu)
L79: 
L80: 
L81: Calculate the first four moments:
L82: 
L83:     >>> mean, var, skew, kurt = poisson.stats(mu, moments='mvsk')
L84: Display the probability mass function (`pmf`):
L85: 
L86:     >>> x = np.arange(poisson.ppf(0.01, mu),
L87:     ...               poisson.ppf(0.99, mu))
L88:     >>> ax.plot(x, poisson.pmf(x, mu), 'bo', ms=8, label='poisson pmf')
L89:     >>> ax.vlines(x, 0, poisson.pmf(x, mu), colors='b', lw=5, alpha=0.5)
L90: 
L91: 
L92: Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function) to fix the shape and location. This returns a “frozen” RV object holding the given parameters fixed.
L93: Freeze the distribution and display the frozen `pmf`:
L94: 
L95:     >>> rv = poisson(mu)
L96:     >>> ax.vlines(x, 0, rv.pmf(x), colors='k', linestyles='-', lw=1,
L97:     ...         label='frozen pmf')
L98:     >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
L99:     >>> plt.show()
L100: 
L101: 
L102: cite23†Image: ../../_images/scipy-stats-poisson-1_00_00.png L103: 
L104: Check accuracy of `cdf` and `ppf`:
L105: 
L106:     >>> prob = poisson.cdf(x, mu)
L107:     >>> np.allclose(x, poisson.ppf(prob, mu))
L108:     True
L109: Generate random numbers:
L110: 
L111:     >>> r = poisson.rvs(mu, size=1000)

External Resources, Videos and Talks L73: # 1.9. Naive Bayescite66†# L74: 
L75: Naive Bayes methods are a set of supervised learning algorithms based on applying Bayes’ theorem with the “naive” assumption of conditional independence between every pair of features given the value of the class variable. Bayes’ theorem states the following relationship, given class variable \(y\) and dependent feature vector \(x_1\) through \(x_n\):
L76: 
L77: \[P(y \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) = \frac{P(y) P(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid y)} {P(x_1, \dots, x_n)}\]
L78: Using the naive conditional independence assumption that
L79: 
L80: \[P(x_i | y, x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \dots, x_n) = P(x_i | y),\]
L81: 
L82: for all \(i\), this relationship is simplified to
L83: 
L84: \[P(y \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) = \frac{P(y) \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i \mid y)} {P(x_1, \dots, x_n)}\]
L85: 
L86: Since \(P(x_1, \dots, x_n)\) is constant given the input, we can use the following classification rule:
L87: \[ \begin{align}\begin{aligned}P(y \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) \propto P(y) \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i \mid y)\\\Downarrow\\\hat{y} = \arg\max_y P(y) \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i \mid y),\end{aligned}\end{align} \]
L88: 
L89: and we can use Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation to estimate \(P(y)\) and \(P(x_i \mid y)\); the former is then the relative frequency of class \(y\) in the training set.
L90: 
L91: The different naive Bayes classifiers differ mainly by the assumptions they make regarding the distribution of \(P(x_i \mid y)\).
L92: In spite of their apparently over-simplified assumptions, naive Bayes classifiers have worked quite well in many real-world situations, famously document classification and spam filtering. They require a small amount of training data to estimate the necessary parameters. (For theoretical reasons why naive Bayes works well, and on which types of data it does, see the references below.)
L93: Naive Bayes learners and classifiers can be extremely fast compared to more sophisticated methods. The decoupling of the class conditional feature distributions means that each distribution can be independently estimated as a one-dimensional distribution. This in turn helps to alleviate problems stemming from the curse of dimensionality.
L94: On the flip side, although naive Bayes is known as a decent classifier, it is known to be a bad estimator, so the probability outputs from `predict_proba` are not to be taken too seriously.
L95: 
L96: Referencescite67†# L97: 
L98:   * H. Zhang (2004). cite68†The optimality of Naive Bayes.†www.cs.unb.ca Proc. FLAIRS.
L99: ## 1.9.1. Gaussian Naive Bayescite69†# L100: 
L101: cite70†`GaussianNB` implements the Gaussian Naive Bayes algorithm for classification. The likelihood of the features is assumed to be Gaussian:
L102: 
L103: \[P(x_i \mid y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2_y}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x_i - \mu_y)^2}{2\sigma^2_y}\right)\]
L104: The parameters \(\sigma_y\) and \(\mu_y\) are estimated using maximum likelihood.
L105: 
L106:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
L107:     >>> from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
L108:     >>> from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
L109:     >>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
L110:     >>> X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
L111:     >>> gnb = GaussianNB()
L112:     >>> y_pred = gnb.fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_test)
L113:     >>> print("Number of mislabeled points out of a total %d points : %d"
L114:     ...       % (X_test.shape[0], (y_test != y_pred).sum()))
L115:     Number of mislabeled points out of a total 75 points : 4
L116: ## 1.9.2. Multinomial Naive Bayescite71†# L117: cite72†`MultinomialNB` implements the naive Bayes algorithm for multinomially distributed data, and is one of the two classic naive Bayes variants used in text classification (where the data are typically represented as word vector counts, although tf-idf vectors are also known to work well in practice).
L118: The distribution is parametrized by vectors \(\theta_y = (\theta_{y1},\ldots,\theta_{yn})\) for each class \(y\), where \(n\) is the number of features (in text classification, the size of the vocabulary) and \(\theta_{yi}\) is the probability \(P(x_i \mid y)\) of feature \(i\) appearing in a sample belonging to class \(y\).
L119: The parameters \(\theta_y\) are estimated by a smoothed version of maximum likelihood, i.e. relative frequency counting:
L120: 
L121: \[\hat{\theta}_{yi} = \frac{ N_{yi} + \alpha}{N_y + \alpha n}\]
L122: 
L123: where \(N_{yi} = \sum_{x \in T} x_i\) is the number of times feature \(i\) appears in all samples of class \(y\) in the training set \(T\), and \(N_{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} N_{yi}\) is the total count of all features for class \(y\).
L124: The smoothing priors \(\alpha \ge 0\) account for features not present in the learning samples and prevent zero probabilities in further computations. Setting \(\alpha = 1\) is called Laplace smoothing, while \(\alpha < 1\) is called Lidstone smoothing.
L125: ## 1.9.3. Complement Naive Bayescite73†# L126: cite74†`ComplementNB` implements the complement naive Bayes (CNB) algorithm. CNB is an adaptation of the standard multinomial naive Bayes (MNB) algorithm that is particularly suited for imbalanced data sets. Specifically, CNB uses statistics from the complement of each class to compute the model’s weights. The inventors of CNB show empirically that the parameter estimates for CNB are more stable than those for MNB.
L127: Further, CNB regularly outperforms MNB (often by a considerable margin) on text classification tasks.
L128: Weights calculationcite75†# L129: 
L130: The procedure for calculating the weights is as follows:
L131: 
L132: \[ \begin{align}\begin{aligned}\hat{\theta}_{ci} = \frac{\alpha_i + \sum_{j:y_j \neq c} d_{ij}} {\alpha + \sum_{j:y_j \neq c} \sum_{k} d_{kj}}\\w_{ci} = \log \hat{\theta}_{ci}\\w_{ci} = \frac{w_{ci}}{\sum_{j} |w_{cj}|}\end{aligned}\end{align} \]
L133: where the summations are over all documents \(j\) not in class \(c\), \(d_{ij}\) is either the count or tf-idf value of term \(i\) in document \(j\), \(\alpha_i\) is a smoothing hyperparameter like that found in MNB, and \(\alpha = \sum_{i} \alpha_i\). The second normalization addresses the tendency for longer documents to dominate parameter estimates in MNB. The classification rule is:
L134: 
L135: \[\hat{c} = \arg\min_c \sum_{i} t_i w_{ci}\]
L136: i.e., a document is assigned to the class that is the poorest complement match.
L137: 
L138: Referencescite76†# L139: 
L140:   * Rennie, J. D., Shih, L., Teevan, J., & Karger, D. R. (2003). cite77†Tackling the poor assumptions of naive bayes text classifiers.†people.csail.mit.edu In ICML (Vol. 3, pp. 616-623).
L141: ## 1.9.4. Bernoulli Naive Bayescite78†# L142: cite79†`BernoulliNB` implements the naive Bayes training and classification algorithms for data that is distributed according to multivariate Bernoulli distributions; i.e., there may be multiple features but each one is assumed to be a binary-valued (Bernoulli, boolean) variable. Therefore, this class requires samples to be represented as binary-valued feature vectors; if handed any other kind of data, a cite79†`BernoulliNB` instance may binarize its input (depending on the `binarize` parameter).
L143: The decision rule for Bernoulli naive Bayes is based on
L144: 
L145: \[P(x_i \mid y) = P(x_i = 1 \mid y) x_i + (1 - P(x_i = 1 \mid y)) (1 - x_i)\]
L146: 
L147: which differs from multinomial NB’s rule in that it explicitly penalizes the non-occurrence of a feature \(i\) that is an indicator for class \(y\), where the multinomial variant would simply ignore a non-occurring feature.
L148: In the case of text classification, word occurrence vectors (rather than word count vectors) may be used to train and use this classifier. cite79†`BernoulliNB` might perform better on some datasets, especially those with shorter documents. It is advisable to evaluate both models, if time permits.
L149: 
L150: Referencescite80†# L151: 
L152:   * C.D. Manning, P. Raghavan and H. Schütze (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press, pp. 234-265.
L153:   * A. McCallum and K. Nigam (1998). cite81†A comparison of event models for Naive Bayes text classification.†cdn.aaai.org Proc. AAAI/ICML-98 Workshop on Learning for Text Categorization, pp. 41-48.
L154: 
L155:   * V. Metsis, I. Androutsopoulos and G. Paliouras (2006). cite82†Spam filtering with Naive Bayes – Which Naive Bayes?†www2.aueb.gr 3rd Conf. on Email and Anti-Spam (CEAS).
L156: ## 1.9.5. Categorical Naive Bayescite83†# L157: 
L158: cite84†`CategoricalNB` implements the categorical naive Bayes algorithm for categorically distributed data. It assumes that each feature, which is described by the index \(i\), has its own categorical distribution.
L159: For each feature \(i\) in the training set \(X\), cite84†`CategoricalNB` estimates a categorical distribution for each feature i of X conditioned on the class y. The index set of the samples is defined as \(J = \{ 1, \dots, m \}\), with \(m\) as the number of samples.
L160: 
L161: Probability calculationcite85†# L162: 
L163: The probability of category \(t\) in feature \(i\) given class \(c\) is estimated as:
L164: 
L165: \[P(x_i = t \mid y = c \: ;\, \alpha) = \frac{ N_{tic} + \alpha}{N_{c} + \alpha n_i},\]
L166: where \(N_{tic} = |\{j \in J \mid x_{ij} = t, y_j = c\}|\) is the number of times category \(t\) appears in the samples \(x_{i}\), which belong to class \(c\), \(N_{c} = |\{ j \in J\mid y_j = c\}|\) is the number of samples with class c, \(\alpha\) is a smoothing parameter and \(n_i\) is the number of available categories of feature \(i\).
L167: cite84†`CategoricalNB` assumes that the sample matrix \(X\) is encoded (for instance with the help of cite86†`OrdinalEncoder` ) such that all categories for each feature \(i\) are represented with numbers \(0, ..., n_i - 1\) where \(n_i\) is the number of available categories of feature \(i\).
L168: ## 1.9.6. Out-of-core naive Bayes model fittingcite87†# L169: 
L170: Naive Bayes models can be used to tackle large scale classification problems for which the full training set might not fit in memory. To handle this case, cite72†`MultinomialNB` , cite79†`BernoulliNB` , and cite70†`GaussianNB` expose a `partial_fit` method that can be used incrementally as done with other classifiers as demonstrated in cite88†Out-of-core classification of text documents . All naive Bayes classifiers support sample weighting.
L171: Contrary to the `fit` method, the first call to `partial_fit` needs to be passed the list of all the expected class labels.
L172: 
L173: For an overview of available strategies in scikit-learn, see also the cite89†out-of-core learning documentation.
L174: 
L175: Note
L176: 
L177: The `partial_fit` method call of naive Bayes models introduces some computational overhead. It is recommended to use data chunk sizes that are as large as possible, that is as the available RAM allows.

L18: ► cite4†Keras 3 API documentation / cite7†Callbacks API / EarlyStopping
L19: # EarlyStopping
L20: 
L21: cite41†[source]†github.com L22: ### `EarlyStopping` class
L23: 
L24:     `keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
L25:         monitor="val_loss",
L26:         min_delta=0,
L27:         patience=0,
L28:         verbose=0,
L29:         mode="auto",
L30:         baseline=None,
L31:         restore_best_weights=False,
L32:         start_from_epoch=0,
L33:     )
L34:     `
L35: 
L36: Stop training when a monitored metric has stopped improving.
L37: Assuming the goal of a training is to minimize the loss. With this, the metric to be monitored would be `'loss'`, and mode would be `'min'`. A `model.fit()` training loop will check at end of every epoch whether the loss is no longer decreasing, considering the `min_delta` and `patience` if applicable. Once it's found no longer decreasing, `model.stop_training` is marked True and the training terminates.
L38: The quantity to be monitored needs to be available in `logs` dict. To make it so, pass the loss or metrics at `model.compile()`.
L39: 
L40: Arguments
L41:   * monitor: Quantity to be monitored. Defaults to `"val_loss"`.
L42:   * min_delta: Minimum change in the monitored quantity to qualify as an improvement, i.e. an absolute change of less than min_delta, will count as no improvement. Defaults to `0`.
L43:   * patience: Number of epochs with no improvement after which training will be stopped. Defaults to `0`.
L44:   * verbose: Verbosity mode, 0 or 1. Mode 0 is silent, and mode 1 displays messages when the callback takes an action. Defaults to `0`.
L45:   * mode: One of `{"auto", "min", "max"}`. In `min` mode, training will stop when the quantity monitored has stopped decreasing; in `"max"` mode it will stop when the quantity monitored has stopped increasing; in `"auto"` mode, the direction is automatically inferred from the name of the monitored quantity. Defaults to `"auto"`.
L46:   * baseline: Baseline value for the monitored quantity. If not `None`, training will stop if the model doesn't show improvement over the baseline. Defaults to `None`.
L47:   * restore_best_weights: Whether to restore model weights from the epoch with the best value of the monitored quantity. If `False`, the model weights obtained at the last step of training are used. An epoch will be restored regardless of the performance relative to the `baseline`. If no epoch improves on `baseline`, training will run for `patience` epochs and restore weights from the best epoch in that set. Defaults to `False`.
L48:   * start_from_epoch: Number of epochs to wait before starting to monitor improvement. This allows for a warm-up period in which no improvement is expected and thus training will not be stopped. Defaults to `0`.
L49: Example
L50: 
L51:     `>>> callback = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor='loss',
L52:     ...                                               patience=3)
L53:     >>> # This callback will stop the training when there is no improvement in
L54:     >>> # the loss for three consecutive epochs.
L55:     >>> model = keras.models.Sequential([keras.layers.Dense(10)])
L56:     >>> model.compile(keras.optimizers.SGD(), loss='mse')
L57:     >>> history = model.fit(np.arange(100).reshape(5, 20), np.zeros(5),
L58:     ...                     epochs=10, batch_size=1, callbacks=[callback],
L59:     ...                     verbose=0)
L60:     >>> len(history.history['loss'])  # Only 4 epochs are run.
L61:     4
L62:     `

Use transfer learning to fine-tune one of the available pretrained models on your own dataset, even if a large amount of image data is not available. The object detection algorithm takes an image as input and outputs a list of bounding boxes.
L7: Training datasets must consist of images in .`jpg`, `.jpeg`, or `.png` format. This page includes information about Amazon EC2 instance recommendations and sample notebooks for Object Detection - TensorFlow.

L2: Get Insights On Data and Data Quality - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Summary cite2†Target column cite3†Quick model cite4†Feature summary cite5†Samples cite6†Definitions L5: # Get Insights On Data and Data Quality
L6: Use the Data Quality and Insights Report to perform an analysis of the data that you've imported into Data Wrangler. We recommend that you create the report after you import your dataset. You can use the report to help you clean and process your data. It gives you information such as the number of missing values and the number of outliers. If you have issues with your data, such as target leakage or imbalance, the insights report can bring those issues to your attention.
L7: Use the following procedure to create a Data Quality and Insights report. It assumes that you've already imported a dataset into your Data Wrangler flow.
L8: ###### To create a Data Quality and Insights report
L9: 
L10:   1. Choose a + next to a node in your Data Wrangler flow.
L11: 
L12:   2. Select Get data insights.
L13: 
L14:   3. For Analysis name, specify a name for the insights report.
L15: 
L16:   4. (Optional) For Target column, specify the target column.
L17: 
L18:   5. For Problem type, specify Regression or Classification.
L19: 
L20:   6. For Data size, specify one of the following:
L21: 
L22:      * 50 K – Uses the first 50000 rows of the dataset that you've imported to create the report.
L23:      * Entire dataset – Uses the entire dataset that you've imported to create the report.
L24: ###### Note
L25: 
L26: Creating a Data Quality and Insights report on the entire dataset uses an Amazon SageMaker processing job. A SageMaker Processing job provisions the additional compute resources required to get insights for all of your data. For more information about SageMaker Processing jobs, see cite7†Data transformation workloads with SageMaker Processing .
L27: 
L28:   7. Choose Create.
L29: 
L30: The following topics show the sections of the report:
L31: ###### Topics
L32: 
L33:   * cite1†Summary L34: 
L35:   * cite2†Target column L36: 
L37:   * cite3†Quick model L38: 
L39:   * cite4†Feature summary L40: 
L41:   * cite5†Samples L42: 
L43:   * cite6†Definitions L44: 
L45: You can either download the report or view it online. To download the report, choose the download button at the top right corner of the screen. The following image shows the button.
L46: 
L47: cite8†Image: Example showing the download button. L48: ## Summary
L49: 
L50: The insights report has a brief summary of the data that includes general information such as missing values, invalid values, feature types, outlier counts, and more. It can also include high severity warnings that point to probable issues with the data. We recommend that you investigate the warnings.
L51: 
L52: The following is an example of a report summary.
L53: 
L54: cite9†Image: Example report summary. L55: ## Target column
L56: 
L57: When you create the data quality and insights report, Data Wrangler gives you the option to select a target column. A target column is a column that you're trying to predict. When you choose a target column, Data Wrangler automatically creates a target column analysis. It also ranks the features in the order of their predictive power. When you select a target column, you must specify whether you’re trying to solve a regression or a classification problem.
L58: For classification, Data Wrangler shows a table and a histogram of the most common classes. A class is a category. It also presents observations, or rows, with a missing or invalid target value.
L59: 
L60: The following image shows an example target column analysis for a classification problem.
L61: 
L62: cite10†Image: Example target column analysis. L63: 
L64: For regression, Data Wrangler shows a histogram of all the values in the target column. It also presents observations, or rows, with a missing, invalid, or outlier target value.
L65: The following image shows an example target column analysis for a regression problem.
L66: 
L67: cite11†Image: Example target column analysis. L68: ## Quick model
L69: 
L70: The Quick model provides an estimate of the expected predicted quality of a model that you train on your data.
L71: Data Wrangler splits your data into training and validation folds. It uses 80% of the samples for training and 20% of the values for validation. For classification, the sample is stratified split. For a stratified split, each data partition has the same ratio of labels. For classification problems, it's important to have the same ratio of labels between the training and classification folds. Data Wrangler trains the XGBoost model with the default hyperparameters.
L72: It applies early stopping on the validation data and performs minimal feature preprocessing.
L73: For classification models, Data Wrangler returns both a model summary and a confusion matrix.
L74: 
L75: The following is an example of a classification model summary. To learn more about the information that it returns, see cite6†Definitions .
L76: 
L77: cite12†Image: Example classification model summary. L78: 
L79: The following is an example of a confusion matrix that the quick model returns.
L80: 
L81: cite13†Image: Example confusion matrix. L82: 
L83: A confusion matrix gives you the following information:
L84:   * The number of times the predicted label matches the true label.
L85: 
L86:   * The number of times the predicted label doesn't match the true label.
L87: 
L88: The true label represents an actual observation in your data. For example, if you're using a model to detect fraudulent transactions, the true label represents a transaction that is actually fraudulent or non-fraudulent. The predicted label represents the label that your model assigns to the data.
L89: You can use the confusion matrix to see how well the model predicts the presence or the absence of a condition. If you're predicting fraudulent transactions, you can use the confusion matrix to get a sense of both the sensitivity and the specificity of the model. The sensitivity refers to the model's ability to detect fraudulent transactions. The specificity refers to the model's ability to avoid detecting non-fraudulent transactions as fraudulent.
L90: The following is an example of the quick model outputs for a regression problem.
L91: 
L92: cite14†Image: Example of the quick model outputs for a regression problem. L93: ## Feature summary
L94: 
L95: When you specify a target column, Data Wrangler orders the features by their prediction power. Prediction power is measured on the data after it was split into 80% training and 20% validation folds. Data Wrangler fits a model for each feature separately on the training fold. It applies minimal feature preprocessing and measures prediction performance on the validation data.
L96: It normalizes the scores to the range [0,1]. Higher prediction scores indicate columns that are more useful for predicting the target on their own. Lower scores point to columns that aren’t predictive of the target column.
L97: 
L98: It’s uncommon for a column that isn’t predictive on its own to be predictive when it’s used in tandem with other columns. You can confidently use the prediction scores to determine whether a feature in your dataset is predictive.
L99: A low score usually indicates the feature is redundant. A score of 1 implies perfect predictive abilities, which often indicates target leakage. Target leakage usually happens when the dataset contains a column that isn’t available at the prediction time. For example, it could be a duplicate of the target column.
L100: 
L101: The following are examples of the table and the histogram that show the prediction value of each feature.
L102: 
L103: cite15†Image: Example summary table showing the prediction value of each feature. L104: cite16†Image: Example histogram showing the prediction value of each feature. L105: ## Samples
L106: 
L107: Data Wrangler provides information about whether your samples are anomalous or if there are duplicates in your dataset.
L108: Data Wrangler detects anomalous samples using the isolation forest algorithm. The isolation forest associates an anomaly score with each sample (row) of the dataset. Low anomaly scores indicate anomalous samples. High scores are associated with non-anomalous samples. Samples with a negative anomaly score are usually considered anomalous and samples with positive anomaly score are considered non-anomalous.
L109: When you look at a sample that might be anomalous, we recommend that you pay attention to unusual values. For example, you might have anomalous values that result from errors in gathering and processing the data. We recommend using domain knowledge and business logic when you examine anomalous samples.
L110: Data Wrangler detects duplicate rows and calculates the ratio of duplicate rows in your data. Some data sources could include valid duplicates. Other data sources could have duplicates that point to problems in data collection. Duplicate samples that result from faulty data collection could interfere with machine learning processes that rely on splitting the data into independent training and validation folds.
L111: 
L112: The following are elements of the insights report that can be impacted by duplicated samples:
L113:   * Quick model
L114: 
L115:   * Prediction power estimation
L116: 
L117:   * Automatic hyperparameter tuning
L118: 
L119: You can remove duplicate samples from the dataset using the Drop duplicates transform under Manage rows. Data Wrangler shows you the most frequently duplicated rows.
L120: ## Definitions
L121: 
L122: The following are definitions for the technical terms that are used in the data insights report.
L123: 
L124: Feature types
L125: 
L126: 
L127: The following are the definitions for each of the feature types:
L128: 
L129:   * Numeric – Numeric values can be either floats or integers, such as age or income. The machine learning models assume that numeric values are ordered and a distance is defined over them. For example, 3 is closer to 4 than to 10 and 3 < 4 < 10.
L130:   * Categorical – The column entries belong to a set of unique values, which is usually much smaller than the number of entries in the column. For example, a column of length 100 could contain the unique values `Dog`, `Cat`, and `Mouse`. The values could be numeric, text, or a combination of both. `Horse`, `House`, `8`, `Love`, and `3.1` would all be valid values and could be found in the same categorical column.
L131: The machine learning model does not assume order or distance on the values of categorical features, as opposed to numeric features, even when all the values are numbers.
L132:   * Binary – Binary features are a special categorical feature type in which the cardinality of the set of unique values is 2.
L133: 
L134:   * Text – A text column contains many non-numeric unique values. In extreme cases, all the elements of the column are unique. In an extreme case, no two entries are the same.
L135: 
L136:   * Datetime – A datetime column contains information about the date or time. It can have information about both the date and time.
L137: 
L138: Feature statistics
L139: The following are definitions for each of the feature statistics:
L140: 
L141:   * Prediction power – Prediction power measures how useful the column is in predicting the target.
L142:   * Outliers (in numeric columns) – Data Wrangler detects outliers using two statistics that are robust to outliers: median and robust standard deviation (RSTD). RSTD is derived by clipping the feature values to the range [5 percentile, 95 percentile] and calculating the standard deviation of the clipped vector. All values larger than median + 5 * RSTD or smaller than median - 5 * RSTD are considered to be outliers.
L143:   * Skew (in numeric columns) – Skew measures the symmetry of the distribution and is defined as the third moment of the distribution divided by the third power of the standard deviation. The skewness of the normal distribution or any other symmetric distribution is zero. Positive values imply that the right tail of the distribution is longer than the left tail. Negative values imply that the left tail of the distribution is longer than the right tail.
L144: As a rule of thumb, a distribution is considered skewed when the absolute value of the skew is larger than 3.
L145:   * Kurtosis (in numeric columns) – Pearson's kurtosis measures the heaviness of the tail of the distribution. It's defined as the fourth moment of the distribution divided by the square of the second moment. The kurtosis of the normal distribution is 3. Kurtosis values lower than 3 imply that the distribution is concentrated around the mean and the tails are lighter than the tails of the normal distribution. Kurtosis values higher than 3 imply heavier tails or outliers.
L146:   * Missing values – Null-like objects, empty strings and strings composed of only white spaces are considered missing.
L147: 
L148:   * Valid values for numeric features or regression target – All values that you can cast to finite floats are valid. Missing values are not valid.
L149: 
L150:   * Valid values for categorical, binary, or text features, or for classification target – All values that are not missing are valid.
L151:   * Datetime features – All values that you can cast to a datetime object are valid. Missing values are not valid.
L152: 
L153:   * Invalid values – Values that are either missing or you can't properly cast. For example, in a numeric column, you can't cast the string `"six"` or a null value.
L154: 
L155: Quick model metrics for regression
L156: 
L157: 
L158: The following are the definitions for the quick model metrics:
L159:   * R2 or coefficient of determination) – R2 is the proportion of the variation in the target that is predicted by the model. R2 is in the range of [-infty, 1]. 1 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly and 0 is the score of the trivial model that always predicts the target mean.
L160: 
L161:   * MSE or mean squared error – MSE is in the range [0, infty]. 0 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly.
L162:   * MAE or mean absolute error – MAE is in the range [0, infty] where 0 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly.
L163: 
L164:   * RMSE or root mean square error – RMSE is in the range [0, infty] where 0 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly.
L165: 
L166:   * Max error – The maximum absolute value of the error over the dataset. Max error is in the range [0, infty]. 0 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly.
L167:   * Median absolute error – Median absolute error is in the range [0, infty]. 0 is the score of the model that predicts the target perfectly.
L168: 
L169: Quick model metrics for classification
L170: 
L171: 
L172: The following are the definitions for the quick model metrics:
L173: 
L174:   * Accuracy – Accuracy is the ratio of samples that are predicted accurately. Accuracy is in the range [0, 1]. 0 is the score of the model that predicts all samples incorrectly and 1 is the score of the perfect model.
L175:   * Balanced accuracy – Balanced accuracy is the ratio of samples that are predicted accurately when the class weights are adjusted to balance the data. All classes are given the same importance, regardless of their frequency. Balanced accuracy is in the range [0, 1]. 0 is the score of the model that predicts all samples wrong. 1 is the score of the perfect model.
L176:   * AUC (binary classification) – This is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. AUC is in the range [0, 1] where a random model returns a score of 0.5 and the perfect model returns a score of 1.
L177:   * AUC (OVR) – For multiclass classification, this is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve calculated separately for each label using one versus rest. Data Wrangler reports the average of the areas. AUC is in the range [0, 1] where a random model returns a score of 0.5 and the perfect model returns a score of 1.
L178:   * Precision – Precision is defined for a specific class. Precision is the fraction of true positives out of all the instances that the model classified as that class. Precision is in the range [0, 1]. 1 is the score of the model that has no false positives for the class. For binary classification, Data Wrangler reports the precision of the positive class.
L179:   * Recall – Recall is defined for a specific class. Recall is the fraction of the relevant class instances that are successfully retrieved. Recall is in the range [0, 1]. 1 is the score of the model that classifies all the instances of the class correctly. For binary classification, Data Wrangler reports the recall of the positive class.
L180:   * F1 – F1 is defined for a specific class. It's the harmonic mean of the precision and recall. F1 is in the range [0, 1]. 1 is the score of the perfect model. For binary classification, Data Wrangler reports the F1 for classes with positive values.
L181: 
L182: Textual patterns
L183: 
L184: 
L185: Patterns describe the textual format of a string using an easy to read format. The following are examples of textual patterns:
L186: 
L187:   * "{digits:4-7}" describes a sequence of digits that have a length between 4 and 7.
L188:   * "{alnum:5}" describes an alpha-numeric string with a length of exactly 5.
L189: 
L190: Data Wrangler infers the patterns by looking at samples of non-empty strings from your data. It can describe many of the commonly used patterns. The confidence expressed as a percentage indicates how much of the data is estimated to match the pattern. Using the textual pattern, you can see which rows in your data you need to correct or drop.
L191: 
L192: The following describes the patterns that Data Wrangler can recognize:
L193: Pattern  | Textual Format
L194: --- | ---
L195: {alnum}  | Alphanumeric strings
L196: {any}  | Any string of word characters
L197: {digits}  | A sequence of digits
L198: {lower}  | A lowercase word
L199: {mixed}  | A mixed-case word
L200: {name}  | A word beginning with a capital letter
L201: {upper}  | An uppercase word
L202: {whitespace}  | whitespace characters
L203: A word character is either an underscore or a character that might appear in a word in any language. For example, the strings 'Hello_word' and 'écoute' both consist of word characters. 'H' and 'é' are both examples of word characters.
