L6: 
L7: This section explains how Amazon SageMaker AI interacts with a Docker container that runs your own inference code for hosting services. Use this information to write inference code and create a Docker image.
L8: ###### Topics
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†How SageMaker AI Runs Your Inference Image L11: 
L12:   * cite2†How SageMaker AI Loads Your Model Artifacts L13: 
L14:   * cite3†How Your Container Should Respond to Inference Requests L15: 
L16:   * cite4†How Your Container Should Respond to Health Check (Ping) Requests L17: 
L18:   * cite5†Container Contract to Support Bidirectional Streaming Capabilities L19: 
L20:   * cite6†Use a Private Docker Registry for Real-Time Inference Containers L21: ## How SageMaker AI Runs Your Inference Image
L22: 
L23: To configure a container to run as an executable, use an `ENTRYPOINT` instruction in a Dockerfile. Note the following:
L24: 
L25:   * For model inference, SageMaker AI runs the container as:
L26: 
L27:     `docker run `image` serve`
L28: 
L29: SageMaker AI overrides default `CMD` statements in a container by specifying the `serve` argument after the image name. The `serve` argument overrides arguments that you provide with the `CMD` command in the Dockerfile.
L30:   * SageMaker AI expects all containers to run with root users. Create your container so that it uses only root users. When SageMaker AI runs your container, users that do not have root-level access can cause permissions issues.
L31: 
L32: 
L33: 
L34:   * We recommend that you use the `exec` form of the `ENTRYPOINT` instruction:
L35: 
L36:     `ENTRYPOINT ["executable", "param1", "param2"]`
L37: 
L38: For example:
L39: 
L40:     `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "k_means_inference.py"]`
L41: The `exec` form of the `ENTRYPOINT` instruction starts the executable directly, not as a child of `/bin/sh`. This enables it to receive signals like `SIGTERM` and `SIGKILL` from the SageMaker API operations, which is a requirement.
L42: 
L43: 
L44: 
L45: For example, when you use the cite7†`CreateEndpoint` API to create an endpoint, SageMaker AI provisions the number of ML compute instances required by the endpoint configuration, which you specify in the request. SageMaker AI runs the Docker container on those instances.
L46: If you reduce the number of instances backing the endpoint (by calling the cite8†`UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities` API), SageMaker AI runs a command to stop the Docker container on the instances that are being terminated. The command sends the `SIGTERM` signal, then it sends the `SIGKILL` signal thirty seconds later.
L47: If you update the endpoint (by calling the cite9†`UpdateEndpoint` API), SageMaker AI launches another set of ML compute instances and runs the Docker containers that contain your inference code on them. Then it runs a command to stop the previous Docker containers. To stop a Docker container, command sends the `SIGTERM` signal, then it sends the `SIGKILL` signal 30 seconds later.
L48:   * SageMaker AI uses the container definition that you provided in your cite10†`CreateModel` request to set environment variables and the DNS hostname for the container as follows:
L49: 
L50: 
L51: 
L52:     * It sets environment variables using the `ContainerDefinition.Environment` string-to-string map.
L53: 
L54:     * It sets the DNS hostname using the `ContainerDefinition.ContainerHostname`.
L55:   * If you plan to use GPU devices for model inferences (by specifying GPU-based ML compute instances in your `CreateEndpointConfig` request), make sure that your containers are `nvidia-docker` compatible. Don't bundle NVIDIA drivers with the image. For more information about `nvidia-docker`, see cite11†NVIDIA/nvidia-docker†github.com .
L56: 
L57: 
L58: 
L59:   * You can't use the `tini` initializer as your entry point in SageMaker AI containers because it gets confused by the `train` and `serve` arguments.
L60: ## How SageMaker AI Loads Your Model Artifacts
L61: 
L62: In your cite10†`CreateModel` API request, you can use either the `ModelDataUrl` or `S3DataSource` parameter to identify the S3 location where model artifacts are stored. SageMaker AI copies your model artifacts from the S3 location to the `/opt/ml/model` directory for use by your inference code. Your container has read-only access to `/opt/ml/model`. Do not write to this directory.
L63: The `ModelDataUrl` must point to a tar.gz file. Otherwise, SageMaker AI won't download the file.
L64: 
L65: If you trained your model in SageMaker AI, the model artifacts are saved as a single compressed tar file in Amazon S3. If you trained your model outside SageMaker AI, you need to create this single compressed tar file and save it in a S3 location. SageMaker AI decompresses this tar file into /opt/ml/model directory before your container starts.
L66: For deploying large models, we recommend that you follow cite12†Deploying uncompressed models .
L67: ## How Your Container Should Respond to Inference Requests
L68: 
L69: To obtain inferences, the client application sends a POST request to the SageMaker AI endpoint. SageMaker AI passes the request to the container, and returns the inference result from the container to the client.
L70: 
L71: For more information about the inference requests that your container will receive, see the following actions in the Amazon SageMaker AI API Reference:
L72: 
L73:   * cite13†InvokeEndpoint L74: 
L75:   * cite14†InvokeEndpointAsync L76:   * cite15†InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream L77: 
L78:   * cite16†InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream L79: ###### Requirements for inference containers
L80: 
L81: To respond to inference requests, your container must meet the following requirements:
L82: 
L83:   * SageMaker AI strips all `POST` headers except those supported by `InvokeEndpoint`. SageMaker AI might add additional headers. Inference containers must be able to safely ignore these additional headers.
L84:   * To receive inference requests, the container must have a web server listening on port 8080 and must accept `POST` requests to the `/invocations` and `/ping` endpoints.
L85: 
L86:   * A customer's model containers must accept socket connection requests within 250 ms.
L87:   * A customer's model containers must respond to requests within 60 seconds. The model itself can have a maximum processing time of 60 seconds before responding to the `/invocations`. If your model is going to take 50-60 seconds of processing time, the SDK socket timeout should be set to be 70 seconds.
L88: 
L89:   * A customer’s model container that supports bidirectional streaming must:
L90: 
L91:     * support WebSockets connections on port 8080 to /invocations-bidirectional-stream by default.
L92:     * have a web server listening on port 8080 and must accept POST requests to the /ping endpoints.
L93: 
L94:     * In addition to container health checks over HTTP, container must respond with Pong Frame per (cite17†RFC6455†datatracker.ietf.org ), for WebSocket Ping Frame sent.
L95: ###### Example invocation functions
L96: 
L97: The following examples demonstrate how the code in your container can process inference requests. These examples handle requests that client applications send by using the InvokeEndpoint action.
L98: 
L99: FastAPI
L100: FastAPI is a web framework for building APIs with Python.
L101: 
L102:     `from fastapi import FastAPI, status, Request, Response
L103:     . . .
L104:     app = FastAPI()
L105:     . . .
L106:     @app.post('/invocations')
L107:     async def invocations(request: Request):
L108:         # model() is a hypothetical function that gets the inference output:
L109:         model_resp = await model(Request)
L110: 
L111:         response = Response(
L112:             content=model_resp,
L113:             status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK,
L114:             media_type="text/plain",
L115:         )
L116:         return response
L117:     . . .`
L118: In this example, the `invocations` function handles the inference request that SageMaker AI sends to the `/invocations` endpoint.
L119: 
L120: Flask
L121: Flask is a framework for developing web applications with Python.
L122: 
L123:     `import flask
L124:     . . .
L125:     app = flask.Flask(__name__)
L126:     . . .
L127:     @app.route('/invocations', methods=["POST"])
L128:     def invoke(request):
L129:         # model() is a hypothetical function that gets the inference output:
L130:         resp_body = model(request)
L131:         return flask.Response(resp_body, mimetype='text/plain')
L132:         `
L133: In this example, the `invoke` function handles the inference request that SageMaker AI sends to the `/invocations` endpoint.
L134: ###### Example invocation functions for streaming requests
L135: 
L136: The following examples demonstrate how the code in your inference container can process streaming inference requests. These examples handle requests that client applications send by using the InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream action.
L137: When a container handles a streaming inference request, it returns the model's inference as a series of parts incrementally as the model generates them. Client applications start receiving responses immediately when they're available. They don't need to wait for the model to generate the entire response. You can implement streaming to support fast interactive experiences, such as chatbots, virtual assistants, and music generators.
L138: 
L139: FastAPI
L140: FastAPI is a web framework for building APIs with Python.
L141: 
L142:     `from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse
L143:     from fastapi import FastAPI, status, Request
L144:     . . .
L145:     app = FastAPI()
L146:     . . .
L147:     @app.post('/invocations')
L148:     async def invocations(request: Request):
L149:         # Streams inference response using HTTP chunked encoding
L150:         async def generate():
L151:             # model() is a hypothetical function that gets the inference output:
L152:             yield await model(Request)
L153:             yield "\n"
L154: 
L155:         response = StreamingResponse(
L156:             content=generate(),
L157:             status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK,
L158:             media_type="text/plain",
L159:         )
L160:         return response
L161:     . . .`
L162: In this example, the `invocations` function handles the inference request that SageMaker AI sends to the `/invocations` endpoint. To stream the response, the example uses the `StreamingResponse` class from the Starlette framework.
L163: 
L164: Flask
L165: Flask is a framework for developing web applications with Python.
L166: 
L167:     `import flask
L168:     . . .
L169:     app = flask.Flask(__name__)
L170:     . . .
L171:     @app.route('/invocations', methods=["POST"])
L172:     def invocations(request):
L173:         # Streams inference response using HTTP chunked encoding
L174: 
L175:         def generate():
L176:             # model() is a hypothetical function that gets the inference output:
L177:             yield model(request)
L178:             yield "\n"
L179:         return flask.Response(
L180:             flask.stream_with_context(generate()), mimetype='text/plain')
L181:     . . .`
L182: In this example, the `invocations` function handles the inference request that SageMaker AI sends to the `/invocations` endpoint. To stream the response, the example uses the `flask.stream_with_context` function from the Flask framework.
L183: ###### Example invocation functions for bidirectional streaming
L184: 
L185: The following examples demonstrate how the code in your container can process streaming inference request and responses. These examples handle streaming requests that client applications send by using the InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream action.
L186: A container with bidirectional streaming capability handles streaming inference requests where parts are incrementally generated at the client and streamed to the container. It returns the model's inference back to the client as a series of parts as the model generates them. Client applications start receiving responses immediately when they're available. They don't need to wait for request to the fully generated at the client or for the model to generate the entire response.
L187: You can implement bidirectional streaming to support fast interactive experiences, such as chatbots, interactive voice AI assistants and real-time translations for a more real-time experience.
L188: FastAPI
L189: FastAPI is a web framework for building APIs with Python.
L190: 
L191:     `import sys
L192:     import asyncio
L193:     import json
L194:     from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect
L195:     from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
L196:     import uvicorn
L197: 
L198:     app = FastAPI()
L199:     ...
L200:     @app.websocket("/invocations-bidirectional-stream")
L201:     async def websocket_invoke(websocket: WebSocket):
L202:         """
L203:         WebSocket endpoint with RFC 6455 ping/pong and fragmentation support
L204: 
L205:         Handles:
L206:         - Text messages (JSON) - including fragmented frames
L207:         - Binary messages - including fragmented frames
L208:         - Ping frames (automatically responds with pong)
L209:         - Pong frames (logs receipt)
L210:         - Fragmented frames per RFC 6455 Section 5.4
L211:         """
L212:         await manager.connect(websocket)
L213: 
L214:         # Fragment reassembly buffers per RFC 6455 Section 5.4
L215:         text_fragments = []
L216:         binary_fragments = []
L217: 
L218:         while True:
L219:             # Use receive() to handle all WebSocket frame types
L220:             message = await websocket.receive()

L223:                 if "text" in message:
L224:                     # Handle text frames (including fragments)
L225:                     text_data = message["text"]
L226:                     more_body = message.get("more_body", False)

L228:                     if more_body:
L229:                         # This is a fragment, accumulate it
L230:                         text_fragments.append(text_data)

L243:                             await handle_text_message(websocket, text_data)

L246:                     binary_data = message["bytes"]

L249:                     if more_body:
L250:                         # This is a fragment, accumulate it
L251:                         binary_fragments.append(binary_data)
L252:                         print(f"Received binary fragment: {len(binary_data)} bytes (more coming)")
L253:                     else:
L254:                         # This is the final frame or a complete message
L255:                         if binary_fragments:

L266:             elif message["type"] == "websocket.ping":
L267:                 # Handle ping frames - RFC 6455 Section 5.5.2
L268:                 ping_data = message.get("bytes", b"")
L269:                 print(f"Received PING frame with payload: {ping_data}")
L270:                 # FastAPI automatically sends pong response
L271:

L273:                 # Handle pong frames
L274:                 pong_data = message.get("bytes", b"")

L329: In this example, the `websocket_invoke` function handles the inference request that SageMaker AI sends to the `/invocations-bidirectional-stream` endpoint. It shows handling stream requests and stream responses back to the client.
L330: ## How Your Container Should Respond to Health Check (Ping) Requests
L331: 
L332: SageMaker AI launches new inference containers in the following situations:
L333: 
L334:   * Responding to `CreateEndpoint`, `UpdateEndpoint`, and `UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities` API calls
L335: 
L336:   * Security patching
L337: 
L338:   * Replacing unhealthy instances
L339: 
L340: Soon after container startup, SageMaker AI starts sending periodic GET requests to the `/ping` endpoint.
L341: The simplest requirement on the container is to respond with an HTTP 200 status code and an empty body. This indicates to SageMaker AI that the container is ready to accept inference requests at the `/invocations` endpoint.
L342: If the container does not begin to pass health checks by consistently responding with 200s during the 8 minutes after startup, the new instance launch fails. This causes `CreateEndpoint` to fail, leaving the endpoint in a failed state. The update requested by `UpdateEndpoint` isn't completed, security patches aren't applied, and unhealthy instances aren't replaced.
L343: While the minimum bar is for the container to return a static 200, a container developer can use this functionality to perform deeper checks. For example, the container can verify that the model is loaded into memory and can serve inference requests. The request timeout on `/ping` attempts is 2 seconds.
L344: We strongly recommend implementing meaningful health checks rather than returning a static 200. The `/ping` endpoint is the main signal SageMaker AI uses to determine whether an instance is healthy. If your container always returns 200 — even when the model has failed to load, run out of memory, or entered a bad state — SageMaker AI continues routing inference requests to that instance.
L345: This results in sustained invocation errors for your application until the instance is manually replaced or the endpoint is updated.
L346: A well-implemented `/ping` handler should verify that:
L347: 
L348:   * The model artifact is loaded and ready to serve
L349: 
L350:   * Critical resources (memory, disk, GPU if applicable) are available
L351: 
L352:   * The inference code path is functional (for example, a lightweight test prediction succeeds)
L353: When `/ping` correctly reports an unhealthy state by returning a non-200 response, SageMaker AI detects the failure and automatically replaces the instance (excluding endpoints that use inference components), minimizing downtime for your application.
L354: Additionally, a container that is capable of handling bidirectional streaming requests must respond with a Pong Frame (per WebSocket protocol cite17†RFC6455†datatracker.ietf.org ) to a Ping Frame. If no Pong Frame is received for 5 consecutive Pings, the connection to container will be closed by SageMaker AI platform. SageMaker AI platform will also respond to Ping Frames from model container with Pong Frames.
L355: ## Container Contract to Support Bidirectional Streaming Capabilities
L356: 
L357: If you want to host your model container as SageMaker AI endpoint that supports bidirectional streaming capabilities, the model container must support the contract below:
L358: 
L359: 1. Bidirectional Docker Label
L360: 
L361: The model container should have a Docker label indicating to the SageMaker AI platform that bidirectional streaming capability is supported on this container.
L362: 
L363:     `com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true`
L364: 2. Support WebSocket Connection for invocations
L365: 
L366: A customer’s model container that supports bi-directional streaming must support WebSockets connections on port 8080 to `/invocations-bidirectional-stream` by default.
L367: This path can be overridden by passing X-Amzn-SageMaker-Model-Invocation-Path header when invoking InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream API. Additionally, users can specify a query string to be appended to this path by passing X-Amzn-SageMaker-Model-Query-String header when invoking InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream API.
L368: 
L369: 3. Request Stream Handling
L370: The InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream API input payloads are streamed in as a series of PayloadParts, which is just a wrapper of a binary chunk (“Bytes”: <Blob>):
L371: 
L372:     `{
L373:        "PayloadPart": {
L374:           "Bytes": <Blob>,
L375:           "DataType": <String: UTF8 | BINARY>,
L376:           "CompletionState": <String: PARTIAL | COMPLETE>
L377:           "P": <String>
L378:        }
L379:     }`
L380: 
L381: 3.1. Data Frames
L382: SageMaker AI passes the input PayloadParts to Model container as WebSocket Data Frames (cite18†RFC6455-Section-5.6†datatracker.ietf.org )
L383: 
L384:   1. SageMaker AI does not inspect into the binary chunk.
L385: 
L386:   2. On receiving an input PayloadPart
L387: 
L388:      * SageMaker AI creates exactly one WebSocket Data Frame from `PayloadPart.Bytes`, then pass it to model container.
L389: 
L390:      * If `PayloadPart.DataType = UTF8`, SageMaker AI creates a Text Data Frame
L391:      * If `PayloadPart.DataType` does not present or `PayloadPart.DataType = BINARY`, SageMaker AI creates a Binary Data Frame
L392: 
L393:   3. For a sequence of PayloadParts with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = PARTIAL`, and terminated by a PayloadPart with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = COMPLETE`, SageMaker AI translates them into WebSocket fragmented message cite19†RFC6455-Section-5.4: Fragmentation†datatracker.ietf.org :
L394:      * The initial PayloadPart with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = PARTIAL` will be translated into a WebSocket Data Frame, with FIN bit clear.
L395: 
L396:      * The subsequent PayloadParts with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = PARTIAL` will be translated into WebSocket Continuation Frames with FIN bit clear.
L397: 
L398:      * The final PayloadPart with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = COMPLETE` will be translated into WebSocket Continuation Frame with FIN bit set.
L399:   4. SageMaker AI does not encode or decode the binary chunk from the input PayloadPart, the bytes are passed to model container as-is.
L400: 
L401:   5. SageMaker AI does not combine multiple input PayloadParts into one BinaryDataFrame.
L402: 
L403:   6. SageMaker AI does not chunk one input PayloadPart into multiple BinaryDataFrames.
L404: Example: Fragmented Message Flow
L405: 
L406:     `Client sends:
L407:     PayloadPart 1: {Bytes: "Hello ", DataType: "UTF8", CompletionState: "PARTIAL"}
L408:     PayloadPart 2: {Bytes: "World", DataType: "UTF8", CompletionState: "COMPLETE"}
L409: 
L410:     Container receives:
L411:     Frame 1: Text Data Frame with "Hello " (FIN=0)
L412:     Frame 2: Continuation Frame with "World" (FIN=1)`
L413: 
L414: 3.2. Control Frames
L415: 
L416: Besides Data Frames, SageMaker AI also sends Control Frames to model container (cite20†RFC6455-Section-5.5†datatracker.ietf.org ):
L417:   1. Close Frame: SageMaker AI may send Close Frame (cite21†RFC6455-Section-5.5.1†datatracker.ietf.org ) to model container should the connection be closed for any reason.
L418: 
L419:   2. Ping Frame: SageMaker AI send Ping Frame (cite22†RFC6455-Section-5.5.2†datatracker.ietf.org ) once every 60 seconds, model container must respond with Pong Frame. If no Pong Frame (cite17†RFC6455-Section-5.5.3†datatracker.ietf.org ) is received for 5 consecutive Pings, the connection will be closed by SageMaker AI.
L420:   3. Pong Frame: SageMaker AI will respond to Ping Frames from model container with Pong Frames.
L421: 
L422: 4. Response Stream Handling
L423: The output are streamed out as a series of PayloadParts, ModelStreamErrors or InternalStreamFailures.
L424: 
L425:     `{
L426:        "PayloadPart": {
L427:           "Bytes": <Blob>,
L428:           "DataType": <String: UTF8 | BINARY>,
L429:           "CompletionState": <String: PARTIAL | COMPLETE>,
L430:        },
L431:        "ModelStreamError": {
L432:           "ErrorCode": <String>,
L433:           "Message": <String>
L434:        },
L435:        "InternalStreamFailure": {
L436:           "Message": <String>
L437:        }
L438:     }`
L439: 
L440: 4.1. Data Frames
L441: SageMaker AI convert Data Frames received from model container into output PayloadParts:
L442: 
L443:   1. On receiving a WebSocket Text Data Frame from the model container, SageMaker AI gets the raw bytes from the Text Data Frame, and wraps it into a response PayloadPart, meanwhile set `PayloadPart.DataType = UTF8`.
L444:   2. On receiving a WebSocket Binary Data Frame from the model container, SageMaker AI directly wraps the bytes from the data frame into a response PayloadPart, meanwhile set `PayloadPart.DataType = BINARY`.
L445: 
L446:   3. For fragmented message as defined in cite19†RFC6455-Section-5.4: Fragmentation†datatracker.ietf.org :
L447: 
L448:      * The initial Data Frame with FIN bit clear will be translated into a PayloadPart with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = PARTIAL`.
L449:      * The subsequent Continuation Frames with FIN bit clear will be translated into PayloadParts with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = PARTIAL`.
L450: 
L451:      * The final Continuation Frame with FIN bit set will be translated into PayloadPart with `PayloadPart.CompletionState = COMPLETE`.
L452: 
L453:   4. SageMaker AI does not encode or decode the bytes received from model containers, the bytes are passed to model container as-is.
L454:   5. SageMaker AI does not combine multiple Data Frames received from model container into one response PayloadPart.
L455: 
L456:   6. SageMaker AI does not chunk a Data Frame received from model container into multiple response PayloadParts.
L457: Example: Streaming Response Flow
L458: 
L459:     `Container sends:
L460:     Frame 1: Text Data Frame with "Generating" (FIN=0)
L461:     Frame 2: Continuation Frame with " response..." (FIN=1)
L462: 
L463:     Client receives:
L464:     PayloadPart 1: {Bytes: "Generating", DataType: "UTF8", CompletionState: "PARTIAL"}
L465:     PayloadPart 2: {Bytes: " response...", DataType: "UTF8", CompletionState: "COMPLETE"}`
L466: 
L467: 4.2. Control Frames
L468: 
L469: SageMaker AI responds to the following Control Frames from the model container:
L470:   1. On receiving a Close Frame (cite21†RFC6455-Section-5.5.1†datatracker.ietf.org ) from model container, SageMaker AI will wrap the status code (cite23†RFC6455-Section-7.4†datatracker.ietf.org ) and failure messages into ModelStreamError, and stream it back to the end user.
L471: 
L472:   2. On receiving a Ping Frame (cite22†RFC6455-Section-5.5.2†datatracker.ietf.org ) from model container, SageMaker AI will respond with Pong Frame.
L473:   3. Pong Frame(cite17†RFC6455-Section-5.5.3†datatracker.ietf.org ): If no Pong Frame is received for 5 consecutive Pings, the connection will be closed by SageMaker AI.

L3: # CloudWatch Logs for Amazon SageMaker AI
L4: 
L5: To help you debug your compilation jobs, processing jobs, training jobs, endpoints, transform jobs, notebook instances, and notebook instance lifecycle configurations, anything an algorithm container, a model container, or a notebook instance lifecycle configuration sends to `stdout` or `stderr` is also sent to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. In addition to debugging, you can use these for progress analysis.
L6: By default, log data is stored in CloudWatch Logs indefinitely. However, you can configure how long to store log data in a log group. For information, see cite1†Change Log Data Retention in CloudWatch Logs in the Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide.
L7: 
L8: Logs
L9: 
L10: The following table lists all of the logs provided by Amazon SageMaker AI.
L11: 
L12: Logs
L13: Log Group Name  | Log Stream Name
L14: --- | ---
L15: `/aws/sagemaker/CompilationJobs`  | `[compilation-job-name]`
L16: `/aws/sagemaker/Endpoints/[EndpointName]`  | `[production-variant-name]/[instance-id]`
L17: (For Asynchronous Inference endpoints) `[production-variant-name]/[instance-id]/data-log`
L18: (For Inference Pipelines) `[production-variant-name]/[instance-id]/[container-name provided in SageMaker AI model]`
L19: `/aws/sagemaker/groundtruth/WorkerActivity`  | `aws/sagemaker/groundtruth/worker-activity/[requester-AWS-Id]-[region]/[timestamp]`

L22: `[inference-recommendations-job-name]/Endpoint/[endpoint-name]`
L23: `/aws/sagemaker/LabelingJobs`  | `[labeling-job-name]`
L24: `/aws/sagemaker/NotebookInstances`  | `[notebook-instance-name]/[LifecycleConfigHook]`
L25: `[notebook-instance-name]/jupyter.log`
L26: `/aws/sagemaker/ProcessingJobs`  | `[processing-job-name]/[hostname]-[epoch_timestamp]`

L29: `/aws/sagemaker/TrainingJobs`  | `[training-job-name]/algo-[instance-number-in-cluster]-[epoch_timestamp]`

L4: cite1†Maintenance cite2†Machine Learning with the SageMaker Python SDK L5: # Amazon SageMaker notebook instances
L6: An Amazon SageMaker notebook instance is a machine learning (ML) compute instance running the Jupyter Notebook application. One of the best ways for machine learning (ML) practitioners to use Amazon SageMaker AI is to train and deploy ML models using SageMaker notebook instances.
L7: The SageMaker notebook instances help create the environment by initiating Jupyter servers on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and providing preconfigured kernels with the following packages: the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK, AWS SDK for Python (Boto3), AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), Conda, Pandas, deep learning framework libraries, and other libraries for data science and machine learning.
L8: Use Jupyter notebooks in your notebook instance to:
L9: 
L10:   * prepare and process data
L11: 
L12:   * write code to train models
L13: 
L14:   * deploy models to SageMaker hosting
L15: 
L16:   * test or validate your models
L17: 
L18: For information about pricing with Amazon SageMaker notebook instance, see cite3†Amazon SageMaker Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L19: ## Maintenance
L20: 
L21: SageMaker AI updates the underlying software for Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances at least once every 90 days. Some maintenance updates, such as operating system upgrades, may require your application to be taken offline for a short period of time. It is not possible to perform any operations during this period while the underlying software is being updated. We recommend that you restart your notebooks at least once every 30 days to automatically consume patches.
L22: If the notebook instance isn't updated and is running unsecure software, SageMaker AI might periodically update the instance as part of regular maintenance. During these updates, data outside of the folder `/home/ec2-user/SageMaker` is not persisted.
L23: 
L24: For more information, contact cite4†AWS Support†aws.amazon.com .
L25: ## Machine Learning with the SageMaker Python SDK
L26: To train, validate, deploy, and evaluate an ML model in a SageMaker notebook instance, use the SageMaker Python SDK. The SageMaker Python SDK abstracts AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) and SageMaker API operations.
L27: It enables you to integrate with and orchestrate other AWS services, such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for saving data and model artifacts, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) for importing and servicing the ML models, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) for training and inference.
L28: You can also take advantage of SageMaker AI features that help you deal with every stage of a complete ML cycle: data labeling, data preprocessing, model training, model deployment, evaluation on prediction performance, and monitoring the quality of model in production.
L29: 
L30: If you're a first-time SageMaker AI user, we recommend you to use the SageMaker Python SDK, following the end-to-end ML tutorial. To find the open source documentation, see the cite5†Amazon SageMaker Python SDK†sagemaker.readthedocs.io .

What is AWS Site-to-Site VPN? - AWS Site-to-Site VPN (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPC_VPN.html)
citeturn216view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPC_VPN.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 130

L2: What is AWS Site-to-Site VPN? - AWS Site-to-Site VPN
L3: 
L4: cite1†Concepts cite2†Site-to-Site VPN features cite3†Site-to-Site VPN limitations cite4†Site-to-Site VPN resources cite5†Pricing L5: # What is AWS Site-to-Site VPN?
L6: 
L7: By default, an instance that you launch within an Amazon VPC can't communicate with a local (AWS Cloud) network and a remote device — for example, this might be a site or an on-premises device. You can enable access to your remote devices from your VPC by creating an AWS Site-to-Site VPN (Site-to-Site VPN) connection, and configuring routing to pass traffic through the connection.
L8: Although the term VPN connection is a general term, in this documentation, a VPN connection refers to the connection between your VPC and your own on-premises network. Site-to-Site VPN supports Internet Protocol security (IPsec) VPN connections.
L9: ###### Contents
L10: 
L11:   * cite1†Concepts L12: 
L13:   * cite2†Site-to-Site VPN features L14: 
L15:   * cite3†Site-to-Site VPN limitations L16: 
L17:   * cite4†Site-to-Site VPN resources L18: 
L19:   * cite5†Pricing L20: ## Concepts
L21: 
L22: The following are the key concepts for Site-to-Site VPN:
L23: 
L24:   * VPN connection: A secure connection between your on-premises equipment and your VPCs.
L25: 
L26:   * VPN tunnel: An encrypted link where data can pass from the customer network to or from AWS.
L27: 
L28: Each VPN connection includes two VPN tunnels which you can simultaneously use for high availability.
L29: 
L30:   * Customer gateway: An AWS resource which provides information to AWS about your customer gateway device.
L31:   * Customer gateway device: A physical device or software application on your side of the Site-to-Site VPN connection.
L32: 
L33:   * Target gateway: A generic term for the VPN endpoint on the Amazon side of the Site-to-Site VPN connection.
L34: 
L35:   * Virtual private gateway: A virtual private gateway is the VPN endpoint on the Amazon side of your Site-to-Site VPN connection that can be attached to a single VPC.
L36:   * Transit gateway: A transit hub that can be used to interconnect multiple VPCs and on-premises networks, and as a VPN endpoint for the Amazon side of the Site-to-Site VPN connection.
L37: 
L38:   * Large Bandwidth Tunnel : A tunnel configuration that supports up to 5 Gbps bandwidth per tunnel, compared to the standard 1.25 Gbps. Available for VPN connections attached to Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN.
L39: ## Site-to-Site VPN features
L40: 
L41: The following features are supported on AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections:
L42: 
L43:   * Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2)
L44: 
L45:   * NAT traversal
L46: 
L47:   * 4-byte ASN in the range of 1–2147483647 for Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) configuration. See cite6†Customer gateway options for your AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for more information.
L48:   * 2-byte ASN for Customer Gateway (CGW) in the range of 1–65535. See cite6†Customer gateway options for your AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for more information.
L49: 
L50:   * CloudWatch metrics
L51: 
L52:   * Reusable IP addresses for your customer gateways
L53: 
L54:   * Additional encryption options; including AES 256-bit encryption, SHA-2 hashing, and additional Diffie-Hellman groups
L55: 
L56:   * Configurable tunnel options
L57: 
L58:   * Custom private ASN for the Amazon side of a BGP session
L59:   * Private Certificate from a subordinate CA from AWS Private Certificate Authority
L60: 
L61:   * Support for IPv6 support for AWS Site-to-Site VPN
L62: 
L63:     * IPv6 for inner tunnel IP addresses (packet IP)
L64: 
L65:     * IPv6 for outer tunnel IP addresses (tunnel IP) on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN
L66: 
L67:   * Full IPv6 migration support with the following combinations:
L68: 
L69:     * IPv6 outer tunnel IP with IPv6 inner packet IP (IPv6-in-IPv6)
L70: 
L71:     * IPv6 outer tunnel IP with IPv4 inner packet IP (IPv4-in-IPv6)
L72: ## Site-to-Site VPN limitations
L73: 
L74: A Site-to-Site VPN connection has the following limitations.
L75: 
L76:   * IPv6 traffic is not supported for VPN connections on a virtual private gateway. IPv6 for outer tunnel IPs is only supported on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN.
L77: 
L78:   * An Site-to-Site VPN connection does not support Path MTU Discovery.
L79: 
L80:   * A single Site-to-Site VPN connection cannot support both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic simultaneously. You need separate VPN connections to transport IPv4 and IPv6 packets.
L81:   * Private IP VPN connections do not support IPv6 addresses for outer tunnel IPs.
L82: 
L83:   * You cannot modify an existing IPv4 VPN connection to use IPv6. You must delete the existing connection and create a new one.
L84: 
L85: In addition, take the following into consideration when you use Site-to-Site VPN.
L86: 
L87:   * When connecting your VPCs to a common on-premises network, we recommend that you use non-overlapping CIDR blocks for your networks.
L88: ## Site-to-Site VPN resources
L89: 
L90: You can create, access, and manage your Site-to-Site VPN resources using any of the following interfaces:
L91: 
L92:   * AWS Management Console— Provides a web interface that you can use to access your Site-to-Site VPN resources.
L93: 
L94:   * AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) — Provides commands for a broad set of AWS services, including Amazon VPC, and is supported on Windows, macOS, and Linux. the AWS Site-to-Site VPN command lines are included in the larger EC2 command line reference
L95:     * For general information about the command line interface, see cite7†AWS Command Line Interface†aws.amazon.com .
L96: 
L97:     * For the list of available EC2 commands, including the Site-to-Site VPN commands, see cite8†EC2 Command Line Reference .
L98: ###### Note
L99: 
L100: The command line reference does not differentiate between the Site-to-Site VPN commands and the larger set of EC2 commands
L101: 
L102:   * AWS SDKs — Provide language-specific APIs and takes care of many of the connection details, such as calculating signatures, handling request retries, and error handling. For more information, see cite9†AWS SDKs†aws.amazon.com .
L103:   * Query API— Provides low-level API actions that you call using HTTPS requests. Using the Query API is the most direct way to access Amazon VPC, but it requires that your application handle low-level details such as generating the hash to sign the request, and error handling. For more information, see the cite10†Amazon EC2 API Reference .
L104: ## Pricing
L105: 
L106: You are charged for each VPN connection hour that your VPN connection is provisioned and available. For more information, see cite11†AWS Site-to-Site VPN and Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN Connection pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L107: 
L108: You are charged for data transfer out from Amazon EC2 to the internet. For more information, see cite12†Data Transfer†aws.amazon.com on the Amazon EC2 On-Demand Pricing page.
L109: When you create an accelerated VPN connection, we create and manage two accelerators on your behalf. You are charged an hourly rate and data transfer costs for each accelerator. For more information, see cite13†AWS Global Accelerator pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L110: 
L111: There are no additional charges for using IPv6 addresses with your Site-to-Site VPN VPN connections.

Preprocessing Data Using a Lambda Function - Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications Developer Guide (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kinesisanalytics/latest/dev/lambda-preprocessing.html)
citeturn217view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 4 days ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kinesisanalytics/latest/dev/lambda-preprocessing.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 205
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Preprocessing Data Using a Lambda Function - Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications Developer Guide
L3: 
L4: cite1†Using a Lambda Function for Preprocessing Records cite2†Lambda Preprocessing Permissions cite3†Lambda Preprocessing Metrics cite4†Using AWS Lambda with the Kinesis Producer Library cite5†Data Preprocessing Event Input Data Model/Record Response Model cite6†Common Data Preprocessing Failures L5: After careful consideration, we have decided to discontinue Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications:
L6: 
L7: 1. From September 1, 2025, we won't provide any bug fixes for Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications because we will have limited support for it, given the upcoming discontinuation.
L8: 
L9: 2. From October 15, 2025, you will not be able to create new Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications.
L10: 3. We will delete your applications starting January 27, 2026. You will not be able to start or operate your Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications. Support will no longer be available for Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL from that time. For more information, see cite7†Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications discontinuation .
L11: # Preprocessing Data Using a Lambda Function
L12: ###### Note
L13: 
L14: After September 12, 2023, you will not able to create new applications using Kinesis Data Firehose as a source if you do not already use Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL. For more information, see cite8†Limits .
L15: 
L16: If the data in your stream needs format conversion, transformation, enrichment, or filtering, you can preprocess the data using an AWS Lambda function. You can do this before your application SQL code executes or before your application creates a schema from your data stream.
L17: Using a Lambda function for preprocessing records is useful in the following scenarios:
L18: 
L19:   * Transforming records from other formats (such as KPL or GZIP) into formats that Kinesis Data Analytics can analyze. Kinesis Data Analytics currently supports JSON or CSV data formats.
L20: 
L21:   * Expanding data into a format that is more accessible for operations such as aggregation or anomaly detection. For instance, if several data values are stored together in a string, you can expand the data into separate columns.
L22:   * Data enrichment with other Amazon services, such as extrapolation or error correction.
L23: 
L24:   * Applying complex string transformation to record fields.
L25: 
L26:   * Data filtering for cleaning up the data.
L27: ## Using a Lambda Function for Preprocessing Records
L28: 
L29: When creating your Kinesis Data Analytics application, you enable Lambda preprocessing in the Connect to a Source page.
L30: ###### To use a Lambda function to preprocess records in a Kinesis Data Analytics application
L31: 
L32:   1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the Managed Service for Apache Flink console at cite9†https://console.aws.amazon.com/kinesisanalytics†console.aws.amazon.com .
L33: 
L34:   2. On the Connect to a Source page for your application, choose Enabled in the Record pre-processing with AWS Lambda section.
L35:   3. To use a Lambda function that you have already created, choose the function in the Lambda function drop-down list.
L36: 
L37:   4. To create a new Lambda function from one of the Lambda preprocessing templates, choose the template from the drop-down list. Then choose View <template name> in Lambda to edit the function.
L38:   5. To create a new Lambda function, choose Create new. For information about creating a Lambda function, see cite10†Create a HelloWorld Lambda Function and Explore the Console in the AWS Lambda Developer Guide.
L39: 
L40:   6. Choose the version of the Lambda function to use. To use the latest version, choose $LATEST.
L41: 
L42: When you choose or create a Lambda function for record preprocessing, the records are preprocessed before your application SQL code executes or your application generates a schema from the records.
L43: ## Lambda Preprocessing Permissions
L44: 
L45: To use Lambda preprocessing, the application's IAM role requires the following permissions policy:
L46: 
L47:     `     {
L48:            "Sid": "UseLambdaFunction",
L49:            "Effect": "Allow",
L50:            "Action": [
L51:                "lambda:InvokeFunction",
L52:                "lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration"
L53:            ],
L54:            "Resource": "<FunctionARN>"
L55:        }
L56:     `
L57: ## Lambda Preprocessing Metrics
L58: 
L59: You can use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the number of Lambda invocations, bytes processed, successes and failures, and so on. For information about CloudWatch metrics that are emitted by Kinesis Data Analytics Lambda preprocessing, see cite11†Amazon Kinesis Analytics Metrics .
L60: ## Using AWS Lambda with the Kinesis Producer Library
L61: 
L62: The cite12†Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) aggregates small user-formatted records into larger records up to 1 MB to make better use of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams throughput. The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) for Java supports deaggregating these records. However, you must use a special module to deaggregate the records when you use AWS Lambda as the consumer of your streams.
L63: To get the necessary project code and instructions, see the cite13†Kinesis Producer Library Deaggregation Modules for AWS Lambda†github.com on GitHub. You can use the components in this project to process KPL serialized data within AWS Lambda in Java, Node.js, and Python. You can also use these components as part of a cite14†multi-lang KCL application†github.com .
L64: ## Data Preprocessing Event Input Data Model/Record Response Model
L65: 
L66: To preprocess records, your Lambda function must be compliant with the required event input data and record response models.
L67: ### Event Input Data Model
L68: 
L69: Kinesis Data Analytics continuously reads data from your Kinesis data stream or Firehose delivery stream. For each batch of records it retrieves, the service manages how each batch gets passed to your Lambda function. Your function receives a list of records as input. Within your function, you iterate through the list and apply your business logic to accomplish your preprocessing requirements (such as data format conversion or enrichment).
L70: The input model to your preprocessing function varies slightly, depending on whether the data was received from a Kinesis data stream or a Firehose delivery stream.
L71: 
L72: If the source is a Firehose delivery stream, the event input data model is as follows:
L73: 
L74: Kinesis Data Firehose Request Data Model
L75: Field  | Description
L76: --- | ---
L77: `invocationId`  | The Lambda invocation Id (random GUID).
L78: `applicationArn`  | Kinesis Data Analytics application Amazon Resource Name (ARN)
L79: `streamArn`  | Delivery stream ARN
L80: records
L81: Field Description
L82: `recordId` record ID (random GUID)
L83: `kinesisFirehoseRecordMetadata`
L84: Field Description
L85: `approximateArrivalTimestamp` Delivery stream record approximate arrival time
L86: `data` Base64-encoded source record payload
L87: The following example shows input from a Firehose delivery stream:
L88: 
L89:     `{
L90:        "invocationId":"00540a87-5050-496a-84e4-e7d92bbaf5e2",
L91:        "applicationArn":"arn:aws:kinesisanalytics:us-east-1:12345678911:application/lambda-test",
L92:        "streamArn":"arn:aws:firehose:us-east-1:AAAAAAAAAAAA:deliverystream/lambda-test",
L93:        "records":[
L94:           {
L95:              "recordId":"49572672223665514422805246926656954630972486059535892482",
L96:              "data":"aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=",
L97:              "kinesisFirehoseRecordMetadata":{
L98:                 "approximateArrivalTimestamp":1520280173
L99:              }
L100:           }
L101:        ]
L102:     }
L103:     `
L104: If the source is a Kinesis data stream, the event input data model is as follows:
L105: 
L106: Kinesis Streams Request Data Model
L107: Field  | Description
L108: --- | ---
L109: `invocationId`  | The Lambda invocation Id (random GUID).
L110: `applicationArn`  | Kinesis Data Analytics application ARN
L111: `streamArn`  | Delivery stream ARN
L112: records
L113: Field Description
L114: `recordId` record ID based off of Kinesis record sequence number
L115: `kinesisStreamRecordMetadata`
L116: Field Description
L117: `sequenceNumber` Sequence number from the Kinesis stream record
L118: `partitionKey` Partition key from the Kinesis stream record
L119: `shardId` `ShardId` from the Kinesis stream record
L120: `approximateArrivalTimestamp` Delivery stream record approximate arrival time
L121: data Base64-encoded source record payload
L122: The following example shows input from a Kinesis data stream:
L123: 
L124:     `
L125:     {
L126:       "invocationId": "00540a87-5050-496a-84e4-e7d92bbaf5e2",
L127:       "applicationArn": "arn:aws:kinesisanalytics:us-east-1:12345678911:application/lambda-test",
L128:       "streamArn": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:AAAAAAAAAAAA:stream/lambda-test",
L129:       "records": [
L130:         {
L131:           "recordId": "49572672223665514422805246926656954630972486059535892482",
L132:           "data": "aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=",
L133:           "kinesisStreamRecordMetadata":{
L134:                 "shardId" :"shardId-000000000003",
L135:                 "partitionKey":"7400791606",
L136:                 "sequenceNumber":"49572672223665514422805246926656954630972486059535892482",
L137:                 "approximateArrivalTimestamp":1520280173
L138:              }
L139:         }
L140:       ]
L141:     }
L142:     `
L143: ### Record Response Model
L144: 
L145: All records returned from your Lambda preprocessing function (with record IDs) that are sent to the Lambda function must be returned. They must contain the following parameters, or Kinesis Data Analytics rejects them and treats it as a data preprocessing failure. The data payload part of the record can be transformed to accomplish preprocessing requirements.
L146: 
L147: Response Data Model
L148: records
L149: Field Description
L150: `recordId` The record ID is passed from Kinesis Data Analytics to Lambda during the invocation. The transformed record must contain the same record ID. Any mismatch between the ID of the original record and the ID of the transformed record is treated as a data preprocessing failure.
L151: `result` The status of the data transformation of the record. The possible values are:
L152:   * `Ok`: The record was transformed successfully. Kinesis Data Analytics ingests the record for SQL processing.
L153:   * `Dropped`: The record was dropped intentionally by your processing logic. Kinesis Data Analytics drops the record from SQL processing. The data payload field is optional for a `Dropped` record.
L154:   * `ProcessingFailed`: The record could not be transformed. Kinesis Data Analytics considers it unsuccessfully processed by your Lambda function and writes an error to the error stream. For more information about the error stream, see cite15†Error Handling . The data payload field is optional for a `ProcessingFailed` record.
L155: `data` The transformed data payload, after base64-encoding. Each data payload can contain multiple JSON documents if the application ingestion data format is JSON. Or each can contain multiple CSV rows (with a row delimiter specified in each row) if the application ingestion data format is CSV. The Kinesis Data Analytics service successfully parses and processes data with either multiple JSON documents or CSV rows within the same data payload.
L156: The following example shows output from a Lambda function:
L157: 
L158:     `{
L159:       "records": [
L160:         {
L161:           "recordId": "49572672223665514422805246926656954630972486059535892482",
L162:           "result": "Ok",
L163:           "data": "SEVMTE8gV09STEQ="
L164:         }
L165:       ]
L166:     }
L167:     `
L168: ## Common Data Preprocessing Failures
L169: 
L170: The following are common reasons why preprocessing can fail.
L171: 
L172:   * Not all records (with record IDs) in a batch that are sent to the Lambda function are returned back to the Kinesis Data Analytics service.
L173: 
L174:   * The response is missing either the record ID, status, or data payload field. The data payload field is optional for a `Dropped` or `ProcessingFailed` record.
L175: 
L176:   * The Lambda function timeouts are not sufficient to preprocess the data.
L177:   * The Lambda function response exceeds the response limits imposed by the AWS Lambda service.
L178: 
L179: For data preprocessing failures, Kinesis Data Analytics continues to retry Lambda invocations on the same set of records until successful. You can monitor the following CloudWatch metrics to gain insight into failures.
L180: 
L181:   * Kinesis Data Analytics application `MillisBehindLatest`: Indicates how far behind an application is reading from the streaming source.
L182:   * Kinesis Data Analytics application `InputPreprocessing` CloudWatch metrics: Indicates the number of successes and failures, among other statistics. For more information, see cite11†Amazon Kinesis Analytics Metrics .
L183: 
L184:   * AWS Lambda function CloudWatch metrics and logs.
L185:

L238: ## General
L239: 
L240: cite86†Open all L241: ### What is Amazon Transcribe?
L242: 
L243: Amazon Transcribe is an AWS Artificial Intelligence (AI) service that makes it easy for you to convert speech to text. Using Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology, you can use Amazon Transcribe for a variety of business applications, including transcription of voice-based customer service calls, generation of subtitles on audio/video content, and conduct (text-based) content analysis on audio/video content.
L244: ### How does Amazon Transcribe interact with other AWS products?
L245: Amazon Transcribe converts audio input into text, which opens the door for various text analytics applications on voice input. For instance, by using Amazon Comprehend on the converted text data from Amazon Transcribe, you can perform sentiment analysis or extract entities and key phrases. Similarly, by integrating with Amazon Translate and Amazon Polly, you can accept voice input in one language, translate it into another, and generate voice output, effectively enabling multilingual conversations.
L246: It is also possible to integrate Amazon Transcribe with Amazon Kendra or Amazon OpenSearch to index and perform text-based search across an audio/video library. To learn more, check out the cite87†Live Call Analytics and Agent Assist , cite88†Post Call Analytics , cite89†MediaSearch , or cite90†Content Analysis solution.
L247: ### What else should I know before using Amazon Transcribe?
L248: Amazon Transcribe is designed to handle a wide range of speech and acoustic characteristics, including variations in volume, pitch, and speaking rate. The quality and content of the audio signal (including but not limited to factors such as background noise, overlapping speakers, accented speech, or switches between languages within a single audio file) may affect the accuracy of service output.
L249: We are constantly updating the service to improve its ability to accommodate additional acoustic variation and content types.
L250: ## Using Amazon Transcribe
L251: 
L252: cite86†Open all L253: 
L254: ### How will developers access Amazon Transcribe?
L255: 
L256: The easiest way to get started is to submit a job using the console to transcribe an audio file. You can also call the service directly from the AWS Command Line Interface, or use one of the supported SDKs of your choice to integrate with your applications. Either way, you can start using Amazon Transcribe to generate automated transcripts for your audio files with just a few lines of code.
L257: ### Does Amazon Transcribe support real-time transcriptions?
L258: 
L259: Yes. Amazon Transcribe allows you to open a bidirectional stream over HTTP2. You can send an audio stream to the service while receiving a text stream in return in real time. Please refer to the cite91†documentation page†docs.aws.amazon.com for more details.
L260: ### What encoding does real-time transcription support?
L261: 
L262: Supported media types differ between batch transcriptions and streaming transcriptions, though lossless formats are recommended for both. Please refer to the cite92†documentation page†docs.aws.amazon.com for more details.
L263: 
L264: ### What languages does Amazon Transcribe support?
L265: 
L266: For information on language support, please refer to this cite93†documentation†docs.aws.amazon.com page.
L267: ### What devices does Amazon Transcribe work with?
L268: Amazon Transcribe for the most part is device agnostic. In general, it works with any device that includes an on-device microphone such as phones, PCs, tablets, and IoT devices (such as car audio systems). Amazon Transcribe API will be able to detect the quality of the audio stream being input at the device (8kHz VS 16kHz) and will appropriately select the acoustic models for converting speech to text.
L269: Furthermore, developers can call Amazon Transcribe API through their applications to access speech-to-text conversion capability.
L270: ### Are there size restrictions on the audio content that Amazon Transcribe can process?
L271: 
L272: Amazon Transcribe service calls are limited to four hours (or 2 GB) per API call for our batch service. The streaming service can accommodate open connections up to four hours long.
L273: ### What programming languages does Amazon Transcribe support?
L274: 
L275: Amazon Transcribe batch service supports .NET, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, and Ruby. Amazon Transcribe real-time service supports Java SDK, Ruby SDK, and C++ SDK. Additional SDK support is coming. For more details, visit the cite94†Resources and cite95†documentation page†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L276: ### My custom vocabulary words are not being recognized. What can I do?
L277: 
L278: The speech recognition output depends on a number of factors in addition to custom vocabulary entries, so there can be no assurance that if a term is included in the custom vocabulary, it will be correctly recognized. However, one of the most frequent reasons for this is that the words are pronounced significantly different than they are written.
L279: In these cases, it is recommended to create multiple phrase entries in the custom vocabulary file for the same word to cover for the possible variations in pronounciation. You may use DisplayAs column for the desired output for these phrase entries. Refer to the cite96†custom vocabulary documentation†docs.aws.amazon.com for more information.
L280: ### Why do I see too many custom words in my output?
L281: Custom vocabularies are optimized for a small list of targeted words; larger vocabularies may lead to over-generation of custom words, especially when they contain words that are pronounced in a similar way. If you have a large list, please try reducing it to rare words and words that are actually expected to occur in your audio files. If you have a large vocabulary covering multiple use cases, split it into separate lists for different use cases.
L282: The words that are short and sound similar to many other words may lead to over-generation (too many custom words appearing in the output). It is preferable to combine these words with surrounding words and list them as hyphen-separated phrases. For example, the custom word “A.D.” could be included as part of a phrase such as “A.D.-converter.”
L283: ### When using DisplayAs forms, can I display character sets unrelated to the original language being transcribed (for example, output “Street” as “街道“)?
L284: 
L285: Yes. While phrases may only use a restricted set of characters for the specific language, UTF-8 characters apart from \t (TAB) are permitted in the DisplayAs column.
L286: ### Is automatic content redaction or personally identifiable information (PII) redaction available with both batch and streaming APIs for Transcribe?
L287: 
L288: Yes, Amazon Transcribe supports cite97†automatic content redaction or PII redaction†docs.aws.amazon.com for both batch and streaming APIs.
L289: ### What languages are supported for automatic content redaction / PII identification and redaction?
L290: 
L291: Please refer to the Amazon Transcribe documentation for information on the cite93†language availability of automatic content redaction / PII redaction†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L292: ### Does Automatic content redaction also redact sensitive personal information from the source audio?
L293: No, this feature does not remove sensitive personal information from the source audio. However, Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics removes sensitive personal information from both the transcripts and the source audio. Visit this link for more details on how call analytics can redact audio. You can also redact personal information from the source audio yourself using the start and end timestamps that are provided in the redacted transcripts for each instance of an identified PII utterance.
L294: Please refer to this cite98†audio redaction solution for standard Transcribe APIs.
L295: However, the specialized Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics APIs remove sensitive personal information from both the transcripts and the source audio. To learn more, review the cite99†Call Analytics audio redaction documentation†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L296: ### Can I use automatic content redaction for redacting personal information from the existing text transcripts?
L297: 
L298: No, automatic content redaction only works on audio as an input.
L299: ### What else should I know before using automatic content redaction?
L300: 
L301: Automatic content redaction is designed to identify and remove personally identifiable information (PII), but due to the predictive nature of machine learning, it may not identify and remove all instances of PII in a transcript generated by the service. You should review any output provided by Automatic content redaction to ensure it meets your needs.
L302: ### Are there any differences between automatic content redaction for streaming and batch APIs?
L303: Yes, there are two additional capabilities supported by automatic content redaction for the streaming API that are not supported by the batch API. You can decide to only identify PII and not redact when using content redaction with streaming API. Also you have the ability to cite100†identify or redact specific PII types†docs.aws.amazon.com with streaming API. For example, you can redact just the social security number and credit card information and keep other PII like names and email addresses.
L304: ### In which AWS Regions is automatic content redaction or PII redaction available?
L305: 
L306: Please refer to the cite101†Amazon Transcribe documentation for information on the availability of automatic content redaction and PII redaction for batch and streaming APIs in the AWS Regions.
L307: 
L308: ### Which APIs support automatic language identification?
L309: 
L310: Automatic language identification is currently supported for batch and streaming APIs.
L311: ### What languages can Amazon Transcribe automatically identify?
L312: 
L313: Amazon Transcribe can identify any of the languages supported by the batch and streaming APIs. Go here for cite93†details on supported languages and language-specific features†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L314: 
L315: ### Does Amazon Transcribe identify multiple languages in the same audio file?
L316: 
L317: Amazon Transcribe supports multi-language ID for batch. See cite102†this link†docs.aws.amazon.com for more details.
L318: ### Is there any way to restrict the list of languages to choose from for automatic language identification?
L319: Yes, you can specify a list of languages that might be present in your media library. When you provide a list of languages, the identified language will be chosen from that list. If no languages are specified, the system will process the audio file against all the languages supported by Amazon Transcribe and select the most probable one. The accuracy of language identification is better when a select list of languages is provided. See cite103†this link†docs.aws.amazon.com for more details.

L332: ## Data Privacy
L333: 
L334: cite86†Open all L335: ### Are voice inputs processed by Amazon Transcribe stored, and how are they used by AWS?
L336: Amazon Transcribe may store and use voice inputs processed by the service solely to provide and maintain the service and to improve and develop the quality of Amazon Transcribe and other Amazon machine-learning/artificial-intelligence technologies. Use of your content is important for continuous improvement of your Amazon Transcribe customer experience, including the development and training of related technologies.
L337: We do not use any personally identifiable information that may be contained in your content to target products, services, or marketing to you or your end users. Your trust, privacy, and the security of your content are our highest priority, and we implement appropriate and sophisticated technical and physical controls, including encryption at rest and in transit, designed to prevent unauthorized access to, or disclosure of, your content and ensure that our use complies with our commitments to you.
L338: Please see cite106†https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy-faq/ for more information. You may opt out of having your content used to improve and develop the quality of Amazon Transcribe and other Amazon machine-learning/artificial-intelligence technologies by using an AWS Organizations opt-out policy. For information about how to opt out, see cite107†AI services opt-out policy†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L339: ### Can I delete data and artifacts associated with transcription jobs stored by Amazon Transcribe?
L340: 
L341: Yes. You can use available cite108†Delete APIs†docs.aws.amazon.com to delete data and other artifacts associated with transcription jobs. If you have issues doing so, contact AWS support.
L342: ### Who has access to my content that is processed and stored by Amazon Transcribe?
L343: Only authorized employees will have access to your content that is processed by Amazon Transcribe. Your trust, privacy, and the security of your content are our highest priority, and we implement appropriate and sophisticated technical and physical controls, including encryption at rest and in transit, designed to prevent unauthorized access to, or disclosure of, your content and ensure that our use complies with our commitments to you.
L344: Please see cite106†https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy-faq/ for more information.
L345: ### Do I still own my content that is processed and stored by Amazon Transcribe?
L346: 
L347: You always retain ownership of your content, and we will only use your content with your consent.
L348: ### What happens to my data used in training custom language models? Will I still own it?
L349: 
L350: When submitting text data that is used to train a dedicated model, you have ownership of the original text data and the generated custom model. The text data will neither be stored, nor used to improve our general speech recognition engine. Models produced by using CLM are self-contained and accessibly by only you.
L351: ### Since the service will not be retaining my training data, are there any drawbacks or degradation to the transcription quality or overall service experience?
L352: There will be no transcription quality degradation resulting from our service not storing your training data. Once the training data is used to actually produce a custom language model, the model itself becomes available for repeated use at your discretion. The original training set you uploaded is expunged from our systems. The only drawback is if you require technical support.
L353: Because we do not retain your original training data, we would not have convenient access to those assets or related intermediate artifacts, should you require support team to investigate potential service issues. Support would still be available, but not as expedient because we may need to ask for additional information from you.
L354: ### How can I reuse the data for future model updates or improvements?
L355: 
L356: Since training data is not stored, the same data set and any additional data will have to be uploaded again to train new models. When there is an update to the base model provided by Amazon Transcribe, you will be notified. To take advantage of the latest base model, you should submit your data to train a new model. You will then have both the original custom model that you previously generated and also the new version to use.
L357: ### How do I delete a model?
L358: 
L359: You can delete any customer language model that you generated, at your discretion.
L360: ### Is the content processed by Amazon Transcribe moved outside the AWS region where I am using Amazon Transcribe?
L361: Any content processed by Amazon Transcribe is encrypted and stored at rest in the AWS region where you are using Amazon Transcribe. Some portion of content processed by Amazon Transcribe may be stored in another AWS region solely in connection with the continuous improvement and development of your Amazon Transcribe customer experience and other Amazon machine-learning/artificial-intelligence technologies.
L362: If you opt out of having your content used to develop the quality of Amazon Transcribe and other Amazon machine-learning/artificial-intelligence technologies by contacting AWS Support, your content will not be stored in another AWS region. You can request deletion of voice inputs associated with your account by contacting AWS Support.
L363: Your trust, privacy, and the security of your content are our highest priority and we implement appropriate and sophisticated technical and physical controls, including encryption at rest and in transit, designed to prevent unauthorized access to, or disclosure of, your content and ensure that our use complies with our commitments to you. Please see cite106†https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy-faq/ for more information.
L364: ### Can I use Amazon Transcribe in connection with websites, programs or other applications that are directed or targeted to children under age 13 and subject to the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)?
L365: Yes, subject to your compliance with the Amazon Transcribe Service Terms, including your obligation to provide any required notices and obtain any required verifiable parental consent under COPPA, you may use Amazon Transcribe in connection with websites, programs, or other applications that are directed or targeted, in whole or in part, to children under age 13.
L366: ### How do I determine whether my website, program, or application is subject to COPPA?
L367: For information about the requirements of COPPA and guidance for determining whether your website, program, or other application is subject to COPPA, please refer directly to the resources provided and maintained by the cite109†United States Federal Trade Commission†www.ftc.gov . This site also contains information regarding how to determine whether a service is directed or targeted, in whole or in part, to children under age 13.
L368: ## Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics
L369: 
L370: cite86†Open all L371: ### What is Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics?
L372: Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics is an AI-powered API that provides rich call transcripts and actionable conversation insights that you can add into call applications to improve customer experience and agent productivity. It combines powerful speech-to-text and custom natural language processing (NLP) models that are trained specifically to understand customer care and outbound sales calls.
L373: As a part of cite110†AWS Contact Center Intelligence (CCI) solutions , this API is contact center agnostic and makes it easier for customers and ISVs to add call analytics capabilities into their applications.
L374: ### What can I do with Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics?
L375: Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics can do both real-time and post-call analytics. With Call Analytics, developers can quickly add valuable intelligence such as customer and agent sentiment scores, call drivers, call categories, call summarization as an API output to any inbound or outbound call application. Common use cases include agent assist, summarization, supervisor alerts, and call analytics.
L376: Here are two open source sample solutions that are based on Transcribe Call Analytics: cite87†Real-time Call Analytics with Agent Assist and cite88†Post Call Analytics .
L377: ### How do I get started with Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics?
L378: 
L379: You can use Transcribe Call Analytics through the APIs and AWS Management Console. Analytics jobs can be created and monitored through the API or the Console. In the Console, you will see a list of analytics jobs, and a job detail page with input parameters, and a JSON output preview. In addition to this, you will be able to create and edit categories through the APIs or Console for the automated contact categorization feature.
L380: ### Which languages does Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics support?
L381: 
L382: Please refer to the cite93†Amazon Transcribe documentation†docs.aws.amazon.com for information on the cite93†language availability of Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L383: ### In which AWS Regions is Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics available?
L384: 
L385: Please refer to the cite101†AWS regional services documentation for information on AWS Region coverage for Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics. Please note that Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics generative call summarization is currently available only in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).
L386: ### Is generative call summarization available with both post-call and real-time Transcribe Call Analytics API?
L387: 
L388: Currently, generative call summarization is only available with Transcribe Call Analytics API for post-call analytics.
L389: 
L390: ### How does the pricing work for Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics?
L391: 
L392: Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics API is priced separately from the standard Amazon Transcribe APIs. Please see the Amazon cite104†Transcribe pricing page for more details.
L393: ## Amazon Transcribe Medical
L394: 
L395: cite86†Open all L396: ### What is Amazon Transcribe Medical?
L397: 
L398: Amazon Transcribe Medical is an automatic speech recognition (ASR) service that makes it easy for developers to add medical speech-to-text capabilities to their applications. Using Amazon Transcribe Medical, you can quickly and accurately transcribe medical dictation and conversational speech into text for a variety of purposes, such as recording physician notes or processing in downstream text analytics to extract meaningful insights.
L399: ### What can I do with Amazon Transcribe Medical?
L400: 
L401: Amazon Transcribe Medical uses advanced machine learning models to accurately transcribe medical speech into text. Transcribe Medical can generate text transcripts that can be used to support a variety of use cases, spanning clinical documentation workflow and drug safety monitoring (pharmacovigilance) to subtitling for telemedicine and even contact center analytics in the healthcare and life sciences domains.
L402: ### Do I need to be an expert in automatic speech recognition (ASR) to use Amazon Transcribe Medical?
L403: 
L404: No, you don’t need any ASR or machine learning expertise to use Amazon Transcribe Medical. You only need to call Transcribe Medical’s API, and the service will handle the required machine learning in the backend to transcribe medical speech to text.
L405: ### How do I get started with Amazon Transcribe Medical?
L406: 
L407: You can get started with Amazon Transcribe Medical from the AWS Management console or by using the SDK. Please refer to this cite111†technical documentation page†docs.aws.amazon.com for details.
L408: 
L409: Amazon Transcribe Medical provides a free tier so that you can test the service. Refer to this pricing page for more information.
L410: ### Which languages does Amazon Transcribe Medical support?
L411: 
L412: Amazon Transcribe Medical currently supports medical transcription in US English.
L413: 
L414: ### Which medical specialties does Amazon Transcribe Medical support?
L415: 
L416: Amazon Transcribe Medical supports transcription for an expanding list of primary care and specialty care specialties. Visit our cite112†documentation†docs.aws.amazon.com for a full list of supported medical specialties.
L417: ### In which AWS regions is Amazon Transcribe Medical available?
L418: 
L419: Please refer to the cite101†AWS regional services documentation for information on AWS Region coverage for Amazon Transcribe Medical.
L420: 
L421: ### How is Amazon Transcribe Medical priced?
L422: 
L423: Refer to the cite104†Amazon Transcribe Medical pricing page to learn more about pricing details.
L424: 
L425: ### Is Amazon Transcribe Medical HIPAA eligible?
L426: 
L427: Yes.
L428: ### Is the content processed by Amazon Transcribe Medical used for any purpose other than to provide the service?
L429: 
L430: Amazon Transcribe Medical does not use content processed by the service for any reason other than to provide and maintain the service. Content processed by the service is not used to develop or improve the quality for Amazon Transcribe Medical or any other Amazon machine-learning/artificial-intelligence technologies.
L431: ### Does Amazon Transcribe Medical learn over time?
L432: 
L433: Yes, Amazon Transcribe Medical uses machine learning and is continuously being trained to make it better for customer use cases. Amazon Transcribe medical does not store or use customer data used with the service to train the models
L434: ### What else should I know before using the Amazon Transcribe Medical service?
L435: Amazon Transcribe Medical is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. You and your end users are responsible for exercising your and their own discretion, experience, and judgment in determining the correctness, completeness, timeliness, and suitability of any information provided by Amazon Transcribe Medical. You and your end users are solely responsible for any decisions, advice, actions, and/or inactions based on the use of Amazon Transcribe Medical.
L436: Amazon Transcribe Medical may not accurately identify protected health information in all circumstances, and does not meet the requirements for de-identification of protected health information in accordance with HIPAA. You are responsible for reviewing any output provided by Amazon Transcribe Medical to ensure it meets your needs.
L437: ## Custom language models
L438: 
L439: cite86†Open all L440: 
L441: ### What functionality does custom language models provide today?
L442: 
L443: You can use custom language models (CLM) to train and develop language models that are domain-specific. CLM currently supports Australian English, British English, Hindi, US English and US Spanish for batch transcriptions and US English for streaming transcriptions. CLM supports the simultaneous use of custom vocabulary for batch transcriptions.
L444: ### How much and what type of training data do I need? How do I obtain the data? Does the data need to have a specific format?
L445: The text data should be relevant to the audio that will be transcribed using the custom model; it should contain as many of the domain-specific words, phrases, and word combinations as possible. We recommend using at least 100k and at most 10M words of running text. Text data resources can be obtained from any in-house or public sources (e.g., using text from customers’ websites). We recommend each plain text file contain 200,000 words or more, but not exceeding 1 GB in overall file size.
L446: The text should be in UTF-8, and use one sentence per line. Each sentence should contain punctuation. Users are responsible for spell-checking, removing formatting characters, and validating the encoding.
